front: Identify the diagnostic signs of a tension pneumothorax and its mandatory immediate intervention.
back:
* Signs: Respiratory distress, distended neck veins, hyper-resonance, and decreased breath sounds on the affected side.
* Intervention: Immediate surgical decompression (needle or finger thoracostomy) based on clinical diagnosis, without waiting for radiological confirmation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation. ... Treatment consists of immediate decompression... or, in extremis, a fnger thoracostomy at the same location.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: What clinical signs characterize a retrobulbar haemorrhage surgical emergency?
back:
- Tense proptosis
- Reduced visual acuity
- Loss of pupillary response
- Increasing pain
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness... It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: Describe the immediate pathophysiological consequences of an untreated tension pneumothorax.
back:
- Lung collapse via 'one-way valve' air leak
- Mediastinal shift to opposite side
- Decreased venous return
- Compression of the contralateral lung
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing and then compressing the affected lung. The mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side, decreasing venous return and compressing the opposite lung.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: Contrast the immediate management of traumatic cardiac tamponade versus non-traumatic tamponade.
back:
- Traumatic: Immediate operative repair (sternotomy/thoracotomy) is required.
- Non-traumatic: Pericardiocentesis is utilized; however, it has no role in penetrating myocardial trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury. The correct immediate treatment of tamponade is operative...]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: A patient with an open tibial fracture develops pain out of proportion and on passive stretch. Next step?
back:
- Immediate suspected diagnosis: Compartment syndrome
- Action: Split all casts/dressings to skin and perform emergency fasciotomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis characterised by pain out of proportion... Emergency treatment involves splitting casts and/or dressings to the skin and elevating the extremity... perform defnitive treatment with fasciotomies.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: What is the critical time-limited window for administering Tranexamic acid (TXA) after trauma?
back:
- Ideally within the first hour of injury.
- Must not be administered more than 3 hours post-injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [It needs to be administered as early as possible and ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: What criteria render Emergency Department Thoracotomy (EDT) futile in trauma patients?
back:
- CPR >15 minutes (penetrating trauma)
- CPR >10 minutes (blunt trauma)
- Blunt trauma with no signs of life at the scene
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 398 (Book Page): [EDT is considered futile: CPR for more than 15 minutes... in the presence of penetrating thoracic trauma; CPR for more than 10 minutes... in the presence of blunt thoracic trauma; blunt trauma when there have been no signs of life at the scene.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: Why is 'c' (exsanguinating external haemorrhage) prioritized over 'A' (Airway) in war/blast trauma?
back: Massive arterial bleeding can lead to death faster than airway obstruction and must be controlled immediately by direct pressure or tourniquet.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: A patient presents with a knee (tibiofemoral) dislocation. What specific vascular emergency must be ruled out?
back:
- Popliteal artery injury (occurs in 30% of cases).
- Requires urgent angiography or continuous monitoring as intimal flaps can progress to thrombosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): [In 30% of knee dislocations (tibiofemoral dislocation) a vascular injury will occur... An intimal fap may develop, progress and thrombose over time. Repeated evaluation is necessary...]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: Identify the three physiological components of the trauma 'triad of death.'
back:
1. Acidosis
2. Coagulopathy
3. Hypothermia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: Define the anatomical boundaries of the 'safe triangle' for emergency chest decompression.
back:
- Posterior: Latissimus dorsi
- Anterior: Lateral border of pectoralis major
- Inferior: Line perpendicular to the nipple level
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [safe triangle – defned posteriorly by latissimus dorsi, anteriorly by the lateral border of pectoralis major and inferiorly by a line perpendicular to the nipple...]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What is the prioritized sequence for identifying life-threatening pathologies during the trauma primary survey?
back:
cABCDE:
- c: Exsanguinating external hemorrhage.
- A: Airway with C-spine control.
- B: Breathing/ventilation.
- C: Circulation/hemorrhage control.
- D: Disability.
- E: Exposure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [The primary survey aims to identify and manage the most immediately life-threatening pathologies frst and follows cABCDE.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What is the physiological purpose and time-limitation for permissive hypotension in trauma resuscitation?
back: Maintains vital organ perfusion (brain, heart, kidneys) while avoiding hemodilution and coagulopathy caused by excessive fluids. It is time-limited until surgical control of hemorrhage is achieved.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page)-377: [The initial aim of resuscitation is to maintain the blood supply to the vital organs: the brain, heart and kidneys... However, the key to this approach of permissive hypotension is that it is time limited.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: How is pericardial tamponade clinically distinguished from tension pneumothorax during the primary survey?
back:
- Both: Shock and distended neck veins.
- Tension PTX: Hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds.
- Tamponade: Muffled heart sounds and clear lungs on auscultation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [Pericardial tamponade needs to be diferentiated from a tension pneumothorax in the shocked patient with distended neck veins.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: A hemodynamically unstable blunt trauma patient requires immediate surgery. Where exactly should the pelvic binder be placed?
back: At the level of the greater trochanters. Correct positioning allows for trauma laparotomy to proceed without removing the binder.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Why is 'c' (catastrophic hemorrhage) managed before 'A' (airway) in military or blast trauma?
back: Massive arterial bleeding can cause exsanguination faster than airway compromise causes death. Immediate control via direct pressure, packs, or tourniquets is required.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed... Bleeding must be controlled immediately by the application of packs and pressure.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What blood product ratio defines an established massive transfusion protocol (MTP)?
back:
A 1:1:1 ratio consisting of:
- 1 part Packed Red Cells.
- 1 part Fresh-Frozen Plasma.
- 1 part Platelets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Describe the stepwise progression of managing a compromised airway during the primary survey.
back:
1. Suction secretions/blood.
2. Simple maneuvers (jaw thrust/chin lift).
3. Oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal adjuncts.
4. Definitive airway (endotracheal intubation or surgical airway).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [A compromised airway requires a stepwise progression, frst clearing the airway by suctioning secretions or blood, followed by simple airway manoeuvres... Advanced airway manoeuvres necessitate the insertion of a cufed endotracheal tube.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What is the specific systolic blood pressure target in trauma patients with suspected head injury?
back: Systolic BP >90 mmHg. This higher threshold is necessary to maintain adequate cerebral perfusion pressure compared to standard permissive hypotension (70–90 mmHg).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What three physiological states constitute the 'triad of death' in trauma patients?
back:
1. Acidosis.
2. Coagulopathy.
3. Hypothermia.
This cycle leads to multi-organ failure and necessitates damage control surgery rather than early total care.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Why is formal log-rolling deferred until after the primary survey in blunt trauma patients?
back: It adds minimal information and can disrupt blood clots in severe pelvic fractures, potentially causing fatal hemorrhage. Use inline stabilization or scoop stretchers instead.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [Log-rolling should not occur until a pelvic fracture has been radiographically excluded... It should be deferred until after the primary survey.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What is the primary objective of the secondary survey in trauma?
back: To perform a detailed top-to-toe examination identifying all injuries after life-threatening pathologies have been managed during the primary survey.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [All severely injured patients require a detailed top-to-toe examination after life-threatening injuries have been identifed and managed during the primary survey.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Which six potentially life-threatening chest injuries must be identified during the secondary survey?
back:
1. Aortic injuries
2. Tracheobronchial injuries
3. Myocardial contusion
4. Diaphragm rupture
5. Oesophageal injuries
6. Pulmonary contusion
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [six are potentially life-threatening and should be detected during the secondary survey (Table 29.3)]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Differentiate between a secondary survey and a tertiary survey.
back:
Secondary: Detailed top-to-toe exam after stabilization.
Tertiary: Re-examination when the patient is alert/extubated to identify missed 'minor' injuries (e.g., scaphoid fractures).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Such patients should have a ‘tertiary survey’ when extubated and alert to identify any missed ‘minor’ injuries, such as a scaphoid fracture in the wrist]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: A trauma patient is unconscious. How is the secondary survey spine evaluation conducted?
back: Maintain spinal immobilization (collar/blocks); log-roll to palpate for thoracic/lumbar deformity; perform per rectum exam; check for priapism as a cord injury sign.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [The patient will need to be log-rolled to palpate for thoracic or lumbar deformity... A per rectum examination is also performed at log-roll... Priapism is a strong predictor of severe cord injury even in intubated patients.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What precautions are necessary for the 'Exposure' phase of the secondary survey?
back: Adequately expose for systematic examination while using warmed blankets, trolleys, and fluids to maintain normal temperature and prevent hypothermia-induced coagulopathy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [The patient must be adequately exposed to allow a thorough and systematic clinical examination during the secondary survey but they must be kept warm.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Which clinical signs during the secondary survey indicate a possible skull base fracture?
back: Battle's sign (mastoid bruising), Raccoon eyes (periorbital bruising), haemotympanum, and CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Clinical evidence of a skull base fracture may include Battle’s sign... ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes... CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea are also highly suggestive of a fracture of the base of the skull.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: How are the cranial nerves assessed during the secondary survey head examination?
back: Check facial/vestibulocochlear function (for base fracture), gaze paresis or dysconjugate gaze (for brainstem dysfunction), and perform an ophthalmoscopic retinal inspection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [A complete examination of the cranial nerves will reveal, for example, facial or vestibulocochlear nerve damage associated with skull base fracture. Midbrain or brainstem dysfunction may produce gaze paresis]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: When is formal log-rolling contraindicated during the initial secondary survey steps?
back: Log-rolling should not occur until a pelvic fracture has been radiographically excluded to avoid disrupting established blood clots.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [Log-rolling should not occur until a pelvic fracture has been radiographically excluded.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What specific per rectum findings are assessed during the secondary survey log-roll?
back:
1. Anal tone
2. Perianal sensation (if awake)
3. Anal wink (contraction in response to pinprick stimulus)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [A per rectum examination is also performed at log-roll, assessing for anal tone, sensation in the awake patient and anal wink]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Identify the specific facial structures that must be inspected during the secondary survey.
back: Scalp for haematomas, orbital rims, zygoma, maxilla, eyes (for hyphaema or papilloedema), and the mouth for blood or tongue-biting.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Examine the face for evidence of fractures, especially to the orbital rim, zygoma and maxilla... Inspect the conjunctiva and cornea... looking for hyphaema... Blood in the mouth]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What is the recommended sequence for the primary survey in modern trauma management?
back:
- c: Control of exsanguinating external haemorrhage
- A: Airway with C-spine control
- B: Breathing and ventilation
- C: Circulation and haemorrhage control
- D: Disability
- E: Exposure
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [The primary survey aims to identify and manage the most immediately life-threatening pathologies frst and follows cABCDE.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Why is exsanguinating external haemorrhage (c) prioritized before airway (A) in the primary survey?
back:
- Massive arterial bleeding from blast or gunshot injuries leads to rapid death.
- It must be controlled immediately with direct pressure or tourniquets to prevent exsanguination before other interventions.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed... Failure to control bleeding in the limb by direct pressure... should be followed by the application of a tourniquet]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Differentiate between simple and advanced airway manoeuvres in trauma stabilization.
back:
- Simple: Suctioning, jaw thrust, chin lift, oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal adjuncts.
- Advanced: Cuffed endotracheal tube insertion (intubation) or creating a surgical airway.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [simple airway manoeuvres such as a jaw thrust, chin lift and insertion of an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway. Advanced airway manoeuvres necessitate the insertion of a cufed endotracheal tube... or a surgical airway.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: A blunt trauma patient is haemodynamically unstable; what immediate mechanical step is mandatory during 'C'?
back:
- Application of a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters.
- Precaution: Do not remove until a pelvic fracture has been radiographically excluded.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [A pelvic binder should be applied to all haemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma and not removed until after a pelvic fracture has been excluded.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What are the systolic blood pressure targets for 'permissive hypotension' during primary survey resuscitation?
back:
- Standard Target: 70–90 mmHg (to maintain a palpable radial pulse).
- Suspected Head Injury: >90 mmHg to ensure adequate cerebral perfusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected. Small boluses of IV fuids... should be administered... which should result in a palpable radial pulse.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What specific blood product ratio is utilized in a massive transfusion protocol?
back:
- 1 unit Packed Red Cells
- 1 unit Fresh-Frozen Plasma
- 1 unit Platelets
- Standard Ratio: (1:1:1).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Why is formal log-rolling deferred until after the primary survey in blunt trauma patients?
back:
- It delays time-critical investigations (Whole-body CT).
- It adds minimal useful clinical data early.
- It risks disrupting clots in potential pelvic fractures, causing further haemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [Formal log-rolling of the blunt trauma patient to examine the back during the primary survey adds minimal useful clinical information, delays the WBCT scan and may cause harm to a patient with a pelvic fracture.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Why is 'springing the pelvis' strictly contraindicated in the emergency department?
back:
- It Disrupts established blood clots around a pelvic fracture.
- It does not replace the gold standard of radiographic diagnosis.
- It may exacerbate internal bleeding.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Mechanical testing of the pelvis in the emergency room (‘springing the pelvis’) adds no useful clinical examination and will disrupt any blood clot that has formed around a pelvic fracture. It should never be performed]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: How is haemodynamic status clinically assessed to identify 'shock' during the primary survey (C)?
back:
- Skin: Cool, pale, and sweaty.
- Heart Rate: Tachycardia (>100 beats per minute).
- Blood Pressure: Low (hypotension).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [An assessment of the haemodynamic status should be made to identify shocked patients: the skin may be cool and sweaty, the pulse rate raised to over 100 per minute and the blood pressure low.]

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What is the mandatory anatomical precaution during airway assessment (A)?
back:
- The cervical spine must be strictly immobilised and protected throughout the survey.
- Immobilisation uses a rigid collar and blocks until spinal injury is excluded.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [All trauma patients should have their cervical spine immobilised and protected throughout. An immediate assessment of the patient’s airway is made.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: What is the first priority (the 'c' stage) in the primary survey of trauma?
back: Control of exsanguinating external hemorrhage. Must be managed even before the airway using direct pressure, packs, or tourniquets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [Experience from war zones over the past 20 years has shown that exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: Describe the clinical presentation of Cushing’s triad in brain herniation.
back:
1. Hypertension
2. Bradycardia
3. Irregular respiration
Indicates brainstem compromise and impending death.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. The patient is then said to be ‘coning’, and brainstem death will result without immediate intervention.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: Why is tension pneumothorax defined strictly as a clinical diagnosis?
back: Decompression must never be delayed for radiological confirmation to avoid fatal cardiovascular collapse and mediastinal shift.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: Differentiate neurogenic shock from hypovolaemic shock in a spinal trauma patient.
back:
● Neurogenic: Hypotension, bradycardia (or normal HR), warm peripheries.
● Hypovolaemic: Hypotension, tachycardia, cold clammy peripheries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page): [Neurogenic shock. This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries... Hypovolaemic shock. Hypotension with tachycardia and cold clammy peripheries.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: What is the specific timing and dose for Tranexamic acid in traumatic hemorrhage?
back: 1g IV over 10 minutes, then 1g over 8 hours. Ideally administered within 1 hour; never after 3 hours from injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: What defines 'Massive Haemothorax' requiring urgent surgical thoracotomy?
back: Initial drainage of >1500 mL blood or ongoing loss exceeding 200 mL/hour over 3–4 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: Where must a pelvic binder be positioned to ensure life-saving hemorrhage control?
back: At the level of the greater trochanters. Correct placement reduces pelvic volume without obstructing a potential trauma laparotomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: A trauma patient presents with transient loss of consciousness followed by a 'lucid interval' before rapid decline. Diagnosis?
back: Extradural haematoma. Usually involves middle meningeal artery rupture; mandates urgent transfer for surgical evacuation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Transient loss of consciousness is typical, and the patient may then present in the subsequent lucid interval with headache but without any neurological defcit... although this ‘talk and die’ pattern of deterioration occurs in only one-third of cases]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: Explain the physiological triggers of life-threatening autonomic dysreflexia in spinal cord injuries.
back: Triggered by noxious stimuli below injury level (T6 or higher), typically bladder distension or rectal loading. Causes paroxysmal hypertension and bradycardia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Autonomic dysrefexia... is most commonly triggered by bladder distension or rectal loading from faecal impaction.]

category: Identify immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention
front: Q: Why is pericardiocentesis contraindicated in traumatic myocardial tamponade?
back: Blood in traumatic injury is usually clotted, preventing aspiration. Immediate treatment is operative (sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [In penetrating injury to the heart there is usually a substantial clot in the pericardium, which may prevent aspiration. Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What is the primary timing and scope of the secondary survey in trauma?
back:
Performed only after:
- Life-threatening injuries are identified/managed (Primary Survey).
- Initial stabilization is achieved.
- Scope: Detailed top-to-toe clinical examination.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [All severely injured patients require a detailed top-to-toe examination after life-threatening injuries have been identifed and managed during the primary survey.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Which physical signs identified during the head/face secondary survey suggest a basal skull fracture?
back:
- Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising).
- 'Racoon' or 'Panda' eyes (periorbital bruising).
- Haemotympanum or CSF rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Clinical evidence of a skull base fracture may include Battle’s sign ( Figure 28.3 ) and ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes (bilateral periorbital bruising). Haemotympanum... and CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea are also highly suggestive of a fracture of the base of the skull.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What specific spinal assessments must be performed during the log-roll in a secondary survey?
back:
- Palpation of the entire spine for tenderness, steps, or deformity.
- Per rectum (PR) examination for anal tone, sensation, and anal wink.
- Identification of posterior torso wounds (penetrating trauma).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [The patient will need to be log-rolled to palpate for thoracic or lumbar deformity... A per rectum examination is also performed at log-roll, assessing for anal tone, sensation in the awake patient and anal wink.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: How is the limb neurological status assessed in the detailed secondary survey examination?
back:
- Peripheral nerve examination.
- Documentation of limb tone, power, reflexes, and sensation.
- Identification of specific sensory levels (e.g., thoracic levels).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [A peripheral nerve examination with documentation of limb tone, power, refexes and sensation needs to be performed early to identify spinal pathology.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What environmental precaution is mandatory while the patient is exposed for the secondary survey?
back:
- Keep the patient warm.
- Use warmed blankets, warmed trolleys, and warmed fluids.
- Minimise unnecessary exposure to prevent hypothermia-induced coagulopathy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [The patient must be adequately exposed to allow a thorough and systematic clinical examination during the secondary survey but they must be kept warm. Trauma patients are frequently hypothermic and this will further increase coagulopathy.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Why is the secondary survey often limited in accuracy for patients who remain intubated?
back:
- Patient is unresponsive.
- Clinical examination cannot rely on feedback for pain or sensory levels.
- Requires follow-up 'Tertiary Survey' when the patient is extubated and alert.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Patients may be intubated and unresponsive at this point, limiting the accuracy of clinical examination. Such patients should have a ‘tertiary survey’ when extubated and alert to identify any missed ‘minor’ injuries.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
coreConcept: Secondary Survey: Spinal Cord Injury Signs
front: Q: What clinical finding during the secondary survey predicts severe spinal cord injury in intubated patients?
back:
- Priapism.
- This sign is reliable even when the patient is unresponsive to other stimuli.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Priapism is a strong predictor of severe cord injury even in intubated patients.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: How should a suspected cervical spine injury be managed while examining the neck in a secondary survey?
back:
- Maintain hard collar immobilization.
- Remove collar only temporarily to allow palpation of the cervical spine.
- Replace collar immediately after palpation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [These patients should be managed in a hard collar until the neck can be cleared clinically... any cervical collar should be removed at this stage to allow palpation of the cervical spine before it is then replaced again.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What specific anatomical areas must be inspected for wounds during the secondary survey log-roll?
back:
- Scalp (subgaleal haematoma).
- Back and buttocks.
- Perineum and sacral area.
- Posterior neck.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Examination of the head should include inspection and palpation of the scalp... The patient will need to be log-rolled to palpate for thoracic or lumbar deformity... Perineum or sacral area, indicating an open pelvic fracture.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Which specific facial structures require palpation for fractures during the secondary survey?
back:
- Orbital rims.
- Zygoma.
- Maxilla.
- Scalp for underlying skull fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Examine the face for evidence of fractures, especially to the orbital rim, zygoma and maxilla... inspection and palpation of the scalp for evidence of subgaleal haematoma... potentially overlie fractures.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: When is the trauma secondary survey initiated and what is its primary clinical objective?
back:
Initiation: Performed only after the primary survey (cABCDE) is complete and life-threatening injuries are managed.
Objective: A systematic, 'top-to-toe' physical examination to identify all injuries, including seemingly 'minor' ones that could cause long-term disability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [All severely injured patients require a detailed top-to-toe examination after life-threatening injuries have been identifed and managed during the primary survey.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Outline the essential examination components of the head and spine during a secondary survey.
back:
• Head: Palpate scalp/face for fractures; check for Battle’s sign, raccoon eyes, and CSF leaks (rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea).
• Spine/Neurology: Full log-roll to palpate for bony steps or tenderness; motor/sensory assessment of limbs.
• Perineum: Digital rectal exam for anal tone and sensation; check for priapism.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [A full secondary survey will be required. Particular attention must be paid to the head, neck and spine... The patient will need to be log-rolled to palpate for thoracic or lumbar deformity... A per rectum examination is also performed at log-roll, assessing for anal tone...]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: When is the secondary survey initiated in a trauma patient?
back:
- After the primary survey (cABCDE) is completed.
- Vital functions must be stabilized.
- Life-threatening injuries must be actively managed.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): All severely injured patients require a detailed top-to-toe examination after life-threatening injuries have been identifed and managed during the primary survey.

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What physical signs during the secondary survey indicate a base of skull fracture?
back:
- Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising).
- Raccoon/Panda eyes (periorbital bruising).
- Haemotympanum (blood behind the eardrum).
- CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): Clinical evidence of a skull base fracture may include Battle’s sign and ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes (bilateral periorbital bruising). Haemotympanum... and CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea are also highly suggestive.

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: How is the spine assessed during the secondary survey?
back:
- Whole-spine palpation via formal log-roll.
- Check for bony tenderness, 'steps', or gaps.
- Maintain manual in-line stabilization or hard collar until cleared.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): The entire spine must be palpated. A formal spinal log roll must be performed to achieve this... Signifcant swelling, tenderness, palpable steps or gaps suggest a spinal injury.

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What are the mandatory components of the digital rectal examination in trauma?
back:
- Assessment of anal sphincter tone.
- Evaluation of perianal sensation.
- Identification of rectal wall discontinuity or blood.
- Palpation of prostate position (high-riding suggests urethral avulsion).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): A per rectum examination is also performed at log-roll, assessing for anal tone, sensation in the awake patient and anal wink... Page 384 (Book Page): in male patients, the prostate is palpated; a high-riding prostate indicates a complete urethral avulsion.

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: List the 'potentially life-threatening' chest injuries identified in the secondary survey.
back:
- Aortic injuries.
- Tracheobronchial injuries.
- Myocardial contusion.
- Rupture of the diaphragm.
- Oesophageal injuries.
- Pulmonary contusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): six are potentially life-threatening and should be detected during the secondary survey (Table 29.3)... Aortic injuries, Tracheobronchial injuries, Myocardial contusion, Rupture of the diaphragm, Oesophageal injuries, Pulmonary contusion.

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What specific neurological findings must be documented during the secondary survey?
back:
- Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score.
- Pupil size and reactivity.
- Peripheral limb tone, power, and reflexes.
- Dermatomal sensation level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): A peripheral nerve examination with documentation of limb tone, power, refexes and sensation needs to be performed early to identify spinal pathology.

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What finding on perineal inspection during the secondary survey suggests urethral trauma?
back:
- Blood at the urethral meatus.
- Perineal haematoma or bruising.
- Lacerations in the groin or scrotum area.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): Inspection of the urethral meatus may reveal a drop of blood, indicating urethral damage... Evidence of perineal injury or haematuria mandates radiological evaluation.

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Why is 'springing the pelvis' contraindicated during the secondary survey?
back:
- It provides no useful clinical information.
- It disrupts established blood clots around pelvic fractures.
- It significantly increases the risk of massive haemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): Mechanical testing of the pelvis in the emergency room (‘springing the pelvis’) adds no useful clinical examination and will disrupt any blood clot... It should never be performed.

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What intraoral findings should be checked during the top-to-toe examination?
back:
- Tongue-biting (suggests seizure).
- Displaced or missing teeth (aspiration risk).
- Evidence of jaw fractures or soft tissue lacerations.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): Blood in the mouth may be due to tongue-biting at seizure... Page 407 (Book Page): teeth should be examined and their presence or absence noted... aspiration is a major risk.

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Define the 'Tertiary Survey' in the trauma assessment sequence.
back:
- A full re-examination performed 24 hours later (or once alert).
- Aim: To identify 'minor' missed injuries (e.g., scaphoid fractures, rotator cuff tears).
- Essential for reducing long-term disability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): Such patients should have a ‘tertiary survey’ when extubated and alert to identify any missed ‘minor’ injuries, such as a scaphoid fracture in the wrist or a rotator cuf tear.

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What is the primary objective and timing of the secondary survey in trauma?
back: Detailed top-to-toe examination performed only after the primary survey (cABCDE) is complete and the patient is stabilized. It identifies non-lethal injuries that may cause long-term disability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [All severely injured patients require a detailed top-to-toe examination after life-threatening injuries have been identified and managed during the primary survey.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Explain the significance of finding Battle’s sign and 'raccoon eyes' during the head survey.
back:
- Battle's sign: Bruising over the mastoid process.
- Raccoon eyes: Bilateral periorbital bruising.
- Both indicate a fracture of the base of the skull.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Clinical evidence of a skull base fracture may include Battle’s sign (Figure 28.3) and ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes (bilateral periorbital bruising).]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Contrast the timing and purpose of a secondary survey versus a tertiary survey.
back:
- Secondary Survey: Immediate post-stabilization exam to identify major injuries.
- Tertiary Survey: Performed when patient is alert/extubated; identifies missed "minor" injuries like scaphoid fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Such patients should have a ‘tertiary survey’ when extubated and alert to identify any missed ‘minor’ injuries, such as a scaphoid fracture in the wrist or a rotator cuff tear in the shoulder.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: A blunt trauma patient has a suspected pelvic fracture. How should the spinal survey proceed?
back:
- Defer formal log-rolling until radiographs exclude a pelvic fracture.
- Rolling can disrupt clots, leading to lethal hemorrhage.
- Use 20° rolls with inline stabilization if movement is essential.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [Log-rolling should not occur until a pelvic fracture has been radiographically excluded. If patients need to be moved during their primary survey, such as when moving onto the CT scanning gantry, a 20° roll with inline spinal stabilisation should be used.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: When should prophylactic antibiotics be administered during the evaluation of penetrating abdominal trauma?
back:
- Administer prior to any surgery identified during the survey.
- A single dose is usually sufficient unless major contamination is present.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 408 (Book Page): [prophylactic antibiotics prior to surgery should be used in all cases of penetrating abdominal trauma. Unless there is major contamination, a single dose is sufficient.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Which three components must be assessed to calculate the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) during the secondary survey?
back:
1. Best eye response (1–4).
2. Best verbal response (1–5).
3. Best motor response (1–6).
- GCS provides an index for potential secondary brain injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [On admission, the GCS score should be calculated (Table 27.1), the pupils assessed for size and reaction to light and the patient observed to determine whether they are moving all four limbs.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: How is the spine clinically 'cleared' during the secondary survey of an alert patient?
back:
- Remove cervical collar to palpate the cervical spine.
- Log-roll to palpate the whole spine for steps or tenderness.
- Perform peripheral nerve exam for tone, power, and sensation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [The patient will need to be log-rolled to palpate for thoracic or lumbar deformity, and any cervical collar should be removed at this stage to allow palpation of the cervical spine before it is then replaced again.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: During a secondary survey log-roll, what does finding priapism or loss of anal tone indicate?
back:
- Priapism: Strong predictor of severe spinal cord injury.
- Loss of anal tone: Indicates spinal cord or cauda equina damage.
- Requires immediate neurosurgical consultation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [A per rectum examination is also performed at log-roll, assessing for anal tone... Priapism is a strong predictor of severe cord injury even in intubated patients.]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: Why must the patient be kept warm during the extensive exposure required for the secondary survey?
back:
- Hypothermia exacerbates coagulopathy and the "triad of death."
- Use warmed blankets and warmed fluids.
- Minimize unnecessary exposure during the systematic clinical examination.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [Trauma patients are frequently hypothermic and this will further increase coagulopathy. Every effort should be made to maintain normal temperature by minimising unnecessary exposure of the patient and by using warmed blankets...]

category: Outline the steps of secondary survey for detailed evaluation after initial stabilization
front: Q: What clinical signs in the perineal survey suggest a male urethral injury?
back:
- Blood at the urethral meatus.
- Scrotal/perineal bruising.
- High-riding prostate on digital rectal examination.
- Contraindicates blind catheterization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [Inspection of the urethral meatus may reveal a drop of blood, indicating urethral damage... In male patients, the prostate is palpated; a high-riding prostate indicates a complete urethral avulsion.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What is the preferred fluid and ratio for resuscitating severely hypovolaemic trauma patients?
back: Warmed blood and blood products are used in a ratio of 1:1:1 (packed red cells : fresh-frozen plasma : platelets).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What is the recommended dosing regimen and timing for Tranexamic acid in trauma?
back: 1g IV over 10 minutes, then 1g over 8 hours. Ideally within 1 hour; do not give after 3 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... the first dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: How are venous lactate levels used to distinguish between suitability for ETC versus DCS?
back:
● <2 mmol/L: Resuscitated (ETC).
● 2–3 mmol/L: Monitor trend.
● >5 mmol/L: Under-resuscitated (DCS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.6 Venous lactate is an essential marker of resuscitation ● <2 mmol/L – ETC... ● >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What are the systolic blood pressure targets during the limited phase of permissive hypotension?
back: Target 70–90 mmHg generally, or >90 mmHg if a head injury is suspected.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What investigation is the gold standard for trauma patients with deranged physiology or signs of multiple injury?
back: Whole-body computed tomography (WBCT) from head to pelvis with IV contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Why should excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions be avoided in severe trauma?
back: They cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy, and elevate the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: When should a pelvic binder be applied and when can it be safely removed?
back: Applied to all haemodynamically unstable blunt trauma patients; removed only after pelvic fracture is radiographically excluded.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [A pelvic binder should be applied to all haemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma and not removed until after a pelvic fracture has been excluded.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: When is a FAST scan most useful in the management of unstable trauma patients?
back: To locate major haemorrhage sources in patients too haemodynamically unstable for CT before immediate surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [A focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan (if immediately available) may also be useful in this scenario to locate the major source of haemorrhage.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Contrast the primary goals of Damage Control Surgery (DCS) versus Early Total Care (ETC).
back:
● DCS: Rapid life/limb-saving procedures (haemorrhage control/decompression) in unstable patients.
● ETC: Definitive management of all injuries within 36 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.5 ETC versus DCS ● ETC describes the definitive management... within 36 hours... ● DCS describes simultaneous resuscitation with early rapid life- and limb-saving surgery.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What three clinical indicators are used during the primary survey to identify a shocked patient?
back:
1. Cool, sweaty skin
2. Pulse rate >100 per minute
3. Low blood pressure
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [An assessment of the haemodynamic status should be made to identify shocked patients: the skin may be cool and sweaty, the pulse rate raised to over 100 per minute and the blood pressure low.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What is the target systolic blood pressure in permissive hypotension for trauma resuscitation?
back:
● 70–90 mmHg (aiming for a palpable radial pulse).
● Target >90 mmHg if head injury is suspected.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Why should excessive IV crystalloid solutions be avoided during initial trauma resuscitation?
back:
● Causes haemodilution.
● Increases coagulopathy.
● Increases risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Contrast the role of Whole-Body CT (WBCT) with selective body system scanning in multiple injuries.
back:
● WBCT with IV contrast is the gold standard for sign/symptoms of multiple injury.
● Selective scanning has no role in severely injured trauma patients.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [WBCT from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology... There is no role for scanning selective body systems in the severely injured trauma patient.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What immediate mechanical intervention is required for a haemodynamically unstable blunt trauma patient?
back:
● Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters.
● Do not remove until pelvic fracture is radiographically excluded.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [A pelvic binder should be applied to all haemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma and not removed until after a pelvic fracture has been excluded.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What is the recommended dosing regimen for Tranexamic Acid in trauma patients suspected of significant hemorrhage?
back:
● 1 g IV over 10 minutes.
● Followed by 1 g IV over 8 hours.
● Administer within 3 hours of injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: List the three components of the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) used to monitor neurological status.
back:
● Best eye response (1-4).
● Best verbal response (1-5).
● Best motor response (1-6).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [Table 27.1 Glasgow Coma Scale. Best eye response (E)... Best verbal response (V)... Best motor response (M).]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: How does a venous lactate level of >5 mmol/L influence trauma surgical management decisions?
back:
● Indicates severe under-resuscitation.
● Mandates Damage Control Surgery (DCS) rather than Early Total Care (ETC).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.6 Venous lactate is an essential marker of resuscitation... >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Distinguish between Damage Control Surgery (DCS) and Early Total Care (ETC) in trauma management.
back:
● ETC: Definitive injury management within 36 hours.
● DCS: Rapid life/limb-saving surgery (hemorrhage control) while deferring time-consuming procedures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.5 ETC versus DCS ● ETC describes the defnitive management of a patient’s injuries within 36 hours... ● DCS describes simultaneous resuscitation with early rapid life- and limb-saving surgery.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Describe the physiological components of the trauma 'triad of death'.
back:
● Acidosis.
● Coagulopathy.
● Hypothermia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What is the preferred ratio of blood products in a massive transfusion protocol for trauma?
back:
● 1 Packed Red Cells.
● 1 Fresh-Frozen Plasma.
● 1 Platelets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What is the target systolic blood pressure range in permissive hypotension for a trauma patient without head injury?
back: 70–90 mmHg (aiming for a palpable radial pulse). If head injury is suspected, target >90 mmHg.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Why is excessive crystalloid resuscitation avoided in early trauma management?
back:
● Causes haemodilution
● Increases coagulopathy
● Increases risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Contrast the timing and patient selection for Early Total Care (ETC) versus Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
back:
● ETC: Definitive management within 36 hours for physiologically stable patients.
● DCS: Early rapid life/limb-saving surgery for physiologically compromised patients; definitive surgery deferred.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [ETC describes the defnitive management of a patient’s injuries within 36 hours of injury... DCS describes simultaneous resuscitation with early rapid life- and limb-saving surgery. Time-consuming defnitive surgery is deferred]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: A haemodynamically unstable blunt trauma patient requires immediate laparotomy. What adjunct is mandatory before/during transfer?
back: A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters; it must not be removed until pelvic fracture is radiographically excluded.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All patients undergoing immediate laparotomy in the operating theatre should have a pelvic binder applied and not removed. A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What is the intravenous administration protocol for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in trauma patients suspected of major bleeding?
back: 1g IV over 10 minutes, followed by another 1g over 8 hours. Ideally given within 1 hour and no later than 3 hours post-injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What is the gold standard investigation for a physiologically stable adult with signs of multiple blunt trauma?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from head to pelvis with intravenous (IV) contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: How do venous lactate levels guide the decision to proceed with definitive surgery?
back:
● <2 mmol/L: Resuscitated; suitable for ETC.
● 3–5 mmol/L: Under-resuscitated; further resuscitation or DCS required.
● >5 mmol/L: Indicates DCS.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [<2 mmol/L – ETC... >3 mmol/L – may be under-resuscitated; should either have further resuscitation or DCS if surgery is urgent... >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
coreConcept: FAST Scan Role in Unstable Patients
front: Q: In an unstable trauma patient, when should a FAST scan be utilized instead of CT?
back: When the patient is too haemodynamically unstable for CT transfer and requires immediate identification of intra-abdominal or pericardial haemorrhage before theatre.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Some patients will be so haemodynamically unstable on arrival that they need immediate surgical control... A focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan (if immediately available) may also be useful in this scenario to locate the major source of haemorrhage.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Define the component ratios required for a Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP) in severe hypovolaemia.
back: 1 unit Packed Red Cells : 1 unit Fresh-Frozen Plasma (FFP) : 1 unit Platelets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What are the specific target neurointensive care parameters for Intracranial Pressure (ICP) and Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP)?
back:
● ICP: <20 mmHg
● CPP: >60 mmHg
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Table 28.5 Key parameters... ICP <20 mmHg... CPP >60 mmHg]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Which biochemical marker is the essential monitor for determining successful resuscitation and suitability for early total care?
back:
• Venous Lactate.
• Threshold: <2 mmol/L indicates adequate resuscitation (suitable for ETC).
• Values >3 mmol/L suggest under-resuscitation; >5 mmol/L necessitates Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Venous lactate is a useful marker of resuscitation and physiological state. A normal lactate (<2 mmol/L) is a sign that the patient is probably resuscitated and suitable for ETC. An elevated lactate (>3 mmol/L) suggests the patient is under-resuscitated... >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Explain the physiological basis and systolic blood pressure targets for permissive hypotension during trauma resuscitation.
back:
• Basis: Limits clot disruption and prevents dilutional coagulopathy or ARDS caused by excessive crystalloid/colloid volumes.
• Standard Target: Systolic 70–90 mmHg (confirmed by palpable radial pulse).
• Head Injury Exception: >90 mmHg to maintain adequate cerebral perfusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected. ... Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
coreConcept: Absolute Surgical Indication in Spinal Trauma
front: Q: What is the only absolute surgical indication for acute spinal trauma management?
back: - Deteriorating neurological function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Why is prompt surgical drainage mandatory in native joint septic arthritis?
back:
- Prevents leukocyte proteases from destroying collagen matrix.
- Avoids avascular necrosis from high intra-articular pressure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage. AVN may occur secondary to pressure effects or ischaemic infarction.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: When is DAIR indicated versus total implant removal in prosthetic joint infections?
back:
- DAIR (Debridement, Antibiotics, and Implant Retention): Indicated for early, well-fixed prostheses.
- Removal: Mandatory for loose or chronically infected implants.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [DAIR... can only be undertaken if the prosthesis is well fxed... loose infected implants should always be removed.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: A child with an orbital fracture presents with bradycardia and nausea; what is the urgent management?
back:
- Urgent surgical release of the entrapped inferior rectus muscle.
- Diagnosis: Oculocardiac reflex (indicates imminent muscle necrosis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. This needs to be treated as an emergency because irreversible damage related to muscle necrosis can occur within hours.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
coreConcept: Surgical Phase of Open Fracture Management
front: Q: What defines the definitive management of an open fracture during the surgical phase?
back:
- Radical debridement of non-vital tissue.
- Bone stabilization (internal or external fixation).
- Dead-space management and soft-tissue reconstruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [The aim of open fracture management is to achieve bony union, optimise function and avoid infection... stable fxation of the bony injury is very important... Thorough debridement of any contaminated or non-vital soft tissue is important.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Which specific scenario in acute osteomyelitis warrants urgent referral for surgical debridement?
back:
- Failure of patient to respond rapidly to initial medical treatment.
- Evidence of limb deterioration or radiological progression of disease/abscess.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 625 (Book Page): [If the patient does not respond rapidly, if the limb deteriorates or if there is imaging evidence of progression of disease, surgery is indicated to prevent bone destruction...]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: How is an unhealed fracture with unstable fixation managed in the setting of infection?
back:
- Removal of the unstable infected implant.
- Radical excision of the infected fracture site.
- Stabilization using an external fixator.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [If the implant is not stable, it should be removed and replaced by an external fxator. Radical excision of the infected fracture is needed...]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What surgical maneuver is required for acute retrobulbar hemorrhage with loss of pupillary response?
back:
- Immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis.
- Goal: Decompress orbit to prevent optic nerve ischemia/blindness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness... preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis...]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What is the definitive reconstruction strategy for BACH 'complex' segmental chronic osteomyelitis?
back:
- Segmental curative resection of dead bone.
- Stabilization with external fixation (e.g., Ilizarov method).
- Distraction osteogenesis to fill bone defects.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 627 (Book Page): [When the infection is segmental (BACH complex)... Curative resection must be segmental and bone stabilisation will always be required. The Ilizarov method... is a powerful and successful technique.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What is the mandatory surgical management for an acute unstable Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis?
back:
- Urgent gentle repositioning and internal fixation within 24 hours.
- Surgical capsulotomy to reduce intracapsular tamponade.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 643 (Book Page): [an acute unstable SCFE is an emergency... A gentle repositioning... A capsulotomy reduces the tamponade efect... such treatment should take place within 24 hours.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What is the target systolic blood pressure range in permissive hypotension for trauma patients without head injury?
back: 70–90 mmHg. This maintains vital organ supply while minimizing the risk of increasing hemorrhage and coagulopathy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Why should excessive intravenous crystalloid or colloid solutions be avoided during initial trauma resuscitation?
back:
• Causes hemodilution
• Increases coagulopathy
• Elevates risk of Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Distinguish between the venous lactate levels indicating Early Total Care (ETC) versus Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
back:
• <2 mmol/L: Suitable for ETC
• >5 mmol/L: Indicator for DCS
• 2–3 mmol/L: Monitor trend (upward/downward)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [<2 mmol/L – ETC... >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: In the cABCDE trauma sequence, which specific clinical condition takes priority even before airway management?
back: Exsanguinating external hemorrhage. Control immediately using direct pressure, packs, or proximal tourniquets to prevent rapid exsanguination.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed]
