category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What is the recommended dosage and administration timing for Tranexamic acid (TXA) in suspected major hemorrhage?
back:
• Dose: 1g IV over 10 minutes, then 1g over 8 hours
• Timing: Ideally within the first hour; must be within 3 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Which imaging modality is the gold standard for trauma patients with deranged physiology and multisystem injury?
back: Whole-body Computed Tomography (WBCT). Scans from head to pelvis with IV contrast for rapid identification of life-threatening pathology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What specific ratio of blood products defines a modern massive transfusion protocol (MTP) for trauma patients?
back: 1:1:1 ratio. 1 Unit Packed Red Cells : 1 Unit Fresh-Frozen Plasma : 1 Unit Platelets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What immediate adjunct must be applied to all hemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma before pelvic fracture exclusion?
back: Pelvic binder. Apply at the level of greater trochanters; do not remove until pelvic fracture is radiographically excluded.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [A pelvic binder should be applied to all haemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma and not removed until after a pelvic fracture has been excluded.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: Describe the three components of the 'Triad of Death' resulting from immune and physiological derangement in trauma.
back:
A cycle of:
• Acidosis
• Coagulopathy
• Hypothermia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Discuss the role of resuscitation, monitoring, and adjunct investigations in trauma management
front: Q: What minimum hourly urine output threshold indicates a satisfactory physiological response to trauma resuscitation?
back: >30 mL/h. This serves as a key physiological index for evaluating resuscitation success and readiness for Early Total Care (ETC).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [A number of physiological indices are used to evaluate the response to resuscitation, including... urine output >30 mL/h.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: When is immediate laparotomy indicated in blunt trauma patients?
back:
* Haemodynamic instability on arrival.
* Suspected abdominal or pelvic haemorrhage requiring immediate control.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): Some patients will be so haemodynamically unstable on arrival that they need immediate surgical control of their haemorrhage before a CT scan. The most likely sources are abdominal or pelvic bleeding.

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Why is an acute unstable SCFE treated as a surgical emergency?
back:
* Pathophysiology mimics a displaced intracapsular neck fracture.
* Requires reduction within 24 hours to prevent high risk of Avascular Necrosis (AVN).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 643 (Book Page): This means that an acute unstable SCFE is an emergency. The AVN risk is considerable. To be effective such treatment should take place within 24 hours of injury.

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What chest drain output levels mandate urgent surgical thoracotomy?
back:
* Initial drainage >1500 mL of blood.
* Ongoing haemorrhage >200 mL/h for 3–4 consecutive hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Management of a child with bradycardia following an orbital floor fracture?
back:
* Immediate surgical emergency.
* Indicates inferior rectus entrapment (oculocardiac reflex).
* Requires prompt release to prevent irreversible muscle necrosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac reflex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. This needs to be treated as an emergency because irreversible damage related to muscle necrosis can occur within hours.

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What is the definitive emergency management for suspected retrobulbar haemorrhage?
back:
* Immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis.
* Goal is orbital decompression to prevent retinal artery ischemia and permanent blindness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency... preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under LA to allow the globe to bulge forwards and relieve the pressure.

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What is the definitive surgical management for established compartment syndrome?
back:
* Urgent fasciotomies.
* Requires splitting all fascial compartments of the affected limb to restore tissue perfusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): Emergency treatment involves splitting casts and/or dressings to the skin and elevating the extremity... arrangements put in place to perform definitive treatment with fasciotomies.

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: When is surgical debridement indicated in acute osteomyelitis?
back:
* Failure to respond rapidly to high-dose intravenous antibiotics.
* Imaging evidence of disease progression or bone destruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 625 (Book Page): If the patient does not respond rapidly, if the limb deteriorates or if there is imaging evidence of progression of disease, surgery is indicated to prevent bone destruction and the onset of chronic osteomyelitis.

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Immediate management of a 'white pulseless hand' in supracondylar fractures?
back:
* Urgent surgical emergency.
* Requires immediate assessment and fracture reduction to restore vascular flow.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 441 (Book Page): The white pulseless hand is a surgical emergency and requires immediate attention, assessment and urgent reduction.

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Why is surgery required for penetrating pericardial tamponade?
back:
* Pericardiocentesis is ineffective due to substantial clotting.
* Requires operative repair (sternotomy or thoracotomy) for haematoma evacuation and myocardial repair.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury. The correct immediate treatment of tamponade is operative, either via a subxiphoid window or by open surgery.

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What are the primary surgical goals for open fracture management?
back:
* Prompt thorough debridement of contaminated or non-vital tissue.
* Immediate stabilisation of the bony injury to allow soft-tissue recovery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): Stable fxation of the bony injury is very important to prevent deterioration of the soft tissues... Thorough debridement of any contaminated or non-vital soft tissue is important.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Define Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) based on the timing of injury components.
back:
TBI is the combination of:
- Primary injury: Sustained on impact (not medically modifiable).
- Secondary injury: Developing in the following hours and days.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Why is the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) the gold standard for classifying TBI severity?
back:
- Best predictor of neurological outcome.
- The motor score is the most significant prognostic component.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): The severity of head injury is classifed according to the post-resuscitation Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score... as it is the GCS score – and in particular the motor score – that is the best predictor of neurological outcome.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Classify TBI severity based on post-resuscitation GCS scores.
back:
- Minor/Mild: GCS 14–15.
- Moderate: GCS 9–13.
- Severe: GCS 3–8 (Comatose).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): Table 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation. Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC; Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC; Moderate head injury GCS 9–13; Severe head injury GCS 3–8.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Differentiate between Minor and Mild TBI regarding consciousness status.
back:
- Minor TBI: GCS 15 with no loss of consciousness (LOC).
- Mild TBI: GCS 14 or 15 with loss of consciousness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): Table 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation. Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC; Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Define the pathological mechanism and classical clinical progression of Extradural Haematoma (EDH).
back:
- Mechanism: Rupture of middle meningeal artery/vein associated with skull fracture.
- Progression: Transient loss of consciousness, a 'lucid interval,' then rapid neurological deterioration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): Extradural haematoma... results from rupture of an artery, vein or venous sinus, in association with a skull fracture... Transient loss of consciousness is typical, and the patient may then present in the subsequent lucid interval... with rapid deterioration.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: List the four clinical hallmarks suggestive of a fracture of the skull base.
back:
1. Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising).
2. 'Panda' or 'raccoon' eyes (periorbital bruising).
3. Haemotympanum.
4. CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): Clinical evidence of a skull base fracture may include Battle’s sign... and ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes (bilateral periorbital bruising). Haemotympanum... and CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea are also highly suggestive.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Explain the anatomical reason for Chronic Subdural Haematoma (SDH) prevalence in elderly patients.
back: Cerebral atrophy stretches cortical-dural bridging veins, making them susceptible to rupture from minor or trivial impacts.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): Cerebral atrophy in this age group results in stretching of the cortical–dural bridging veins, which are then vulnerable to rupture.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Contrast the CT radiological appearances of Extradural (EDH) vs. Subdural (SDH) Haematomas.
back:
- EDH: Lentiform (biconvex) hyperdense lesion limited by dural adhesions.
- SDH: Diffuse concave (crescentic) appearance spreading across the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page)-388: On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... Since the dura is not as adherent to the brain as it is to the skull, subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Define Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) and its clinical presentation.
back:
- Definition: Axonal shearing from extreme acceleration/deceleration in high-energy trauma.
- Presentation: Patient is typically comatose with poor outcomes; CT may only show minor haemorrhagic foci.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [DAI] is a form of primary brain injury seen in high-energy accidents that usually renders the patient comatose; it is associated with poor outcomes... [results] from extreme accelerations of the skull contents.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Define 'Coup' versus 'Contre-coup' cerebral contusions.
back:
- Coup: Brain injury at the primary site of impact.
- Contre-coup: Injury distant to impact site, caused by brain impacting the skull interior during asynchronous deceleration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): ‘Coup contre-coup’ contusions refer to brain injury both at the site of impact and distant to this, where the brain impacts on the inside of the skull as the skull and brain accelerate and then decelerate out of synchrony.

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
coreConcept: Indications for Urgent Thoracotomy in Massive Hemothorax
front: Q: What specific volume of initial blood drainage from a chest tube indicates urgent thoracotomy?
back:
- More than 1500 mL of blood initially
- Ongoing hemorrhage exceeding 200 mL/hour over 3–4 hours
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Why is retrobulbar hemorrhage defined as an acute surgical emergency?
back:
- Causes pressure-induced reduced flow in the retinal artery
- Leads to permanent ischaemic damage to the optic nerve and blindness
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness secondary to pressureinduced reduced fow on the retinal artery, leading to ischaemic damage to the optic nerve.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
coreConcept: Predictors for Urgent Septic Joint Referral
front: Q: What clinical predictors indicate a 93% probability of septic arthritis requiring urgent surgical washout?
back:
- Fever >38.5°C
- Non-weight-bearing status
- ESR >40 mm/h
- White cell count >12 × 10^9/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [History of fever >38.5°C, Non-weight-bearing, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h, White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L... Predicted probability of joint sepsis: 4 predictors = 93.0%]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
coreConcept: Emergency Management of Vascular Compromise in Fractures
front: Q: A pediatric supracondylar fracture presents with a white, pulseless hand. What is the mandatory management?
back:
- Immediate attention and urgent fracture reduction
- If pulse fails to return post-reduction, immediate surgical vessel exploration is required
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 462 (Book Page): [The white pulseless hand is a surgical emergency and requires immediate attention, assessment and urgent reduction. If the pulse does not return with reduction, then the vessels should be explored by appropriately trained surgeons.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What is the definitive definitive management for an infected unhealed fracture with unstable fixation?
back:
- Removal of unstable existing implant
- Radical excision of infected bone/tissue
- Stabilization using an external fixator
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 625 (Book Page): [Stability is essential for bone healing and eradication of infection. If the implant is not stable, it should be removed and replaced by an external fxator. Radical excision of the infected fracture is needed]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Which clinical patterns mandate urgent surgical referral for immediate evacuation of an extradural haematoma?
back:
- Deteriorating consciousness or comatose state
- Large bleeds identified on CT
- Development of contralateral hemiparesis or ipsilateral pupillary dilatation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Significant extradural haematoma mandates urgent transfer to the most accessible neurosurgical facility for immediate evacuation in deteriorating or comatose patients or those with large bleeds]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What definitive surgical management is required for a clinical diagnosis of compartment syndrome?
back:
- Immediate splitting of all casts/dressings to the skin
- Urgent definitive surgical fasciotomies of all affected compartments
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 466 (Book Page): [Emergency treatment involves splitting casts and/or dressings to the skin and elevating the extremity... perform defnitive treatment with fasciotomies.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Why does inferior rectus muscle entrapment in an orbital fracture require emergency surgical referral?
back:
- Risk of irreversible muscle necrosis within hours
- Triggering of the oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, nausea, syncope)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. This needs to be treated as an emergency because irreversible damage related to muscle necrosis can occur within hours.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Which six chest injuries are classified as the 'deadly dozen' requiring immediate management during the primary survey?
back:
1. Airway obstruction
2. Tension pneumothorax
3. Pericardial tamponade
4. Open pneumothorax
5. Massive haemothorax
6. Flail chest
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Table 29.3 The ‘deadly dozen’ threats to life from chest injury. Immediately life-threatening: Airway obstruction, Tension pneumothorax, Pericardial tamponade, Open pneumothorax, Massive haemothorax, Flail chest.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Where is the recommended anatomical site for the urgent surgical decompression of a tension pneumothorax?
back:
Decompression is performed in the 'safe triangle':
1. Posteriorly by latissimus dorsi
2. Anteriorly by pectoralis major
3. Inferiorly by the 5th intercostal space (nipple level)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [current teaching advocates undertaking decompression in the safe triangle – defned posteriorly by latissimus dorsi, anteriorly by the lateral border of pectoralis major and inferiorly by a line perpendicular to the nipple going to the back, just anterior to the mid-axillary line]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Why is pericardiocentesis contraindicated in the definitive management of traumatic cardiac tamponade?
back:
1. Substantial clotted blood in the pericardium prevents successful aspiration.
2. Definitive treatment requires operative evacuation and myocardial repair via sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury. The correct immediate treatment of tamponade is operative... with repair of the heart in the operating theatre.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: At what drainage thresholds is a massive haemothorax an indication for urgent thoracotomy?
back:
1. Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood.
2. Ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What are the specific pharmacological indications for administering Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in trauma patients?
back:
Suspected significant haemorrhage, including:
1. Systolic blood pressure <110 mmHg.
2. Pulse over 110 beats per minute.
3. Administration must occur within 3 hours of injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have signifcant haemorrhage, including those with a systolic blood pressure of <110 mmHg or a pulse of over 110 per minute. It needs to be administered as early as possible... not more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What is the only absolute indication for urgent surgical intervention in patients with spinal trauma?
back: Deteriorating neurological function is the only absolute surgical indication in acute spinal trauma management.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Which markers indicate a patient is physiologically stable enough for Early Total Care (ETC) vs Damage Control Surgery?
back:
1. Pulse <100/min and normal BP.
2. Urine output >30 mL/h.
3. Normal coagulation screen.
4. Venous lactate <2 mmol/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [A number of physiological indices are used to evaluate the response to resuscitation, including a pulse rate less than 100 per minute, normal blood pressure... urine output >30 mL/h... normal coagulation screen. Lactate levels... normal.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: In which penetrating trauma scenario is Emergency Department Thoracotomy (EDT) indicated versus futile?
back:
Indications: Signs of life and electrical activity must be present.
Futile: CPR >15 minutes in penetrating thoracic trauma or >10 minutes in blunt trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): [EDT should be reserved for those patients with penetrating injury in whom signs of life are still present... In certain situations, EDT is considered futile: CPR for more than 15 minutes... penetrating thoracic trauma; CPR for more than 10 minutes... blunt thoracic trauma.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
coreConcept: Triad of Death in Damage Control
front: Q: Describe the 'triad of death' and its effect on definitive surgical management.
back:
1. Components: Acidosis, Coagulopathy, and Hypothermia.
2. Effect: Mandates Damage Control Surgery (DCS), deferring time-consuming definitive reconstructions until physiology is restored.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death... surgical interventions... are limited to rapid life- and limb-saving procedures... definitive reconstructive procedures are deferred.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What are the cardinal clinical signs of compartment syndrome requiring urgent fasciotomy?
back:
1. Pain out of proportion to injury.
2. Pain on passive stretch.
3. Paraesthesia, paralysis, and pallor.
4. Pulselessness (late sign).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis characterised by pain out of proportion, increasing pain, and pain on passive stretch, with paraesthesia possible. Paralysis, numbness and pallor are late signs and pulselessness is an extremely late sign.]

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Define traumatic brain injury (TBI) and its two distinct pathological categories.
back:
TBI is the result of physical impact to the head. It consists of:
- Primary injury: Occurs at impact; medically non-modifiable.
- Secondary injury: Develops hours/days later; potentially preventable by managing intracranial pressure and oxygenation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Classify traumatic brain injury severity based on GCS scores and loss of consciousness (LOC) status.
back:
- Minor: GCS 15, no LOC.
- Mild: GCS 14–15 with LOC.
- Moderate: GCS 9–13.
- Severe: GCS 3–8 (comatose).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): TABLE 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation. Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC; Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC; Moderate head injury GCS 9–13; Severe head injury GCS 3–8.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: How is Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) defined regarding the timing of injury components?
back:
- Primary injury: Sustained at the moment of impact.
- Secondary injury: Develops in the hours and days following the initial event.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.]

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Contrast the medical modifiability of primary and secondary brain injuries.
back:
- Primary injury: Not medically modifiable (irreversible impact damage).
- Secondary injury: Modifiable through management of intracranial pressure (ICP) and systemic parameters.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.]

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
coreConcept: Minor vs Mild Head Injury Classification
front: Q: Classify the severity difference between Minor and Mild head injuries using GCS and consciousness.
back:
- Minor: GCS 15 with no loss of consciousness (LOC).
- Mild: GCS 14 or 15 with a history of loss of consciousness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Table 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation. Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC; Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC]

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: A patient presents with a post-resuscitation GCS of 7; what is the injury severity classification?
back: - Severe head injury (defined as GCS 3–8).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Table 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation... Severe head injury GCS 3–8]

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: What GCS range identifies a Moderate head injury classification?
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Table 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation... Moderate head injury GCS 9–13]

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Classify traumatic intracranial haemorrhage by CT appearance: which type is lentiform or biconvex?
back: - Extradural haematoma (EDH).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain]

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Which specific GCS component is the best predictor of neurological outcome in TBI classification?
back: - The motor score.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [The severity of head injury is classifed according to the post-resuscitation Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score ( Table 28.1 ), as it is the GCS score – and in particular the motor score – that is the best predictor of neurological outcome.]

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Classify Acute vs. Chronic Subdural Haematoma by CT density and patient type.
back:
- Acute: Hyperdense, concave; high-energy or elderly/anticoagulated.
- Chronic: Diffuse hypodensity; older adults/cerebral atrophy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 387 (Book Page): [Acute subdural... concave appearance... Chronic subdural... Imaging reveals diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface.]

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Define the "Coup contre-coup" type of cerebral contusion injury.
back:
- Coup: Injury at impact site.
- Contre-coup: Injury distant to impact site, caused by skull and brain accelerating/decelerating out of synchrony.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [‘ Coup contre-coup ’ contusions refer to brain injury both at the site of impact and distant to this, where the brain impacts on the inside of the skull as the skull and brain accelerate and then decelerate out of synchrony with each other.]

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Define Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) by its clinical presentation and diagnostic basis.
back:
- High-energy primary injury resulting in immediate coma.
- Strictly a pathological diagnosis at postmortem, though MRI is highly sensitive.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [Diffuse axonal injury: This is a form of primary brain injury seen in high-energy accidents that usually renders the patient comatose; it is associated with poor outcomes. It is strictly a pathological diagnosis made at postmortem]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: How is traumatic brain injury (TBI) categorized based on the timing and modifiability of the physical insult?
back:
- Primary injury: Sustained at the moment of impact; not medically modifiable.
- Secondary injury: Develops in the following hours and days; potentially preventable with medical intervention.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifiable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological cycle that drives progressive secondary brain injury following initial head trauma.
back:
- Mass lesions or swelling increase Intracranial Pressure (ICP).
- Elevated ICP reduces cerebral perfusion and oxygenation.
- Resultant ischaemia and inflammation trigger further necrosis and swelling, exacerbating the cycle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Brain swelling and mass lesions contribute to raised intracranial pressure, which compromises perfusion, leading to secondary brain injury and further swelling.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: How is Primary Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) distinguished from Secondary TBI?
back:
● Primary Injury: Sustained at the immediate moment of impact.
● Secondary Injury: Develops in the subsequent hours and days following the initial trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifiable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Describe the physiological 'cycle of deterioration' leading to secondary brain injury.
back:
● Brain swelling/mass lesions cause raised ICP.
● Raised ICP reduces cerebral perfusion pressure.
● This leads to hypoxia and ischemia, causing further brain injury and swelling.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Raised intracranial pressure ... compromises perfusion, leading to secondary brain injury and further swelling. (Figure 28.9)]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Contrast the medical modifiability of primary and secondary brain injuries.
back:
● Primary injury: Not medically modifiable (irreversible at impact).
● Secondary injury: Modifiable through therapeutic interventions like avoiding hypoxia and controlling intracranial pressure (ICP).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifiable, and secondary injury... Understanding the importance of intracranial pressure (ICP) and related parameters is key to minimising secondary injury.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: In a comatose high-energy accident victim, identify the specific primary injury pathophysiology.
back:
● Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI).
● Pathophysiology: Caused by extreme acceleration/deceleration forces of the skull contents during the initial impact.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [Diffuse axonal injury: This is a form of primary brain injury seen in high-energy accidents that usually renders the patient comatose... results from extreme accelerations of the skull contents.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Which two systemic insults are the primary targets for preventing secondary brain injury?
back:
● Hypoxia (PaO2 <11 kPa).
● Hypotension (MAP <80 mmHg).
● Both drastically reduce oxygen delivery to an already injured brain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [medical management strategies aim to minimise secondary brain injury through avoidance of hypoxia and hypotension and control of ICP.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: What defines 'coning' in the context of raised ICP pathophysiology?
back:
● Herniation of cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum.
● Results in compression of medullary vasomotor and respiratory centers (Cushing’s triad).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres, classically producing Cushing’s triad... The patient is then said to be ‘ coning ’.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Apply the Monro–Kellie doctrine to explain the exponential rise in TBI intracranial pressure.
back:
● The cranium is a rigid, non-expandable box.
● Once compensatory expulsion of CSF and venous blood is exhausted, small increases in mass (swelling/blood) cause rapid ICP spikes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [The Monro–Kellie doctrine accounts for the ability of the intracranial compartment to accommodate expanding mass lesions, primarily by excluding venous blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and the rapid rise in pressure associated with exhaustion of this compensation.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: How do metabolic factors like pyrexia and seizures contribute to secondary brain injury?
back:
● They increase cerebral metabolic requirements.
● This exacerbates the mismatch between oxygen supply and demand in the compromised brain tissue.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Increased metabolic requirements – seizure, pyrexia, inflammation ... compromises perfusion, leading to secondary brain injury and further swelling. (Figure 28.9)]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Why is the brain more vulnerable to hypotension after a traumatic injury?
back:
● Disturbance or loss of cerebral autoregulation.
● The brain becomes dependent on Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) for perfusion instead of maintaining constant flow automatically.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [ensuring uninterrupted perfusion of the brain... is especially important after a head injury, given the disturbance to intracranial autoregulation and the sensitivity of the primary injured brain tissue to further insult.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: State the mathematical formula used to calculate Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP).
back:
● CPP = Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) – Intracranial Pressure (ICP).
● Normal range: 75–105 mmHg.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Flow depends on cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), which is the difference between the mean arterial pressure (MAP) and the intracranial pressure (ICP): CPP (75–105 mmHg) = MAP (90–110 mmHg) – ICP (5–15 mmHg)]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
coreConcept: Primary vs Secondary Brain Injury Definition
front: Compare primary and secondary brain injury in terms of timing and modifiability.
back:
● Primary Injury: Occurs at the moment of impact; not medically modifiable.
● Secondary Injury: Develops in the following hours/days; manageable through intervention.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Explain the Monro-Kellie doctrine's effect on intracranial pressure (ICP).
back:
● The cranium is a rigid, incompressible box.
● Expansion (haematoma/swelling) is initially compensated by excluding venous blood and CSF.
● Once compensation is exhausted, ICP rises exponentially.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Alexander Monro observed in 1783 that the cranium is a ‘rigid box’ containing a ‘nearly incompressible brain’. Any expansion... initially accommodated by exclusion of fuid components... Further expansion is associated with an exponential rise in ICP

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Distinguish between the blood flow thresholds for cerebral ischaemia and infarction.
back:
● Normal CBF: ~55 mL/min per 100g.
● Ischaemia: Occurs when CBF drops below 20 mL/min per 100g.
● Infarction: Occurs at levels even lower than the ischaemic threshold.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Normal cerebral blood fow (CBF) is about 55 mL/min for every 100 g of brain tissue. Ischaemia results when this rate drops below 20 mL/min, and even lower levels will result in infarction

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: A patient with an extradural haematoma develops an ipsilateral dilated pupil. Explain the anatomical pathophysiology.
back:
● Uncal herniation compresses the third cranial nerve (oculomotor).
● Parasympathetic supply is compromised.
● Result: Unopposed sympathetic activity causes a sluggish or fixed dilated pupil.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): Uncal herniation ( Figure 28.2 ) can compress the third nerve, compromising the parasympathetic supply to the pupil. Unopposed sympathetic activity produces a sluggish enlarged pupil, progressing to fxed and dilated

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: How does mannitol administration pathophysiologically manage raised intracranial pressure (ICP)?
back:
● Temporises ICP by reducing brain swelling.
● Used to maintain perfusion and prevent secondary injury during critical periods (scanning/transfer).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): A bolus of mannitol or hypertonic saline may be administered to temporise ICP, for example while scanning and transferring the patient.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: State the three clinical components of Cushing’s triad.
back:
1. Hypertension.
2. Bradycardia.
3. Irregular respiration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): cerebellar tonsillar herniation... classically producing Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: How is cerebral perfusion maintained differently in a traumatized brain compared to a normal brain?
back:
● Normal: Autoregulation maintains constant CBF across MAP 50–150 mmHg.
● Trauma: Autoregulation is impaired; MAP and ICP must be actively regulated to ensure perfusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Autoregulation can be impaired in the context of trauma, so that MAP and ICP must be actively regulated in these patients to maintain proper perfusion.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Differentiate the focal structures compressed in uncal versus cerebellar tonsillar herniation.
back:
● Uncal: Compresses the Oculomotor (III) nerve at the tentorium.
● Tonsillar: Compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres at the foramen magnum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): herniation of the uncus of the temporal lobe over the tentorium results in pupil abnormalities... Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Describe the physiological loop linking raised ICP to the progression of secondary injury.
back: ● Swelling/Mass lesion → Raised ICP → Reduced cerebral perfusion → Hypoxia/Ischaemia → Inflammation/Necrosis → Further swelling.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): Figure 28.9 Brain swelling and mass lesions contribute to raised intracranial pressure, which compromises perfusion, leading to secondary brain injury and further swelling.

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Define the physical mechanism underlying coup-contrecoup brain contusions.
back:
● Primary injury at the site of impact (coup) and distant to it (contrecoup).
● Result of the brain impacting the skull interior as they accelerate/decelerate out of synchrony.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): ‘Coup contre-coup’ contusions refer to brain injury both at the site of impact and distant to this, where the brain impacts on the inside of the skull as the skull and brain accelerate and then decelerate out of synchrony

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Distinguish between primary and secondary traumatic brain injury (TBI).
back:
• Primary: Sustained at impact; not medically modifiable.
• Secondary: Develops over following hours/days; manageable through resuscitation and ICP control.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifiable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of intracranial pressure (ICP) compensation via the Monro–Kellie doctrine.
back:
• Cranium is a rigid box.
• Expansion (haematoma/swelling) is initially accommodated by excluding venous blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
• Exhaustion leads to exponential ICP rise.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [the cranium is a ‘rigid box’ containing a ‘nearly incompressible brain’. Any expansion in the contents... may be initially accommodated by exclusion of fluid components, venous blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Further expansion is associated with an exponential rise in ICP.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: What is the physiological formula for calculating Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP)?
back:
• CPP = MAP (Mean Arterial Pressure) – ICP (Intracranial Pressure).
• Normal range: 75–105 mmHg.
• Ischaemia occurs if CBF drops below 20 mL/min/100g.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [CPP (75–105 mmHg) = MAP (90–110 mmHg) – ICP (5–15 mmHg)]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: How is cerebral autoregulation affected in the context of severe trauma?
back:
• Normal: Constant CBF maintained between 50–150 mmHg MAP.
• Trauma: Autoregulation is often impaired.
• Result: MAP and ICP must be actively regulated to maintain perfusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [variations in vascular tone maintain a constant CBF across a range of MAP between 50 and 150 mmHg... Autoregulation can be impaired in the context of trauma, so that MAP and ICP must be actively regulated.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: List two primary systemic insults that drive the pathophysiology of secondary brain injury.
back:
• 1. Hypoxia (Low oxygen delivery).
• 2. Hypotension (Reduced MAP compromising CPP).
• Both exacerbate the injury-swelling cycle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [medical management strategies aim to minimise secondary brain injury through avoidance of hypoxia and hypotension and control of ICP.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Explain the mechanical cause of ‘Coup contre-coup’ cerebral contusions.
back:
• Brain injury occurs at the site of impact and distant to it.
• Result of the brain and skull accelerating/decelerating out of synchrony with each other.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [‘Coup contre-coup’ contusions refer to brain injury both at the site of impact and distant to this, where the brain impacts on the inside of the skull as the skull and brain accelerate and then decelerate out of synchrony.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Describe the self-perpetuating cycle of secondary brain injury and swelling.
back: • Raised ICP -> Reduced cerebral perfusion -> Hypoxia and Ischaemia -> Necrosis and Inflammation -> Increased swelling -> Further ICP rise.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Figure 28.9: Brain swelling and mass lesions contribute to raised intracranial pressure, which compromises perfusion, leading to secondary brain injury and further swelling.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: What mechanical forces characterize the development of Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI)?
back:
• High-energy extreme accelerations/decelerations of the skull contents.
• Leads to widespread axonal shearing; often results in immediate coma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Diffuse axonal injury results from extreme accelerations of the skull contents... seen in high-energy accidents that usually renders the patient comatose.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiology of Cushing’s triad during brain herniation.
back:
• Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum.
• Compression of medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres.
• Signs: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres, classically producing Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: List factors that increase cerebral metabolic requirements and exacerbate secondary injury.
back:
• Seizures.
• Pyrexia (fever).
• Inflammation.
• All increase oxygen/glucose demand in an already compromised brain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Figure 28.9: Increased metabolic requirements – seizure, pyrexia, inflammation... leading to secondary brain injury.]

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Define traumatic brain injury (TBI) by its two constituent phases of clinical development.
back:
- Primary injury: Occurs at the moment of impact; not medically modifiable.
- Secondary injury: Develops over subsequent hours/days; manageable through clinical intervention.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: What physiological insults must be avoided to prevent the progression of secondary traumatic brain injury?
back:
- Hypoxia
- Hypotension
- Raised Intracranial Pressure (ICP)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Understanding the importance of intracranial pressure (ICP) and related parameters is key to minimising secondary injury and improving outcomes. Page 390 (Book Page): Medical management strategies aim to minimise secondary brain injury through avoidance of hypoxia and hypotension and control of ICP.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Distinguish between 'Minor' and 'Mild' head injury severity using the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS).
back:
- Minor: GCS 15 with no loss of consciousness (LOC).
- Mild: GCS 14 or 15 with history of loss of consciousness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): TABLE 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation. Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC. Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: A comatose patient presents with a post-resuscitation GCS of 7. Classify this injury by severity.
back: - Severe traumatic brain injury (GCS 3–8).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): Severe head injury GCS 3–8. ... comatose patients have severe injuries.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Which specific pharmacological agent is typically administered as prophylaxis against early post-traumatic seizures?
back: - Phenytoin.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 391 (Book Page): Antiepileptics, typically phenytoin, are administered prophylactically to patients at high risk of seizures.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: State the GCS score range used to classify a 'Moderate' traumatic brain injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): TABLE 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation. ... Moderate head injury GCS 9–13.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Why is primary traumatic brain injury considered non-modifiable compared to secondary injury?
back: - Primary injury occurs instantly at impact, whereas secondary injury involves modifiable physiological cascades like inflammation, hypotension, and ischemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Differentiate the anatomical type of TBI seen in extradural vs. subdural haematomas on CT imaging.
back:
- Extradural: Lentiform (biconvex/lens-shaped); constrained by sutures.
- Subdural: Diffuse concave appearance; free to expand across the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion. Page 388 (Book Page): Since the dura is not as adherent to the brain as it is to the skull, subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Describe the metabolic cycle by which raised intracranial pressure (ICP) causes worsening secondary brain injury.
back:
- Raised ICP decreases cerebral perfusion.
- Reduced perfusion leads to hypoxia and ischemia.
- Ischemia causes further brain swelling, which further increases ICP.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): Figure 28.9 Brain swelling and mass lesions contribute to raised intracranial pressure, which compromises perfusion, leading to secondary brain injury and further swelling.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Q: Which specific artery is most commonly ruptured in traumatic extradural haematoma of the squamous temporal bone?
back: - The middle meningeal artery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): The classical injury is a fracture to the thin squamous temporal bone, with associated damage to the middle meningeal artery.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Define Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) based on its temporal clinical components.
back: Primary injury: sustained on impact (non-modifiable). Secondary injury: develops post-impact in subsequent hours/days (medically modifiable through ICP and perfusion control).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Describe the physiological cycle linking intracranial pressure (ICP) to secondary brain injury.
back: Raised ICP reduces Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP), causing ischaemia and necrosis. This triggers further inflammation and brain swelling, resulting in a deteriorating cycle of injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): Brain swelling and mass lesions contribute to raised intracranial pressure, which compromises perfusion, leading to secondary brain injury and further swelling.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Contrast the CT appearance of Subdural Haematoma (SDH) with Extradural Haematoma (EDH).
back: EDH: Lentiform (biconvex) hyperdense lesion constrained by dural adherence. SDH: Diffuse concave or crescentic appearance extending across the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page)/387: extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: A patient wakes from transient unconsciousness only to deteriorate rapidly with a dilated pupil. Identify the TBI type.
back: Extradural Haematoma (EDH). The clinical hallmark is the 'lucid interval' occurring before compensatory mechanisms are exhausted and brain herniation begins.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): The classical injury is a fracture... Transient loss of consciousness is typical... presentation in the subsequent lucid interval... then rapid deterioration... the cardinal signs of brain compression and herniation.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: State the pharmacological steps for reversing coagulopathy in an acute subdural haematoma.
back: Reverse immediately using Vitamin K for non-emergencies, or urgent transfusion of recombinant clotting factors for patients with acute neurological deterioration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 387 (Book Page): Anticoagulation should be reversed, either by administration of vitamin K or urgently by transfusion of recombinant clotting factors in patients who have deteriorated acutely.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Classify head injury severity according to post-resuscitation Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores.
back: Minor: GCS 15 (no LOC). Mild: GCS 14 or 15 (with LOC). Moderate: GCS 9-13. Severe: GCS 3-8.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): Table 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation... Moderate head injury GCS 9-13. Severe head injury GCS 3-8.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Explain the anatomic mechanism of 'Coup-contrecoup' cerebral contusions.
back: Brain injury occurs both at the impact site (Coup) and distant to it (Contrecoup) as brain asynchronous movement causes impact against the irregular internal skull surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): Coup contre-coup contusions refer to brain injury both at the site of impact and distant to this, where the brain impacts on the inside of the skull as the skull and brain accelerate and then decelerate out of synchrony with each other.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Identify the TBI type associated with mastoid bruising and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhoea.
back: Skull base fracture. Classic signs include Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising), Raccoon/Panda eyes (periorbital bruising), and CSF otorrhoea or rhinorrhoea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): Clinical evidence of a skull base fracture may include Battle’s sign... and ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes (bilateral periorbital bruising)... CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea are also highly suggestive.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: Outline the Monro-Kellie doctrine regarding intracranial pressure compensation.
back: The cranium is a rigid box. Expansion of one component (e.g., blood) is initially compensated by excluding venous blood and CSF; exhaustion of this leads to exponential ICP rise.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): The Monro-Kellie doctrine accounts for the ability of the intracranial compartment to accommodate expanding mass lesions, primarily by excluding venous blood and cerebrospinal fuid (CSF), and the rapid rise in pressure associated with exhaustion of this compensation.

category: Define traumatic brain injury and classify it by severity and type
front: State the characteristic anatomic locations of haemorrhagic foci in Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI).
back: Haemorrhagic foci are typically found within the corpus callosum and the dorsolateral rostral brainstem.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): Diffuse axonal injury... haemorrhagic foci in the corpus callosum and dorsolateral rostral brainstem on CT may be suggestive.

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: How is the severity of Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) categorized using the post-resuscitation Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)?
back:
• Minor: GCS 15 with no loss of consciousness (LOC).
• Mild: GCS 14-15 with LOC.
• Moderate: GCS 9–13.
• Severe: GCS 3–8.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Head injury severity: clinical classification. Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC; Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC; Moderate head injury GCS 9–13; Severe head injury GCS 3–8]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Describe the clinical components of Cushing’s triad and its physiological significance in the context of TBI.
back:
• Components: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration.
• Significance: Indicates 'coning' or cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum, compressing medullary centers.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page)-382: [Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres, classically producing Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Distinguish the characteristic clinical presentation of an Extradural Haematoma (EDH) from other intracranial bleeds.
back:
• Transient loss of consciousness followed by a 'lucid interval'.
• Rapid subsequent deterioration with headache.
• Ipsilateral pupillary dilatation and contralateral hemiparesis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Transient loss of consciousness is typical, and the patient may then present in the subsequent lucid interval with headache but without any neurological deficit... contralateral hemiparesis, a reduced conscious level and ipsilateral pupillary dilatation, the cardinal signs of brain compression and herniation.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: A patient presents with 'raccoon eyes' and clear fluid leaking from the nose after a TBI. What is the suspected diagnosis?
back:
• Diagnosis: Basal (skull base) fracture.
• Key Signs: Periorbital bruising (raccoon/panda eyes), Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising), and CSF rhinorrhoea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Clinical evidence of a skull base fracture may include Battle’s sign... and ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes (bilateral periorbital bruising). Haemotympanum... and CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea are also highly suggestive of a fracture of the base of the skull.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Which pharmacological agents are used to temporarily reduce intracranial pressure (ICP) during the transfer of a TBI patient?
back:
• Mannitol (osmotic diuretic).
• Hypertonic saline.
• Purpose: To temporize ICP while scanning or transferring to a neurosurgical unit.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [A bolus of mannitol or hypertonic saline may be administered to temporize ICP, for example while scanning and transferring the patient.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: List the three specific clinical components assessed in the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) for TBI.
back:
• Best Eye response (scored 1–4).
• Best Verbal response (scored 1–5).
• Best Motor response (scored 1–6).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [TABLE 27.1 Glasgow Coma Scale. Best eye response (E)... Best verbal response (V)... Best motor response (M)]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Explain the relationship between Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP), Intracranial Pressure (ICP), and Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP).
back:
• Formula: CPP = MAP – ICP.
• Normal values: CPP (75–105 mmHg), MAP (90–110 mmHg), ICP (5–15 mmHg).
• Goal: Maintenance of CPP >60 mmHg is critical to prevent secondary injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Flow depends on cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), which is the difference between the mean arterial pressure (MAP) and the intracranial pressure (ICP): CPP (75–105 mmHg) = MAP (90–110 mmHg) – ICP (5–15 mmHg)]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: How do the clinical features of an Acute Subdural Haematoma (SDH) typically differ from a Chronic SDH?
back:
• Acute SDH: High-energy injury, rapid deterioration, no lucid interval, often associated with primary brain injury.
• Chronic SDH: Elderly/anticoagulated patients, insidious onset (days/weeks), caused by rupture of bridging veins.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 387 (Book Page): [Acute... high-energy injury mechanisms... results in an expanding haematoma with rapid deterioration... without the lucid interval. Chronic... common cause of acute neurological deterioration in older adults... resulting haematoma can expand over days or weeks by osmosis]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Describe the self-perpetuating cycle of secondary brain injury involving raised intracranial pressure.
back:
• Raised ICP leads to reduced cerebral perfusion.
• Low perfusion causes hypoxia and ischemia.
• Ischemia triggers secondary brain injury and inflammatory swelling, further increasing ICP.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Raised intracranial pressure -> Reduced cerebral perfusion -> Hypoxia -> Secondary brain injury -> Inflammation/Necrosis -> Raised intracranial pressure (Figure 28.9)]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: What pupillary changes are characteristic of uncal herniation in a patient with a traumatic mass lesion?
back:
• Mechanism: Compression of the third (oculomotor) nerve.
• Progression: Sluggish enlarged pupil, progressing to a fixed and dilated pupil (mydriasis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Uncal herniation (Figure 28.2) can compress the third nerve, compromising the parasympathetic supply to the pupil... produces a sluggish enlarged pupil, progressing to fixed and dilated under continued compression.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Define the key pathophysiological difference between primary and secondary brain injury.
back: Primary injury: Immediate damage sustained on impact; not medically modifiable. Secondary injury: Develops in the following hours/days; preventable by managing hypoxia, hypotension, and intracranial pressure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can be considered as the combination of primary injury sustained on impact, and hence not medically modifiable, and secondary injury developing in the following hours and days.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: State the physiological equation for Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) and its normal range.
back: CPP = MAP (Mean Arterial Pressure) – ICP (Intracranial Pressure). Normal range: 75–105 mmHg.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [CPP (75–105 mmHg) = MAP (90–110 mmHg) – ICP (5–15 mmHg)]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Describe the Monro-Kellie doctrine's role in intracranial pressure (ICP) compensation.
back: Cranium is a rigid box; mass expansion is initially compensated by excluding venous blood and CSF. Once compensation is exhausted, ICP rises exponentially.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [The Monro–Kellie doctrine accounts for the ability of the intracranial compartment to accommodate expanding mass lesions, primarily by excluding venous blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and the rapid rise in pressure associated with exhaustion of this compensation.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Identify the three clinical components of Cushing’s triad and its underlying cause.
back: Components: Hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration. Cause: Brainstem compression (coning) due to cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres, classically producing Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. The patient is then said to be ‘coning’]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: What pharmacological intervention is used to acutely temporise raised ICP during patient transfer?
back: Administration of a bolus of mannitol or hypertonic saline to reduce brain swelling and osmotic pressure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [A bolus of mannitol or hypertonic saline may be administered to temporise ICP, for example while scanning and transferring the patient.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Classify head injury severity based on the post-resuscitation Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score.
back: Minor: GCS 15 with no LOC. Mild: GCS 14-15 with LOC. Moderate: GCS 9–13. Severe: GCS 3–8.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Table 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classification. Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC; Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC; Moderate head injury GCS 9–13; Severe head injury GCS 3–8]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: How is cerebral autoregulation affected in the context of traumatic brain injury?
back: Autoregulation (maintaining constant flow across MAP 50–150 mmHg) is often impaired; MAP and ICP must be actively regulated to ensure perfusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Autoregulation can be impaired in the context of trauma, so that MAP and ICP must be actively regulated in these patients to maintain proper perfusion.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Distinguish between traumatic Subarachnoid Haemorrhage (SAH) and aneurysmal SAH.
back: Traumatic SAH is the commonest cause; unlike aneurysmal SAH, it is rarely associated with significant vasospasm.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 387 (Book Page): [Trauma is the commonest cause of subarachnoid haemorrhage... It is not usually associated with significant vasospasm, which characterises aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Differentiate the mechanisms of SIADH and Cerebral Salt Wasting (CSW) in TBI.
back: SIADH: Pituitary damage causes water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia. CSW: Excretory dysregulation causes volume depletion and hyponatraemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Cerebral salt wasting... leads to volume depletion and hyponatraemia. The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) leads to water retention and hyponatraemia in the context of pituitary damage.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of primary and secondary brain injury
front: Q: Explain the "Coup contre-coup" mechanism of cerebral contusion.
back: Brain injury occurs at impact site (coup) and distant site (contre-coup) because the skull and brain accelerate/decelerate out of synchrony.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 387 (Book Page): [‘Coup contre-coup’ contusions refer to brain injury both at the site of impact and distant to this, where the brain impacts on the inside of the skull as the skull and brain accelerate and then decelerate out of synchrony with each other.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Classify Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) severity based on post-resuscitation GCS scores.
back:
• Minor: GCS 15 (no LOC)
• Mild: GCS 14-15 (with LOC)
• Moderate: GCS 9-13
• Severe: GCS 3-8 (comatose)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Head injury severity: clinical classifcation. Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC... Severe head injury GCS 3–8]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: What physiological loop describes the progression of secondary brain injury in TBI?
back:
• Raised ICP reduces cerebral perfusion
• Results in hypoxia and hypotension
• Triggers further brain swelling and necrosis
• Leads to higher ICP, creating a cycle
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [Brain swelling and mass lesions contribute to raised intracranial pressure, which compromises perfusion, leading to secondary brain injury and further swelling.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: List the clinical features diagnostic of a skull base fracture in TBI.
back:
• Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising)
• Racoon eyes (periorbital bruising)
• CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea
• Haemotympanum
