citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Clinical evidence of a skull base fracture may include Battle’s sign... ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes... CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea are also highly suggestive]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Describe the clinical presentation of uncal herniation resulting from TBI.
back:
• Ipsilateral pupillary dilation (fixed and dilated)
• Sluggish pupil reactivity (early sign)
• Contralateral hemiparesis
• Rapidly deteriorating GCS
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Typically, herniation of the uncus... results in pupil abnormalities... occurring frst on the side of any expanding haematoma.] Page 386 (Book Page): [There is contralateral hemiparesis, a reduced conscious level and ipsilateral pupillary dilatation]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: What target parameters are maintained in neurointensive care to prevent secondary TBI?
back:
• ICP <20 mmHg
• CPP >60 mmHg
• MAP 80–90 mmHg
• PaO2 >11 kPa
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [A sustained elevated ICP exceeding 20–25 mmHg is associated with a poor outcome, and maintenance of a CPP of at least 60 mmHg is important in preventing secondary injury.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Which NICE criteria for vomiting and GCS indicate immediate CT in adult TBI?
back:
• GCS <13 at any point
• GCS <15 at 2 hours
• More than one episode of vomiting
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour: GCS <13 at any point, GCS <15 at 2 hours... More than one episode of vomiting]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Why does uncal herniation cause ipsilateral pupillary dilation?
back:
• Compresses the third (oculomotor) nerve
• Compromises parasympathetic supply to the pupil
• Results in unopposed sympathetic activity
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Uncal herniation can compress the third nerve, compromising the parasympathetic supply to the pupil. Unopposed sympathetic activity produces a sluggish enlarged pupil]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Contrast the clinical features of concussion versus post-concussive syndrome.
back:
• Concussion: Acute amnesia, confusion, lethargy, or gait disturbance
• Post-concussive: Chronic headache, dizziness, insomnia, fatigue, and personality change
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Key features include confusion and amnesia... Postconcussive syndrome... headache, dizziness... neurocognitive... disturbances, including difculty with concentration... fatigue, depression and personality change.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: What occurs during the 'compensation phase' of the Monro-Kellie doctrine in TBI?
back:
• Initial mass expansion (swelling/hematoma) is accommodated
• Venous blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are excluded from the cranium
• ICP remains relatively stable before an exponential rise
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Any expansion in the contents... may be initially accommodated by exclusion of fuid components, venous blood and cerebrospinal fuid (CSF).]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Define the clinical hallmarks of Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) in high-energy trauma.
back:
• Immediate coma following impact
• Disproportionately poor outcomes
• Presence of hemorrhagic foci on MRI (corpus callosum/brainstem)
• Minimal initially visible CT changes
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [This is a form of primary brain injury seen in high-energy accidents that usually renders the patient comatose; it is associated with poor outcomes.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Categorize Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) severity based on post-resuscitation GCS and consciousness.
back:
* Minor: GCS 15, no loss of consciousness (LOC).
* Mild: GCS 14-15 with LOC.
* Moderate: GCS 9-13 (obtunded).
* Severe: GCS 3-8 (comatose).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC; Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC; Moderate head injury GCS 9–13; Severe head injury GCS 3–8.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
coreConcept: Clinical Signs of Raised ICP and Brain Herniation
front: Q: Identify the focal and physiological clinical signs indicating raised intracranial pressure (ICP) and herniation.
back:
* Focal: Ipsilateral dilated/fixed pupil (3rd nerve) and contralateral hemiparesis.
* Physiological (Cushing's triad): Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration.
* Progressive: Rapidly deteriorating Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. ... The patient is then said to be ‘coning’] Page 386 (Book Page): [There is contralateral hemiparesis, a reduced conscious level and ipsilateral pupillary dilatation, the cardinal signs of brain compression and herniation.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: According to the GCS classification, what score range defines a 'Severe Head Injury'?
back:
● GCS score 3–8
● Corresponds to comatose patients
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Severe head injury GCS 3–8]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What is the primary advantage of utilizing a trauma team during the ATLS primary survey?
back:
● Activities occur concurrently instead of sequentially
● Allows simultaneous assessment of airway, breathing, and circulation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): [The principal advantage of a trauma team is that this activity can occur concurrently instead of sequentially; while the anaesthetist is assessing and managing the patient’s airway, another team member can be assessing and managing the patient’s breathing, etc.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: Contrast 'Minor' vs 'Mild' head injury using GCS score and Loss of Consciousness (LOC) criteria.
back:
● Minor: GCS 15 with no LOC
● Mild: GCS 14 or 15 with LOC
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC; Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: A trauma patient localizes to pain on the right but shows flexion withdrawal on the left. Calculate the GCS Motor (M) score.
back:
● M5 (Localises to pain)
● Rule: Score represents the best performance elicited from any limb
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Remember that the score represents the best performance elicited, so a patient fexing in response to a painful stimulus on the left and localising on the right scores ‘M5’.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What is the target systolic blood pressure for permissive hypotension when a head injury is suspected?
back:
● >90 mmHg
● Higher than the standard 70–90 mmHg target to maintain cerebral perfusion
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: Which specific component of the Glasgow Coma Scale is the best predictor of neurological outcome?
back: ● The Motor (M) score
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [as it is the GCS score – and in particular the motor score – that is the best predictor of neurological outcome.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: In the revised cABCDE sequence, what pathology necessitates intervention before managing the airway?
back:
● Exsanguinating external hemorrhage
● Controlled via direct pressure, packs, or proximal tourniquets
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: How is the 'D' (Disability) assessment performed during the ATLS primary survey?
back:
● Calculate GCS score
● Assess pupils (size and reaction to light)
● Observe movement in all four limbs
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [On admission, the GCS score should be calculated ( Table 27.1 ), the pupils assessed for size and reaction to light and the patient observed to determine whether they are moving all four limbs.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: How is the GCS Verbal (V) component documented for an intubated trauma patient?
back:
● Documented as 'T'
● Used when the patient cannot produce sounds due to an endotracheal tube
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Verbal... Intubated patient T]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What anatomical landmark defines the correct level for applying a pelvic binder in hemodynamically unstable patients?
back:
● Level of the greater trochanters
● Prevents obstruction of potential trauma laparotomy
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: How is Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) severity classified using the post-resuscitation GCS score?
back:
* Minor: GCS 15, no history of Loss of Consciousness (LOC).
* Mild: GCS 14–15 with history of LOC.
* Moderate: GCS 9–13.
* Severe: GCS 3–8 (comatose).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Head injury severity: clinical classifcation. Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC. Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC. Moderate head injury GCS 9–13. Severe head injury GCS 3–8]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: What pathophysiological mechanism causes the fixed, dilated pupil seen in uncal herniation?
back:
* Anatomy: The temporal lobe uncus herniates over the tentorium, compressing the third cranial (oculomotor) nerve.
* Result: Compromise of the parasympathetic supply leads to unopposed sympathetic pupillary dilation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Uncal herniation ( Figure 28.2 ) can compress the third nerve, compromising the parasympathetic supply to the pupil. Unopposed sympathetic activity produces a sluggish enlarged pupil, progressing to fxed and dilated under continued compression.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Distinguish between the clinical definitions of 'Minor' and 'Mild' head injury.
back:
* Minor: GCS of 15 with zero history of Loss of Consciousness (LOC).
* Mild: GCS of 14 or 15 that specifically includes a history of Loss of Consciousness (LOC).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC. Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: A patient with temporal trauma presents with a 'lucid interval' followed by rapid coma. Likely diagnosis?
back:
* Diagnosis: Extradural haematoma (EDH).
* Mechanism: Arterial rupture (often middle meningeal) associated with temporal bone fracture.
* Clinical Pattern: 'Talk and die' pattern; biconvex lesion on CT.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Transient loss of consciousness is typical, and the patient may then present in the subsequent lucid interval with headache but without any neuro - logical defcit. As the haematoma expands, compensation is exhausted... with rapid deterioration.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Which pharmacological agent is standard for acutely reducing intracranial pressure (ICP) during patient stabilization?
back:
* Agents: Mannitol (bolus) or hypertonic saline.
* Indication: Used to temporise raised ICP while awaiting definitive imaging (CT) or neurosurgical transfer.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [A bolus of mannitol or hypertonic saline may be administered to temporise ICP, for example while scanning and transferring the patient.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: List four typical clinical features of a concussion without radiological abnormalities.
back:
* Amnesia (retrograde or anterograde).
* Confusion/disorientation.
* Headache.
* Somnolence or lethargy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Amnesia, confusion, headaches and somnolence are typical features of concussion]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: If a TBI patient withdraws on the left but localises to pain on the right, what is their GCS Motor score?
back:
* Score: M5.
* Rule: The GCS score represents the best performance elicited (Localising to pain = 5; Withdrawal = 4).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Remember that the score represents the best perfor - mance elicited, so a patient fexing in response to a painful stimulus on the left and localising on the right scores ‘M5’.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: A patient remains comatose after high-speed trauma, but the CT shows no mass lesion. Suspected diagnosis?
back:
* Diagnosis: Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI).
* Hallmark: Comatose state out of proportion to initial CT findings; shearing injury at the corpus callosum or brainstem.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Diffuse axonal injury... form of primary brain injury seen in high-energy acci - dents that usually renders the patient comatose... haemorrhagic foci in the corpus callosum and dorsolateral rostral brainstem on CT may be suggestive.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: How does raised intracranial pressure (ICP) precipitate a cycle of secondary brain injury?
back:
* Lowers CPP: Raised ICP decreases Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP = MAP - ICP).
* Ischaemia: Low CPP causes reduced blood flow and hypoxia.
* Swelling: Hypoxia causes cell death and further brain swelling, which increases ICP.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Brain swelling and mass lesions contribute to raised intra- cranial pressure, which compromises perfusion, leading to secondary brain injury and further swelling.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Which anatomical feature in infants allows for the direct clinical palpation of intracranial pressure (ICP)?
back:
* Anterior fontanelle.
* Finding: A bulging or tense fontanelle directly indicates raised ICP in infants with open skull sutures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): [Children with open sutures can lose substantial blood volumes into the head. Palpating the fontanelle allows direct assessment of ICP]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What is the primary sequence for initial trauma assessment according to current ATLS principles?
back:
cABCDE:
- c: Exsanguinating external haemorrhage control
- A: Airway with cervical spine protection
- B: Breathing and ventilation
- C: Circulation and haemorrhage control
- D: Disability (GCS/Neurology)
- E: Exposure/Environment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [The primary survey aims to identify and manage the most immediately life-threatening pathologies frst and follows cABCDE.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: Why is the motor component of the GCS considered particularly significant in head injury classification?
back:
- It is the best predictor of neurological outcome.
- Allows for monitoring of potentially reversible secondary injury.
- Helps categorize injury severity as minor, moderate, or severe.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [as it is the GCS score – and in particular the motor score – that is the best predictor of neurological outcome.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What distinguishes the diagnostic focus of the Primary Survey from the Secondary Survey?
back:
- Primary Survey: Rapid identification and management of immediately life-threatening pathologies.
- Secondary Survey: Detailed top-to-toe examination performed only after stabilizing life-threatening injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [The primary survey aims to identify and manage the most immediately life-threatening pathologies frst] ... Page 379 (Book Page): [All severely injured patients require a detailed top-to-toe examination after life-threatening injuries have been identifed and managed during the primary survey.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: A trauma patient presents with a post-resuscitation GCS of 7. What is the priority intervention?
back:
- Immediate advanced airway management (intubation).
- A GCS of 3–8 defines severe head injury and a comatose state.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [comatose patients have severe injuries... Severe head injury GCS 3–8] ... Page 376 (Book Page): [Advanced airway manoeuvres necessitate the insertion of a cufed endotracheal tube.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What is the target systolic blood pressure during fluid resuscitation if a head injury is suspected?
back:
- Target systolic BP > 90 mmHg.
- This is higher than the standard permissive hypotension target (70-90 mmHg) to maintain adequate cerebral perfusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What are the three clinical components evaluated to calculate the Glasgow Coma Scale score?
back:
- Best eye response (1–4).
- Best verbal response (1–5).
- Best motor response (1–6).
- Total score ranges from 3 to 15.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [TABLE 27.1 Glasgow Coma Scale. Best eye response (E) ... Best verbal response (V) ... Best motor response (M)]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: How is the GCS recorded if a patient is intubated and cannot provide a verbal response?
back:
- The verbal score is recorded as 'T' (e.g., GCS 10T).
- This indicates the presence of an endotracheal tube preventing speech.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [TABLE 28.4 Glasgow Coma Scale score for head injury. ... Verbal ... Intubated patient T]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: How is the GCS motor score determined for a patient with asymmetrical limb responses?
back:
- The score reflects the best performance elicited across any limb.
- Example: If a patient flexes on the left but localizes on the right, the motor score is M5.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Remember that the score represents the best performance elicited, so a patient fexing in response to a painful stimulus on the left and localising on the right scores ‘M5’.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: How does inadequate circulation (hypotension) contribute to secondary brain injury?
back:
- Hypotension compromises cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP).
- This results in a cycle of ischemia, further brain swelling, and increased intracranial pressure (ICP).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Raised ICP can compromise cerebral perfusion, resulting in a cycle of secondary brain injury and swelling] ... Page 381 (Book Page): [Flow depends on cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), which is the diference between the mean arterial pressure (MAP) and the intracranial pressure (ICP)]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What GCS score range defines a 'Moderate' head injury according to clinical classification?
back:
- GCS 9–13.
- In contrast, Minor is 15 (no LOC), Mild is 14-15 (with LOC), and Severe is 3-8.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [TABLE 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation. ... Moderate head injury GCS 9–13]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: List the three clinical signs comprising Cushing’s triad in patients with raised intracranial pressure.
back: The components are hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration. This triad indicates brainstem compromise due to central or tonsillar herniation and may lead to brainstem death without immediate intervention.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. The patient is then said to be ‘coning’, and brainstem death will result without immediate intervention.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiological basis of the Monro–Kellie doctrine in traumatic brain injury.
back: The cranium is a rigid, non-expansible box. Initial increases in intracranial volume (haematoma/swelling) are accommodated by excluding cerebrospinal fluid and venous blood. Once these compensatory mechanisms are exhausted, intracranial pressure (ICP) rises exponentially.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Monro observed in 1783 that the cranium is a ‘rigid box’ containing a ‘nearly incompressible brain’. Any expansion in the contents... may be initially accommodated by exclusion of fuid components... Further expansion is associated with an exponential rise in ICP.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Distinguish the CT imaging features of acute versus chronic subdural haematomas.
back: Acute SDH appears as a hyperdense (white), crescentic/concave collection on the brain surface. Chronic SDH appears as a diffuse hypodense (dark) collection, commonly resulting from osmotic expansion of a degrading clot over weeks.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 387 (Book Page): [subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.] Page 388 (Book Page): [Chronic subdural haematoma... Imaging reveals difuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: What are the cardinal clinical features of uncal herniation resulting from an expanding mass lesion?
back: Ipsilateral pupillary dilatation (fixed/dilated due to third nerve compression), contralateral hemiparesis, and a reduced conscious level. These features reflect rapid brain compression and shift across the tentorium.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [There is contralateral hemiparesis, a reduced conscious level and ipsilateral pupillary dilatation, the cardinal signs of brain compression and herniation.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Which intravenous bolus agents are used to acutely temporise raised intracranial pressure during patient transfer?
back: A bolus of mannitol or hypertonic saline is administered. These hyperosmolar agents reduce brain swelling and lower ICP temporarily to facilitate safe management, scanning, and transfer.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [A bolus of mannitol or hypertonic saline may be administered to temporise ICP, for example while scanning and transferring the patient.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Define the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score thresholds for minor, moderate, and severe head injury.
back: Minor: GCS 15 with no loss of consciousness (LOC). Mild: GCS 14 or 15 with LOC. Moderate: GCS 9–13. Severe: GCS 3–8.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Table 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation. Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC; Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC; Moderate head injury GCS 9–13; Severe head injury GCS 3–8.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: How is the GCS motor score (M) assigned when a patient exhibits differing bilateral responses?
back: The score represents the best performance elicited. For example, if a patient flexes to pain (M3) on the left but localises (M5) on the right, the final score recorded is M5.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Remember that the score represents the best performance elicited, so a patient fexing in response to a painful stimulus on the left and localising on the right scores ‘M5’.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Contrast the clinical presentations of simple concussion and the rare 'second impact syndrome.'
back: Concussion features confusion, amnesia, headaches, and somnolence without imaging abnormalities. Second impact syndrome involves malignant, rapid brain swelling following a repeat minor impact, progressing quickly to coma and death.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Concussion... Key features include confusion and amnesia... Second impact syndrome following an apparently trivial repeat injury comprises malignant brain swelling that can quickly progress to coma and death.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: Describe the physiological cycle leading to secondary brain injury in traumatic brain injury patients.
back: Initial brain swelling raises ICP, reducing cerebral perfusion and causing hypoxia. This ischemia triggers further swelling, hypotension, and inflammation, creating a self-perpetuating cycle of further secondary brain damage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Figure 28.9 Brain swelling and mass lesions contribute to raised intra-cranial pressure, which compromises perfusion, leading to secondary brain injury and further swelling.]

category: Identify the clinical features of TBI, including altered consciousness, focal neurological deficits, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
front: Q: What is the clinical formula used to calculate Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP)?
back: CPP equals the Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) minus the Intracranial Pressure (ICP). Maintenance of CPP above 60 mmHg is critical to prevent secondary ischemic injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Flow depends on cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), which is the diference between the mean arterial pressure (MAP) and the intracranial pressure (ICP): CPP... = MAP... – ICP...]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: Within the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), which component is the most accurate predictor of neurological outcome?
back: The motor score is the most reliable predictor of neurological outcome in traumatic brain injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [The severity of head injury is classifed according to the post-resuscitation Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score ( Table 28.1 ), as it is the GCS score – and in particular the motor score – that is the best predictor of neurological outcome.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: How is a GCS verbal score recorded specifically for a patient who has been intubated?
back: The verbal score is recorded as 'T' (e.g., GCS 10T) to indicate the presence of an endotracheal tube.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Table 28.4 ... Verbal ... Intubated patient T]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What GCS findings distinguish a 'Minor' head injury from a 'Mild' head injury in clinical classification?
back:
● Minor: GCS 15 with no loss of consciousness (LOC).
● Mild: GCS 14 or 15 with loss of consciousness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [TABLE 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation. Minor head injury GCS 15 with no LOC; Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: A patient opens eyes to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds, and localises to pain. Calculate their GCS score.
back:
GCS 9 (E2, V2, M5).
● Eyes: Pain (2)
● Verbal: Incomprehensible (2)
● Motor: Localises (5)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [TABLE 27.1 Glasgow Coma Scale. Best eye response (E) 2 Eye opening in response to pain; Best verbal response (V) 2 Incomprehensible sounds; Best motor response (M) 5 Localises to pain]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What is the target systolic blood pressure during permissive hypotension if a head injury is suspected (GCS <15)?
back: The target systolic blood pressure should be >90 mmHg to maintain adequate cerebral perfusion pressure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: Define the GCS score range used to classify 'Severe Traumatic Brain Injury' in a comatose patient.
back: A GCS score of 3 to 8 is the criteria for Severe Traumatic Brain Injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [TABLE 28.1 ... Severe head injury GCS 3–8]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: In the ATLS 'Disability' (D) survey, what must be established besides GCS and pupillary response?
back: Determine if the patient is moving all four limbs to screen for lateralising signs or spinal cord injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [D: Disability and E: Exposure. On admission, the GCS score should be calculated ( Table 27.1 ), the pupils assessed for size and reaction to light and the patient observed to determine whether they are moving all four limbs.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: How is the 'Best Motor Response' determined if a patient exhibits different responses on the left versus right side?
back: The score represents the best performance elicited from any limb (e.g., if flexing left but localizing right, score M5).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Remember that the score represents the best performance elicited, so a patient fexing in response to a painful stimulus on the left and localising on the right scores ‘M5’.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: Why is a rapid GCS deterioration clinically significant following a 'lucid interval' in a trauma patient?
back: It indicates a 'talk and die' pattern, characteristic of an expanding extradural haematoma causing sudden brain herniation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Transient loss of consciousness is typical, and the patient may then present in the subsequent lucid interval... As the haematoma expands... rapid deterioration... this ‘ talk and die ’ pattern of deterioration occurs in only one-third of cases]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: List the components of the 'Cushing’s Triad' associated with late-stage brainstem compromise (GCS 3).
back:
1. Hypertension
2. Bradycardia
3. Irregular Respiration
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres, classically producing Cushing’s triad : hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: Which clinical triad indicates life-threatening brainstem compression and imminent coning in traumatic brain injury?
back:
Cushing’s Triad:
• Hypertension
• Bradycardia
• Irregular respiration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. The patient is then said to be ‘ coning ’, and brainstem death will result without immediate intervention.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: What specific pupillary change signals urgent neurosurgical intervention for suspected uncal herniation?
back:
• Ipsilateral sluggish or enlarged pupil
• Progresses to a fixed and dilated pupil
• Caused by third cranial nerve compression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Uncal herniation ( Figure 28.2 ) can compress the third nerve, compromising the parasympathetic supply to the pupil. Unopposed sympathetic activity produces a sluggish enlarged pupil, progressing to fxed and dilated under continued compression.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
coreConcept: NICE Guidelines for Urgent Brain CT
front: Q: Distinguish between the GCS scores requiring immediate CT imaging within one hour of head injury.
back:
• GCS <13 at any point since injury
• GCS <15 at two hours post-injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour: GCS <13 at any point; GCS <15 at 2 hours; Focal neurological defcit; Suspected open, depressed or basal skull fracture]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: A patient presents with a brief loss of consciousness followed by a 'lucid interval.' What red-flag signs follow?
back:
• Rapid neurological deterioration
• Contralateral hemiparesis
• Ipsilateral pupillary dilatation
• Indicates an expanding Extradural Haematoma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [subsequent lucid interval with headache but without any neuro - logical defcit. As the haematoma expands... rapid deterioration. There is contralateral hemiparesis, a reduced conscious level and ipsilateral pupillary dilatation]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: When is a bolus of mannitol or hypertonic saline indicated as a red-flag temporizing measure?
back:
• Indicated to acutely lower intracranial pressure (ICP)
• Used specifically while scanning or transferring a deteriorating patient.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): [A bolus of mannitol or hypertonic saline may be administered to temporise ICP, for example while scanning and transferring the patient.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: List the NICE discharge criteria 'red flag' symptoms requiring immediate return for neurosurgical evaluation.
back:
• Persistent/worsening headache or persistent vomiting
• New drowsiness or visual disturbances
• New limb weakness or numbness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [seek medical attention if: Persistent/worsening headache despite analgesia; Persistent vomiting; Drowsiness; Visual disturbance; Limb weakness or numbness]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
coreConcept: Base of Skull Fracture Red Flags
front: Q: Which clinical signs of a skull base fracture necessitate urgent neurosurgical consultation?
back:
• CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea
• Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising)
• Raccoon eyes (bilateral periorbital bruising)
• Haemotympanum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Battle’s sign ( Figure 28.3 ) and ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes (bilateral periorbital bruising). Haemotympanum... and CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea are also highly suggestive of a fracture of the base of the skull.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: In children, which neuroimaging and clinical findings suggest urgent referral for suspected non-accidental injury?
back:
• Retinal haemorrhages
• Bilateral chronic subdural haematomas
• Multiple skull fractures
• Injuries of disparate age.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Signifcant fndings include delayed presentation, injuries of disparate age, retinal haemorrhages, bilateral chronic subdural haematomas, multiple skull fractures and neurological injury without external signs of trauma.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: Why is the detection of a depressed skull fracture considered a red flag for urgent surgery?
back:
• High incidence of infection
• Risk of late-onset epilepsy
• Likely breach in the dura mater.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Depressed skull fractures... are associated with a high incidence of infection, neurological defcit and late-onset epilepsy. These fractures require exploration and elevation, especially where intracranial air is present, pointing to a breach in the dura mater.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: Which specific component of the GCS is the most critical predictor of neurosurgical outcome?
back:
• The Motor Score (M)
• Used to classify Moderate (GCS 9–13) vs. Severe (GCS 3–8) injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [as it is the GCS score – and in particular the motor score – that is the best predictor of neurological outcome. In broad terms, signifcantly obtunded patients have moderate injuries and comatose patients have severe injuries]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: Which GCS thresholds post-head injury mandate urgent neurosurgical referral or immediate CT imaging?
back:
• GCS <13 at any point.
• GCS <15 at two hours post-injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour... GCS <13 at any point; GCS <15 at 2 hours]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: Which pupillary changes specifically indicate uncal herniation and the need for urgent intervention?
back:
• Ipsilateral sluggish, enlarged pupil.
• Progressing to a fixed and dilated state due to third nerve compression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [herniation of the uncus of the tem - poral lobe over the tentorium results in pupil abnormalities... typically... sluggish enlarged pupil, progressing to fxed and dilated under continued compression.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: What physiological signs constitute Cushing’s triad, indicating brainstem compromise and impending coning?
back:
• Hypertension.
• Bradycardia.
• Irregular respiration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cushing’s triad : hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. The patient is then said to be ‘ coning ’]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
coreConcept: Focal neurological deficit as a red flag
front: Q: A patient develops a focal neurological deficit after head trauma. What urgent investigation is indicated?
back:
• Urgent CT scan of the brain within one hour.
• Immediate neurosurgical consultation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour... Focal neurological defcit]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: What classic progression characterizes an extradural haematoma before rapid neurosurgical deterioration?
back:
• Transient loss of consciousness followed by a 'lucid interval.'
• Subsequent rapid deterioration ('talk and die' pattern) with contralateral hemiparesis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Extradural haematoma (Figure 28.6) is a neurosurgical emer - gency... Transient loss of consciousness is typical... presentation in the subsequent lucid interval... this ‘ talk and die ’ pattern of deterioration]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: What are the pathognomonic physical signs of a base of skull fracture?
back:
• Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising).
• Raccoon eyes (periorbital bruising).
• CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Battle’s sign ( Figure 28.3 ) and ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes (bilateral periorbital bruising). Haemotympanum... and CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea are also highly suggestive of a fracture of the base of the skull.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: Which two clinical events occurring after head trauma are immediate indicators for CT within 1 hour?
back:
• Post-traumatic seizure.
• More than one episode of vomiting.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour... More than one episode of vomiting; Post-traumatic seizure]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: In spinal trauma, what specific neurological change is considered an absolute indication for urgent surgery?
back: • Deteriorating neurological function (progressive loss of motor or sensory levels).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: What specific physical finding in an infant with a head injury indicates raised intracranial pressure?
back: • A tense or bulging fontanelle (allows direct assessment due to open sutures).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): [Children with open sutures can lose substantial blood volumes into the head. Palpating the fontanelle allows direct assessment of ICP]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: Why do depressed skull fractures require urgent neurosurgical evaluation?
back:
• High incidence of infection, neurological deficits, and late-onset epilepsy.
• Often involve breaches in the dura mater requiring elevation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Depressed skull fractures... involve inward displacement... associated with a high incidence of infection, neurological defcit and late-onset epilepsy. These fractures require exploration and elevation]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: What three clinical findings constitute Cushing’s triad, signaling impending brainstem death from raised intracranial pressure?
back:
* Hypertension
* Bradycardia
* Irregular respiration
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): "classically producing Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration."

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: How does uncal herniation specifically affect pupillary response as a neurosurgical red flag?
back:
* Compression of the third nerve
* Initial sluggish enlargement
* Progression to fixed, dilated pupil (usually ipsilateral)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): "Uncal herniation can compress the third nerve... Unopposed sympathetic activity produces a sluggish enlarged pupil, progressing to fxed and dilated..."

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: What characteristic clinical sequence identifies an extradural haematoma as a neurosurgical emergency?
back:
* Initial transient loss of consciousness
* Subsequent "lucid interval"
* Rapid neurological deterioration ("talk and die" pattern)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): "Transient loss of consciousness is typical, and the patient may then present in the subsequent lucid interval... then sudden deterioration."

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: According to NICE guidelines, which specific vomiting pattern following head injury necessitates CT imaging within one hour?
back: * More than one episode of vomiting.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): "Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour... More than one episode of vomiting"

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Which pharmacological agents are used to acutely temporize raised intracranial pressure while awaiting neurosurgical transfer?
back:
* Bolus of Mannitol
* Hypertonic saline
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): "A bolus of mannitol or hypertonic saline may be administered to temporize ICP, for example while scanning and transferring the patient."

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: What Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score range defines a severe traumatic brain injury requiring urgent referral?
back: * GCS 3 to 8.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): "Table 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation... Severe head injury GCS 3–8"

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Which clinical signs of a basal skull fracture serve as urgent indicators of high-energy intracranial injury?
back:
* Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising)
* Raccoon eyes (periorbital bruising)
* CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): "Clinical evidence of a skull base fracture may include Battle’s sign and ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes... CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea"

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: In a trauma patient, why is a sudden drop in GCS score considered a critical neurosurgical red flag?
back:
* Indicates developing secondary brain injury
* Signifies potentially reversible pathologies (e.g., expanding mass lesions)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): "A deterioration in the GCS score is an important index of developing a potentially reversible secondary injury."

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: What cardinal neurological signs during the primary survey signal significant brain compression and impending herniation?
back:
* Contralateral hemiparesis
* Reduced conscious level
* Ipsilateral pupillary dilatation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): "There is contralateral hemiparesis, a reduced conscious level and ipsilateral pupillary dilatation, the cardinal signs of brain compression and herniation."

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Which specific event following head trauma mandates immediate CT imaging and neurosurgical evaluation under NICE guidelines?
back: * Any post-traumatic seizure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): "Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour... Post-traumatic seizure"

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What does the 'D' represent in the ATLS primary survey (cABCDE)?
back: Disability. Assessment focuses on neurological status using the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and pupil size/reaction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.4 The cABCDE of trauma care ... D – Disability (neurological status)]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What pupillary changes signal potential uncal herniation during the Disability assessment?
back: A sluggish or fixed and dilated pupil (mydriasis), usually ipsilateral to the lesion, caused by third nerve compression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Uncal herniation ( Figure 28.2 ) can compress the third nerve ... Unopposed sympathetic activity produces a sluggish enlarged pupil, progressing to fxed and dilated]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: Contrast the GCS score ranges for 'Moderate' vs 'Severe' head injuries.
back:
● Moderate: GCS 9–13.
● Severe: GCS 3–8.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Table 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation ... Moderate head injury GCS 9–13; Severe head injury GCS 3–8]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: Calculate GCS: A patient opens eyes to speech, uses inappropriate words, and withdraws from pain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Table 28.4 Glasgow Coma Scale score for head injury. Eyes open: To verbal command 3; Verbal: Inappropriate/words only 3; Motor: Withdrawal/fexion 4]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: What metabolic assessment must be excluded immediately during the ATLS primary survey 'Disability' phase?
back: Hypoglycaemia. Blood glucose must be measured as it mimics neurological deficits and is rapidly reversible.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [The blood glucose level should also be measured as early as possible as hypoglycaemia is very dangerous and easily reversible.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
coreConcept: Prognostic Value of GCS Motor Component
front: Q: Which component of the Glasgow Coma Scale is the most accurate predictor of neurological outcome?
back: The Motor score.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [as it is the GCS score – and in particular the motor score – that is the best predictor of neurological outcome.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: Define 'Mild head injury' using the GCS and clinical history criteria.
back: GCS 14 or 15 accompanied by a history of Loss of Consciousness (LOC).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Table 28.1 Head injury severity: clinical classifcation ... Mild head injury GCS 14 or 15 with LOC]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: If a patient localizes to pain on the right and extends on the left, what Motor score (M) is assigned?
back: M5. The score represents the best performance elicited from any limb.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Remember that the score represents the best performance elicited, so a patient fexing in response to a painful stimulus on the left and localising on the right scores ‘M5’.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: Under the primary survey (cABCDE), when is hemorrhage control ('c') prioritized over the airway ('A')?
back: In cases of exsanguinating external hemorrhage (massive arterial bleeding), where pressure or tourniquets must be applied first.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: Q: How is the GCS Verbal score documented specifically for an intubated patient?
back: It is recorded with the suffix 'T' (e.g., GCS 10T or V-T) to indicate the presence of an endotracheal tube.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Table 28.4 Glasgow Coma Scale score for head injury ... Verbal: Intubated patient T]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: What is the gold standard imaging investigation for a severely injured adult blunt trauma patient?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from head to pelvis with IV contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): Whole-body CT (WBCT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast is the gold standard investigation of the severely injured adult blunt trauma patient.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: In a hemodynamically unstable patient, which imaging helps locate a major source of hemorrhage before theatre?
back: Focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan and an immediate pelvic radiograph.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): A focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan (if immediately available) may also be useful in this scenario to locate the major source of haemorrhage.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Contrast the CT appearance of an acute extradural hematoma versus an acute subdural hematoma.
back:
● Extradural: Lentiform (biconvex) hyperdense lesion.
● Subdural: Diffuse concave (crescent) appearance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... Page 388 (Book Page): Since the dura is not as adherent to the brain as it is to the skull, subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a diffuse concave appearance.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Which two radiographic criteria on a lateral cervical spine film indicate spinal instability?
back:
1. Sagittal translation of >3.5 mm.
2. Sagittal angulation of >11° compared to the adjacent level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): Assess for instability: a. 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; b. sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: To accurately diagnose a bladder injury during CT, what is the mandatory contrast volume and route?
back: Minimum of 300 mL of contrast instilled via a urethral catheter (CT cystogram).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): For assessment of bladder injury a cystogram should be performed at the time of CT. A minimum of 300 mL of contrast is instilled into the bladder via a urethral catheter.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: List three NICE indications for CT brain imaging within 1 hour of head injury.
back:
● GCS <13 at any point.
● Focal neurological deficit.
● Suspected open or basal skull fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour: GCS <13 at any point... Focal neurological defcit... Suspected open, depressed or basal skull fracture.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: What are the three primary anatomical regions where eFAST is unreliable for diagnosing injury?
back:
1. Hollow viscus (bowel).
2. Retroperitoneum.
3. Penetrating trauma wounds.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): Does not directly identify injury to hollow viscus... Cannot reliably exclude injury in penetrating trauma... Is unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Why is MRI preferred over CT for diagnosing Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI)?
back: MRI is more sensitive to the characteristic small hemorrhagic foci in the corpus callosum or brainstem.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): Magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive and is employed to evaluate for diffuse axonal injury in patients who fail to improve neurologically.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: What is the classic initial radiographic finding in suspected traumatic thoracic aortic disruption?
back: Widened mediastinum on an erect chest radiograph.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Regarding liver trauma follow-up, which specific subset of patients requires mandatory rescanning before discharge?
back: Patients with a suspected vascular component to their liver injury (risk of false aneurysms/fistulae).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 401 (Book Page): Injury in which there is a suggestion of a vascular component should be reimaged... It is advised that all patients should be rescanned prior to discharge.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
coreConcept: Glasgow Coma Scale Components in ATLS
front: Which three clinical parameters are assessed to calculate the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score in the trauma primary survey?
back: • Best Eye response (E) • Best Verbal response (V) • Best Motor response (M)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): TABLE 27.1 Glasgow Coma Scale. Best eye response (E) Best verbal response (V) Best motor response (M)

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
front: How is head injury severity classified by GCS score, and which component most accurately predicts neurological outcome?
back: • Severe: GCS 3–8 • Moderate: GCS 9–13 • Mild/Minor: GCS 14–15 • Superior Outcome Predictor: Motor response score
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): The severity of head injury is classifed according to the post-resuscitation Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score ( Table 28.1 ), as it is the GCS score – and in particular the motor score – that is the best predictor of neurological outcome.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Which imaging modality is the most sensitive for early diagnosis of acute osteomyelitis?
back:
• MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging).
• It detects bone marrow oedema and periosteal elevation within 2–3 days of onset.
• Plain radiographs often remain normal for the first 5–7 days.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 603 (Book Page): [In the early phase (2–3 days) radiographs may be normal but MRI will show bone oedema and periosteal elevation. After 5–7 days, plain radiographs may show subtle abnormality with osteopenia and periosteal new bone formation.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Contrast the age-based selection of ultrasound versus radiography in diagnosing DDH.
back:
• 0–4 months: Ultrasound (defines anatomy/stability; head is not ossified).
• After 4–5 months: Plain Radiography (assesses the ossific nucleus relationship to Perkins’ and Hilgenreiner’s lines).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): [Ultrasonographic assessment... is used as a screening tool... between 4 and 6 weeks of age. Plain radiographs are used from 4–5 months of age, when the relationship of the femoral ossific nucleus to the acetabulum can be assessed.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
coreConcept: NICE Head Injury Discharge Red Flags
front: Q: Which fve post-discharge symptoms indicate a need for urgent medical re-evaluation after a mild head injury?
back: 1. Persistent/worsening headache; 2. Persistent vomiting; 3. Drowsiness; 4. Visual disturbance; 5. Limb weakness or numbness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [seek medical attention if: Persistent/worsening headache despite analgesia; Persistent vomiting; Drowsiness; Visual disturbance; Limb weakness or numbness]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: What is Cushing’s triad and what clinical state does its appearance signify?
back: Components: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration. Signifes: Imminent brainstem compromise or herniation ('coning') due to uncontrolled intracranial pressure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. The patient is then said to be ‘coning’, and brainstem death will result without immediate intervention.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: List four high-risk 'red fag' indications for mandatory CT brain imaging within one hour of injury.
back: 1. GCS <13 at any point; 2. GCS <15 at two hours; 3. Focal neurological defcit; 4. Suspected open, depressed, or basal skull fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour: GCS <13 at any point; GCS <15 at 2 hours; Focal neurological defcit; Suspected open, depressed or basal skull fracture]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: What cardinal triad of signs indicates rapid brain compression from an expanding extradural haematoma?
back: 1. Reduced level of consciousness; 2. Contralateral hemiparesis; 3. Ipsilateral pupillary dilatation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [There is contralateral hemiparesis, a reduced conscious level and ipsilateral pupillary dilatation, the cardinal signs of brain compression and herniation.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: What speciÿc pupillary change is a red fag for uncal herniation compressing the third cranial nerve?
back: A sluggish, enlarged pupil that progresses to being ÿxed and dilated, usually occurring ÿrst on the side of the haematoma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Uncal herniation can compress the third nerve... Unopposed sympathetic activity produces a sluggish enlarged pupil, progressing to fxed and dilated under continued compression.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: Which constellation of clinical ÿndings constitutes a red fag for Non-Accidental Injury (NAI) in children?
back: Delayed presentation; Retinal haemorrhages; Bilateral chronic subdural haematomas; Multiple skull fractures; Neurological injury without external trauma signs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Signifcant fndings include delayed presentation, injuries of disparate age, retinal haemorrhages, bilateral chronic subdural haematomas, multiple skull fractures and neurological injury without external signs of trauma.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: Identify the classic clinical signs of a basal skull fracture requiring urgent neurosurgical consultation.
back: Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising); Raccoon/Panda eyes (periorbital bruising); CSF rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea; Haemotympanum; Cranial nerve defcits.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Clinical signs of skull base fracture include bleeding or CSF leak from the ears (otorrhoea) or nose (rhinorrhoea) and bruising behind the ear (Figure 28.3) or around the eyes.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: What speciÿc clinical course constitutes the 'talk and die' red fag pattern in head trauma?
back: Initial transient loss of consciousness, followed by a 'lucid interval' of apparent recovery, ending in sudden, rapid neurological collapse.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Transient loss of consciousness is typical, and the patient may then present in the subsequent lucid interval... although this ‘talk and die’ pattern of deterioration occurs in only one-third of cases]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: Which 'red fag' symptom triad suggests urgent neurosurgical evaluation for traumatic cerebral arterial dissection?
back: 1. Headache; 2. Neck pain; 3. Focal ischaemic defcits (due to occlusion or thromboembolism).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Cerebral arterial dissection... It presents with headache, neck pain and focal ischaemic defcits due to occlusion by mural haematoma, thrombus and thromboembolism.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Q: What anatomical feature deÿnes a depressed skull fracture as a red fag for urgent surgical intervention?
back: Inward displacement of a bone fragment by at least the thickness of the skull, often compound (open) or associated with dural breach/intracranial air.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Depressed skull fractures involve inward displacement of a bone fragment by at least the thickness of the skull... They are usually compound (open) fractures... require exploration and elevation]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: What is the gold standard investigation for adult blunt trauma patients with multiple injuries?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from head to pelvis with intravenous (IV) contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury...]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Why is a FAST scan considered unreliable for excluding hollow viscus or retroperitoneal injuries?
back:
• Low sensitivity for injuries without haemoperitoneum (29–35%).
• Inability to detect <100 mL of free blood.
• Obscured by bowel gas or obesity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Hollow viscus injury and solid organ injury are difcult to diagnose... eFAST has a low sensitivity (29–35%) for organ injury without haemoperitoneum... unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Contrast the utility of CT and MRI in diagnosing diffuse axonal injury (DAI).
back:
• CT: May show haemorrhagic foci in the corpus callosum or brainstem.
• MRI: More sensitive; preferred for patients failing to improve neurologically.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [haemorrhagic foci in the corpus callosum and dorsolateral rostral brainstem on CT may be suggestive. Magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive and is employed to evaluate for difuse axonal injury...]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: A haemodynamically unstable patient requires immediate trauma laparotomy. Which imaging must be performed first?
back:
• Immediate chest radiograph (excludes catastrophic intrathoracic haemorrhage).
• Immediate pelvic radiograph (excludes pelvic source; must not delay transfer).
• FAST scan (to locate major haemorrhage).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [An immediate chest radio-graph will exclude catastrophic intrathoracic haemorrhage. An immediate pelvic radiograph is essential but should not delay transfer to the operating theatre. A focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan... may also be useful...]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Detail the volume and rationale for contrast administration during CT cystography for bladder injury.
back:
• Minimum 300 mL of contrast is instilled.
• Rationale: Ensures adequate bladder distension to detect small leaks despite cystic muscle contraction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [A minimum of 300 mL of contrast is instilled into the bladder via a urethral catheter. The large volume is essential because a small volume may not distend the bladder enough to produce a leak... once the cystic muscle is contracted.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: List three NICE indications for CT brain imaging within 1 hour of head injury.
back:
• GCS <13 at any point.
• Focal neurological deficit.
• Suspected open, depressed, or basal skull fracture.
• Post-traumatic seizure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour: GCS <13 at any point; GCS <15 at 2 hours; Focal neurological defcit; Suspected open, depressed or basal skull fracture; More than one episode of vomiting; Post-traumatic seizure.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: What is the recommended imaging follow-up for suspected scaphoid fractures with normal initial radiographs?
back:
• Immobilise wrist in cast.
• Repeat scaphoid-view radiographs in 10–14 days.
• Consider MRI, CT, or bone scan for earlier definitive diagnosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [If a fracture is not evident on the initial radiographs... immobilise the wrist and examine again 10–14 days later. If tenderness remains, repeat the scaphoid views. If facilities and resources allow, an earlier diagnosis may be made with a bone scan, MRI or CT.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: How is imaging used to differentiate pediatric septic arthritis from transient synovitis?
back:
• Ultrasound: Identifies joint effusions (distended capsule).
• Clinical/Imaging Core: Combined with Kocher predictors (ESR >40mm/h, Fever >38.5°C, non-weight-bearing, WBC >12x10⁹/L).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Ultrasound scans of deep joints, such as the hip, will identify joint efusions... Four clinical predictors can diferentiate between septic arthritis and transient synovitis (Table 44.17).]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Compare the roles of MRI and 18FDG-PET/CT in managing chronic osteomyelitis.
back:
• MRI: Investigation of choice for anatomical diagnosis and soft-tissue involvement.
• 18FDG-PET/CT: Localises active infection to assist in surgical planning.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 604 (Book Page): [MRI is the imaging test of choice... 18FDG-PET CT scanning can be helpful for surgical planning.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Which specific liver injuries mandate routine CT re-imaging prior to hospital discharge?
back: Injuries with a suspected vascular component to exclude false aneurysms, arteriovenous fistulae, or haemobiliary fistulae.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [Injury in which there is a suggestion of a vascular component should be reimaged... significant risk of the development of subsequent ischaemia, false aneurysms, arteriovenous fstulae or haemobiliary fstula. It is advised that all patients should be rescanned prior to discharge.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
coreConcept: NICE Guidelines for Urgent CT Imaging in TBI
front: What are the primary clinical 'red flag' indications for urgent CT brain imaging within 1 hour of head injury?
back: GCS <13 at any point; GCS <15 at two hours post-injury; focal neurological deficit; suspected open, depressed, or basal skull fracture; post-traumatic seizure; and more than one episode of vomiting.
