citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour: GCS <13 at any point, GCS <15 at 2 hours, Focal neurological defcit, Suspected open, depressed or basal skull fracture, More than one episode of vomiting, Post-traumatic seizure.]

category: Identify red flag signs that indicate urgent neurosurgical referral
front: Which physiological 'red flag' triad indicates dangerously high intracranial pressure and imminent brainstem herniation?
back: Cushing’s Triad: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration. It signifies that the patient is 'coning' and requires immediate neurosurgical intervention to prevent brainstem death.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. The patient is then said to be ‘ coning ’, and brainstem death will result without immediate intervention.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: What is the gold standard imaging investigation for a severely injured adult blunt trauma patient?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology].

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: When is Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) specifically indicated during the assessment of spinal trauma?
back:
• Presence of a neurological deficit.
• Requirement for detailed assessment of ligamentous structures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 414 (Book Page): [MRI is indicated in all patients with neurological defcit and where assessment of ligamentous structures is important].

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Compare the specific diagnostic utility of Ultrasound versus MRI in pediatric hip joint sepsis.
back:
• Ultrasound: Identifies joint effusions in deep joints like the hip.
• MRI: Investigation of choice; detects osteomyelitis but may require general anesthesia in young children.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Ultrasound scans of deep joints, such as the hip, will identify joint efusions... MRI is considered the investigation of choice but this resource is not available to all (in a timely manner) and, in young children, it requires a general anaesthetic].

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Which three imaging studies are prioritized for trauma patients too hemodynamically unstable for CT?
back:
• Immediate chest radiograph (excludes catastrophic hemorrhage).
• Immediate pelvic radiograph.
• Focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Some patients will be so haemodynamically unstable on arrival that they need immediate surgical control of their haemorrhage before a CT scan. The most likely sources are abdominal or pelvic bleeding. An immediate chest radiograph will exclude catastrophic intrathoracic haemorrhage. An immediate pelvic radiograph is essential... A focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan (if immediately available) may also be useful].

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Specify the contrast administration requirements for evaluating bladder injury during a trauma CT scan.
back: A minimum of 300 mL of contrast must be instilled into the bladder via a urethral catheter.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 403 (Book Page): [For assessment of bladder injury a cystogram should be performed at the time of CT. A minimum of 300 mL of contrast is instilled into the bladder via a urethral catheter].

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: List three NICE criteria for performing a CT brain scan within one hour of head injury.
back:
• GCS <13 at any point.
• Focal neurological deficit.
• Suspected open, depressed, or basal skull fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour: GCS <13 at any point... Focal neurological defcit... Suspected open, depressed or basal skull fracture].

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: According to the Ottawa rules, when are ankle radiographs mandatory following an injury?
back:
• Bone tenderness at distal 6cm/tip of lateral or medial malleolus.
• Inability to bear weight at time of injury or examination.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 526 (Book Page): [Radiographs of the ankle are indicated if the patient fulfls any of the Ottawa ankle rules... Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the lateral malleolus... Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the medial malleolus... Inability to bear weight at the time of the accident or at the time of examination].

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Which specific radiographic views are required to exclude a mandibular fracture, and why?
back:
• Views: Orthopantomogram (OPT) and Posteroanterior (PA) mandible.
• Rationale: Two orthogonal views (right angles) ensure fractures are not missed in different planes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 408 (Book Page): [If a mandibular fracture is suspected, an orthopantomogram (OPT) and a posteroanterior (PA) radiograph of the mandible should be obtained... It is extremely important to have two views at right angles to each other to avoid missing any fractures].

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: What is the follow-up imaging protocol for suspected scaphoid fractures with normal initial radiographs?
back:
• Immobilize the wrist in a cast.
• Re-examine and repeat scaphoid view radiographs after 10–14 days.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 496 (Book Page): [The standard protocol of a suspected scaphoid fracture is to immobilise the wrist and examine again 10–14 days later. If tenderness remains, repeat the scaphoid views].

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: What three radiographic views constitute a standard 'full cervical spine series' for trauma clearance?
back:
• Anteroposterior (AP) view.
• Lateral view.
• Open mouth (odontoid peg) view.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [A full cervical spine series includes anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the whole cervical spine, and open mouth views].

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: What is the gold-standard investigation for a severely injured blunt trauma patient with signs of multiple injury?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from the head to the pelvis with IV contrast. It should be performed as early as possible during resuscitation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Why is eFAST considered unreliable for excluding internal organ injury in blunt abdominal trauma?
back: It fails to detect less than 100 mL of free blood and has low sensitivity (29–35%) for organ injury that lacks haemoperitoneum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): [eFAST is accurate at detecting >100 mL of free blood... has a low sensitivity (29–35%) for organ injury without haemoperitoneum. eFAST is also unreliable for excluding injury in penetrating trauma.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Compare the diagnostic sensitivity of radiographs and MRI for detecting early acute osteomyelitis.
back: Radiographs may remain normal for 5–7 days; MRI is the investigation of choice, identifying bone oedema and periosteal elevation within 2–3 days.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [In the early phase (2–3 days) radiographs may be normal but MRI will show bone oedema and periosteal elevation. After 5–7 days, plain radiographs may show subtle abnormality]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: A pediatric patient presents with a 'white eye' blow-out fracture and bradycardia. What does imaging likely reveal?
back: A minimally displaced 'trapdoor' orbital floor fracture with entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle, causing an oculocardiac reflex.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac reflex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope... the orbital floor may appear undisplaced or minimally displaced, which means that a trapdoor defect has opened and then closed again, entrapping the muscle.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: What pharmacological step is utilized during a CT scan to improve the diagnosis of duodenal trauma?
back: Administration of oral contrast is used to identify leakages or fluid collections in the periduodenal tissue.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): [if duodenal injury is suspected from the mechanism of injury, oral contrast may be helpful... CT is the diagnostic modality of choice. The only sign may be gas or a fuid collection in the periduodenal tissue, and leakage of oral contrast, administration of which may improve accuracy of diagnosis.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: List three fracture patterns on radiographic imaging with high specificity for non-accidental injury (NAI).
back:
1. Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures.
2. Posterior rib fractures.
3. Scapular fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [TABLE 44.21 Fracture patterns with a high specifcity for non-accidental injury. ● Multiple fractures at different stages of healing/old fractures ● Posterior rib fractures ● Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures ● Scapular fractures]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Why must formal log-rolling be deferred until a pelvic fracture is radiographically excluded in trauma care?
back: Log-rolling can disturb established blood clots in severe pelvic fractures, causing further harm; a 20-degree roll with inline stabilization is used instead.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [Log-rolling patients with severe pelvic fractures may harm the patient by disturbing established blood clots. Log-rolling should not occur until a pelvic fracture has been radiographically excluded.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: Why is follow-up CT recommended 6–12 months after surgery for complex frontal sinus fractures?
back: To ensure normal sinus function and screen for latent, life-threatening complications such as meningitis, mucocele, or Pott’s puffy tumour.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 435 (Book Page): [A CT scan at 6 months to 1 year is recommended to ensure that there are no signs of complications... including meningitis, Pott’s pufy tumour and mucocele.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: If a single spinal fracture is identified on imaging, what mandatory follow-up imaging must occur?
back: Radiological imaging of the entire spine is required because 10-15% of cases involve a second spinal injury at a remote level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [A second spinal injury at a remote level may be present in 10% of cases... If a spinal fracture is identifed then further imaging of the whole spine is required because there is a 15% incidence of a further spinal fracture.]

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
front: Q: What is the investigation of first choice in the routine diagnostic assessment of chest injuries?
back: A supine anteroposterior (AP) chest radiograph. It identifies tracheal deviation, lung/mediastinal pathology, and skeletal injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [A chest radiograph is the investigation of frst choice... an anteroposterior (AP) supine chest radiograph is usually the simplest initial investigation.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: What are the mandatory acute management steps for a suspected septic arthritis?
back: 1. Joint aspiration for microscopy and culture. 2. Urgent surgical joint washout (arthroscopic or open). 3. Empirical systemic antibiotic therapy followed by 3–6 weeks of targeted treatment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 600 (Book Page): [The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint and appropriate adequate antibiotic therapy. ... Management is prompt surgical joint washout, followed by 3–6 weeks of antibiotics.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Why is an acute unstable slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) treated as a surgical emergency?
back: It is functionally equivalent to a displaced intracapsular neck fracture. High risk of avascular necrosis (AVN). Requires gentle reduction and pinning within 24 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 622 (Book Page): [This situation is equivalent to a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. This means that an acute unstable SCFE is an emergency. The AVN risk is considerable.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Outline the sequence of the Ponseti method for managing congenital club foot.
back: C: Correct forefoot cavus. A: Gradual abduction. V: Correct hindfoot varus. E: Correct equinus via percutaneous Achilles tenotomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 626 (Book Page): [C – correction of the apparent forefoot cavus... A – gradual forefoot abduction... V – correction of the hindfoot varus... E – correction of hindfoot equinus usually follows a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: What criteria determine the suitability for a 'DAIR' strategy in prosthetic joint infection?
back: 1. Prosthesis must be well-fixed. 2. Requires full excision of infected soft tissue and modular component exchange. 3. Followed by long-term suppressive antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 602 (Book Page): [Debridement, antibiotics and implant retention - ‘DAIR’. This can only be undertaken if the prosthesis is well fxed. DAIR is not a form of washout as all infected soft tissue and necrotic bone must be fully excised and modular components exchanged.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Identify the four critical factors in the BACH classification for chronic osteomyelitis management.
back: B: Bone anatomy (cavitary vs segmental). A: Antimicrobial susceptibility. C: Coverage of soft tissue (need for plastic surgery). H: Host systemic health status.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 605 (Book Page): [The BACH classifcation divides patients into ... based on the four important features of the infection ... anatomical location in the bone (B), the antimicrobial profle (A), the need for soft-tissue cover (C) and the health of the host (H).]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: When is surgical debridement mandatory in the management of acute childhood osteomyelitis?
back: 1. Failure of conservative high-dose intravenous antibiotic treatment. 2. Evidence of abscess formation. 3. Progression of clinical toxaemia or bone destruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 604 (Book Page): [Late diagnosis and/or failure of medical treatment requires surgical debridement. ... Acute bone infection has a good prognosis with a 90% cure rate. Failure to treat adequately produces chronicity.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: State the definitive pressure thresholds used to confirm acute compartment syndrome.
back: 1. Absolute fascial pressure ≥30 mmHg. 2. Differential pressure (Diastolic BP minus Compartment Pressure) ≤30 mmHg.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Generally accepted pressure thresholds include an absolute pressure greater than or equal to 30 mmHg or pressure diference (diastolic pressure – compartment pressure) less than or equal to 30 mmHg.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Outline the 'top-down' sequencing priority for the surgical repair of panfacial fractures.
back: 1. Frontal bone and zygomatic arch. 2. Orbital rim and nasoethmoidal complex. 3. Mandible. 4. Maxillary Le Fort I level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 415 (Book Page): [One of the most common sequencing techniques is a ‘topdown’ and ‘outsidein’ approach. This includes frst repairing the frontal bone and zygomatic arch fractures followed by orbital rim, nasoethmoidal and mandible fractures. The Le Fort I level... repaired last.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Identify the specific clinical presentation of neurogenic shock in cervical spinal trauma.
back: 1. Hypotension. 2. Bradycardia (unopposed vagal tone). 3. Warm peripheries (loss of sympathetic outflow below T5). Contrast with hypovolaemic shock.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Neurogenic shock . This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries. This is due to unopposed vagal tone resulting from cervical spinal cord injury at or above the level of sympathetic outfow (T5).]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Which specific fracture patterns are considered pathognomonic for non-accidental injury in children?
back: 1. Multiple fractures at different healing stages. 2. Posterior rib fractures. 3. Metaphyseal corner/bucket-handle fractures. 4. Fractures in non-ambulant children.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [Fracture patterns with a high specifcity for non-accidental injury: Multiple fractures at different stages of healing/old fractures; Posterior rib fractures; Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures; Any fracture in a child below walking age.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: What is the mandatory immediate surgical management for a native joint confirmed with septic arthritis?
back:
● Prompt removal of pus via formal surgical washout (irrigation).
● Immediate initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy.
● Splintage of the joint while the inflammatory process settles.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint and appropriate adequate antibiotic therapy. The joint is aspirated and, if pus is confrmed, a formal washout is mandatory.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: How do leukocytes contribute to permanent joint damage in untreated acute septic arthritis?
back:
● Leukocytes produce proteases that destroy the bacteria and the collagen matrix of articular cartilage.
● Secondary pressure effects or ischemic infarction cause avascular necrosis (AVN).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint is destructive: the proteases produced by leukocytes destroy both the bacteria and the collagen matrix of the articular cartilage. AVN may occur secondary to pressure efects or ischaemic infarction.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Contrast the acute surgical strategy for fixed versus loose prosthetic joint infections (PJI).
back:
● Well-fixed implants: Managed via DAIR (Debridement, Antibiotics, and Implant Retention).
● Loose implants: Mandatory removal followed by single-stage or two-stage revision surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 602 (Book Page): [loose infected implants should always be removed... Well-fxed prostheses may be Debrided, treated with Antibiotics and the Implant Retained (‘DAIR’ approach)]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: What is the critical management window for an acute unstable slip of the capital femoral epiphysis?
back:
● This is a surgical emergency requiring intervention within 24 hours.
● Treatment involves gentle repositioning and internal screw fixation to minimize avascular necrosis risk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 622 (Book Page): [This situation is equivalent to a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. This means that an acute unstable SCFE is an emergency. To be efective such treatment should take place within 24 hours of injury.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: What is the recommended antibiotic duration for complex chronic osteomyelitis following radical debridement?
back:
● Typical duration is 6–12 weeks.
● Therapy is initially parenteral followed by oral, tailored to specific culture and sensitivity results.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 606 (Book Page): [In total segmental excision of infection a short course may be indicated, but in most chronic infections 6–12 weeks is often advised.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Identify the most significant complication related to the late treatment of neonatal septic hip arthritis.
back:
● Destruction of the femoral head and physis.
● Permanent joint subluxation and avascular necrosis secondary to pressure or ischemic infarction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Pus in a joint destroys articular cartilage and causes avascular necrosis of intra-articular epiphyses... Joint instability, particularly in the hip joint, may require the reduced joint to be splinted.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: What is the mandatory immediate management step for an unhealed fracture with unstable hardware and infection?
back:
● Removal of the unstable internal hardware.
● Radical debridement of infected tissue.
● Stabilization of the bone using an external fixator.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 603 (Book Page): [Stability is essential for bone healing and eradication of infection. If the implant is not stable, it should be removed and replaced by an external fxator. Radical excision of the infected fracture is needed.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Differentiate the primary management plans for flexible postural clubfoot versus structural idiopathic clubfoot.
back:
● Postural: Physiotherapy stretching exercises; normal by 3 months.
● Structural: The Ponseti method (serial manipulation and casting) followed by percutaneous Achilles tenotomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 626 (Book Page): [The postural club foot may beneft from physiotherapy stretches... structural idiopathic club foot... The Ponseti method corrects foot deformity in 95% of idiopathic cases.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Why is emergency fasciotomy required as the definitive acute management for suspected compartment syndrome?
back:
● Fasciotomy immediately lowers intra-fascial pressure.
● This restores microperfusion to prevent irreversible muscle anoxia and ischemic necrosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [The pathophysiology involves increased tissue pressure, which leads to reduced microperfusion... Emergency treatment involves... performing defnitive treatment with fasciotomies.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: What anatomical position is used in harness management for neonatal developmental dysplasia of the hip?
back:
● Reduction is maintained with the hip held in abduction and flexion.
● This biomechanical environment encourages acetabular remodelling via the Pavlik harness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Hips that remain unstable... are treated with harnesses or splints that obtain and maintain reduction with the hip abducted and fexed.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: What are the three primary AO classifications of spinal fractures based on mechanism?
back:
• Type A: Compression fractures of the vertebral body.
• Type B: Distraction injuries of anterior or posterior elements.
• Type C: Rotational injuries (often coexisting with A or B).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): [The system developed by the AO... can be used to classify these fractures. There are three main injury types, A, B and C... Type A fractures are vertebral body compression fractures. Type B injuries involve distraction of the anterior or posterior elements and type C injuries are rotational]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Describe the Denis three-column model used to determine spinal stability.
back:
• Anterior, middle, and posterior columns.
• Instability is defined as injury involving two or more columns.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Spinal stability... The spine can be divided into three columns: anterior, middle and posterior... If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Compare the common outcomes of upper cervical vs. subaxial cervical (C3-C7) trauma.
back:
• Upper cervical (Skull-C2): Frequently non-operative or fatal; neurological injury rare (except C1/C2 instability).
• Subaxial: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is more commonly associated with these levels.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): [The majority of upper cervical spinal injuries are treated non-operatively... Spinal cord injury is more commonly associated with subaxial cervical spinal injuries.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: What is the specific mechanism and stability criterion for a Jefferson (Atlas) fracture?
back:
• Mechanism: Axial loading of the cervical spine.
• Instability: Present if transverse ligament rupture causes combined lateral mass deviation >6.9 mm.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Fracture of the C1 ring is associated with axial loading... Rupture of the transverse ligament is present when the combined lateral mass deviation exceeds 6.9 mm.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: How are Odontoid peg fractures classified by anatomical level?
back:
• Type I: Avulsion of the tip.
• Type II: Fracture through the neck/base of the dens.
• Type III: Fracture extending into the body of C2.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [There are three types of odontoid peg fracture... Type I, Type II, Type III (as illustrated in Figure 30.27)]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Identify the mechanism and anatomical level of a Hangman’s fracture.
back:
• Level: Traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 on C3.
• Mechanism: Hyperextension and distraction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (hangman’s fracture)... This is a traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 on C3.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Why are the cervicothoracic and thoracolumbar junctions prone to injury?
back: • They are transitional zones where the spine changes from mobile segments (cervical/lumbar) to fixed segments (thoracic).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [The cervicothoracic and thoracolumbar junctions are transitional zones where the spine changes from a mobile section (cervical and lumbar) to a more fxed one (thoracic). These two areas are common sites of injury.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: What defines a Chance fracture by mechanism and level?
back:
• Mechanism: Flexion-distraction (classically lap-belt injury).
• Level: Thoracolumbar junction (T11-L2).
• Associations: Duodenal, pancreatic, or aortic ruptures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 401 (Book Page): [Chance fractures are fexion–distraction injuries of the thoracolumbar junction and are classically associated with the use of lap belts... Duodenal, pancreatic and/or aortic ruptures are also associated with these injuries.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: List the mechanisms associated with specific subaxial (C3-C7) cervical injuries.
back:
• Compression fractures: Hyperflexion.
• Burst fractures: Axial compression.
• Facet subluxation/dislocation: Distraction-flexion.
• Teardrop fractures: Hyperextension.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 398 (Book Page): [The pattern of lower cervical spine injury depends on the mechanism of trauma. These include compression fractures (hyperfexion), burst fractures (axial compression), facet subluxation/dislocation injuries (distraction–fexion), teardrop fractures (hyperextension)]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Which radiographic measurements on a lateral cervical spine series indicate instability?
back:
• Sagittal translation >3.5 mm.
• Sagittal angulation >11° compared to the adjacent level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 392 (Book Page): [Assess for instability... 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: What is the mandatory immediate management plan for a clinically diagnosed tension pneumothorax?
back:
1. Immediate decompression via needle thoracocentesis (safe triangle or 2nd ICS).
2. Finger thoracostomy in the safe triangle.
3. Definitively hold with intercostal chest tube insertion (5th ICS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Treatment consists of immediate decompression. This was historically taught by rapid insertion of a large-bore cannula into the second intercostal space... current teaching advocates undertaking decompression in the safe triangle... or, in extremis, a fnger thoracostomy... followed by insertion of a chest tube through the ffth intercostal space]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiology of compartment syndrome and the primary complication if left untreated.
back:
Pathophysiology: Increased tissue pressure within a fascial compartment reduces microperfusion.
Complication: Cellular anoxia leads to irreversible muscle damage and nerve necrosis (Volkmann’s Ischaemic Contracture).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [The pathophysiology involves increased tissue pressure, which leads to reduced microperfusion, resulting in tissue ischaemia and irreversible muscle damage from cellular anoxia.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Outline the management difference between suspected paediatric septic arthritis and transient synovitis.
back:
Septic Arthritis: Requires urgent joint aspiration, formal surgical washout (arthrotomy/irrigation), and systemic antibiotics.
Transient Synovitis: Managed conservatively with relative rest and analgesia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint and appropriate adequate antibiotic therapy... a formal washout is mandatory; standard teaching states that the joint must be opened, irrigated and free drainage encouraged]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Plan the management for a haemodynamically unstable patient with an 'open book' pelvic fracture.
back:
1. Immediate application of pelvic binder/sheet at greater trochanters.
2. Resuscitation (1:1:1 ratio).
3. If arterial bleeding persists, perform interventional angioembolisation or extraperitoneal packing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Initial management requires the use of a compression binder or a sheet, applied around the true pelvis at the level of the greater trochanters... If the bleeding is of arterial origin, interventional angioembolisation is the next choice.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: State the acute administration protocol for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in severe trauma patients.
back:
Indication: Significant haemorrhage (SBP <110, HR >110).
Dose: 1g IV over 10 minutes, then 1g infusion over 8 hours.
Timing: Ideally within 1 hour; contra-indicated after 3 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours. Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have signifcant haemorrhage... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: What are the three primary goals of Damage Control Surgery (DCS)?
back:
1. Stopping active surgical haemorrhage.
2. Controlling contamination (GI leakage).
3. Restoring normal physiology in the ICU before definitive reconstruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Damage control surgery is restricted to only three goals: ● stopping any active surgical bleeding; ● controlling any contamination; ● restoring normal physiology.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Outline the management plan for an acute unstable Slip of the Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE).
back:
1. Orthopaedic emergency (AVN risk).
2. Urgent gentle repositioning under GA (within 24 hours).
3. Capsulotomy to reduce tamponade.
4. Single-screw fixation in situ.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 622 (Book Page): [An acute unstable SCFE is an emergency. The AVN risk is considerable... gentle repositioning of the femoral epiphysis occurs as the externally rotated limb is lifted into the neutral position... To be efective such treatment should take place within 24 hours of injury.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Describe the 'DAIR' approach for early prosthetic joint or fracture-related infection.
back:
Application: Well-fixed implants with early infection.
Steps: 1. Thorough surgical Debridement. 2. Exchange modular components. 3. Systemic Antibiotics. 4. Implant Retention.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 602 (Book Page): [Debridement, antibiotics and implant retention - ‘DAIR’. This can only be undertaken if the prosthesis is well fxed. DAIR is not a form of washout as all infected soft tissue and necrotic bone must be fully excised and modular components exchanged.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: What is the recommended dosing and timing for Tranexamic acid (TXA) in major trauma?
back:
- 1g IV over 10 minutes, followed by 1g over 8 hours.
- Administer within the first hour; must not be given after 3 hours post-injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: How are venous lactate levels used to decide between ETC and Damage Control Surgery?
back:
- <2 mmol/L: Safe for ETC (definitive repair).
- >3 mmol/L: Under-resuscitated; consider DCS.
- >5 mmol/L: Mandatory DCS.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.6... <2 mmol/L – ETC; >3 mmol/L – may be under-resuscitated... >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: In which adult blunt trauma patients is Whole-Body CT (WBCT) indicated?
back:
- Signs or symptoms of multiple injury.
- Deranged physiology.
- Note: Not performed based on mechanism of injury alone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [WBCT... is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology, but note that WBCT should not be performed on the basis of the mechanism of injury alone.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: What drainage volumes constitute an indication for urgent thoracotomy in massive haemothorax?
back:
- Initial drainage of >1500 mL of blood.
- Ongoing haemorrhage >200 mL/hour for 3–4 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Where should a pelvic binder be positioned to ensure it does not obstruct a trauma laparotomy?
back: - Correctly positioned at the level of the greater trochanters.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: What criteria define the 'unstable' category in a slip of the capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)?
back: - Defined as a slip where the patient is unable to bear weight, even with crutches.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [An unstable slip is defned by Loder as one in which the patient cannot bear weight on the limb.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: What is the goal timeline for Early Total Care (ETC) in musculoskeletal trauma?
back: - Definitive fixation of all unstable long bone, spinal, and pelvic fractures within 36 hours of injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [For musculoskeletal injuries, ETC allows defnitive fxation of all unstable long bone, spinal and pelvic fractures within 36 hours of injury.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Identify the immediate surgical management for a trauma patient with acute retrobulbar haemorrhage.
back: - Bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under local anaesthesia to prevent blindness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [If this is suspected, preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under LA to allow the globe to bulge forwards and relieve the pressure posteriorly.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: What physiological loop constitutes the 'Triad of Death' in trauma patients?
back:
- Acidosis
- Coagulopathy
- Hypothermia
- These lead to multiorgan failure and death.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: What pressure thresholds are diagnostic for Acute Compartment Syndrome?
back:
- Absolute pressure ≥30 mmHg.
- Delta pressure (Diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) ≤30 mmHg.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Generally accepted pressure thresholds include an absolute pressure greater than or equal to 30 mmHg or pressure diference (diastolic pressure – compartment pressure) less than or equal to 30 mmHg.]

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Outline the urgent acute management plan for a patient with a lentiform hyperdense lesion on CT.
back:
- Immediate transfer to a neurosurgical facility.
- Surgical evacuation via craniotomy for deteriorating or comatose patients.
- Serial imaging and close observation if neurologically intact.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): Significant extradural haematoma mandates urgent transfer to the most accessible neurosurgical facility for immediate evacuation in deteriorating or comatose patients or those with large bleeds and for close observation with serial imaging in other cases.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Describe the emergency management of a paediatric 'white eye' blowout orbital floor fracture with oculocardiac reflex.
back:
- Immediate surgical release of entrapped muscle to prevent necrosis.
- Identified by bradycardia, nausea, and syncope.
- Requires urgent intervention within hours of presentation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac reflex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. This needs to be treated as an emergency because irreversible damage related to muscle necrosis can occur within hours.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Contrast the surgical management strategies for acute versus chronic subdural haematomas in symptomatic patients.
back:
- Acute: Prompt evacuation via craniotomy or craniectomy.
- Chronic: Preferred drainage using burr holes.
- Both: Urgent correction of clotting function/anticoagulation reversal.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [Acute] collections require prompt evacuation, typically by craniotomy or craniectomy... [Chronic] For the majority drainage is performed using burr holes.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Outline the immediate management sequence for a neonate presenting with a hot, immobile 'pseudoparalyzed' hip.
back:
- Urgent ultrasound to identify effusion.
- Immediate joint aspiration; if pus confirmed, mandatory formal washout (arthrotomy).
- Start empiric IV antibiotics (e.g., flucloxacillin + gentamicin).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint and appropriate adequate antibiotic therapy... if pus is confirmed, a formal washout is mandatory.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: What are the specific target partial pressure limits for PaCO2 and PaO2 in neurointensive TBI management?
back:
- PaCO2: 4.5–5.0 kPa.
- PaO2: >11 kPa.
- Clinical Goal: Maintenance of cerebral perfusion and prevention of secondary injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): Table 28.5 Key parameters to maintain in head-injured patients in neurointensive care: PaCO 2 = 4.5–5.0 kPa; PaO 2 >11 kPa.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Outline the acute management plan for an unstable Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE).
back:
- Treat as a surgical emergency (similar to neck fracture).
- Perform gentle repositioning and single-screw internal fixation in situ.
- Include capsulotomy to reduce tamponade and AVN risk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 643 (Book Page): This situation is equivalent to a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. This means that an acute unstable SCFE is an emergency... gentle repositioning... A capsulotomy reduces the tamponade effect.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Outline the 'DAIR' management plan for early fracture-related infections (FRI) with stable fixation.
back:
- Radical debridement of infected soft tissue and necrotic bone.
- Retention of stable metalwork to facilitate union.
- Systemic antibiotic suppression until the fracture is fully healed.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): Unhealed fracture with stable fixation... managed with deep sampling, debridement of infected tissues... systemic antibiotics must be given to suppress infection until bone union.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Outline the stepwise acute management for an open tibial fracture with associated vascular injury.
back:
- Step 1: Immediate manual reduction and spanning external fixation.
- Step 2: Creation of an arterial shunt for urgent inflow.
- Step 3: Definitive vascular grafting and plastic surgery cover.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): immediate surgical attention through rapid spanning of the limb, creation of an arterial shunt to provide urgent inflow and subsequent vascular grafting.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: List the three primary goals of Damage Control Surgery (DCS) in trauma patients.
back:
- Immediate control of active surgical haemorrhage.
- Control of contamination (e.g., bowel stapling).
- Restoration of normal physiology (acidosis/coagulopathy) in the ICU.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): Damage control surgery is restricted to only three goals: stopping any active surgical bleeding; controlling any contamination; restoring normal physiology.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
front: Q: Identify three potential late complications of inadequately treated acute osteomyelitis in children.
back:
- Development of chronic osteomyelitis (sequestrum formation).
- Permanent growth plate damage (limb length discrepancy/deformity).
- Joint destruction if secondary septic arthritis occurs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 625 (Book Page): In children, the adjacent growth plates and joints may be affected with subsequent deformity and joint destruction. [Page 626 (Book Page)]: Failure to treat adequately produces chronicity.

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Which anatomical levels define the 'Upper Cervical Spine' and 'Subaxial Cervical Spine'?
back:
• Upper Cervical: Skull to C2 (Atlas and Axis)
• Subaxial Cervical: C3 to C7
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Upper cervical spine (skull–C2)... Subaxial cervical spine (C3–C7)]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: What is the primary mechanism and level associated with a Jefferson fracture?
back:
• Level: C1 (Atlas ring)
• Mechanism: Axial loading of the cervical spine
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Atlas fracture (Jefferson fracture) Fracture of the C1 ring is associated with axial loading of the cervical spine]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Define a 'Hangman’s Fracture' by its level and anatomical displacement.
back:
• Level: C2 on C3
• Definition: Traumatic spondylolisthesis (forward slip) of the Axis (C2) on C3
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (hangman’s fracture) This is a traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 on C3.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: A patient presents with a flexion-distraction injury at T12-L1 after a lap-belt collision. Diagnosis?
back:
• Chance fracture
• Classically involves the thoracolumbar junction
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 401 (Book Page): [Chance fractures are fexion–distraction injuries of the thoracolumbar junction and are classically associated with the use of lap belts]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Classify the three types of Odontoid (Dens) fractures based on anatomical level.
back:
• Type I: Fracture of the tip
• Type II: Fracture at the base/junction with the body (most common)
• Type III: Fracture extending into the C2 vertebral body
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Odontoid fractures There are three types of odontoid peg fracture (Figure 30.27).]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Based on the three-column model, what defines spinal instability?
back: • Injury to two or more columns (Anterior, Middle, or Posterior columns)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [The spine can be divided into three columns: anterior, middle and posterior... If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Match the subaxial (C3-C7) fracture types to their specific mechanisms: Burst and Teardrop.
back:
• Burst Fracture: Axial compression
• Teardrop Fracture: Hyperextension
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 398 (Book Page): [These include compression fractures (hyperfexion), burst fractures (axial compression)... teardrop fractures (hyperextension)]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Distinguish between AO Classification Types A, B, and C for thoracic fractures.
back:
• Type A: Vertebral body compression (axial loading)
• Type B: Distraction (anterior or posterior elements)
• Type C: Rotation (usually associated with Type A or B)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): [Type A fractures are vertebral body compression fractures. Type B injuries involve distraction... and type C injuries are rotational]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: What level of the spinal column is most prone to injury due to its role as a transitional zone?
back:
• The thoracolumbar junction (T11–L2)
• Transition from fixed thoracic to mobile lumbar spine
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): [Thoracolumbar spinal fractures (T11–L2) The thoracolumbar junction is especially prone to injury.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Which subaxial cervical injury involves distraction-flexion forces?
back: • Facet subluxation or dislocation injuries
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 398 (Book Page): [facet subluxation/dislocation injuries (distraction–fexion)]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Describe the specific mechanical force and anatomical injury level defining a Jefferson fracture.
back:
• Level: Atlas (C1) ring.
• Mechanism: Axial loading of the cervical spine.
• Classification: Can be stable or unstable based on transverse ligament integrity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [Atlas fracture (Jefferson fracture). Fracture of the C1 ring is associated with axial loading of the cervical spine and may be stable or unstable.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Classify thoracolumbar fractures into the three primary types established by the AO system.
back:
• Type A: Vertebral body compression fractures.
• Type B: Distraction of anterior or posterior elements.
• Type C: Rotational injuries (often coexisting with A or B).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [The system developed by the AO... can be used to classify these fractures. There are three main injury types, A, B and C... Type A fractures are vertebral body compression fractures. Type B injuries involve distraction... type C injuries are rotational.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Contrast the anatomical level and mechanism of a Hangman’s fracture versus a Jefferson fracture.
back:
• Hangman’s: Traumatic spondylolisthesis of Axis (C2) on C3.
• Jefferson: Burst fracture of the Atlas (C1) ring.
• Mechanism: Hangman's is often hyperextension; Jefferson is axial loading.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 417 (Book Page): [Traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (hangman’s fracture). This is a traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 on C3.] Page 416 (Book Page): [Atlas fracture (Jefferson fracture). Fracture of the C1 ring is associated with axial loading.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: A patient wearing a lap-belt sustains a flexion-distraction injury at T11-L2. Identify this injury.
back:
• Diagnosis: Chance fracture.
• Mechanism: Flexion-distraction injury.
• Level: Commonly the thoracolumbar junction (T11-L2).
• Risk: Associated with duodenal, pancreatic, or aortic ruptures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Chance fractures are flexion–distraction injuries of the thoracolumbar junction and are classically associated with the use of lap belts.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: List the four primary patterns of subaxial cervical spine (C3-C7) injuries classified by mechanism.
back:
• Hyperflexion: Compression fractures.
• Axial compression: Burst fractures.
• Distraction-flexion: Facet subluxation/dislocation.
• Hyperextension: Teardrop fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): [The pattern of lower cervical spine injury depends on the mechanism of trauma. These include compression fractures (hyperflexion), burst fractures (axial compression), facet subluxation/dislocation injuries (distraction–flexion), teardrop fractures (hyperextension)]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: How are Odontoid peg fractures classified based on anatomical level?
back:
• Type I: Fracture of the tip of the dens.
• Type II: Fracture through the base of the dens (most common).
• Type III: Fracture extends into the body of the axis (C2).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 417 (Book Page): [Odontoid fractures. There are three types of odontoid peg fracture (Figure 30.27).]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: According to the three-column model, what specific finding classifies a spinal injury as unstable?
back:
• Definition: Injury involving two or more columns.
• Columns: Anterior, Middle, and Posterior.
• Clinical Significance: Predicts progressive deformity or neurological deficit.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 410 (Book Page): [The spine can be divided into three columns: anterior, middle and posterior... If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Classify the three directions of displacement in potentially fatal occipitoatlantal dislocations.
back:
• Anterior dislocation.
• Posterior dislocation.
• Vertical dislocation.
• Assessment: Powers' ratio is used to determine translation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 415 (Book Page): [Occipitoatlantal dislocation. This injury is usually caused by high-energy trauma and is often fatal. The dislocation may be anterior, posterior or vertical.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Why are the cervicothoracic and thoracolumbar junctions specifically prone to traumatic injury?
back:
• Reason: These are transitional zones.
• Level Change: Transition from a mobile section (cervical/lumbar) to a more fixed section (thoracic).
• Mechanical stress: Focal point for force concentration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 409 (Book Page): [The cervicothoracic and thoracolumbar junctions are transitional zones where the spine changes from a mobile section (cervical and lumbar) to a more fixed one (thoracic). These two areas are common sites of injury.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Which specific spinal assessment confirms rotational (Type C) injury at the thoracolumbar junction?
back:
• Clinical Sign: Multiple posterior rib fractures or rib dislocations at the injury level.
• Radiological Sign: Asymmetrical rotation of vertebral bodies on imaging.
• Risk: Associated with major vascular and pulmonary injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [Multiple posterior rib fractures and rib dislocations above and below a thoracic spinal injury signify a major rotational injury to the chest.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: What is the primary mechanism of injury for a Jefferson fracture of the C1 ring?
back:
● Axial loading of the cervical spine.
● May be stable or unstable based on transverse ligament integrity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 417 (Book Page): [Fracture of the C1 ring is associated with axial loading of the cervical spine and may be stable or unstable.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Which subaxial cervical spine injuries result from distraction–flexion versus hyperextension mechanisms?
back:
● Distraction–flexion: Facet subluxation/dislocation injuries.
● Hyperextension: Teardrop fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [These include... facet subluxation/dislocation injuries (distraction–flexion), teardrop fractures (hyperextension)]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: In the AO spine classification, differentiate Type B from Type C injuries by mechanism.
back:
● Type B: Distraction of the anterior or posterior elements.
● Type C: Rotational injuries (often coexist with A or B).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 420 (Book Page): [Type B injuries involve distraction of the anterior or posterior elements and type C injuries are rotational and often coexist with type A or type B injuries.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Identify the level and mechanism associated with seatbelt-induced "Chance fractures."
back:
● Level: Thoracolumbar junction (T11–L2).
● Mechanism: Flexion–distraction injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Chance fractures are flexion–distraction injuries of the thoracolumbar junction and are classically associated with the use of lap belts.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Define the anatomical level and pathological nature of a "Hangman’s fracture."
back:
● Level: Axis (C2) on C3.
● Pathology: Traumatic spondylolisthesis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): [Traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (hangman’s fracture) This is a traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 on C3.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: According to the three-column model, when is a spinal injury classified as unstable?
back:
● When two or more columns of the spine are injured.
● Columns include: Anterior, middle, and posterior.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 410 (Book Page): [If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable. The spine can be divided into three columns: anterior, middle and posterior.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Classify the three levels of odontoid fractures shown in the standard classification system.
back:
● Type I: Tip fracture.
● Type II: Fracture through the base of the dens (common).
● Type III: Fracture into the C2 body.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): [Types of odontoid fracture. Type I, Type II, Type III (as shown in Figure 30.27)]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: What radiographic feature distinguishes a lumbar burst fracture from a simple compression fracture?
back:
● Widening of the distance between the pedicles (interpedicular distance).
● Often associated with retropulsion of bone fragments into the canal.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Burst fractures... are characterised by widening of the distance between the pedicles and can be associated with retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Define "spinal stability" regarding physiological loads and neurological function.
back:
● The ability to withstand physiological loads with acceptable pain.
● Prevents progressive deformity or neurological deficit.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 410 (Book Page): [Spinal stability is the ability of the spine to withstand physiological loads with acceptable pain, avoiding progressive deformity or neurological deficit.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Why are the cervicothoracic and thoracolumbar junctions common sites for traumatic injury?
back: ● They are transitional zones where the spine changes from a mobile section to a fixed one.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 409 (Book Page): [The cervicothoracic and thoracolumbar junctions are transitional zones where the spine changes from a mobile section (cervical and lumbar) to a more fixed one (thoracic).]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: How is spinal stability classified according to the three-column model?
back:
• The spine is divided into anterior, middle, and posterior columns.
• Injury to two or more columns renders the spine unstable.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [The spine can be divided into three columns: anterior, middle and posterior (Figure 30.7). If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: What is the mechanism of injury and anatomical site for a Jefferson fracture?
back:
• Mechanism: Axial loading of the cervical spine.
• Site: Fracture of the C1 ring (Atlas).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Atlas fracture (Jefferson fracture). Fracture of the C1 ring is associated with axial loading of the cervical spine and may be stable or unstable.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Distinguish between AO types A, B, and C for thoracic and thoracolumbar fractures.
back:
• Type A: Vertebral body compression fractures.
• Type B: Distraction of anterior or posterior elements.
• Type C: Rotational injuries (highest risk of neurological damage).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): [Type A fractures are vertebral body compression fractures. Type B injuries involve distraction of the anterior or posterior elements and type C injuries are rotational and often coexist with type A or type B injuries.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: A patient with lap-belt bruising has a flexion-distraction injury at T11-L2. Diagnosis?
back:
• Chance fracture.
• Highly associated with visceral injuries, including duodenal, pancreatic, and aortic ruptures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page)-401: [Chance fractures are flexion–distraction injuries of the thoracolumbar junction and are classically associated with the use of lap belts... Duodenal, pancreatic and/or aortic ruptures are also associated with these injuries.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: What is the pharmacological status of corticosteroids in acute traumatic spinal cord injury?
back:
• No longer indicated for acute trauma due to lack of efficacy evidence.
• Only indicated for non-traumatic compression (e.g., malignancy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support efficacy. Steroids do have a role in non-traumatic spinal cord compression, e.g. malignant spinal cord compression.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Identify the specific mechanisms for Burst and Teardrop subaxial (C3-C7) injuries.
back:
• Burst fractures: Axial compression.
• Teardrop fractures: Hyperextension.
• Facet subluxation: Distraction-flexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 398 (Book Page): [These include compression fractures (hyperflexion), burst fractures (axial compression), facet subluxation/dislocation injuries (distraction–flexion), teardrop fractures (hyperextension) and fracture of posterior elements.]

category: Classify spinal and cervical spine trauma injuries by mechanism and level
front: Q: Define Hangman's fracture including its anatomical level and structural injury.
back:
• Traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 on C3.
• Involves distraction and extension forces causing bilateral fractures of the C2 pars interarticularis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (hangman’s fracture). This is a traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2 on C3.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: Define the primary injury process in spinal cord trauma.
back: The direct mechanical insult and damage to the neural elements occurring at the exact time of the initial impact.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [The primary injury: This is the direct insult to the neural elements and occurs at the time of the initial injury.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: What is the mechanism behind the secondary injury process in spinal cord trauma?
back: A biochemical cascade involving haemorrhage, oedema, and ischaemia that develops in the hours and days following the initial impact.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [The secondary injury: Haemorrhage, oedema and ischaemia result in a biochemical cascade that causes the secondary injury.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: Which systemic physiological states can exacerbate the secondary injury cascade in spinal trauma?
back:
● Hypotension
● Hypoxia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [This [secondary injury] may be accentuated by hypotension, hypoxia, spinal instability and/or persistent compression of the neural elements.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: What is the pathophysiology of spinal shock?
back: A temporary physiological disorganisation of spinal cord function occurring within minutes of injury, independent of anatomical cord transection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Spinal shock is a temporary physiological disorganisation of spinal cord function that starts within minutes following the injury.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: List the clinical hallmarks of spinal shock.
back:
● Flaccid paralysis
● Decreased muscle tone
● Hyporeflexia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [It [spinal shock] is characterised by paralysis, decreased tone and hyporeflexia.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: Which reflex return signifies the resolution of spinal shock?
back: The bulbocavernosus reflex.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Once it [spinal shock] has resolved the bulbocavernosus reflex (Figure 30.39) returns.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: Describe the physiological mechanism behind neurogenic shock.
back: Loss of sympathetic outflow leading to unopposed vagal tone, typically occurring in injuries at or above T5.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [This [neurogenic shock] is due to unopposed vagal tone resulting from cervical spinal cord injury at or above the level of sympathetic outflow (T5).]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: What is the standard clinical finding for distinguishing an incomplete spinal cord injury?
back: Preservation of perianal sensation (indicating some sacral sparing).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 403 (Book Page): [A spinal cord injury is incomplete when there is preservation of perianal sensation.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: How does persistent compression impact the spinal cord pathophysiology?
back: It acts as a mechanical driver for secondary injury by causing ongoing ischaemia and feeding the biochemical destruction cascade.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Management of spinal cord injury must focus on minimising secondary injury... [which] may be accentuated by... persistent compression of the neural elements.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: In the three-column model, how many columns must be injured for the spine to be considered unstable?
back: Two or more columns (anterior, middle, or posterior).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: Define 'primary injury' in the context of traumatic spinal cord injury pathophysiology.
back:
* The direct mechanical insult to the neural elements.
* Occurs at the exact moment of initial trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [The primary injury. This is the direct insult to the neural elements and occurs at the time of the initial injury.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: Describe the biochemical progression involved in the secondary injury phase of spinal cord trauma.
back:
* A biochemical cascade following initial trauma.
* Involves haemorrhage, oedema, and ischaemia resulting in neural damage extension.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [The secondary injury. Haemorrhage, oedema and ischaemia result in a biochemical cascade that causes the secondary injury.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: Contrast neurogenic shock and spinal shock based on mechanism and physiological presentation.
back:
* Neurogenic shock: Loss of sympathetic outflow (T5+), presenting with hypotension/bradycardia.
* Spinal shock: Temporary physiological disorganisation (paralysis/hyporeflexia).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Neurogenic shock... due to unopposed vagal tone... Spinal shock is a temporary physiological disorganisation of spinal cord function... characterised by paralysis, decreased tone and hyporeflexia.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: A patient presents with hypotension and bradycardia following a C6 injury. Identify the specific mechanism.
back:
* Neurogenic shock.
* Caused by unopposed vagal tone due to injury above the level of sympathetic outflow (T5).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Neurogenic shock. This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries. This is due to unopposed vagal tone resulting from cervical spinal cord injury at or above the level of sympathetic outflow (T5).]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: What is the current clinical consensus regarding corticosteroid use in acute spinal cord trauma?
back:
* No longer indicated for acute injury.
* Research lacks evidence to support clinical efficacy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 417 (Book Page): [Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support efficacy.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: Which specific reflex return signifies the resolution of the spinal shock phase?
back:
* The bulbocavernosus reflex.
* Recovery marks the end of temporary physiological disorganisation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Spinal shock... length of effect is variable, but it can last 6 weeks or longer... Once it has resolved the bulbocavernosus reflex... returns.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: List four physiological factors that exacerbate the secondary injury cascade in spinal trauma.
back:
* Hypotension.
* Hypoxia.
* Spinal instability.
* Persistent compression of neural elements.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [This may be accentuated by hypotension, hypoxia, spinal instability and/or persistent compression of the neural elements.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: Define 'incomplete' spinal cord injury based on the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) standards.
back:
* Preservation of any perianal sensation.
* Categorized as ASIA Impairment Scale B, C, or D.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [A spinal cord injury is incomplete when there is preservation of perianal sensation.]

category: Describe the pathophysiology of spinal cord injury, including primary and secondary injury processes
front: Q: Explain the lateral spinothalamic tract's function and decussation pattern within the spinal cord.
back:
* Transmits pain and temperature sensation.
* Crosses to the opposite side within three levels of cord entry.
