- E: Exposure and environment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [The primary survey aims to identify and manage the most immediately life-threatening pathologies frst and follows cABCDE.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What are the target systolic blood pressure and physiological rationale for time-limited permissive hypotension in trauma patients?
back:
- Target: 70–90 mmHg (or >90 mmHg if head injury suspected).
- Rationale: Maintains perfusion to vital organs (brain, heart, kidneys) while preventing haemodilution, ARDS, and worsened coagulopathy from excessive crystalloids.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected... Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Why is Whole-body CT (WBCT) considered the gold standard over selective scanning for blunt trauma assessment?
back:
- It provides rapid diagnosis for patients with multiple injuries or deranged physiology.
- There is no clinical role for scanning selective systems in severely injured patients; WBCT ensures no hidden haemorrhage sites are missed.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology... There is no role for scanning selective body systems in the severely injured trauma patient.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: How must exsanguinating limb haemorrhage be managed if direct pressure and dressings fail during the 'c' stage?
back:
- Apply a proximal tourniquet immediately.
- Record the application time on the patient.
- Arrange urgent surgical control to reperfuse the ischaemic limb.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [Failure to control bleeding in the limb by direct pressure with surgical dressings should be followed by the application of a tourniquet proximal to the wound... the length of time for which the tourniquet is applied must be recorded on the patient and the patient requires urgent surgical control of the bleeding in order to reperfuse the limb.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: State the intravenous dosing regimen and optimal timing for Tranexamic acid (TXA) administration in trauma.
back:
- Dose: 1g IV over 10 minutes, followed by 1g IV over 8 hours.
- Timing: Ideally within the first hour; must not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... It needs to be administered as early as possible and ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What venous lactate thresholds guide the selection between Early Total Care (ETC) and Damage Control Surgery (DCS)?
back:
- <2 mmol/L: Indicates successful resuscitation; suitable for ETC.
- >3 mmol/L: Indicates under-resuscitation; consider DCS if surgery is urgent.
- >5 mmol/L: Strong indication for DCS.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.6 Venous lactate is an essential marker of resuscitation: <2 mmol/L – ETC; 2–3 mmol/L – look at the trend...; >3 mmol/L – may be under-resuscitated; should either have further resuscitation or DCS if surgery is urgent; >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What are the application criteria and the correct anatomical placement for a pelvic binder in trauma stabilization?
back:
- Criteria: All haemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma (until fracture is radiographically excluded).
- Placement: Centred over the greater trochanters.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [A pelvic binder should be applied to all haemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma and not removed until after a pelvic fracture has been excluded... A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Why is formal log-rolling deferred for blunt trauma patients during the primary survey, and what is the exception?
back:
- Reason: It provides minimal clinical info and may harm pelvic fracture patients by disrupting established blood clots.
- Exception: Penetrating trauma patients, to identify posterior torso wounds.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [Log-rolling patients with severe pelvic fractures may harm the patient by disturbing established blood clots... Formal log-rolling... should be deferred until after the primary survey, with the exception of patients with penetrating trauma, where it is important to identify the presence of a posterior torso wound.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Define the physiological components of the trauma 'triad of death' and its implication for surgical strategy.
back:
- Components: Acidosis, Coagulopathy, and Hypothermia.
- Implication: If present, complex reconstructions are deferred for Damage Control Surgery (DCS) to prevent multiorgan failure and death.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [...the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death. Consequently, surgical interventions in the trauma patient with physiological abnormality are limited to rapid life- and limb-saving procedures...]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: What blood product ratio is used in the massive transfusion protocol for severely injured hypovolaemic patients?
back:
A ratio of 1:1:1, consisting of:
- 1 unit Packed Red Cells.
- 1 unit Fresh-Frozen Plasma (FFP).
- 1 unit Platelets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What is the mandatory definitive surgical management for confirmed native joint septic arthritis?
back:
• Prompt formal joint washout (irrigation)
• Removal of all purulent material
• Synovectomy if aggressive synovitis or erosions exist
• Joint splintage and antibiotic therapy
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [the treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint and appropriate adequate antibiotic therapy... a formal washout is mandatory]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Which specific chest drainage thresholds indicate an urgent referral for thoracotomy in massive haemothorax?
back:
• Initial drainage >1500 mL of blood
• Ongoing haemorrhage >200 mL/h over 3–4 hours
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Define the goal and timing of Early Total Care (ETC) in definitive trauma management.
back:
• Definitive management of all injuries within 36 hours
• Stabilization of all unstable long bone, spinal, and pelvic fractures
• Reduces pulmonary complications and ICU stay
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [For musculoskeletal injuries, ETC allows defnitive fxation of all unstable long bone, spinal and pelvic fractures within 36 hours of injury. This... allows early mobilisation of the patient and reduces pulmonary complications]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: A patient with a tibial fracture develops pain out of proportion. What urgent referral is indicated?
back:
• Urgent referral for definitive fasciotomy
• Split all dressings/casts to skin
• Elevate extremity to heart level
• Monitor pressures if diagnosis is uncertain
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Emergency treatment involves splitting casts and/or dressings to the skin and elevating the extremity... perform defnitive treatment with fasciotomies.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What are the immediate management priorities for an open fracture in the emergency department?
back:
• Photograph wound; remove macroscopic dirt
• Sterile moist saline dressing and splintage
• Prompt broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
• Tetanus prophylaxis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Apply a moist saline dressing to the wound. It is acceptable to irrigate... Administer intravenous antibiotics according to local protocols. It has been shown that early administration of intravenous antibiotics is one of the most important steps.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What is the definitive clinical management for a suspected tension pneumothorax before radiology?
back:
• Immediate needle decompression in the 'safe triangle'
• Rapid insertion of an intercostal chest tube
• Never delay for radiological confirmation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation... Treatment consists of immediate decompression... in the safe triangle]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: How is a 'white pulseless hand' managed in a pediatric supracondylar humeral fracture?
back:
• Classed as a surgical emergency
• Immediate fracture reduction
• Urgent surgical vessel exploration if pulse fails to return post-reduction
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 441 (Book Page): [The white pulseless hand is a surgical emergency and requires immediate attention, assessment and urgent reduction. If the pulse does not return with reduction, then the vessels should be explored]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: What is the only absolute surgical indication for urgent referral in spinal trauma?
back: • Deteriorating neurological function
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 415 (Book Page): [The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: When is Damage Control Surgery (DCS) indicated over definitive reconstructive procedures?
back:
• Presence of the 'triad of death': acidosis, coagulopathy, and hypothermia
• Hemodynamic instability
• Inability to achieve immediate surgical haemostasis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop... Consequently, surgical interventions... are limited to rapid life- and limb-saving procedures: control of haemorrhage, decompression of cavities]

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
front: Q: Which clinical findings mandate urgent neurosurgical evacuation of an extradural haematoma?
back:
• Rapid neurological deterioration
• Comatose state
• Large bleeds seen on CT (lentiform shape)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Signifcant extradural haematoma mandates urgent transfer to the most accessible neurosurgical facility for immediate evacuation in deteriorating or comatose patients or those with large bleeds]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What is the gold standard radiological investigation for a severely injured adult blunt trauma patient?
back:
- Whole-body CT (WBCT) from head to pelvis.
- Requires intravenous (IV) contrast.
- Performed as early as possible during resuscitation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): WBCT from the head to pelvis with IV contrast is the gold standard investigation of the severely injured adult blunt trauma patient

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Which radiological findings on chest radiograph and CT confirm a traumatic thoracic aortic disruption?
back:
- Chest X-ray: Widened mediastinum.
- CT: Direct visualization of aortic wall disruption.
- Essential to control systolic BP before confirmatory imaging.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): The most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum. The diagnosis is confrmed by a CT scan of the mediastinum.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What is the gold standard radiological investigation for diagnosing mechanical spinal trauma?
back:
- Computed tomography (CT) scanning.
- Requires two-dimensional (2D) reconstruction.
- Superior to plain films for bony detail.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction remains the gold standard in spinal trauma

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: How is spinal stability defined radiologically using the three-column model?
back:
- Spine divided into anterior, middle, and posterior columns.
- Instability is confirmed if two or more columns are injured.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What are the specific indications for Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) in spinal trauma assessment?
back:
- Presence of neurological deficits.
- Requirement to assess ligamentous structures.
- Suspicion of spinal cord contusion or compression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): MRI is indicated in all patients with neurological defcit and where assessment of ligamentous structures is important

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What are the essential 'Rule of 2s' for the radiographic evaluation of extremity trauma?
back:
- 2 views: Orthogonal planes (90 degrees).
- 2 joints: Joint above and below injury.
- 2 occasions: Repeat after 10–14 days for occult fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 429 (Book Page): The rule of 2s should be remembered: 2 views... 2 joints... 2 occasions

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Which investigation is mandatory to exclude occult vascular injury in a suspected knee dislocation?
back:
- Computed Tomography (CT) Angiogram.
- Necessary because palpable pulses do not exclude intimal faps or thrombosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): In injuries commonly associated with vascular injury, such as knee dislocations, occult injury should be actively excluded with an angiogram.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What specific measurements on a lateral cervical spine radiograph define mechanical instability?
back:
- Sagittal translation: >3.5 mm.
- Sagittal angulation: >11° compared to the adjacent level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 392 (Book Page): 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What are the three primary clinical indications for performing eFAST in trauma?
back:
- Detection of intraperitoneal hemorrhage (free fuid).
- Identification of pericardial tamponade.
- Diagnosis of pneumothorax or hemothorax.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): eFAST is becoming the most common investigation... looking for a cardiac tamponade or free blood and air in the hemithoraces, and assessment for blood in the abdominal cavity

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Why is CT preferred over plain X-ray for definitive assessment of pelvic ring stability?
back:
- Precise visualization of fracture anatomy.
- CT angiography identifies active arterial vs. venous bleeding.
- Binders do not obscure CT detail.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): CT is the diagnostic modality of choice... CT angiography is particularly helpful in providing details of both the anatomy of the fracture and the origin of the bleeding

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What is the gold standard radiological investigation for a stable adult with signs of multiple blunt trauma?
back:
* Whole-body CT (WBCT) with IV contrast
* Scans from head to pelvis
* Provides rapid identification of life-threatening pathology
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: In Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), which radiological modality is most sensitive for evaluating Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI)?
back: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is more sensitive than CT, especially in patients who fail to improve neurologically.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive and is employed to evaluate for difuse axonal injury in patients who fail to improve neurologically.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Distinguish between the standard radiological views required for midface fractures versus mandibular fractures.
back:
* Midface: Occipitomental (OM) views (10° and 30°)
* Mandible: Orthopantomogram (OPT) and Posteroanterior (PA) views
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 408 (Book Page): [If a mandibular fracture is suspected, an orthopantomogram (OPT) and a posteroanterior (PA) radiograph... For a suspected midface fracture, occipitomental (OM) radiographs at 10° and 30° should be obtained.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: In a hemodynamically stable patient with a pelvic fracture, which investigation differentiates arterial from venous bleeding?
back: CT angiography provides anatomical fracture details and identifies the specific origin of bleeding (venous vs. arterial).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [CT is the diagnostic modality of choice in the physiologically non-compromised patient, and CT angiography is particularly helpful in providing details of both the anatomy of the fracture and the origin of the bleeding (venous or arterial).]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What must be administered during whole-body CT scanning to ensure adequate visualization of vascular and solid organ injury?
back: Intravenous (IV) contrast is mandatory to achieve gold-standard sensitivity in patients with multiple injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: State the 'Rule of 2s' required for adequate radiographic evaluation of extremity trauma.
back:
* 2 views (orthogonal planes)
* 2 joints (above and below injury)
* 2 occasions (repeat if symptoms persist)
* 2 sides (comparison)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [The rule of 2s should be remembered: 2 views... 2 joints... 2 occasions... 2 sides]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Which radiographic finding on an erect chest film is most suggestive of traumatic thoracic aortic disruption?
back: A widened mediastinum; this must be confirmed by CT scanning of the mediastinum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: How is a suspected scaphoid fracture radiologically managed if the initial scaphoid view radiographs are normal?
back:
* Immobilize the wrist in a cast
* Repeat scaphoid view radiographs in 10–14 days
* Consider MRI or bone scan if facilities allow
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [The standard protocol of a suspected scaphoid fracture is to immobilise the wrist and examine again 10–14 days later. If tenderness remains, repeat the scaphoid views.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Why is clinical diagnosis superior to CT scanning for detecting acute diaphragmatic rupture without visceral herniation?
back: CT scans lack sensitivity (positive predictive value) for isolated ruptures; these often remain hidden unless abdominal contents migrate into the chest.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [although the presence of an isolated rupture of the diaphragm with migration of abdominal contents into the chest can be detected by CT scan, in injury without migration the diagnosis will not be obvious.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What is the gold standard radiological modality for assessing fracture stability and bony anatomy in spinal trauma?
back: Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional (2D) reconstruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction remains the gold standard in spinal trauma]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
coreConcept: Gold Standard Investigation for Major Trauma
front: Q: What is the gold standard radiological investigation for adult blunt trauma patients with deranged physiology?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast. It should be obtained as early as possible during resuscitation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: State the "Rule of 2s" used for standard radiographic assessment of extremity trauma.
back:
● 2 views (orthogonal planes)
● 2 joints (above and below injury)
● 2 occasions (repeat in 10–14 days if symptoms persist)
● 2 sides (comparison in children)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [The rule of 2s should be remembered: 2 views... 2 joints... 2 occasions... 2 sides]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Which imaging modality is the gold standard for diagnosing bony injury in spinal trauma?
back: Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction. It is indicated for all patients with suspected or visible injuries on plain films.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction remains the gold standard in spinal trauma]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: How is a stable hip distinguished from a dislocatable hip on dynamic ultrasound in infants?
back: Stable hips have a high alpha angle and a Morin index ≥50%. Unstable (Barlow positive) hips show a low alpha angle and <50% head coverage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): [Normal hip with a high α angle and a Morin index of 50%... Grossly dysplastic hip with a low α angle and a Morin index of <50%]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Why is an axillary view mandatory in radiographic assessment of the shoulder?
back: It is the only reliable view to identify a posterior glenohumeral dislocation, which is frequently missed on standard AP and lateral scapula views.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 420 (Book Page): [Axillary view – true value of the axillary view shown with obvious posterior dislocation of the glenohumeral joint.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What is the specific radiological requirement to exclude bladder rupture during trauma CT?
back: A CT cystogram using a minimum of 300 mL of contrast instilled into the bladder via a urethral catheter. Small volumes may fail to show leaks.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [For assessment of bladder injury a cystogram should be performed at the time of CT. A minimum of 300 mL of contrast is instilled into the bladder via a urethral catheter.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: In a child suspected of Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE), which radiographic view is most sensitive?
back: The 'frog' lateral pelvic radiograph. Slips are often more obvious on the lateral view and can be missed on standard AP views.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [Displacement is often more obvious on a lateral view and the diagnosis can be missed if only the anteroposterior radiograph is checked.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Which radiographic displacement measurement indicates true pelvic ring instability in an 'open book' injury?
back: Symphysis pubis widening (anterior pelvis displacement) greater than 2 cm indicates at least partial instability and risk of venous plexus tearing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Displacement of the anterior pelvis by greater than 2 cm indicates at least partial instability.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What radiographic finding on the lateral cervical spine is indicative of soft-tissue instability?
back:
● Sagittal translation ≥3.5 mm
● Sagittal angulation >11° compared to the adjacent level
● Prevertebral soft-tissue swelling (indicates hematoma)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): [3.5 mm of sagittal translation... sagittal angulation of >11°... prevertebral soft-tissue swelling]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Identify the pathognomonic radiological signs of non-accidental injury (NAI) in an infant's long bones.
back: Metaphyseal 'corner' or 'bucket-handle' fractures. These are highly specific for child abuse/neglect.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [metaphyseal corner fractures that are considered to be pathognomonic of non-accidental injury.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Which specific imaging modality is considered the gold standard for assessing a physiologically deranged blunt trauma patient?
back: Whole-body Computed Tomography (WBCT) from head to pelvis with IV contrast. It is performed early to identify life-threatening pathology during resuscitation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: How does Computed Tomography identify impending brain herniation in patients with expanding intracranial haematomas?
back: CT visualises 'mass effect' characterized by compression of surrounding brain tissue and significant midline shift towards the opposite hemisphere.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... A mass effect may be evident, with compression of the surrounding brain and midline shift.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Contrast the diagnostic utility of eFAST against CT for solid organ injuries in abdominal trauma.
back: eFAST detects free fluid (>100mL) but has low sensitivity (29–35%) for organ injury without haemoperitoneum; CT is superior for specific organ and retroperitoneal diagnosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): [Hollow viscus injury and solid organ injury are diffcult to diagnose... eFAST has a low sensitivity (29–35%) for organ injury without haemoperitoneum.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: In a hemodynamically unstable patient needing immediate laparotomy, which two initial radiographs must be obtained?
back: 1. Immediate chest radiograph (excludes catastrophic intrathoracic haemorrhage). 2. Immediate pelvic radiograph (excludes fracture; essential despite use of pelvic binder).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [An immediate chest radiograph will exclude catastrophic intrathoracic haemorrhage. An immediate pelvic radiograph is essential but should not delay transfer to the operating theatre.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What radiological study identifies urethral damage in male patients presenting with a high-riding prostate?
back: A retrograde urethrogram. This identifies urethral avulsion or damage before further urological instrumentation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [Evidence of perineal injury or haematuria mandates radiological evaluation of the urinary tract from below upwards (retrograde urethrogram followed by cystogram).]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Identify the gold standard radiological investigation for assessing stability in patients with suspected spinal trauma.
back: Computed Tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction. Plain radiographs are limited as they miss approximately 15% of cervical injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 414 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction remains the gold standard in spinal trauma... Plain cervical spine radiographs fail to identity 15% of injuries.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Applying the 'Rule of 2s,' what constitutes a complete radiographic evaluation of an extremity fracture?
back: 1. Two views (orthogonal planes). 2. Two joints (above and below). 3. Two occasions (initial and delayed/repeat). 4. Two sides (comparative, especially in children).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 440 (Book Page): [The rule of 2s should be remembered: 2 views... 2 joints... 2 occasions... 2 sides.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Which radiological findings on a chest radiograph and CT suggest traumatic aortic disruption?
back: X-ray shows a widened mediastinum; CT confirms disruption distal to the ligamentum arteriosum, often following high-energy falls or collisions.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum... The diagnosis is confrmed by a CT scan of the mediastinum.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Under what specific clinical circumstance is Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) indicated in spinal trauma assessments?
back: MRI is mandatory for all patients presenting with neurological deficits or when assessment of ligamentous structures is essential.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 414 (Book Page): [MRI is indicated in all patients with neurological defcit and where assessment of ligamentous structures is important.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Which specific measurement on an AP pelvic radiograph indicates partial instability in a lateral compression injury?
back: Displacement of the anterior pelvis by greater than 2 cm. This suggests the pelvis is no longer fully stable.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [Displacement of the anterior pelvis by greater than 2 cm indicates at least partial instability.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What is the gold standard radiological investigation for an adult blunt trauma patient with multi-system injuries?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from head to pelvis with intravenous contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Why must pelvic stability be assessed radiographically rather than by manual 'springing' in trauma?
back: Manual testing disrupts established blood clots and provides no useful clinical information; imaging is the only safe diagnostic method.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Mechanical testing of the pelvis in the emergency room (‘springing the pelvis’) adds no useful clinical examination and will disrupt any blood clot that has formed around a pelvic fracture. It should never be performed – a pelvic fracture should always be diagnosed radiographically.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Contrast the CT appearances of acute extradural haematoma and acute subdural haematoma.
back: Extradural: Lentiform (biconvex), hyperdense lesion constrained by dural adherence. Subdural: Diffuse, concave (crescentic) appearance expanding across the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... Page 388 (Book Page): Since the dura is not as adherent to the brain as it is to the skull, subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: In an unstable patient requiring immediate laparotomy, which two radiographs must be obtained before transfer to theatre?
back: 1. Immediate chest radiograph (excludes catastrophic intrathoracic hemorrhage). 2. Immediate pelvic radiograph.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [An immediate chest radio- graph will exclude catastrophic intrathoracic haemorrhage. An immediate pelvic radiograph is essential but should not delay transfer to the operating theatre.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What is the initial radiological marker of traumatic thoracic aortic disruption on an erect chest X-ray?
back: A widened mediastinum (which necessitates confirmation via CT of the mediastinum).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum. The diagnosis is confrmed by a CT scan of the mediastinum]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: According to NICE guidelines, what GCS threshold necessitates a CT brain within 1 hour of head injury?
back: GCS < 13 at any point, or GCS < 15 at two hours post-injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour: GCS <13 at any point; GCS <15 at 2 hours]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Why is eFAST considered unreliable for ruling out retroperitoneal hemorrhage or hollow viscus injury?
back: It cannot visualize the retroperitoneum, requires >100 mL of free fluid for detection, and cannot directly identify visceral perforation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): [Utilisation of eFAST: Will not reliably detect less than 100 mL of free blood; Does not directly identify injury to hollow viscus; Is unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: List the sequential components of the primary survey in severe trauma management.
back:
• c: Control massive external haemorrhage
• A: Airway with cervical spine protection
• B: Breathing and ventilation
• C: Circulation and haemorrhage control
• D: Disability (neurological status)
• E: Exposure and environment
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.4 The cABCDE of trauma care ● c – Control of massive external haemorrhage ● A – Airway with cervical spine protection ● B – Breathing and ventilation ● C – Circulation and haemorrhage control ● D – Disability (neurological status) ● E – Exposure (assess for other injuries)]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Explain the physiological rationale and target for 'permissive hypotension' in initial trauma resuscitation.
back:
• Rationale: Prevents haemodilution, coagulopathy, and ARDS by avoiding excessive IV fluids.
• Target: Systolic BP 70–90 mmHg for short periods.
• Exception: Target >90 mmHg if head injury is suspected.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected. Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Contrast the role of crystalloids versus blood products in severe hypovolaemic trauma resuscitation.
back:
• Blood Products: Primary choice; given in a 1:1:1 ratio (packed cells:FFP:platelets).
• Crystalloids: Limited role; used in small boluses only while awaiting blood products.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.2 ● Severely hypovolaemic trauma patients should be resuscitated using blood and blood products ● The only role for crystalloids in the initial management of severely hypovolaemic patients is for the administration of small quantities to maintain blood pressure while waiting for blood products to become available]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: A blunt trauma patient presents haemodynamically unstable with a suspected pelvic fracture. State the immediate stabilization step.
back:
• Action: Apply a pelvic binder or sheet immediately.
• Position: Place at the level of the greater trochanters.
• Constraint: Do not remove until pelvic fracture is radiographically excluded.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Any patient undergoing immediate trauma laparotomy after blunt trauma without a WBCT scan should have a pelvic binder applied and not removed until a pelvic fracture is excluded... A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Outline the dosage and administration criteria for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in adult trauma patients.
back:
• Dose: 1g IV over 10 minutes, then 1g over 8 hours.
• Criteria: Suspected significant haemorrhage, systolic BP <110 mmHg, or HR >110 bpm.
• Timing: Must be administered within 3 hours of injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours. Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have signifcant haemorrhage, including those with a systolic blood pressure of <110 mmHg or a pulse of over 110 per minute... the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: List the clinical triggers for an enhanced 'Code Red' trauma team activation.
back:
• Haemodynamic instability (shock).
• Acute airway compromise.
• Pre-hospital initiation of massive transfusion protocols.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): [Patients identifed before reaching hospital as being haemodynamically unstable or having acute airway compromise may initiate ‘code red’, triggering the automatic attendance of the most senior clinicians... and prehospital activation of massive transfusion protocols.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: State the clinical indications for performing a Whole-Body CT (WBCT) in a trauma patient.
back:
• Symptoms or signs of multiple injury.
• Deranged physiology.
• Exclusion: Do not perform based on the mechanism of injury alone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology, but note that WBCT should not be performed on the basis of the mechanism of injury alone.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Differentiate the findings of Tension Pneumothorax from Pericardial Tamponade in a shocked trauma patient.
back:
• Tension Pneumothorax: Distended neck veins, unilateral absent breath sounds, hyper-resonance.
• Pericardial Tamponade: Distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, bilateral breath sounds present.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Pericardial tamponade needs to be diferentiated from a tension pneumothorax in the shocked patient with distended neck veins... hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds over the afected hemithorax.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: Identify the components of the 'triad of death' addressed by damage control surgery.
back:
• Acidosis
• Coagulopathy
• Hypothermia
• Significance: This cycle leads to multiorgan failure in physiologically compromised patients.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Prolonged procedures result in additional trauma and further immune and physiological derangement; the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
front: Q: State the venous lactate levels used to distinguish suitability for Early Total Care (ETC) versus Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
back:
• <2 mmol/L: Suitable for Early Total Care (ETC).
• >3 mmol/L: Under-resuscitated; consider DCS if surgery is urgent.
• >5 mmol/L: Direct indication for Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.6 Venous lactate is an essential marker of resuscitation ● <2 mmol/L – ETC ● 2–3 mmol/L – look at the trend ● >3 mmol/L – may be under-resuscitated; should either have further resuscitation or DCS if surgery is urgent ● >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the mandatory initial management step for all suspected spine trauma patients?
back: Immediate immobilization using full spinal precautions (cervical collar, blocks, and straps) on the assumption that an injury exists until proven otherwise.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): [The spine should initially be immobilised using full spinal precautions, on the assumption that every trauma patient has a spinal injury until proven otherwise.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Distinguish neurogenic shock from hypovolaemic shock in a spinal trauma patient.
back: Neurogenic shock presents with hypotension, bradycardia (loss of sympathetic tone), and warm peripheries, whereas hypovolaemic shock typically shows tachycardia and cold, clammy peripheries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Neurogenic shock. This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries. This is due to unopposed vagal tone resulting from cervical spinal cord injury]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Why is imaging of the entire spine required if a single spinal fracture is identified?
back: There is a 10–15% incidence of finding a second non-contiguous spinal fracture at a remote level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 392 (Book Page): [If a spinal fracture is identifed then further imaging of the whole spine is required because there is a 15% incidence of a further spinal fracture.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the gold standard imaging investigation for identifying bony spinal trauma?
back: Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction remains the gold standard in spinal trauma and is indicated for patients with suspected or visible injuries on plain radiographs]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Describe the current consensus on using corticosteroids in acute traumatic spinal cord injury.
back: Corticosteroids are no longer indicated due to a lack of evidence for clinical efficacy in acute spinal cord trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support efcacy.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What are the cardinal features and common triggers of autonomic dysreflexia?
back: Features: Paroxysmal hypertension, bradycardia, and headache. Triggers: Bladder distension or rectal loading (faecal impaction) in injuries above T6.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): [Autonomic dysrefexia... paroxysmal syndrome of hypertension, hyperhidrosis (above the level of injury), bradycardia, fushing and headache... most commonly triggered by bladder distension or rectal loading]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
coreConcept: Prevention of Pressure Ulcers in SCI
front: Q: Why should spinal boards be used only for patient transfer and not long-term immobilization?
back: They cause rapid skin breakdown and pressure ulcers (sores), especially in insensate patients.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): [Spinal boards lead to skin breakdown in insensate patients... They should only be used for transferring patients.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
coreConcept: Clinical Signs of Severe Cord Injury
front: Q: A patient presents with priapism following high-velocity trauma. What does this indicate?
back: Priapism is a strong clinical predictor of severe spinal cord injury, even in intubated or unconscious patients.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Priapism is a strong predictor of severe cord injury even in intubated patients.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the clinical significance of the bulbocavernosus reflex in spinal trauma?
back: Its return signifies the resolution of spinal shock; if the patient remains paralyzed afterward, the cord injury is confirmed as complete.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Spinal shock is a temporary physiological disorganisation of spinal cord function... Once it has resolved the bulbocavernosus refex returns.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Describe the clinical presentation of post-traumatic syringomyelia.
back: Occurs years later with segmental pain at/above the injury level, sensory loss, progressive weakness, or increased spasticity due to intramedullary cavities.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): [Post-traumatic syringomyelia... clinically, patients present with segmental pain at or above the level of injury, sensory loss, progressive asymmetrical weakness or increased spasticity.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the priority for cervical spine management during 'Airway' (A) survey in trauma?
back: Immediate immobilization and protection using a hard collar and blocks until a spinal injury is radiographically excluded.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [All trauma patients should have their cervical spine immobilised and protected throughout.] ... Page 377 (Book Page): [Patients are managed with cervical spine protection (cervical collar and blocks)]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the correct method for moving a patient during primary survey to exclude spinal injury?
back: Protection of the thoracolumbar spine using standard log roll techniques or a 20° roll with inline spinal stabilization if a pelvic fracture is suspected.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [protection of the thoracolumbar spine using standard log roll techniques until a spinal injury has been excluded.] Page 378 (Book Page): [If patients need to be moved... a 20° roll with inline spinal stabilisation should be used.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Which imaging is the current gold standard for rapidly identifying spinal pathology in polytrauma patients?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from the head to the pelvis with IV contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury] ... [Early WBCT scan will rapidly identify the majority of intracranial and spinal pathology.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Which specific physical finding in an unconscious patient is a strong predictor of severe spinal cord injury?
back: Priapism.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Priapism is a strong predictor of severe cord injury even in intubated patients.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What are the hemodynamic targets (MAP and SBP) in the initial management of spinal cord injury?
back:
● MAP: 80–90 mmHg
● SBP: >90 mmHg (if head injury suspected/present)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.] Page 389 (Book Page): [MAP = 80–90 mmHg]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: How is the severity of spinal cord injury graded using the ASIA Impairment Scale?
back:
● A: Complete injury
● B: Sensation present, motor absent
● C: Motor present (grade <3/5)
● D: Motor present (grade ≥3/5)
● E: Normal function
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): [A: complete spinal cord injury; B: sensation present, motor absent; C: sensation present, motor present but not useful (MRC grade <3/5); D: sensation present, motor useful (MRC grade ≥3/5); E: normal function.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Define the clinical components of Neurogenic Shock in spinal trauma patients.
back:
● Hypotension
● Bradycardia (or normal heart rate)
● Warm peripheries
● Caused by loss of sympathetic outflow (above T5).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Neurogenic shock. This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries. This is due to unopposed vagal tone resulting from cervical spinal cord injury at or above the level of sympathetic outflow (T5).]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the only absolute indication for surgery in acute spinal trauma?
back: Deteriorating neurological function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: List the components of the 'Autonomic Dysreflexia' syndrome seen in spinal cord injuries.
back:
● Paroxysmal hypertension
● Bradycardia
● Headache
● Flushing/Hyperhidrosis (above injury level)
● Usually triggered by bladder/rectal distension.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [Autonomic dysreflexia. This is a paroxysmal syndrome of hypertension, hyperhidrosis (above the level of injury), bradycardia, flushing and headache in response to noxious visceral and other stimuli. It is most commonly triggered by bladder distension or rectal loading]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What late neurological complication occurs in 28% of patients with spinal cord injury?
back: Post-traumatic syringomyelia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [Post-traumatic syringomyelia may occur in around 28% of patients with spinal cord injury up to 30 years following injury.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the mandatory initial step for managing a spine trauma patient during the primary survey?
back: A: Strict cervical spine protection and immobilization of the entire vertebral column to prevent secondary injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 411 (Book Page): [The spine should initially be immobilised using full spinal precautions, on the assumption that every trauma patient has a spinal injury until proven otherwise.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Contrast the clinical presentation of hypovolaemic shock versus neurogenic shock in spinal trauma.
back:
● Hypovolaemic: Hypotension with tachycardia and cold/clammy peripheries.
● Neurogenic: Hypotension with bradycardia (or normal rate) and warm peripheries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Neurogenic shock. This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries... Hypovolaemic shock. Hypotension with tachycardia and cold clammy peripheries.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Distinguish between 'spinal shock' and 'neurogenic shock' regarding their clinical duration and nature.
back:
● Neurogenic: Hemodynamic failure due to loss of sympathetic tone (T5 or above).
● Spinal: Temporary physiological loss of all reflex activity, lasting 6+ weeks.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Spinal shock is a temporary physiological disorganisation of spinal cord function... it can last 6 weeks or longer. Neurogenic shock... is due to unopposed vagal tone resulting from cervical spinal cord injury at or above... T5.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: A spinal injury patient presents with paroxysmal hypertension and bradycardia. What is the diagnosis and trigger?
back:
● Diagnosis: Autonomic dysreflexia.
● Common Triggers: Bladder distension (blocked catheter) or rectal loading (faecal impaction).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [Autonomic dysreflexia... paroxysmal syndrome of hypertension, hyperhidrosis... bradycardia... most commonly triggered by bladder distension or rectal loading from faecal impaction.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the current standard of care regarding corticosteroid use in acute traumatic spinal cord injury?
back: A: Corticosteroids are no longer indicated or recommended for acute injury due to a lack of evidence for efficacy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support effcacy.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Which imaging modality is the gold standard for assessing acute spinal column trauma?
back: A: Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 414 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction remains the gold standard in spinal trauma.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What clinical finding signals the resolution of spinal shock in a trauma patient?
back: A: The return of the bulbocavernosus reflex (anal sphincter contraction in response to glans penis/clitoris pressure or Foley catheter traction).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Spinal shock... is characterised by paralysis, decreased tone and hyporefexia. Once it has resolved the bulbocavernosus refex returns.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Which late spinal complication presents with segmental pain, sensory loss, and progressive asymmetrical weakness years post-injury?
back: A: Post-traumatic syringomyelia (expanding cystic cavity within the spinal cord).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [Post-traumatic syringomyelia may occur in around 28% of patients... patients present with segmental pain at or above the level of injury, sensory loss, progressive asymmetrical weakness.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of three-column spinal stability described by Denis.
back:
● Columns: Anterior, Middle, and Posterior.
● Instability: Defined if two or more columns are injured.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 410 (Book Page): [The spine can be divided into three columns: anterior, middle and posterior... If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: List three common musculoskeletal complications associated with chronic spinal cord injury.
back:
● Disuse osteoporosis.
● Heterotopic ossification (hips, knees, shoulders).
● Soft-tissue contractures (due to spasticity).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [Disuse osteoporosis is an inevitable consequence... Heterotopic ossifcation may afect the hips, knees... Soft-tissue contractures around joints may occur as a result of spasticity.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the mandatory initial management for suspected spine injuries during the primary survey?
back:
- Continuous cervical spine immobilization (rigid collar and blocks).
- Protection of the thoracolumbar spine.
- Maintenance of immobilization using standard log roll techniques until cleared.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Patients are managed with cervical spine protection (cervical collar and blocks) and protection of the thoracolumbar spine using standard log roll techniques until a spinal injury has been excluded.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: How is neurogenic shock clinically distinguished from hypovolemic shock in spinal trauma?
back:
- Hypotension associated with bradycardia (due to unopposed vagal tone).
- Warm peripheries (vasodilation).
- Typically occurs with injuries at or above the T5 level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Neurogenic shock. This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries. This is due to unopposed vagal tone resulting from cervical spinal cord injury at or above the level of sympathetic outflow (T5).]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What clinical finding marks the physiological end of the spinal shock phase?
back:
- Return of the bulbocavernosus reflex.
- Followed by the transition from flaccid paralysis to spasticity/hyperreflexia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Spinal shock is a temporary physiological disorganisation... characterized by paralysis, decreased tone and hyporefexia. Once it has resolved the bulbocavernosus refex... returns.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: How should a patient with both spinal trauma and suspected pelvic fractures be moved?
back:
- Avoid formal log-rolling to prevent disturbing pelvic blood clots.
- Utilize a 20° roll with inline spinal stabilization.
- Use a scoop stretcher to minimize rotational forces.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [Log-rolling patients with severe pelvic fractures may harm the patient by disturbing established blood clots... If patients need to be moved... a 20° roll with inline spinal stabilisation should be used. Modern 'scoop stretchers' mean that there is no requirement to roll any patient more than 20° until a pelvic fracture has been excluded.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the current standard regarding corticosteroid use in acute traumatic spinal cord injury?
back:
- Corticosteroids are no longer indicated for acute trauma.
- Lack of clinical evidence for efficacy.
- Reserved primarily for non-traumatic compression (e.g., malignancy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 417 (Book Page): [Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support efcacy.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the gold standard imaging modality for diagnosing unstable spinal injuries in trauma?
back:
- Computed Tomography (CT) with 2D/3D reconstruction.
- Plain radiographs miss approximately 15% of injuries, particularly at the cervicothoracic junction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 415 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction remains the gold standard in spinal trauma... Plain cervical spine radiographs fail to identity 15% of injuries.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Which physical finding is a strong predictor of severe cord injury in intubated patients?
back:
- Priapism (persistent erection).
- Absence of anal tone or anal wink reflex on rectal examination.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Priapism is a strong predictor of severe cord injury even in intubated patients.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What are the cardinal clinical features and primary triggers of Autonomic Dysreflexia?
back:
- Features: Sudden hypertension, bradycardia, and flushing above the injury level.
- Triggers: Bladder distension (commonest) or rectal loading/impaction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [Autonomic dysrefexia. This is a paroxysmal syndrome of hypertension, hyperhidrosis (above the level of injury), bradycardia, fushing and headache... most commonly triggered by bladder distension or rectal loading from faecal impaction.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the primary absolute surgical indication for stabilization/decompression in spine trauma?
back:
- Deteriorating neurological function.
- Evidence of residual neural compression by bone fragments or haematoma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 417 (Book Page): [The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the reported clinical incidence of DVT in patients with spinal cord injury?
back:
- Incidence: 30% of patients.
- Thromboprophylaxis with compression stockings and low-molecular-weight heparin is mandatory.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [Deep vein thrombosis occurs in 30% of patients with spinal cord injury... Thromboprophylaxis with compression stockings and low-molecular-weight heparin is indicated.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What is the gold standard radiological investigation for an adult with signs of multisystem blunt trauma?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from head to pelvis with intravenous (IV) contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Why must a pelvic radiograph precede log-rolling of a blunt trauma patient during the primary survey?
back: To exclude pelvic fractures; log-rolling an unstable fracture can disturb established blood clots and cause catastrophic hemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [Log-rolling should not occur until a pelvic fracture has been radiographically excluded. ... Log-rolling patients with severe pelvic fractures may harm the patient by disturbing established blood clots.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: When is MRI preferred over CT in the assessment of acute spinal trauma?
back:
1. Presence of a neurological deficit.
2. When assessment of ligamentous structures is required.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [MRI is indicated in all patients with neurological defcit and where assessment of ligamentous structures is important]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: A hemodynamically unstable patient requires immediate laparotomy; which two radiographs must be obtained first?
back:
1. Chest radiograph (excludes catastrophic intrathoracic hemorrhage).
2. Pelvic radiograph (identifies pelvic fracture sources).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [An immediate chest radiograph will exclude catastrophic intrathoracic haemorrhage. An immediate pelvic radiograph is essential but should not delay transfer to the operating theatre.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Which specific step is required to diagnose traumatic bladder rupture during a CT cystogram?
back: Instillation of a minimum of 300 mL of contrast into the bladder via a urethral catheter.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [For assessment of bladder injury a cystogram should be performed at the time of CT. A minimum of 300 mL of contrast is instilled into the bladder via a urethral catheter.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What is the preferred radiological screening tool for Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH) before age 4 months?
back: Dynamic Ultrasound (plain radiographs are unreliable until the femoral head ossifies at 4–5 months).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): [Screening scans should be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of age ... Plain radiographs are used from 4–5 months of age, when the relationship of the femoral ossifc nucleus to the acetabulum can be assessed]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: On infant hip ultrasound, what 'Morin index' measurement indicates a stable, normal hip joint?
back: 50% or more (the percentage of the femoral head covered by the acetabulum).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): [Morin index of 50% (defned as the percentage of the femoral head covered by the acetabulum, i.e. the portion lying below the horizontal red line).]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: Which investigation distinguishes traumatic Subarachnoid Haemorrhage (SAH) from spontaneous aneurysmal SAH following head injury?
back: Formal angiography or CT angiography (to exclude underlying aneurysm).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [The possibility of spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage actually leading to collapse and so causing a head injury needs to be borne in mind, and formal or CT angiography may be required to exclude this.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: How is the radiological progression of bone healing distinguished between 'union' and 'consolidation'?
back:
Union: Callus bridges the fracture site.
Consolidation: Return of the normal cortical pattern.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Radiologically a fracture has united when the callus bridges the fracture site. ... Consolidation ... demonstrated by the return of the normal cortical pattern.]

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
front: Q: What lateral cervical radiograph measurements indicate potential spinal instability?
back:
1. Sagittal translation >3.5 mm.
2. Sagittal angulation >11° compared to the adjacent level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 392 (Book Page): [Assess for instability (Figure 30.16): a 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; b sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What standard techniques must be used to protect the thoracolumbar spine during initial trauma assessment?
back:
• Rigid cervical collar and blocks for the neck.
• Log roll technique for moving.
• Maintain full spinal precautions until injury is radiographically excluded.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Patients are managed with cervical spine protection (cervical collar and blocks) and protection of the thoracolumbar spine using standard log roll techniques until a spinal injury has been excluded.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Distinguish neurogenic shock from spinal shock in acute spinal trauma presentation.
back:
• Neurogenic: Hypotension, bradycardia, and warm peripheries (loss of sympathetic tone).
• Spinal: Temporary cord dysfunction characterized by flaccid paralysis and hyporeflexia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page): [Neurogenic shock ... presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries. ... Spinal shock is a temporary physiological disorganisation of spinal cord function ... characterised by paralysis, decreased tone and hyporeflexia.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Which imaging modality is the gold standard for evaluating bony injury in spinal trauma?
back:
• Computed tomography (CT) scan.
• Must include two-dimensional reconstruction.
• Mandatory for suspected injuries or poorly visualized cervicothoracic junctions on radiographs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 414 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction remains the gold standard in spinal trauma and is indicated for patients with suspected or visible injuries on plain radiographs]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Identify the common triggers and cardinal signs of autonomic dysreflexia in chronic SCI patients.
back:
• Triggers: Bladder distension or rectal loading (fecal impaction).
• Signs: Hypertension, bradycardia, headache, and hyperhidrosis above the level of injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [Autonomic dysreflexia ... paroxysmal syndrome of hypertension, hyperhidrosis (above the level of injury), bradycardia, flushing and headache ... most commonly triggered by bladder distension or rectal loading from faecal impaction.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the current evidence-based recommendation for corticosteroid use in acute spinal cord injury?
back:
• No longer indicated for acute management.
• Reason: Lack of evidence supporting clinical efficacy in spinal cord trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support efficacy.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
coreConcept: Absolute Surgical Indication in Spine Trauma
front: Q: What specific neurological finding constitutes the only absolute indication for surgery in spine trauma?
back:
• Deteriorating neurological function.
