• Relative indications include spinal instability, fracture pattern, and severe pain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Why is the use of spinal boards restricted strictly to patient transfer in trauma management?
back:
• Cause rapid pressure ulcers/skin breakdown in insensate patients.
• Extremely uncomfortable for those with normal sensation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 411 (Book Page): [Spinal boards lead to skin breakdown in insensate patients, and are very uncomfortable ... They should only be used for transferring patients.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Describe the diagnostic criteria for an ASIA Grade A 'complete' spinal cord injury.
back:
• Complete absence of sensory and motor function.
• Must specifically involve the S4-S5 sacral segments.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): [A: complete spinal cord injury; ... Incomplete = Any sensory or motor function in S4-5]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Enumerate three common thromboembolic and metabolic complications of spinal cord injury.
back:
• Deep vein thrombosis (30% risk).
• Heterotopic ossification (25% risk).
• Disuse osteoporosis leading to fragility fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [Deep vein thrombosis occurs in 30% of patients with spinal cord injury. ... Disuse osteoporosis is an inevitable consequence ... Heterotopic ossification ... occurs in 25% of patients]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: At which vertebral level does the adult spinal cord end as the conus medullaris?
back:
• L1/L2 level.
• The cauda equina lies inferior to this termination point.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 410 (Book Page): [The spinal cord extends from the foramen magnum to the L1/L2 level, where it ends as the conus medullaris in adults]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the mandatory protocol for managing the thoracolumbar spine before ruling out injury?
back:
1. Spinal protection using standard log-roll techniques.
2. Maintenance of neutral alignment.
3. Immobilisation continues until injury is excluded by imaging (Whole-body CT).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Patients are managed with cervical spine protection (cervical collar and blocks) and protection of the thoracolumbar spine using standard log roll techniques until a spinal injury has been excluded.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What pathophysiological mechanism differentiates neurogenic shock from hypovolaemic shock in spinal trauma?
back:
1. Unopposed vagal tone (loss of sympathetic outflow).
2. Resultant bradycardia (hypovolaemia causes tachycardia).
3. Warm peripheries due to vasodilation (hypovolaemia causes cold peripheries).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Neurogenic shock . . . presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries. This is due to unopposed vagal tone resulting from cervical spinal cord injury at or above the level of sympathetic outfow (T5).]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Contrast the clinical presentation of spinal shock with neurogenic shock.
back:
1. Spinal shock: Temporary loss of all reflex activity, flaccid paralysis, and hyporeflexia.
2. Neurogenic shock: Hemodynamic instability (hypotension/bradycardia) from autonomic disruption.
3. Spinal shock ends when bulbocavernosus reflex returns.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [Spinal shock is a temporary physiological disorganisation of spinal cord function . . . It is characterised by paralysis, decreased tone and hyporefexia. Once it has resolved the bulbocavernosus refex returns.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: A patient has an irreducible cervical spine dislocation. What are the planned surgical steps?
back:
1. Formal open reduction.
2. Stabilisation using internal fixation.
3. Direct decompression of neural elements if bone fragments or hematoma cause residual compression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [In many cases of spinal trauma, formal open reduction and stabilisation using internal fxation is also required. . . A direct decompression of the neural elements may also be indicated if there are bone fragments causing residual compression.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What is the current pharmacological recommendation regarding corticosteroids in acute spinal cord trauma?
back:
1. Corticosteroids are no longer indicated.
2. Lack of evidence for efficacy in acute trauma.
3. Use is restricted to non-traumatic compression (e.g., malignancy).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support efcacy. Steroids do have a role in non-traumatic spinal cord compression, e.g. malignant spinal cord compression.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: Which imaging modality is the gold standard for identifying the majority of spinal pathology?
back:
1. Whole-body CT (WBCT) with IV contrast.
2. From head to pelvis.
3. Rapidly identifies bone injury; MRI is secondary for ligamentous/cord assessment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Early WBCT scan will rapidly identify the majority of intracranial and spinal pathology. . . WBCT from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation.]

category: Plan initial management and enumerate complications of spine trauma
front: Q: What paroxysmal complication and its primary triggers must be monitored in chronic spinal cord injury?
back:
1. Autonomic dysreflexia (hypertension and bradycardia).
2. Triggered by noxious stimuli below the lesion.
3. Primary triggers: Bladder distension or faecal impaction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [Autonomic dysrefexia . . . is a paroxysmal syndrome of hypertension, hyperhidrosis . . . bradycardia, fushing and headache . . . most commonly triggered by bladder distension or rectal loading from faecal impaction.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the single absolute indication for surgical intervention in cases of spinal trauma?
back: Deteriorating neurological function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: According to the three-column model, when is a spinal injury classified as unstable?
back: When two or more columns (anterior, middle, or posterior) are injured.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 410 (Book Page): [The spine can be divided into three columns: anterior, middle and posterior... If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Contrast the primary management of stable vs. unstable Jefferson (C1) fractures.
back:
- Stable: Non-operative (cervical collar/halo brace).
- Unstable: Surgery (indicated if combined lateral mass deviation >6.9 mm indicating transverse ligament rupture).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [Most are treated non-operatively in a cervical collar or halo brace. Rupture of the transverse ligament is present when the combined lateral mass deviation exceeds 6.9 mm.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What clinical indicators mandate surgical stabilization instead of conservative treatment for a Hangman’s fracture?
back:
- Significant displacement
- Associated facet dislocation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): [Those with signifcant displacement or associated facet dislocation are treated operatively, usually with posterior stabilisation.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Contrast the typical management for Type A versus Type B/C thoracic and thoracolumbar fractures.
back:
- Type A (Compression): Often conservative/cement augmentation.
- Type B (Distraction) and Type C (Rotational): Usually require surgical stabilization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 420 (Book Page): [Type A fractures are vertebral body compression fractures... The majority of type B and type C injuries require surgical stabilisation.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Why are fractures of the lower lumbar spine (L3–S1) frequently managed non-surgically?
back:
1. Neural canal is capacious (cord ends at L1/L2).
2. Lower risk of kyphotic deformity due to natural lumbar lordosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 422 (Book Page): [Most fractures of the lower lumbar spine can be treated non-surgically because the incidence of neurological injury is lower. The neural canal is more capacious at this level (the spinal cord terminates at L1/L2).]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: How does management differ for acute vs. displaced odontoid peg fractures?
back:
- Acute: Non-operative (hard collar/halo for 3 months).
- Displaced: Internal fixation (anterior compression screw).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [The majority of acute injuries are treated non-operatively in a hard collar or halo jacket for 3 months. Internal fxation with an anterior compression screw is indicated for displaced fractures.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Why is surgical stabilization preferred over collars in patients with Ankylosing Spondylitis?
back: High fracture risk, progressive neurological deficit risk, and collars are often contraindicated due to rigid autofusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [These patients have a higher risk of spinal fractures and spinal cord injury than the normal population... application of a cervical collar may be contraindicated... Surgical stabilisation is commonly indicated.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Define the management protocol for Occipital Condyle fractures.
back: Conservative treatment using a hard collar for 6–8 weeks.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [Occipital condyle fracture... This is a relatively stable injury often associated with head injuries and is best treated in a hard collar for 6–8 weeks.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the preferred management for symptomatic osteoporotic wedge compression fractures?
back: Percutaneous bone cement augmentation (vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 420 (Book Page): [Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures... symptomatic fractures can be treated with percutaneous bone cement augmentation, known as vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What primary clinical and radiological factors determine the indication for spinal surgical intervention?
back:
* Injury pattern and degree of instability
* Level of pain
* Presence of a neurological deficit
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): The indication for operative intervention is infuenced by the injury pattern, level of pain, degree of instability and the presence of a neurological defcit.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma?
back: Deteriorating neurological function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Contrast the management of closed linear vs. depressed skull vault fractures.
back:
* Closed linear: Conservative management
* Depressed: Exploration and elevation (if fragment depth > skull thickness or intracranial air present)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): Closed linear fractures of the skull vault are managed conservatively. ... Depressed skull fractures ... require exploration and elevation, especially where intracranial air is present, pointing to a breach in the dura mater.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Which specific patient presentations with Extradural Hematoma (EDH) mandate immediate surgical evacuation?
back:
* Comatose patients
* Deteriorating neurological status
* Patients with large bleeds on imaging
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): Signifcant extradural haematoma mandates urgent transfer ... for immediate evacuation in deteriorating or comatose patients or those with large bleeds.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the current standard of care for using corticosteroids in acute spinal cord injury?
back: They are no longer indicated due to a lack of evidence for efficacy in traumatic settings.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support efcacy.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: How are stable occipital condyle fractures typically managed?
back: Conservative treatment with a hard collar for 6–8 weeks.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): Occipital condyle fracture ... is a relatively stable injury often associated with head injuries and is best treated in a hard collar for 6–8 weeks.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the preferred management for most Jefferson (C1 ring) fractures?
back: Non-operative treatment using a cervical collar or halo brace.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Jefferson fracture] Most are treated non-operatively in a cervical collar or halo brace.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: When is internal fixation indicated for an acute Type II odontoid fracture?
back: When the fracture is displaced; typically achieved via an anterior compression screw.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): Internal fxation with an anterior compression screw is indicated for displaced fractures [Type II odontoid].

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Which features of a Hangman’s fracture (C2 spondylolisthesis) indicate a need for operative stabilization?
back:
* Significant displacement
* Associated facet joint dislocation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): Those [Hangman's fractures] with signifcant displacement or associated facet dislocation are treated operatively, usually with posterior stabilisation.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Which AO classification types of thoracic and thoracolumbar fractures usually require surgical stabilization?
back: The majority of Type B (distraction) and Type C (rotational) injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): The majority of type B and type C injuries require surgical stabilisation.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the only absolute indication for surgery in acute spinal trauma?
back: Deteriorating neurological function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: When is a spinal injury classified as 'unstable' using the three-column model?
back: When two or more columns (anterior, middle, or posterior) are injured.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 409 (Book Page): If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Contrast the management of AO Type A versus Type B and C thoracolumbar fractures.
back: Type A (compression) is often conservative; Types B (distraction) and C (rotational) usually require surgical stabilisation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): The majority of type B and type C injuries require surgical stabilisation.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Under what specific anatomical conditions is direct surgical decompression of neural elements indicated?
back: Residual compression by bone fragments or a significant haematoma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): A direct decompression of the neural elements may also be indicated if there are bone fragments causing residual compression or a significant haematoma.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the current standard regarding corticosteroid use in acute traumatic spinal cord injury?
back: They are no longer indicated due to lack of evidence supporting efficacy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support efficacy.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What criteria mandate internal fixation for an acute odontoid peg fracture?
back: Displacement of the fracture or evidence of non-union.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): Internal fixation with an anterior compression screw is indicated for displaced fractures, and a posterior C1/2 fusion is considered in cases of non-union.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Why are L3-S1 fractures more amenable to non-surgical treatment compared to T11-L2?
back: Lower incidence of neurological injury due to a more capacious canal and spinal cord termination (L1/L2).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 401 (Book Page): Most fractures of the lower lumbar spine can be treated non-surgically because the incidence of neurological injury is lower. The neural canal is more capacious at this level (the spinal cord terminates at L1/L2).

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Which specific upper cervical injury requires immediate surgical stabilization if facet dislocation is present?
back: Traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (Hangman’s fracture).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): Those with significant displacement or associated facet dislocation are treated operatively, usually with posterior stabilisation.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: How is the facial skeleton divided vertically for fracture classification?
back: Upper face (above canthi), midface (maxillary teeth to canthi), and lower face (mandible).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [The facial skeleton can be divided vertically into thirds using horizontal lines: upper face (from the level of the canthi upwards), midface (from the maxillary teeth to the canthi) and lower face (mandible and mandibular teeth).]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Identify the two anatomical subdivisions of the midface and their respective complexes.
back: 1. Central midface (naso-orbital–ethmoidal complex). 2. Lateral midface (zygomaticomaxillary complex).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [The midface can be further divided into central and lateral, with the naso-orbital–ethmoidal complex forming the central and the zygomaticomaxillary complex forming the lateral components.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: List the specific bone fracture types based on their structure or clinical presentation.
back: Simple, compound, comminuted, complicated (neurovascular involvement), greenstick, and pathological.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [Maxillofacial bone fractures can be divided into several types: simple (isolated single), compound (communicates through the skin or oral/nasal mucosal surfaces), comminuted (multiple fragments), complicated (with neurological or vascular injury), greenstick (includes single cortex) and pathological.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Describe the anatomical fracture line involved in a Le Fort I injury.
back: Extends from the pterygoid plates through the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus and the piriform aperture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): [Le Fort I involves a fracture line extending from the pterygoid plates through the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus and piriform aperture of the nose.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Which specific landmarks are involved in the pyramidal-shaped Le Fort II fracture line?
back: The pterygoid plates, the inferior orbital rim, and the bridge of the nose.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): [Le Fort II involves the whole of the dentitionbearing portion of the maxilla and the nasal bones. The fracture line extends from the pterygoid plates to the inferior orbital rim and across the bridge of the nose.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: What anatomical separation defines a Le Fort III (craniofacial disjunction) fracture?
back: Separation of the midface from the skull base; involves pterygoid plates, zygomatic arches, lateral orbital walls, and frontozygomatic (FZ) sutures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): [Le Fort III fracture essentially is where the whole of the midface is separated from the skull base. The fracture line runs from the pterygoid plates to the base of the zygomatic arch, the lateral walls of the orbit through the FZ suture and the nasal bridge.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: How are frontal sinus fractures classified to evaluate surgical priority?
back: Based on anterior table involvement, posterior table involvement, and damage to the frontonasal duct.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [Frontal sinus fractures are classifed into those involving the anterior or posterior table, with or without damage to the frontonasal duct.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Classify isolated orbital fractures based on anatomical site.
back: Orbital floor (blow-out/blow-in), medial wall, lateral wall, or orbital roof.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [Orbital (eye socket) fractures can occur in isolation or in combination with other fractures. Orbital fractures can be classifed into orbital foor, medial and/or lateral walls and the roof of the orbit.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Differentiate facial soft-tissue injuries by mechanism of injury.
back: 1. Lacerations (blunt crushing). 2. Incised wounds (sharp instruments). 3. Through-and-through (communication between skin and mucosa).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [Lacerations are a result of crushing injuries... Sharp implements... cause incised wounds... Where the injury results in a communication between the skin and the mucosa... termed ‘through and through’.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Define a 'panfacial' fracture and state its clinical implication.
back: Involves bony injury at all levels of the facial skeleton (upper, mid, lower); implies high-energy force and potential multisystem trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [The most severe facial fractures involving bony injury at all levels of the facial skeleton are referred to as panfacial fractures. These usually imply that a signifcant degree of force has been involved, suggesting signifcant other injuries such as head, abdominal or chest injuries.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: How is the facial skeleton divided vertically for fracture classification?
back: 1. Upper face (canthi upwards); 2. Midface (maxillary teeth to canthi); 3. Lower face (mandible and mandibular teeth).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): The facial skeleton can be divided vertically into thirds using horizontal lines: upper face (from the level of the canthi upwards), midface (from the maxillary teeth to the canthi) and lower face (mandible and mandibular teeth).

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Describe the anatomical pathway defining a Le Fort I fracture.
back: A horizontal fracture line extending from the pterygoid plates through the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus and the piriform aperture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): Le Fort I involves a fracture line extending from the pterygoid plates through the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus and piriform aperture of the nose.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Contrast the structural involvement of Le Fort II versus Le Fort III fractures.
back: Le Fort II (Pyramidal): Involves the inferior orbital rim and nasal bridge. Le Fort III (Craniofacial Dysjunction): Separation of the entire midface from the skull base via the zygomatic arch and lateral orbital walls.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): Le Fort II involves... the inferior orbital rim and across the bridge of the nose. Le Fort III fracture essentially is where the whole of the midface is separated from the skull base. The fracture line runs from the pterygoid plates to the base of the zygomatic arch, the lateral walls of the orbit through the FZ suture and the nasal bridge.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: A patient presents with a left parasymphyseal fracture and right pre-auricular pain. Which mandibular classification applies?
back: Contralateral site involvement; specifically a right condylar neck or angle fracture, as these frequently occur as a pair with parasymphyseal injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 410 (Book Page): The commonest fracture patterns are parasymphysis and angle fractures, or parasymphysis and condylar fractures (contralateral sites in both cases).

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Classify frontal sinus fractures and name the pharmacological step used for minimally displaced cases.
back: Classified as Anterior Table, Posterior Table, or Both; management of minimally displaced (<2mm) fractures utilizes nasal decongestants.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 414 (Book Page): Frontal sinus fracture may be classified according to whether the anterior, posterior or both tables are involved... Minimally displaced (<2 mm) fractures... can be managed conservatively with nasal decongestants.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: List the six general types used to classify the nature of maxillofacial bone fractures.
back: 1. Simple; 2. Compound (open); 3. Comminuted; 4. Complicated (neurovascular injury); 5. Greenstick; 6. Pathological.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): Maxillofacial bone fractures can be divided into several types: simple (isolated single), compound (communicates through the skin or oral/nasal mucosal surfaces), comminuted (multiple fragments), complicated (with neurological or vascular injury), greenstick (includes single cortex) and pathological.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Classify the four anatomical components (stool legs) assessed in zygomatic bone fractures.
back: 1. Zygomatic arch; 2. Frontozygomatic (FZ) process; 3. Infraorbital rim; 4. Maxillary buttress.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 411 (Book Page): it is helpful to consider the zygomatic bone as a four-legged stool... The four legs comprise the zygomatic arch... the zygomatic process... at the FZ suture, the infraorbital rim... and the maxillary buttress.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Differentiate the Central versus Lateral midface complexes in maxillofacial classification.
back: Central Midface: Naso-orbital–ethmoidal (NOE) complex. Lateral Midface: Zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): The midface can be further divided into central and lateral, with the naso-orbital–ethmoidal complex forming the central and the zygomaticomaxillary complex forming the lateral components.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Distinguish between the orbital classification of 'blow-out' and 'blow-in' fractures.
back: Blow-out: Internal orbital fragments/fat herniate outwards (usually floor) due to pressure. Blow-in: Fracture fragments are driven inwards into the orbital space.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): Isolated orbital injuries are described as ‘blowout’ or ‘blowin’ fractures... Internal rectus muscle entrapment... trapdoor defect has opened and then closed again.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: What is the anatomical definition of a 'panfacial' fracture?
back: Bony injuries simultaneously involving all three vertical levels of the facial skeleton: upper, mid, and lower face.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): The most severe facial fractures involving bony injury at all levels of the facial skeleton are referred to as panfacial fractures.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Which four factors influence the choice between surgical and conservative management of spinal injuries?
back:
1. Injury pattern
2. Level of pain
3. Degree of instability
4. Presence of neurological deficit
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [The indication for operative intervention is infuenced by the injury pattern, level of pain, degree of instability and the presence of a neurological defcit.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the pathophysiological trigger for absolute surgical intervention in spinal trauma?
back: Deteriorating neurological function is the only absolute indication, signifying active neural compression that necessitates immediate surgical decompression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Contrast the management of AO Type A versus Type B/C thoracic spinal fractures.
back:
● Type A (Compression): Most heal with conservative care.
● Type B/C (Distraction/Rotation): Majority require surgical stabilization due to inherent instability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): [Type A fractures are vertebral body compression fractures... heal... The majority of type B and type C injuries require surgical stabilisation.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: In a clinical scenario of a Hangman’s (C2) fracture, when is surgical stabilization indicated over bracing?
back: Surgical posterior stabilization is required if there is significant displacement or associated facet joint dislocation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Those with signifcant displacement or associated facet disloca - tion are treated operatively, usually with posterior stabilisation.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the current status of corticosteroid use in acute traumatic spinal cord injury management?
back: Corticosteroids are no longer indicated for acute traumatic injuries due to a lack of evidence supporting their efficacy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support efcacy.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What radiological criteria define an unstable Jefferson (C1) fracture requiring potential surgical consideration?
back: A combined lateral mass deviation exceeding 6.9 mm on an open-mouth view, indicating transverse ligament rupture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Rupture of the transverse ligament is present when the combined lateral mass deviation exceeds 6.9 mm.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Why is non-operative management conceptually prioritized for lower lumbar (L3–S1) fractures?
back: The lower incidence of neurological injury at this level, as the neural canal is more capacious below the conus medullaris (L1/L2).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 401 (Book Page): [Most fractures of the lower lumbar spine can be treated non-surgically because the incidence of neurological injury is lower. The neural canal is more capacious at this level.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Differentiate the clinical presentation of neurogenic shock from hypovolemic shock in spinal injury.
back:
● Neurogenic: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm peripheries.
● Hypovolemic: Hypotension with tachycardia and cold, clammy peripheries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Hypovolaemic shock... tachycardia and cold clammy peripheries. This is most often due to haemorrhage... Neurogenic shock... normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: How does surgical intervention break the metabolic loop of secondary spinal cord injury?
back: Direct decompression interrupts the cascade of hemorrhage and edema by removing bone fragments or hematomas causing persistent neural compression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Management of spinal cord injury must focus on minimising secondary injury. ...persistent compression of the neural elements. ...A direct decompression of the neural elements may also be indicated if there are bone fragments causing residual compression or a signifcant haematoma.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the standard management for a stable occipital condyle fracture?
back: Conservative treatment involving immobilization in a hard cervical collar for 6–8 weeks.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Occipital condyle fracture... is best treated in a hard collar for 6–8 weeks.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: How is the facial skeleton divided vertically for fracture classification purposes?
back:
* Upper face: From the canthi upwards.
* Midface: From maxillary teeth to canthi.
* Lower face: Mandible and mandibular teeth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [The facial skeleton can be divided vertically into thirds using horizontal lines: upper face (from the level of the canthi upwards), midface (from the maxillary teeth to the canthi) and lower face (mandible and mandibular teeth).]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Classify the midface into its two primary anatomical complexes.
back:
* Central midface: Naso-orbital-ethmoidal (NOE) complex.
* Lateral midface: Zygomaticomaxillary complex.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [The midface can be further divided into central and lateral, with the naso-orbital–ethmoidal complex forming the central and the zygomaticomaxillary complex forming the lateral components.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: List the three levels of maxillary fractures defined in the Le Fort classification.
back:
* Le Fort I: Horizontal fracture above the teeth (floating palate).
* Le Fort II: Pyramidal fracture involving the nasal bridge.
* Le Fort III: Craniofacial dysjunction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [Maxillary fractures are classifed according to their anatomical level, as originally described by René Le Fort... Le Fort I... Le Fort II... Le Fort III...]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Which specific fracture lines define a Le Fort III craniofacial dysjunction?
back:
The midface separates from the skull base via the:
* Pterygoid plates.
* Zygomatic arches.
* Lateral orbital walls (Frontozygomatic suture).
* Nasal bridge.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [Le Fort III fracture essentially is where the whole of the midface is separated from the skull base. The fracture line runs from the pterygoid plates to the base of the zygomatic arch, the lateral walls of the orbit through the FZ suture and the nasal bridge.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: How are frontal sinus fractures classified to determine airway and surgical risk?
back:
* Anatomical: Anterior table, posterior table, or both.
* Functional: Involvement of the frontonasal duct (risk of mucocele or infection).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 435 (Book Page): [Frontal sinus fracture may be classifed according to whether the anterior, posterior or both tables are involved with or without fracture of the sinus foor, which raises concern for possible injury to the nasofrontal duct]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: What diagnostic criteria classify a facial fracture as "compound"?
back:
Direct communication of the fracture line with the:
* External skin surface.
* Oral mucosa.
* Nasal mucosa.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [Maxillofacial bone fractures can be divided into several types... compound (communicates through the skin or oral/nasal mucosal surfaces)]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Describe the "four-legged stool" classification model for zygomatic fractures.
back:
* Zygomatic arch (Anteroposterior leg).
* Zygomatic process (Vertical/FZ suture leg).
* Infraorbital rim (Horizontal leg).
* Maxillary buttress (Vertical leg).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 432 (Book Page): [it is helpful to consider the zygomatic bone as a fourlegged stool... zygomatic arch running anteroposteriorly, the zygomatic process running vertically... infraorbital rim running horizontally and the maxillary buttress running vertically.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Define panfacial fractures and list their primary clinical management implication.
back:
* Definition: Fractures involving all vertical levels of the facial skeleton.
* Implication: High-impact injury; mandates exclusion of concomitant head, thoracic, and abdominal trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 428 (Book Page): [The most severe facial fractures involving bony injury at all levels of the facial skeleton are referred to as panfacial fractures. These usually imply that a signifcant degree of force has been involved, suggesting signifcant other injuries such as head, abdominal or chest injuries.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: How are orbital fractures classified based on the anatomical wall involved?
back:
* Orbital floor (common "blowout").
* Medial wall.
* Lateral wall.
* Orbital roof.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [Orbital (eye socket) fractures can be classifed into orbital foor, medial and/or lateral walls and the roof of the orbit.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: List the three most common anatomical sites for mandibular fractures.
back:
* Condylar neck (most frequent).
* Angle of the mandible.
* Parasymphysis (region of the mental foramen).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 431 (Book Page): [The commonest fracture patterns are parasymphysis and angle fractures, or parasymphysis and condylar fractures... Figure 31.8... (1) The neck of the condyle is the most common site, followed by (2) the angle of the mandible. (3) The third point of weakness is in the region of the mental foramen.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: How is the facial skeleton vertically classified into thirds?
back:
- Upper face: Canthi upwards.
- Midface: Maxillary teeth to canthi.
- Lower face: Mandible and its teeth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [The facial skeleton can be divided vertically into thirds using horizontal lines: upper face (from the level of the canthi upwards), midface (from the maxillary teeth to the canthi) and lower face (mandible and mandibular teeth).]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Classify the midface skeleton into central and lateral complexes.
back:
- Central: Naso-orbital-ethmoidal (NOE) complex.
- Lateral: Zygomaticomaxillary (ZMC) complex.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [The midface can be further divided into central and lateral, with the naso-orbital–ethmoidal complex forming the central and the zygomaticomaxillary complex forming the lateral components.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: List the morphological types used to classify maxillofacial bone fractures.
back:
- Simple, compound, comminuted.
- Complicated (neuro/vascular injury).
- Greenstick, pathological.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [Maxillofacial bone fractures can be divided into several types: simple (isolated single), compound... comminuted... complicated (with neurological or vascular injury), greenstick... and pathological]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: What are the common anatomical sites for mandibular fractures?
back:
- Condylar neck (most common).
- Angle of mandible.
- Parasymphysis/Mental foramen region.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 432 (Book Page): [The commonest fracture patterns are parasymphysis and angle fractures, or parasymphysis and condylar fractures... The neck of the condyle is the most common site]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Define the anatomical level of a Le Fort I fracture.
back:
- Horizontal fracture extending from pterygoid plates.
- Passes through lateral maxillary sinus wall and piriform aperture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [Le Fort I involves a fracture line extending from the pterygoid plates through the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus and piriform aperture of the nose.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Identify the structures involved in a Le Fort II (pyramidal) fracture.
back:
- Pterygoid plates.
- Inferior orbital rim.
- Bridge of the nose.
- Entire dentition-bearing portion of maxilla.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [Le Fort II involves the whole of the dentitionbearing portion of the maxilla and the nasal bones. The fracture line extends from the pterygoid plates to the inferior orbital rim and across the bridge of the nose.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: What defines a Le Fort III fracture (craniofacial disjunction)?
back:
- Complete separation of midface from skull base.
- Line runs through pterygoid plates, zygomatic arches, lateral orbital walls, and nasal bridge.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [Le Fort III fracture essentially is where the whole of the midface is separated from the skull base. The fracture line runs from the pterygoid plates to the base of the zygomatic arch, the lateral walls of the orbit through the FZ suture and the nasal bridge.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: List the 'four legs' of the zygomatic bone stool used for classification.
back:
1. Zygomatic arch (anteroposterior).
2. Zygomatic process (vertical/frontal bone).
3. Infraorbital rim (horizontal).
4. Maxillary buttress (vertical).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 431 (Book Page): [it is helpful to consider the zygomatic bone as a fourlegged stool... The four legs comprise the zygomatic arch... zygomatic process... infraorbital rim... and the maxillary buttress.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Classify common orbital fractures by location and mechanism.
back:
- Location: Floor (most common), medial/lateral walls, roof.
- Mechanism: Isolated 'blow-out' (internal) or 'blow-in' fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [Orbital (eye socket) fractures... can be classified into orbital floor, medial and/or lateral walls and the roof... Isolated orbital injuries are described as ‘blowout’ or ‘blowin’ fractures.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: How are frontal sinus fractures primarily classified for management?
back:
- Anterior table involvement.
- Posterior table involvement.
- Integrity of the frontonasal duct.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 435 (Book Page): [Frontal sinus fracture may be classified according to whether the anterior, posterior or both tables are involved with or without fracture of the sinus floor, which raises concern for possible injury to the nasofrontal duct]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: How is the facial skeleton divided vertically for fracture classification?
back:
- Upper face (above the canthi)
- Midface (maxillary teeth to canthi)
- Lower face (mandible and teeth)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [The facial skeleton can be divided vertically into thirds using horizontal lines: upper face (from the level of the canthi upwards), midface (from the maxillary teeth to the canthi) and lower face (mandible and mandibular teeth).]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Classify the midface skeleton into its central and lateral components.
back:
- Central: Naso-orbital-ethmoidal (NOE) complex
- Lateral: Zygomaticomaxillary complex
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [The midface can be further divided into central and lateral, with the naso-orbital–ethmoidal complex forming the central and the zygomaticomaxillary complex forming the lateral components.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Contrast the anatomical involvement of Le Fort I versus Le Fort II fractures.
back:
- Le Fort I: Horizontal; involves pterygoid plates, lateral maxillary sinus, and piriform aperture.
- Le Fort II: Pyramidal; involves pterygoid plates, inferior orbital rim, and nasal bridge.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): [Le Fort I involves a fracture line extending from the pterygoid plates through the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus and piriform aperture... Le Fort II involves... the pterygoid plates to the inferior orbital rim and across the bridge of the nose.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: A patient has a parasymphyseal mandibular fracture. Which other sites should be prioritized for secondary fractures?
back: Contralateral angle or condylar fractures are the most common patterns seen with multiple mandibular injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 410 (Book Page): [The commonest fracture patterns are parasymphysis and angle fractures, or parasymphysis and condylar fractures (contralateral sites in both cases).]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: List the four key anatomical 'legs' used to classify zygomatic bone stability.
back:
1. Zygomatic arch
2. Frontozygomatic (FZ) suture
3. Infraorbital rim
4. Maxillary buttress
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 411 (Book Page): [it is helpful to consider the zygomatic bone as a fourlegged stool... The four legs comprise the zygomatic arch... the zygomatic process... the infraorbital rim... and the maxillary buttress.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Define a 'compound' facial bone fracture.
back: Any fracture that communicates through the skin or through oral/nasal mucosal surfaces.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [compound (communicates through the skin or oral/nasal mucosal surfaces)]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Classify frontal sinus fractures based on surgical urgency criteria.
back:
- Anterior table involvement
- Posterior table involvement (neurological risk)
- Frontonasal duct involvement (obstruction risk)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 414 (Book Page): [Frontal sinus fracture may be classifed according to whether the anterior, posterior or both tables are involved with or without fracture of the sinus foor, which raises concern for possible injury to the nasofrontal duct]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Distinguish between 'blow-out' and 'blow-in' orbital fracture classifications.
back: Both are isolated orbital injuries; blow-out involves herniation out of the orbit (often floor), whereas blow-in involves fragments displaced into the orbit.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Isolated orbital injuries are described as ‘blowout’ or ‘blowin’ fractures.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Describe the structural impact of a Le Fort III fracture on the midface.
back: Craniofacial disjunction: The entire midface skeleton separates from the skull base via the pterygoid plates, zygomatic arch, and lateral orbital walls.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): [Le Fort III fracture essentially is where the whole of the midface is separated from the skull base. The fracture line runs from the pterygoid plates to the base of the zygomatic arch, the lateral walls of the orbit through the FZ suture and the nasal bridge.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: What defines a panfacial fracture classification?
back: A fracture involving multiple levels across the upper face, midface, and lower face simultaneously.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [The most severe facial fractures involving bony injury at all levels of the facial skeleton are referred to as panfacial fractures.]

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the only absolute indication for surgery in acute spinal trauma?
back: Deteriorating neurological function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: How is clinical instability defined using the three-column model of the spine?
back: Injury involving two or more columns (Anterior, Middle, or Posterior).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Contrast the general management of Thoracic AO Type A versus Type B and C fractures.
back: Type A (compression) usually heals conservatively. The majority of Type B (distraction) and Type C (rotational) injuries require surgical stabilisation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): Type A fractures are vertebral body compression fractures. Most of these fractures heal... The majority of type B and type C injuries require surgical stabilisation.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the definitive management for a displaced Type II odontoid fracture in a young patient?
back: Internal fixation with an anterior compression screw.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): Internal fxation with an anterior compression screw is indicated for displaced fractures (Figure 30.28), and a posterior C1/2 fusion is considered in cases of non-union.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the current clinical indication for corticosteroids in acute traumatic spinal cord injury?
back: They are no longer indicated due to lack of evidence regarding efficacy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support efcacy.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Identify the standard primary treatment for most Jefferson (C1 ring) fractures.
back: Non-operative management using a cervical collar or halo brace.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): Most are treated non-operatively in a cervical collar or halo brace.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Which specific features of a Hangman’s fracture (C2) necessitate operative posterior stabilisation?
back: Significant forward translation (displacement) or associated facet dislocation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): Those with signifcant displacement or associated facet dislocation are treated operatively, usually with posterior stabilisation.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Contrast historical and current surgical principles for managing thoracolumbar burst fractures.
back: Anterior surgery is now rarely used; current treatment principles favor posterior fixation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): Anterior surgery for this type of fracture is now very rarely used and the current treatment principles involve posterior fxation.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: Why is surgical stabilization preferred over collars in patients with ankylosing spondylitis and spinal fracture?
back: High risk of instability and cord injury; collars may be contraindicated due to pre-existing deformity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 398 (Book Page): These patients have a higher risk of spinal fractures and spinal cord injury than the normal population... application of a cervical collar may be contraindicated... Surgical stabilisation is commonly indicated.

category: Identify indications for surgical versus conservative management of spinal injuries
front: Q: What is the recommended management for a stable occipital condyle fracture?
back: Conservative treatment using a hard collar for 6–8 weeks.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): This is a relatively stable injury often associated with head injuries and is best treated in a hard collar for 6–8 weeks.

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Which anatomical combination in midface trauma specifically triggers acute airway compromise?
back:
• Maxilla detached from skull base and displaced postero-inferiorly.
• Bilateral mandibular fracture causing tongue displacement.
• Significant oedema of the soft palate and tongue.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [The patient may present with acute airway compromise if the midface impaction is also combined with a bilateral mandibular fracture, which can displace the tongue backwards. Such injuries are often associated with signifcant oedema of the soft palate and tongue.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Describe the immediate clinical manifestations of a life-threatening tension pneumothorax.
back:
• Increasing restlessness and tachypnoea.
• Distended neck veins.
• Hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds on the affected side.
• Late sign: Tracheal deviation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [The patient is increasingly restless with tachypnoea, dyspnoea and distended neck veins... There will also be hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds over the afected hemithorax. Clinical examination may reveal tracheal deviation; this is a late fnding.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What is the physiological loop known as the 'triad of death' in trauma patients?
back:
• A cycle of Acidosis.
• Coagulopathy.
• Hypothermia.
• These factors result in multiorgan failure and death if not corrected.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Identify the clinical emergency features of a retrobulbar haemorrhage in facial trauma.
back:
• Tense proptosis and increasing pain.
• Reduced visual acuity.
• Loss of pupillary response.
• Altered perception of red color (early sign).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response. One of the early signs may be altered perception of red colour in the afected eye.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: List the specific complications associated with excessive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation in trauma.
back:
• Dilutional coagulopathy.
• Haemodilution.
• Increased risk of Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What are the diagnostic clinical hallmarks and late complications of Acute Compartment Syndrome?
back:
• Hallmark: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch.
• Late signs: Paralysis, numbness, and pulselessness.
• Complication: Irreversible muscle damage from cellular anoxia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [characterized by pain out of proportion, increasing pain, and pain on passive stretch, with paraesthesia possible. Paralysis, numbness and pallor are late signs... irreversible muscle damage from cellular anoxia.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Outline the stepwise clinical progression for managing a compromised trauma airway.
back:
1. Suctioning blood/secretions.
2. Manual maneuvers (Jaw thrust/chin lift).
3. Oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal airway insertion.
4. Cuffed endotracheal tube or surgical airway.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [A compromised airway requires a stepwise progression, frst clearing the airway by suctioning secretions or blood, followed by simple airway manoeuvres such as a jaw thrust, chin lift and insertion of an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway. Advanced airway manoeuvres necessitate the insertion of a cufed endotracheal tube... or a surgical airway.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What are the four clinical predictors used to differentiate paediatric septic arthritis from transient synovitis?
back:
• History of fever >38.5°C.
• Non-weight-bearing status.
• Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) >40 mm/h.
• White cell count (WCC) >12 × 10^9/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Table 44.17: History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10^9/L.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Describe the clinical presentation of a classic Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE).
back:
• Shortened and externally rotated leg.
• Painful limitation of hip internal rotation.
• Referred knee pain (Hilton's law).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [the leg lies short and externally rotated. There is painful limitation of hip movement. Hilton’s law... explains why many children present with knee pain although the pathology is in the hip.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: How is pericardial tamponade clinically differentiated from tension pneumothorax in shocked patients?
back:
• Tamponade: Muffled heart sounds and bilateral breath sounds.
• Tension Pneumothorax: Absent breath sounds on one side and hyper-resonance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [presentation consists of central venous pressure elevation, a decline in arterial pressure with tachycardia and mufed heart sounds... Tension pneumothorax... hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds.]

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: How is the facial skeleton vertically classified into horizontal thirds?
back:
* Upper face: Above the level of the canthi.
* Midface: From the maxillary teeth to the canthi.
* Lower face: Mandible and its dentition.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): The facial skeleton can be divided vertically into thirds using horizontal lines: upper face (from the level of the canthi upwards), midface (from the maxillary teeth to the canthi) and lower face (mandible and mandibular teeth).

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: What are the three primary anatomical sites where the mandible most commonly fractures?
back:
1. Condylar neck (most frequent site).
2. Angle of the mandible.
3. Parasymphysis (region of the mental foramen).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 410 (Book Page): The commonest fracture patterns are parasymphysis and angle fractures, or parasymphysis and condylar fractures... The neck of the condyle is the most common site, followed by the angle of the mandible. The third point of weakness is in the region of the mental foramen.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Contrast Le Fort I and Le Fort II fractures by their primary fracture lines.
back:
* Le Fort I: Horizontal; through pterygoid plates, lateral maxillary wall, and piriform aperture.
* Le Fort II (Pyramidal): Through pterygoid plates, inferior orbital rim, and nasal bridge.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): Le Fort I involves a fracture line extending from the pterygoid plates through the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus and piriform aperture of the nose. Le Fort II involves the whole of the dentition-bearing portion of the maxilla and the nasal bones. The fracture line extends from the pterygoid plates to the inferior orbital rim and across the bridge of the nose.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Identify the classification for a midface fracture resulting in complete separation from the skull base.
back: Le Fort III (Craniofacial disjunction). The fracture line involves the pterygoid plates, zygomatic arches, lateral orbital walls, and the frontozygomatic (FZ) suture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): Le Fort III fracture essentially is where the whole of the midface is separated from the skull base. The fracture line runs from the pterygoid plates to the base of the zygomatic arch, the lateral walls of the orbit through the FZ suture and the nasal bridge.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Define a 'compound' facial fracture and its implications.
back: A fracture that communicates with the external environment through the skin, or through the oral or nasal mucosa. These require prophylactic antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [Fractures can be] compound (communicates through the skin or oral/nasal mucosal surfaces)... Prophylactic antibiotics prior to surgery should be used in all cases of penetrating abdominal trauma [and by extension compound facial fractures].

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Classify orbital fractures based on the anatomical wall involved.
back:
* Orbital floor (e.g., 'blow-out' or 'blow-in').
* Medial wall.
* Lateral wall.
* Orbital roof.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): Orbital (eye socket) fractures can be classified into orbital floor, medial and/or lateral walls and the roof of the orbit. Page 413 (Book Page): Isolated orbital injuries are described as 'blow-out' or 'blow-in' fractures.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: List the four anatomical 'legs' of the zygomatic bone classification model.
back:
1. Zygomatic arch.
2. Frontozgyomatic (FZ) process.
3. Infraorbital rim.
4. Maxillary buttress.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 411 (Book Page): It is helpful to consider the zygomatic bone as a four-legged stool... The four legs comprise the zygomatic arch running anteroposteriorly, the zygomatic process running vertically to join the frontozygomatic (FZ) process... the infraorbital rim running horizontally and the maxillary buttress running vertically.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Distinguish between panfacial and craniofacial fracture classifications.
back:
* Panfacial: Bony injuries involving all levels (upper, mid, and lower) of the facial skeleton.
* Craniofacial: Facial fractures combined with skull fractures (e.g., frontal or ethmoidal sinuses).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): Skull fractures including frontal and ethmoidal sinuses, in combination with facial fractures, are termed craniofacial fractures... The most severe facial fractures involving bony injury at all levels of the facial skeleton are referred to as panfacial fractures.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: How are frontal sinus fractures classified to determine surgical risk?
back:
* Anatomical: Anterior table vs. posterior table involvement.
* Functional: Presence or absence of damage to the frontonasal duct.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): Frontal sinus fractures are classified into those involving the anterior or posterior table, with or without damage to the frontonasal duct.

category: Classify common facial fractures
front: Q: Classify the central and lateral components of midface complex injuries.
back:
* Central midface: Naso-orbital-ethmoidal (NOE) complex.
* Lateral midface: Zygomaticomaxillary complex.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): The midface can be further divided into central and lateral, with the naso-orbital–ethmoidal complex forming the central and the zygomaticomaxillary complex forming the lateral components.

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Which maxillofacial fracture pattern leads to acute airway compromise via posterior tongue displacement?
back:
- Bilateral mandibular fractures.
- Midface skeletal detachment/impaction (maxilla pushed downwards and backwards).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [The patient may present with acute airway compromise if the midface impaction is also combined with a bilateral mandibular fracture, which can displace the tongue backwards.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiological mechanism leading to blindness in traumatic retrobulbar haemorrhage.
back:
- Increased intra-orbital pressure.
- Reduced flow in the retinal artery.
- Ischaemic damage to the optic nerve.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness secondary to pressureinduced reduced fow on the retinal artery, leading to ischaemic damage to the optic nerve.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Contrast the clinical presentations of hypoglobus and enophthalmos in orbital wall fractures.
back:
- Hypoglobus: Inferior positioning of the globe.
- Enophthalmos: Sinking of the globe due to increased orbital volume.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [orbital wall fractures can lead to changes in globe position, with inferior positioning of the globe (hypoglobus) or sinking in of the globe due to an increase in orbital volume (enophthalmos).]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Outline the immediate emergency department maneuvers to relieve airway obstruction from midface impaction.
back:
- Manual maxilla disimpaction (pulling forward).
- Tongue traction (using suture or towel clip).
- High-volume suction of blood and debris.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [In the obtunded or unconscious patient, the maxilla can be disimpacted and pulled forwards using fngers. The tongue can be pulled and held forwards, with a large suture or a towel clip, to help open up the airway.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Identify the pharmacological adjuncts indicated in the medical management of acute retrobulbar haemorrhage.
back:
- Mannitol.
- Acetazolamide.
- Corticosteroids.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Concomitant medical management should also be initiated with mannitol, acetazolamide and steroids.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: List the anatomical structures involved in a Le Fort II (Pyramidal) fracture line.
back:
- Pterygoid plates.
- Lateral wall of the maxillary sinus.
- Inferior orbital rim.
- Bridge of the nose.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): [Le Fort II involves the whole of the dentitionbearing portion of the maxilla and the nasal bones. The fracture line extends from the pterygoid plates to the inferior orbital rim and across the bridge of the nose.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Explain why 'white eye' blowout fractures in children require urgent surgical intervention.
back:
- Entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle.
- Triggers oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, syncope).
- Risk of irreversible muscle necrosis within hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. This needs to be treated as an emergency because irreversible damage related to muscle necrosis can occur within hours.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Interpret the clinical significance of mental nerve paraesthesia following mandibular trauma.
back:
- Indicates a mandibular body fracture.
- Specifically suggests injury to the Inferior Alveolar Nerve within the canal.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 408 (Book Page): [the patient may have altered sensation in the region of the lip and chin, due to damage to the inferior alveolar nerve running along the canal within the mandible and involvement of the mental nerve.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Describe the physiological factors contributing to progressive pharyngeal space restriction in facial trauma.
back:
- Soft tissue oedema of the soft palate and tongue.
- Backward displacement of bony segments.
- Sublingual or cervical haematoma formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [Such injuries are often associated with signifcant oedema of the soft palate and tongue (Figure 31.2). ... maxilla can become detached ... and displaced downwards and backwards.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: State the surface landmark for assessing potential injury to the parotid duct.
back: - Middle third of a line from the tragus to the midpoint between the upper lip and alar base.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 409 (Book Page): [The middle third of a line drawn from the tragus of the ear to the midpoint between the upper lip and the alar base represents the surface landmarking of the parotid duct.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Which three clinical signs constitute Cushing's triad in patients with uncontrolled intracranial pressure?
back:
• Hypertension.
• Bradycardia.
• Irregular respiration.
• This indicates imminent brainstem herniation (coning).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. The patient is then said to be ‘coning’, and brainstem death will result without immediate intervention.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: How does midface skeletal detachment specifically lead to acute airway compromise in trauma?
back:
• Maxilla displaces downwards and backwards.
• Often combined with bilateral mandibular fractures.
• Results in posterior displacement of the tongue obstructing the pharynx.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 415 (Book Page): [In severe injury to the midface skeleton, the maxilla can become detached from the skull base and displaced downwards and backwards... combined with a bilateral mandibular fracture, which can displace the tongue backwards.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Identify the classical clinical triad observed in a patient with acute retrobulbar haemorrhage.
back:
• Tense proptosis.
• Pain and reduced visual acuity.
• Loss of pupillary response.
• Potential loss of red colour perception.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page): [It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response. One of the early signs may be altered perception of red colour in the affected eye.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What clinical signs distinguish a tension pneumothorax from other thoracic injuries?
