back:
• Restlessness with tachypnoea and dyspnoea.
• Distended neck veins.
• Hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds on the affected side.
• Tracheal deviation (late finding).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [The patient is increasingly restless with tachypnoea, dyspnoea and distended neck veins... hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds over the affected hemithorax. Tracheal deviation; this is a late finding.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What specific ocular sign is characteristic of temporal lobe uncal herniation?
back:
• Ipsilateral pupil abnormalities.
• Compression of the third cranial (oculomotor) nerve.
• Progresses from a sluggish enlarged pupil to a fixed and dilated state.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Typically, herniation of the uncus of the temporal lobe over the tentorium results in pupil abnormalities... usually occurring first on the side of any expanding haematoma.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Describe the characteristic clinical presentation of acute native joint septic arthritis.
back:
• Single hot, swollen, painful joint.
• Immobility in the 'position of comfort'.
• 'Pseudoparalysis' in neonates.
• Severe pain on active or passive movement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 599 (Book Page): [Most patients present after an acute or subacute history with a single hot, swollen, painful joint... joint is held immobile in the ‘position of comfort’, with ‘pseudoparalysis’ in neonates.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Why is early intubation critical in patients with traumatic neck haematomas?
back:
• Airway distortion can be insidious and progressive.
• Potential for sudden airway oedema.
• Delay makes subsequent intubation difficult or impossible.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Early intubation is very important, particularly in cases of neck haematoma or possible airway oedema. Airway distortion can be insidious and progressive and can make delayed intubation more difficult if not impossible.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: In male trauma patients, what finding on rectal examination specifically suggests complete urethral avulsion?
back:
• A high-riding prostate.
• Often associated with pelvic fractures and blood at the urethral meatus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [In male patients, the prostate is palpated; a high-riding prostate indicates a complete urethral avulsion.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Define the 'oculocardiac reflex' seen in pediatric trapdoor orbital floor fractures.
back:
• Triad: Bradycardia, nausea, and syncope.
• Caused by entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle.
• Represents a surgical emergency to prevent muscle necrosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac reflex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. This needs to be treated as an emergency.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Where is the specific site of maximal tenderness in a suspected scaphoid fracture?
back:
• The anatomical snuffbox.
• Located on the radial aspect of the wrist between the extensor pollicis longus and abductor pollicis brevis tendons.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 480 (Book Page): [In the trauma setting, palpate the anatomical snuff box: a fracture of the scaphoid may cause tenderness.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: How does severe midface skeleton detachment classically compromise the airway?
back: The maxilla detaches from the skull base and is displaced downwards and backwards, obstructing the pharyngeal space.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): In severe injury to the midface skeleton, the maxilla can become detached from the skull base and displaced downwards and backwards ( Figure 31.1 ). The patient may present with acute airway compromise...

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What is the primary pathophysiology behind tissue damage in compartment syndrome?
back: Increased intrafascial pressure compromises microperfusion, leading to tissue ischemia and irreversible muscle damage from cellular anoxia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 465 (Book Page): The pathophysiology involves increased tissue pressure, which leads to reduced microperfusion, resulting in tissue ischaemia and irreversible muscle damage from cellular anoxia.

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Contrast the four Kocher clinical predictors used to differentiate septic arthritis from transient synovitis.
back:
1. Fever >38.5°C
2. Non-weight-bearing
3. ESR >40 mm/h
4. White cell count >12 × 10^9/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 656 (Book Page): Table 44.17: (a) The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: History of fever >38.5°C, Non-weight-bearing, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h, White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: A patient with midface trauma presents with tense proptosis and loss of pupillary response. What is the immediate management?
back: Perform emergency bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under local anesthesia to relieve posterior pressure on the optic nerve.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response... preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under LA to allow the globe to bulge forwards and relieve the pressure posteriorly.

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What is the high-yield dosing regimen for Tranexamic Acid in severe trauma?
back: 1g given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a second 1g dose infused over the next 8 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours.

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What clinical feature does the "too many toes" sign indicate during foot inspection?
back: It signifies increased forefoot abduction and a splayed forefoot, typically associated with pes planus (flat foot).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 515 (Book Page): The ‘too many toes’ sign demonstrates increased forefoot abduction (pes planus [fat foot]) and a splayed forefoot.

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What specific clinical triggers necessitate the activation of a ‘code red trauma call’?
back: Patients identified as hemodynamically unstable or presenting with acute airway compromise initiate this enhanced trauma team attendance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): Patients identifed before reaching hospital as being haemodynamically unstable or having acute airway compromise may initiate ‘code red’...

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Why must a pediatric "white eye" blowout fracture be treated as a surgical emergency?
back: Entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle can cause a life-threatening oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, nausea, syncope) and irreversible muscle necrosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. This needs to be treated as an emergency because irreversible damage related to muscle necrosis can occur within hours.

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Identify the components of the metabolic "triad of death" in severely traumatized patients.
back: A self-perpetuating cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy, and hypothermia leading to multiorgan failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): ...the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Which classic skull fracture site is associated with middle meningeal artery rupture in extradural hematoma?
back: Fracture of the thin squamous temporal bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): The classical injury is a fracture to the thin squamous temporal bone, with associated damage to the middle meningeal artery.

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What is the stepwise progression for managing a compromised airway in a trauma patient?
back:
- Suctioning blood/secretions.
- Simple manoeuvres (jaw thrust, chin lift).
- Adjuncts (oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal airway).
- Advanced (cuffed endotracheal tube or surgical airway).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [A compromised airway requires a stepwise progression, first clearing the airway by suctioning secretions or blood, followed by simple airway manoeuvres such as a jaw thrust, chin lift and insertion of an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway. Advanced airway manoeuvres necessitate the insertion of a cuffed endotracheal tube... or a surgical airway.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: How do severe midface impaction and mandibular fractures cause acute airway compromise?
back:
- Maxillary detachment from the skull base pushes it downwards and backwards.
- Bilateral mandibular fractures displace the tongue backwards.
- Associated soft palate and tongue oedema.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [the maxilla can become detached from the skull base and displaced downwards and backwards... airway compromise if the midface impaction is also combined with a bilateral mandibular fracture, which can displace the tongue backwards. Such injuries are often associated with signiﬁcant oedema of the soft palate and tongue.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Contrast tension pneumothorax and massive haemothorax based on neck veins and percussion.
back:
- Tension Pneumothorax: Distended neck veins and hyper-resonance.
- Massive Haemothorax: Flat neck veins and dullness to percussion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page)-396: [[Tension Pneumothorax] distended neck veins... hyper-resonance... [Massive Haemothorax] haemorrhagic shock, ﬂat neck veins, unilateral absence of breath sounds and dullness to percussion.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What clinical signs characterize a sight-threatening retrobulbar haemorrhage following orbital trauma?
back:
- Tense proptosis and increasing pain.
- Reduced visual acuity and altered red colour perception.
- Loss of pupillary response.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response. One of the early signs may be altered perception of red colour in the affected eye.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Which specific anatomical indicators suggest potential ongoing internal bleeding in torso trauma?
back:
- Visible external bleeding.
- Injury in close proximity to major vessels.
- Penetrating injury with a retained missile.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [Anatomical [indicators]: Visible bleeding; Injury in close proximity to major vessels; Penetrating injury with a retained missile.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Describe the multi-system physiological complications of Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS).
back:
- Renal: Increased resistance, reduced GFR.
- Cardiovascular: Decreased venous return and cardiac output.
- Respiratory: Increased ventilation pressures and decreased compliance.
- Intracranial: Severe pressure rises.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [Effect of raised intra-abdominal pressure... Renal... reduction in glomerular ﬁltration rate... Cardiovascular... decreased venous return... Respiratory... Increased ventilation pressures... Intracranial... Severe rises in intracranial pressures.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Define the components and terminal risk of the trauma 'triad of death'.
back:
- Components: Acidosis, Coagulopathy, and Hypothermia.
- Result: Leads to multiorgan failure and death.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What findings define the clinical diagnosis of extremity compartment syndrome?
back:
- Pain out of proportion to injury.
- Pain on passive stretch.
- Paraesthesia.
- Late signs: Paralysis, pallor, and pulselessness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis characterised by pain out of proportion, increasing pain, and pain on passive stretch, with paraesthesia possible. Paralysis, numbness and pallor are late signs and pulselessness is an extremely late sign.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What are the defining features of 'code red trauma calls' in severe injury management?
back:
- Initiated for haemodynamic instability or acute airway compromise.
- Triggers automatic attendance of most senior clinicians.
- Prehospital activation of massive transfusion protocols.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): [Patients identiﬁed... as being haemodynamically unstable or having acute airway compromise may initiate ‘code red’, triggering the automatic attendance of the most senior clinicians... and prehospital activation of massive transfusion protocols.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Why is early intubation critical for patients with suspected neck haematomas or airway oedema?
back: Airway distortion can be insidious and progressive, making delayed intubation difficult or impossible.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Early intubation is very important, particularly in cases of neck haematoma or possible airway oedema. Airway distortion can be insidious and progressive and can make delayed intubation more difficult if not impossible.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What anatomical displacement causes airway obstruction in severe midface trauma?
back: The maxilla becomes detached from the skull base and is displaced downwards and backwards, physically obstructing the pharyngeal space and compromising the airway.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [the maxilla can become detached from the skull base and displaced downwards and backwards... acute airway compromise]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: How does a bilateral mandibular fracture combined with midface impaction compromise the airway?
back: This combination results in the posterior displacement of the tongue, significantly restricting pharyngeal space, often exacerbated by soft tissue edema of the palate.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [midface impaction is also combined with a bilateral mandibular fracture, which can displace the tongue backwards.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Contrast the clinical presentation of retrobulbar hemorrhage versus simple periorbital edema.
back: Retrobulbar hemorrhage is a surgical emergency featuring tense proptosis, reduced visual acuity, pain, and loss of pupillary response, requiring immediate intervention to prevent blindness.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: A patient with severe facial trauma is obtunded with acute airway obstruction. List two immediate maneuvers.
back:
1. Manually disimpact and pull the maxilla forward using fingers.
2. Pull and hold the tongue forward using a large suture or towel clip.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [In the obtunded or unconscious patient, the maxilla can be disimpacted and pulled forwards using fingers. The tongue can be pulled and held forwards, with a large suture or a towel clip]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What is the initial prophylactic antibiotic and serological management for human or animal facial bites?
back: Prompt administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics, tetanus vaccination, and (for human bites) testing for HIV and hepatitis serology if the patient is high-risk.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 431 (Book Page): [All facial bites should be cleaned thoroughly and closed primarily... antibiotics must be prescribed according to local microbiology guidelines.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: List four clinical signs suggesting a fracture of the skull base during facial assessment.
back:
1. Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising).
2. Raccoon eyes (periorbital bruising).
3. Hemotympanum/otorrhea.
4. CSF rhinorrhoea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Clinical evidence of a skull base fracture may include Battle’s sign... ‘racoon’ or ‘panda’ eyes... CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Which temporary measure can control midface hemorrhage when direct pressure is ineffective?
back: Application of anterior and posterior nasal packs, or the use of inflatable balloon nasal packs and Foley urinary catheters to exert pressure on internal bleeding points.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [management of severe bleeding may require... placement of anterior and posterior nasal packs. Specifc inflatable balloon nasal packs or Foley urinary catheters]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: A trauma patient has a missing tooth not found at the scene. What priority investigation is required?
back: A chest radiograph is mandatory to exclude aspiration of the tooth or fragments, as this represents a major risk for developing a chest infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 428 (Book Page): [important to account for all missing teeth or tooth fragments as aspiration is a major risk... a chest radiograph should be considered.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Explain the physiological mechanism of the 'oculocardiac reflex' in pediatric orbital floor fractures.
back: Entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle in a 'trapdoor' fracture triggers a vagal response, resulting in the clinical triad of bradycardia, nausea, and syncope.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac reflex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What is the surface landmark for the parotid duct when assessing facial lacerations?
back: The middle third of a line drawn from the tragus of the ear to the midpoint between the upper lip and the alar base.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 430 (Book Page): [middle third of a line drawn from the tragus of the ear to the midpoint between the upper lip and the alar base represents the surface landmarking of the parotid duct.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What is the mandatory first priority in the initial assessment of a patient with facial trauma?
back:
Follow Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) protocols:
• Immediate assessment of Airway (with cervical spine protection).
• Breathing assessment.
• Circulation management (ABC).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [Initial assessment requires a focused history of the mechanism of injury and a general medical and social history, followed by clinical examination. An injury to the body including facial trauma must be managed with an immediate assessment of the airway, breathing and circulation (ABC) in line with the established Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) guidelines.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
coreConcept: Mechanical Airway Obstruction in Facial Trauma
front: Q: How do combined midface and bilateral mandibular fractures physiologically compromise the airway?
back:
• The maxilla detaches from the skull base, displacing downwards and backwards.
• Mandibular fractures allow the tongue to displace posteriorly.
• Associated soft palate and tongue edema further restrict pharyngeal space.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [In severe injury to the midface skeleton, the maxilla can become detached from the skull base and displaced downwards and backwards... combined with a bilateral mandibular fracture, which can displace the tongue backwards. Such injuries are often associated with signifcant oedema of the soft palate and tongue.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Differentiate the likely hemorrhage sources in midface injuries versus penetrating neck injuries.
back:
• Midface: Maxillary artery or pterygoid venous plexus.
• Neck: External carotid artery branches or internal jugular vein tributaries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [The source of such bleeding is likely to be from injury to the maxillary artery or pterygoid venous plexus in the grossly damaged midface, or branches of the external carotid artery or tributaries of the internal jugular vein in penetrating injuries of the neck.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: A facial trauma patient presents with tense proptosis and loss of red color perception. What stabilization step is required?
back: Immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under local anesthesia to relieve orbital pressure and prevent permanent blindness from retrobulbar hemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response. One of the early signs may be altered perception of red colour in the afected eye. If this is suspected, preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under LA to allow the globe to bulge forwards and relieve the pressure posteriorly.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: List the immediate manual stabilization maneuvers to relieve airway obstruction in an obtunded patient with midface impaction.
back:
• Clear blood/debris with high-volume suction.
• Manually disimpact and pull the maxilla forward using fingers.
• Pull the tongue forward with a large suture or towel clip.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [In the obtunded or unconscious patient, the maxilla can be disimpacted and pulled forwards using fngers. The tongue can be pulled and held forwards, with a large suture or a towel clip, to help open up the airway. Highvolume suction must be readily available to clear the blood as well as tooth fragments and debris]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
coreConcept: Masked Head Injury in Facial Trauma
front: Q: Why is a brain CT scan prioritized for patients presenting with interpersonal facial violence?
back: Alcohol or drug intoxication, common in interpersonal violence cases, frequently masks the clinical symptoms of concurrent severe intracranial head injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [Patients with facial injury and particularly those with injury due to interpersonal violence are frequently intoxicated because of alcohol or drug abuse, which may mask the symptoms of head injury. Therefore, clinicians should have a low threshold for requesting a brain computed tomography (CT) scan to exclude signifcant intracranial injury.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: How is an initial ocular assessment safely performed when trauma-induced edema has swollen the eyelids shut?
back: Gently pull the lids apart using dry gauze, cotton buds, or a swab stick; temporary gentle pressure on the lids can reduce edema to facilitate opening.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [Examination is possible even in the most swollen of eyes by gently pulling the eyelids apart with dry gauze, a cotton bud/roll or a microbiology swab stick. Gentle pressure on the eyelid for a brief period may reduce oedema, which may facilitate the opening of the eyelids.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Compare the stabilization of accessible external bleeding versus midface bleeding where direct pressure is impossible.
back:
• Accessible: Direct digital pressure.
• Inaccessible Midface: Anterior and posterior nasal packs, inflatable balloon packs, or Foley urinary catheters to exert internal pressure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [The management of severe bleeding may require application of direct digital pressure or placement of anterior and posterior nasal packs. Specifc infatable balloon nasal packs or Foley urinary catheters may be utilised to exert pressure on the bleeding points.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What is the physiological rationale for positioning a conscious midface-trauma patient in a forward-sitting posture?
back: It utilizes gravity to drain blood away from the oropharynx, minimizing the risk of blood obstructing the airway or causing aspiration while awaiting intubation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [If the patient has midface bleeding where direct pressure cannot be applied, the conscious patient may sit forwards or be placed on their side in the standard recovery position to minimise the risk of blood obstructing the airway.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What clinical finding on oral examination is pathognomonic for a displaced mandibular or maxillary fracture?
back: Altered dental occlusion (malocclusion), which the patient may detect as their bite feeling 'off,' often accompanied by sublingual hematoma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [A key feature of displaced mandibular or maxillary fractures is altered occlusion. The patient may be able to detect even a tiny alteration in their occlusion. If there is a fracture of the mandible, the overlying mucosa is often torn and there may be an associated haematoma in the foor of the mouth]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What is the absolute first priority in the initial assessment of a patient with severe maxillofacial trauma?
back: Assessment of Airway, Breathing, and Circulation (ABC) with simultaneous cervical spine protection, following ATLS guidelines.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [An injury to the body including facial trauma must be managed with an immediate assessment of the airway, breathing and circulation (ABC) in line with the established Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) guidelines.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Describe the anatomical mechanism by which severe midface trauma acutely compromises the airway.
back: The maxilla detaches and displaces downwards/backwards; if combined with bilateral mandibular fractures, the tongue also moves posteriorly to obstruct the pharynx.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [In severe injury to the midface skeleton, the maxilla can become detached from the skull base and displaced downwards and backwards...combined with a bilateral mandibular fracture, which can displace the tongue backwards.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What manual maneuvers are used to stabilize the airway in an unconscious patient with midface impaction?
back:
● Manual disimpaction/anterior traction of the maxilla.
● Pulling the tongue forward using fngers, a large suture, or a towel clip.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [In the obtunded or unconscious patient, the maxilla can be disimpacted and pulled forwards using fngers. The tongue can be pulled and held forwards, with a large suture or a towel clip, to help open up the airway.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Identify the most common vascular sources of life-threatening haemorrhage in midface trauma.
back:
● Maxillary artery
● Pterygoid venous plexus
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [The source of such bleeding is likely to be from injury to the maxillary artery or pterygoid venous plexus in the grossly damaged midface.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Which pharmacological adjuncts are used to medically stabilize a patient with suspected retrobulbar haemorrhage?
back:
● Mannitol
● Acetazolamide
● Corticosteroids
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Concomitant medical management should also be initiated with mannitol, acetazolamide and steroids.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What is the definitive emergency stabilization procedure for sight-threatening retrobulbar haemorrhage?
back: Immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under local anaesthesia to reduce intraorbital pressure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [If this is suspected, preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under LA to allow the globe to bulge forwards and relieve the pressure posteriorly.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What clinical triad identifies the 'oculocardiac reflex' during assessment of pediatric orbital floor fractures?
back:
● Bradycardia
● Nausea
● Syncope
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Which clinical finding during a secondary survey is most indicative of a displaced mandibular fracture?
back: Altered dental occlusion (deranged bite), often accompanied by a sublingual haematoma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [A key feature of displaced mandibular or maxillary fractures is altered occlusion. The patient may be able to detect even a tiny alteration in their occlusion.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: How is torrential midface bleeding stabilized when direct digital pressure is ineffective?
back: Placement of anterior and posterior nasal packs, specifically using inflatable balloon packs or Foley urinary catheters.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [The management of severe bleeding may require application of direct digital pressure or placement of anterior and posterior nasal packs. Specifc infatable balloon nasal packs or Foley urinary catheters may be utilised to exert pressure.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Why is visual acuity assessment vital even in cases of severe periorbital edema preventing eye opening?
back: To rule out sight-threatening injuries like retrobulbar hemorrhage or extraocular muscle entrapment that require immediate surgical intervention.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [such an examination is crucial as inadequate examination may lead to a delay in the diagnosis of serious eye injury that may need urgent intervention to prevent blindness.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What are the immediate priorities in the initial management of facial trauma?
back:
Based on ATLS principles: 
- Airway maintenance with cervical spine protection
- Breathing and ventilation
- Circulation with haemorrhage control
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [An injury to the body including facial trauma must be managed with an immediate assessment of the airway, breathing and circulation (ABC) in line with the established Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) guidelines.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
coreConcept: Airway Obstruction Mechanism in Midface Injury
front: Q: Describe the mechanism by which severe midface trauma causes acute airway compromise.
back:
- Maxilla detaches from the skull base
- Displaced downwards and backwards
- Tongue is displaced backwards (if combined with bilateral mandibular fractures)
- Soft palate/tongue oedema
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [the maxilla can become detached from the skull base and displaced downwards and backwards... combined with a bilateral mandibular fracture, which can displace the tongue backwards.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Contrast the immediate manual techniques used to relieve airway compromise in midface vs. tongue displacement.
back:
- Midface: Disimpact and pull the maxilla forward manually.
- Tongue: Pull and hold the tongue forward using a large suture or towel clip.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [the maxilla can be disimpacted and pulled forwards using fngers. The tongue can be pulled and held forwards, with a large suture or a towel clip, to help open up the airway.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: How is torrential midface haemorrhage managed when direct pressure is ineffective?
back:
- Digital pressure
- Anterior and posterior nasal packs
- Inflatable balloon nasal packs
- Foley urinary catheters
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [The management of severe bleeding may require application of direct digital pressure or placement of anterior and posterior nasal packs. Specifc infatable balloon nasal packs or Foley urinary catheters may be utilised]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What are the clinical hallmarks of an acute retrobulbar haemorrhage?
back:
- Tense proptosis
- Pain (increasing)
- Reduced visual acuity/loss of pupillary response
- Altered perception of red colour
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response. One of the early signs may be altered perception of red colour in the afected eye.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What systematic approach is required during the secondary survey of facial bones?
back:
A top-down approach:
1. Supraorbital ridge
2. Lateral orbital wall/inferior rim
3. Zygoma
4. Nasal bones
5. Temporomandibular joint
6. Mandible
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [A systematic approach would include palpation of the supraorbital ridge followed by the lateral orbital wall, inferior orbital rim, zygomatic bone, nasal bones, temporomandibular joint and the rest of the mandible on both sides.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Which specific physical findings in the oral cavity strongly suggest a mandibular fracture?
back:
- Altered occlusion (bite)
- Torn overlying mucosa
- Haematoma in the floor of the mouth
- Lip/chin paraesthesia (mental nerve damage)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [A key feature of displaced mandibular or maxillary fractures is altered occlusion... if there is a fracture of the mandible, the overlying mucosa is often torn and there may be an associated haematoma in the foor of the mouth]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What is the immediate bedside surgical stabilization for a sight-threatening retrobulbar haemorrhage?
back:
- Lateral canthotomy
- Cantholysis (under local anaesthesia)
- Goal: Allow the globe to bulge forward to relieve optic nerve pressure
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under LA to allow the globe to bulge forwards and relieve the pressure posteriorly.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
coreConcept: Secondary Complication Assessment in Facial Injury
front: Q: Why must a chest radiograph be considered in facial trauma patients with missing teeth?
back: To exclude aspiration of tooth fragments or debris, which poses a major risk for developing chest infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 427 (Book Page): [It is important to account for all missing teeth or tooth fragments as aspiration is a major risk for developing chest infection. If it is unclear about the location of missing teeth, a chest radiograph should be considered.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
coreConcept: Gold Standard Imaging for Midface Injury
front: Q: What is the gold standard imaging for suspected orbital or high-energy midface fractures?
back: Computed Tomography (CT) from the head to facial bones, utilizing 3D reformatting for visualization of complex bony structures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 428 (Book Page): [A CT of the facial bones would be more suitable if an orbital fracture is suspected or in the case of a highimpact injury; this will provide the gold standard detail... A threedimensional (3D) reformatting of the CT scan allows for excellent visualisation]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
coreConcept: ATLS Primary Survey in Facial Trauma
front: Q: What is the mandatory sequence for the initial management of a maxillofacial trauma patient?
back:
● Immediate ABC assessment (Airway, Breathing, Circulation)
● Concurrent cervical spine protection (ATLS guidelines)
● Stabilization of life-threatening or sight-threatening injuries
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [An injury to the body including facial trauma must be managed with an immediate assessment of the airway, breathing and circulation (ABC) in line with the established Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) guidelines.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: In severe midface trauma, in which specific directions is the maxilla typically displaced?
back:
● Downwards
● Backwards (impaction against the skull base)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [In severe injury to the midface skeleton, the maxilla can become detached from the skull base and displaced downwards and backwards.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
coreConcept: Mechanical Airway Obstruction in Facial Injury
front: Q: Which anatomical factor causes acute airway compromise when midface impaction occurs with bilateral mandibular fractures?
back:
● Posterior displacement of the tongue
● Significant oedema of the soft palate and tongue obstructing pharyngeal space
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [The patient may present with acute airway compromise if the midface impaction is also combined with a bilateral mandibular fracture, which can displace the tongue backwards. Such injuries are often associated with signicant oedema of the soft palate and tongue.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What immediate manual maneuvers can relieve airway obstruction in an obtunded patient with midface detachment?
back:
● Digital disimpaction of the maxilla (pulling it forward)
● Traction of the tongue (using a large suture or towel clip)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page): [In the obtunded or unconscious patient, the maxilla can be disimpacted and pulled forwards using ngers. The tongue can be pulled and held forwards, with a large suture or a towel clip, to help open up the airway.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: How is torrential hemorrhage from the maxillary artery managed during initial stabilization?
back:
● Direct digital pressure
● Anterior and posterior nasal packing
● Use of inflatable balloon packs or Foley urinary catheters
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 405 (Book Page)-406: [The management of severe bleeding may require application of direct digital pressure or placement of anterior and posterior nasal packs. Specic inatable balloon nasal packs or Foley urinary catheters may be utilised.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Why must a brain CT be routinely considered for intoxicated patients with facial injuries?
back:
● Alcohol/drugs mask neurologic symptoms of head injury
● High impact mechanism often involves concurrent intracranial trauma
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [Patients with facial injury... are frequently intoxicated because of alcohol or drug abuse, which may mask the symptoms of head injury. Therefore, clinicians should have a low threshold for requesting a brain computed tomography (CT) scan.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What are the clinical indicators of retrobulbar hemorrhage requiring immediate intervention?
back:
● Tense proptosis
● Reduced visual acuity
● Loss of pupillary response
● Altered perception of red color
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency... It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response. One of the early signs may be altered perception of red colour.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What emergency bedside procedure is performed to stabilize a patient with sight-threatening retrobulbar hemorrhage?
back:
● Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under local anesthesia
● Relieves pressure on the retinal artery by allowing the globe to move forward
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [If this is suspected, preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under LA to allow the globe to bulge forwards and relieve the pressure posteriorly.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: How should missing teeth be accounted for during the initial assessment of a facial trauma patient?
back:
● Verify if teeth are avulsed, luxated, or fractured
● Obtain a chest radiograph if teeth are missing to exclude pulmonary aspiration
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 407 (Book Page): [It is important to account for all missing teeth or tooth fragments as aspiration is a major risk for developing chest infection. If it is unclear about the location of missing teeth, a chest radiograph should be considered.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What is the 'milking maneuver' and its significance in medial elbow assessment?
back:
● Provocative maneuver applying valgus stress through elbow range of motion
● Elicits pain at the medial elbow, indicating ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) injury
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 502 (Book Page): [Examination focuses on provocative manoeuvres that are specic for the UCL, including valgus stress and the moving valgus stress tests or milking manoeuvre... Pain at the medial elbow during these manoeuvres is specic for UCL pathology.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What are the immediate maneuvers to stabilize the airway in a patient with a detached midface?
back:
- Manually disimpact the maxilla and pull it forward using fingers.
- Use high-volume suction to clear blood, tooth fragments, and debris.
- Intubate if simple maneuvers fail.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [In the obtunded or unconscious patient, the maxilla can be disimpacted and pulled forwards using fngers. Highvolume suction must be readily available to clear the blood as well as tooth fragments and debris from the oral cavity and upper aerodigestive tract.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: How do bilateral mandibular fractures cause acute airway compromise?
back:
- The fractured segments allow the tongue to displace backwards, obstructing the pharynx.
- Airway narrowing is often exacerbated by significant soft tissue oedema of the palate and tongue.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [midface impaction is also combined with a bilateral mandibular fracture, which can displace the tongue backwards. Such injuries are often associated with signifcant oedema of the soft palate and tongue]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Which methods are used to stabilize life-threatening midface haemorrhage when direct pressure is impossible?
back:
- Insertion of anterior and posterior nasal packs.
- Utilization of inflatable balloon nasal packs or Foley urinary catheters to tamponade internal bleeding.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [management of severe bleeding may require application of direct digital pressure or placement of anterior and posterior nasal packs. Specifc infatable balloon nasal packs or Foley urinary catheters may be utilised to exert pressure on the bleeding points.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What is the emergency treatment for a patient with proptosis and vision loss after facial trauma?
back:
- Immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis.
- This procedure allows the globe to move forward, relieving intraocular pressure from a retrobulbar haemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness... preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under LA to allow the globe to bulge forwards and relieve the pressure]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Which medications supplement surgical stabilization in retrobulbar haemorrhage?
back:
- Mannitol.
- Acetazolamide.
- Corticosteroids.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [Concomitant medical management should also be initiated with mannitol, acetazolamide and steroids.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What is the gold standard investigation for suspected intracranial injury in facial trauma?
back:
- Non-contrast CT scan of the brain.
- Clinicians should include facial bone protocols in the request if intoxication masks symptoms.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [clinicians should have a low threshold for requesting a brain computed tomography (CT) scan to exclude signifcant intracranial injury. In such cases, it is prudent to include the facial bones in the CT request]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: How is the tongue stabilized manually to prevent airway obstruction in an unconscious facial trauma patient?
back:
- Pull and hold the tongue forward using a large suture or a towel clip.
- This prevents the tongue from falling back into the upper aerodigestive tract.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [The tongue can be pulled and held forwards, with a large suture or a towel clip, to help open up the airway.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: Which vessels are the likely sources of torrential bleeding in penetrating neck or midface injuries?
back:
- Maxillary artery.
- Pterygoid venous plexus.
- External carotid artery branches.
- Internal jugular vein tributaries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [source of such bleeding is likely to be from injury to the maxillary artery or pterygoid venous plexus in the grossly damaged midface, or branches of the external carotid artery or tributaries of the internal jugular vein in penetrating injuries]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What stabilization step prevents permanent disfigurement from contaminated facial lacerations?
back:
- Gentle scrubbing of the skin with a soft brush to prevent "dirt tattoo."
- Minimal debridement is required as the rich facial blood supply promotes excellent healing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 429 (Book Page): [If the skin is contaminated with dirt, it should be gently scrubbed with a soft brush to prevent dirt tattoo. Facial skin has a rich blood supply, which contributes to its excellent healing; therefore, wounds should only be debrided of frankly necrotic tissue.]

category: Explain initial assessment and stabilization in facial injuries
front: Q: What is the primary priority during the surgical stabilization of a parotid duct injury?
back:
- Repair over a cannula under high magnification.
- Concomitantly examine the buccal branch of the facial nerve, which closely follows the duct path.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 430 (Book Page): [The repair is best achieved under high magnifcation, over a cannula inserted through the duct opening under GA. The buccal branch of the facial nerve that closely follows the duct may also get transected in the injury; this requires careful examination.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What is the gold standard investigation for a severely injured blunt trauma patient with deranged physiology?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) with IV contrast from the head to the pelvis. This should be obtained as early as possible during resuscitation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: How is a diagnosis of traumatic thoracic aortic disruption confirmed following an initial suspicious chest radiograph?
back: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the mediastinum. The initial radiograph classically demonstrates a widened mediastinum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [The diagnosis is confrmed by a CT scan of the mediastinum ( Figure 29.5 ). In the hypotensive patient, widening of the mediastinum and aortic injury is not the cause of the hypotension.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which imaging modality is the most sensitive for diagnosing Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) in comatose patients?
back: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). CT is less sensitive, though it may show hemorrhagic foci in the corpus callosum or brainstem.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [Magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive and is employed to evaluate for difuse axonal injury in patients who fail to improve neurologically.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What specific technique should be used before X-raying a patient with multiple penetrating missile wounds?
back: Place metal markers (e.g., bent paper clips) on all external wounds. This correlates entry/exit points with retained internal missiles and assesses trajectory.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): [In patients with penetrating injury, metal markers (e.g. bent paper clips) should be placed on all external wounds before plain flms are taken... as this allows an assessment of the trajectory and helps to correlate the number of holes and the number of missiles.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which combination of investigations confirms the diagnosis of traumatic esophageal injury?
back: CT with oral contrast and esophagoscopy. Suspect this in patients presenting with mediastinal or deep cervical emphysema.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [A combination of CT with oral contrast and oesophagoscopy confrms the diagnosis in the great majority of cases.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: How must a suspected pelvic fracture be definitively diagnosed in the emergency department setting?
back: Radiographically (X-ray or CT). Manual mechanical testing ('springing the pelvis') is unreliable and contraindicated as it disrupts blood clots.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [A pelvic fracture should always be diagnosed radiographically... Mechanical testing of the pelvis in the emergency room (‘springing the pelvis’) adds no useful clinical examination and will disrupt any blood clot... It should never be performed.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
coreConcept: The Rule of 2s in Orthopaedic Imaging
front: Q: List the four components of the 'Rule of 2s' regarding radiographs for extremity trauma.
back:
1. 2 Views (orthogonal planes)
2. 2 Joints (above and below injury)
3. 2 Occasions (repeat if initially normal)
4. 2 Sides (comparison)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 432 (Book Page): [The rule of 2s should be remembered: 2 views... 2 joints... 2 occasions... 2 sides.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which specific radiographic projection is optimal for detecting a cam lesion in femoroacetabular impingement (FAI)?
back: 45° Dunn lateral radiograph. This supplements standard anteroposterior (AP) pelvis and false profile views for intra-articular hip derangements.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 524 (Book Page): [Anteroposterior pelvis and false profle views can help determine lateral or anterior coverage... while 45° Dunn lateral radiographs of the hip are the optimal projection for detecting the presence of a cam lesion.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: At what age does the primary screening tool for Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH) shift from ultrasound to radiography?
back: 4–5 months. At this age, plain radiographs become effective as the femoral ossific nucleus begins to appear.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 638 (Book Page): [Ultrasonographic assessment defnes the anatomy... it is used as a screening tool... Plain radiographs are used from 4–5 months of age, when the relationship of the femoral ossifc nucleus to the acetabulum can be assessed.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What standard radiographic views are obtained to identify a fracture of the zygomatic complex?
back: Occipitomental (OM) radiographs at 10° and 30°. These identify step deformities and maxillary sinus opacification (hemosinus).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 429 (Book Page): [For a suspected midface fracture, occipitomental (OM) radiographs at 10° and 30° should be obtained... right maxillary sinus opacifcation, which is one of the radiological hallmarks of zygomatic fracture.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What is the gold standard investigation for a severely injured adult blunt trauma patient?
back: Whole-body Computed Tomography (WBCT) from head to pelvis with intravenous (IV) contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [WBCT from the head to pelvis with IV contrast is the gold standard investigation of the severely injured adult blunt trauma patient]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which specific fracture and MRI finding are pathognomonic for an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture?
back:
• Segond fracture (anterolateral tibia)
• "Kissing lesions" (bone edema on posterolateral tibia and lateral femoral condyle)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 504 (Book Page): [A Segond fracture located on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury... ‘Kissing lesions’ of bony oedema... are also pathognomonic for ACL rupture]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: How is a suspected scaphoid fracture managed if initial radiographs appear normal?
back:
• Immobilize the wrist in a cast
• Repeat dedicated scaphoid view radiographs in 10–14 days
• Consider MRI/CT if earlier diagnosis is required
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [The standard protocol of a suspected scaphoid fracture is to immobilise the wrist and examine again 10–14 days later. If tenderness remains, repeat the scaphoid views.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What is the specific diagnostic protocol for a cystogram to detect traumatic bladder injury?
back: Instill a minimum of 300 mL of contrast into the bladder via a urethral catheter during Computed Tomography (CT).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 403 (Book Page): [For assessment of bladder injury a cystogram should be performed... A minimum of 300 mL of contrast is instilled into the bladder via a urethral catheter.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which four clinical predictors differentiate pediatric septic arthritis from transient synovitis?
back:
• History of fever >38.5°C
• Non-weight-bearing status
• ESR >40 mm/h
• White cell count >12 × 10⁹/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Four clinical predictors can diferentiate between septic arthritis and transient synovitis... History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which two radiographic views are essential to identify a suspected mandibular fracture?
back:
• Orthopantomogram (OPT)
• Posteroanterior (PA) radiograph of the mandible
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 429 (Book Page): [If a mandibular fracture is suspected, an orthopantomogram (OPT) and a posteroanterior (PA) radiograph of the mandible should be obtained]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
coreConcept: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip Screening
front: Q: What is the preferred diagnostic modality for screening neonatal hip instability before four months of age?
back: Ultrasonography defines both anatomy and stability (dynamic scanning) between 4 and 6 weeks of age.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): [Ultrasonography defnes the anatomy and the stability of the hip joint. It is used as a screening tool... Screening scans should be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of age]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which specific diagnostic investigation confirms a suspected traumatic tracheobronchial disruption?
back: Bronchoscopy is the definitive diagnostic modality for confirming airway disruption.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Severe subcutaneous emphysema with respiratory compromise can suggest tracheobronchial disruption... Bronchoscopy is diagnostic.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which specific fracture patterns on a skeletal survey have a high specificity for non-accidental injury?
back:
• Posterior rib fractures
• Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures
• Scapular fractures
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 637 (Book Page): [Fracture patterns with a high specifcity for non-accidental injury... Posterior rib fractures; Corner or bucket-handle metaphyseal fractures; Scapular fractures]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which combination of investigations confirms a traumatic oesophageal injury in the majority of cases?
back: Computed Tomography (CT) using oral contrast combined with oesophagoscopy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [A combination of CT with oral contrast and oesophagoscopy confrms the diagnosis in the great majority of cases.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What is the gold standard imaging investigation for an adult blunt trauma patient with suspected multiple injuries?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from head to pelvis with IV contrast. It should be performed as early as possible during resuscitation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
coreConcept: Imaging Sensitivity for Diffuse Axonal Injury
front: Q: In cases of traumatic brain injury, why is MRI preferred over CT for diagnosing Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI)?
back: MRI has higher sensitivity for detecting non-haemorrhagic microscopic foci in the corpus callosum and brainstem that are often invisible on CT.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): Magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive and is employed to evaluate for difuse axonal injury in patients who fail to improve neurologically.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: How does the imaging modality for screening Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH) change based on the infant's age?
back: ● Neonates (<4-6 months): Ultrasonographic assessment. ● Infants (>4-5 months): Plain radiography (assessing femoral ossific nucleus position).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): Ultrasonographic assessment. . . used as a screening tool. . . Plain radiographs are used from 4–5 months of age, when the relationship of the femoral ossifc nucleus to the acetabulum can be assessed.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which specific CT finding distinguishes a 'lentiform' hyperdense lesion in a patient with a 'talk and die' presentation?
back: Extradural Haematoma (EDH). It appears as a biconvex/lens-shaped hyperdense lesion between the skull and the dura, often associated with a skull fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which biochemical marker is investigated to confirm adequate tissue perfusion before proceeding with Early Total Care (ETC)?
back: Venous Lactate. Levels <2 mmol/L indicate successful resuscitation; >3 mmol/L indicates under-resuscitation and potential need for Damage Control Surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): Venous lactate is a useful marker of resuscitation and physiological state. A normal lactate (<2 mmol/L) is a sign that the patient is probably resuscitated and suitable for ETC.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What are the two specific radiographic measurements used to define acute spinal instability on a lateral cervical view?
back: ● Sagittal translation greater than 3.5 mm. ● Sagittal angulation greater than 11 degrees compared to the adjacent level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): Assess for instability: a 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; b sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
coreConcept: Indications for MRI in Spinal Trauma
front: Q: In the evaluation of spinal trauma, when is MRI indicated over the gold-standard CT scan?
back: Mandatory for all patients presenting with neurological deficits or when detailed assessment of ligamentous structures is required.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 414 (Book Page): MRI is indicated in all patients with neurological defcit and where assessment of ligamentous structures is important.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of the Limping Child
front: Q: Which four clinical predictors on examination and lab results differentiate pediatric Septic Arthritis from Transient Synovitis?
back: ● Fever >38.5°C ● Refusal to weight-bear ● ESR >40 mm/h ● WBC >12,000/L (Kocher Criteria).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 656 (Book Page): The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: History of fever >38.5°C, Non-weight-bearing, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h, White cell count >12 × 10^9 /L.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Why is MRI superior to plain X-ray in the first 48 hours of suspected acute osteomyelitis?
back: MRI detects bone marrow oedema and periosteal elevation early; X-ray findings (osteopenia/bone destruction) are typically delayed for 5–7 days.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 625 (Book Page): In the early phase (2–3 days) radiographs may be normal but MRI will show bone oedema and periosteal elevation.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
coreConcept: Mandatory Radiographic Views for Shoulder Dislocation
front: Q: Which radiographic view must be obtained to avoid missing a posterior glenohumeral dislocation?
back: Axillary view (or modified axillary/Velpeau view). AP and lateral views alone frequently result in a missed diagnosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 455 (Book Page): Axillary view – true value of the axillary view shown with obvious posterior dislocation of the glenohumeral joint.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What is the gold standard investigation for hemodynamically stable patients with multisystem trauma?
back:
* Whole-body CT (WBCT) from head to pelvis with IV contrast.
* It should be performed as early as possible during resuscitation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: How do imaging requirements evolve between the early and late stages of acute osteomyelitis?
back:
* Early (2-3 days): Radiographs are often normal; MRI is required to show bone edema/periosteal elevation.
* Late (5-7 days): Plain radiographs show osteopenia and periosteal new bone formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 603 (Book Page): In the early phase (2–3 days) radiographs may be normal but MRI will show bone oedema and periosteal elevation. After 5–7 days, plain radiographs may show subtle abnormality with osteopenia and periosteal new bone formation.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Contrast the specific radiological roles of chest radiography versus CT in suspected aortic disruption.
back:
* Chest Radiograph: Suggests injury via a widened mediastinum.
* CT Scan: Confirms the diagnosis of mediastinal aortic disruption.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum. The diagnosis is confrmed by a CT scan of the mediastinum.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: A non-weight-bearing child has a fever >38.5°C, ESR >40mm/h, and WCC >12×10⁹/L. Probability of septic arthritis?
back:
* 93.0% predicted probability of joint sepsis.
* Requires immediate aspiration and formal washout if pus is confirmed.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): (a) The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004)... History of fever >38.5°C, Non-weight-bearing, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h, White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L... (b) 4 [positive predictors] = 93.0% [probability].

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What is the diagnostic protocol for suspected scaphoid fracture with normal initial radiographs?
back:
1. Immobilize wrist in a cast.
2. Repeat radiographs in 10–14 days.
3. Consider early MRI, CT, or bone scan if symptoms persist.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): If a fracture is not evident on the initial radiographs and the patient remains tender in the anatomical snuf box, then treat as a suspected scaphoid fracture... protocol... is to immobilise the wrist and examine again 10–14 days later... earlier diagnosis may be made with a bone scan, MRI or CT.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: According to EBJIS criteria, which specific findings confirm a Prosthetic Joint Infection (PJI)?
back:
* Sinus tract communicating with the joint.
* ≥2 positive tissue samples with identical organisms.
* Synovial leukocyte count >3000/µL or positive α-defensin.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 601 (Book Page): Infection is confrmed if there is a sinus communicating with the joint or there is a high synovial fuid WCC (>3000/μL), a positive microbiological culture or positive histology.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which physical examination findings per the Ottawa Ankle Rules mandate radiographic investigation?
back:
* Bone tenderness at distal 6cm posterior margin or tip of lateral/medial malleolus.
* Inability to bear weight immediately and at the time of examination.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): Table 36.1 Ottawa ankle rules. Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the lateral malleolus [or medial malleolus]... Inability to bear weight at the time of the accident or at the time of examination.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Why is retrobulbar hemorrhage a clinical surgical emergency rather than a radiological diagnosis?
back:
* Diagnosis must be clinical (proptosis, pain, vision loss) to prevent blindness.
* High pressure causes irreversible optic nerve ischemia; immediate lateral canthotomy is mandatory.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness secondary to pressure-induced reduced fow on the retinal artery... It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What is the recommended imaging sequence for DDH based on patient age?
back:
* Under 4–5 months: Ultrasound (Dynamic/Static) is the gold standard.
* Over 4–5 months: Plain Radiography (due to ossification of the femoral nucleus).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): [Ultrasound] Screening scans should be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of age... Plain radiographs are used from 4–5 months of age, when the relationship of the femoral ossifc nucleus to the acetabulum can be assessed.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: List pathognomonic radiological signs for an Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) rupture.
back:
* Segond fracture: Anterolateral tibial avulsion on Radiographs.
* 'Kissing lesions': Bony edema on MRI (posterolateral tibia and lateral femoral condyle).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 504 (Book Page): A Segond fracture located on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury. ‘Kissing lesions’ of bony oedema seen on fuid-sensitive sequences on the posterolateral tibia and lateral femoral condyle are also pathognomonic for ACL rupture.

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Which clinical features identify acute airway compromise in severe midface trauma?
back:
● Posterior displacement of the maxilla/soft palate obstructing the pharynx.
● Marked oedema of the tongue and soft palate.
● Presentation with laboured breathing, stridor, or snoring.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 392 (Book Page): [the maxilla can become detached from the skull base and displaced downwards and backwards... acute airway compromise may initiate ‘code red’... associated with signifcant oedema of the soft palate and tongue.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiological mechanism of cardiovascular collapse in a tension pneumothorax.
back:
● One-way valve air leak causes progressive intrapleural pressure rise.
● Mediastinal shift compresses the vena cava, reducing venous return.
● Decreased cardiac output results in rapidly progressive obstructive shock.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape... The mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side, decreasing venous return and compressing the opposite lung.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Contrast the clinical findings of tension pneumothorax versus pericardial tamponade in trauma.
back:
● Both present with shock and distended neck veins.
