● Tension Pneumothorax: Absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance.
● Tamponade: Muffled heart sounds and clear lungs on auscultation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Pericardial tamponade needs to be diferentiated from a tension pneumothorax in the shocked patient with distended neck veins... presentation consists of central venous pressure elevation... mufed heart sounds.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: A febrile child presents with pseudoparalysis and an irritable hip. What is the priority diagnosis?
back:
● Acute septic arthritis of the hip joint.
● Cardinal signs: High fever, systemic toxaemia, and refusal to weight-bear.
● Urgent complication: Irreversible cartilage destruction and avascular necrosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 655 (Book Page): [Classically, the child presents with pain, fever and a reluctance to move the joint; in the lower limb, this implies a reluctance to weight bear. ... held immobile in the ‘position of comfort’... ‘pseudoparalysis’ in neonates.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What is the evidence-based dosing and timing for Tranexamic Acid in major trauma?
back:
● Initial dose: 1 gram IV bolus over 10 minutes.
● Timing: Ideally within 1 hour; contra-indicated if >3 hours post-injury.
● Maintenance: Second 1 gram IV dose infused over 8 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours. ... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: List the four clinical and laboratory predictors of pediatric septic arthritis (Kocher criteria).
back:
● Fever >38.5°C.
● Inability to weight-bear.
● Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) >40 mm/h.
● White Cell Count (WCC) >12,000/mm³.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 656 (Book Page): [Table 44.17... History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10⁹/L.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: What are the target systolic blood pressures for 'permissive hypotension' in trauma management?
back:
● General targets: 70–90 mmHg (aiming for a palpable radial pulse).
● Head injury targets: >90 mmHg (to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure).
● Purpose: Minimize hemorrhage before definitive surgical control.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Identify the hallmark features of a pediatric 'white eye' blowout fracture.
back:
● Minimal external bruising/edema despite significant entrapment.
● Vertical gaze restriction.
● Complication: Bradycardia, nausea, and syncope (oculocardiac reflex) from muscle entrapment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children... oculocardiac refex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. ... also described as a ‘white eye’ blowout fracture.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Describe the physiological consequence of intracranial mass expansion per the Monro-Kellie doctrine.
back:
● Skull is a rigid box; mass expansion first displaces CSF and venous blood.
● Once volume limits are reached, ICP rises exponentially.
● Consequence: Reduced cerebral perfusion pressure and brain herniation syndromes.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [the cranium is a ‘rigid box’ containing a ‘nearly incompressible brain’... expansion... initially accommodated by exclusion of fuid components... Further expansion is associated with an exponential rise in ICP.]

category: Describe key clinical features and complications, including airway compromise
front: Q: Identify the anatomical vessel and classic clinical progression of an extradural haematoma.
back:
● Vessel: Middle meningeal artery (associated with squamous temporal bone fracture).
● Progression: Initial concussion, followed by a 'lucid interval,' then rapid deterioration.
● Hallmark sign: Ipsilateral dilated pupil with contralateral hemiparesis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [fracture to the thin squamous temporal bone, with associated damage to the middle meningeal artery. Transient loss of consciousness is typical... subsequent lucid interval... contralateral hemiparesis... ipsilateral pupillary dilatation.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
coreConcept: WBCT as Gold Standard in Polytrauma
front: Q: What is the current gold standard investigation for an adult blunt trauma patient with multisystem injuries?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) with IV contrast from the head to the pelvis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [WBCT from the head to pelvis with IV contrast is the gold standard investigation of the severely injured adult blunt trauma patient]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which bedside ultrasound technique is used to locate sources of internal haemorrhage in hemodynamically unstable patients?
back:
● eFAST (Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma)
● Used to identify cardiac tamponade and free fluid in the thorax/abdomen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [Extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (eFAST) is becoming the most common investigation. The technique uses sonographic assessment in the chest, looking for a cardiac tamponade or free blood and air... and assessment for blood in the abdominal cavity]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which imaging modality is most sensitive for evaluating suspected Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI)?
back: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive and is employed to evaluate for diffuse axonal injury in patients who fail to improve neurologically.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: According to NICE guidelines, within what timeframe should a CT head be performed for GCS <13?
back: Within 1 hour.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [Table 28.3 Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour: GCS <13 at any point]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What imaging strategy is required if a scaphoid fracture is suspected clinically despite normal initial radiographs?
back:
● Immobilise the wrist
● Repeat scaphoid view radiographs after 10–14 days.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [The standard protocol of a suspected scaphoid fracture is to immobilise the wrist and examine again 10–14 days later. If tenderness remains, repeat the scaphoid views.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Contrast the radiographic appearance of an acute Extradural Haematoma versus a Chronic Subdural Haematoma on CT.
back:
● Extradural: Lentiform (biconvex) hyperdense lesion.
● Chronic Subdural: Diffuse concave hypodense lesion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page)/388: [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... Chronic subdural haematoma... Imaging reveals diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Why is imaging of the entire spinal column required after identifying a single spinal fracture?
back: Because there is a 15% incidence of having a second spinal fracture at a remote level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [If a spinal fracture is identifed then further imaging of the whole spine is required because there is a 15% incidence of a further spinal fracture.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Describe the fundamental 'Rule of 2s' used in the radiographic evaluation of extremity fractures.
back:
● 2 views (orthogonal)
● 2 joints (above and below)
● 2 occasions (repeat for occult injury)
● 2 sides (comparison for pediatric cases)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 420 (Book Page): [The rule of 2s should be remembered: 2 views... 2 joints... 2 occasions... 2 sides]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: Which investigation must be performed to exclude occult popliteal artery injury following a knee dislocation?
back: Angiogram (either formal or CT Angiography).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [In injuries commonly associated with vascular injury, such as knee dislocations, occult injury should be actively excluded with an angiogram.]

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
front: Q: What specific clinical findings necessitate the use of MRI instead of CT in spinal trauma?
back:
● Neurological deficits
● Suspected ligamentous structures injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 414 (Book Page): [MRI is indicated in all patients with neurological defcit and where assessment of ligamentous structures is important]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Which specific medical disciplines are typically included in a multidisciplinary trauma team?
back: Doctors from the emergency department, anaesthetics/critical care, trauma and orthopaedics, and general surgery. Radiology and haematology often contribute during initial assessment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): [The team] will invariably involve doctors from the emergency department, anaesthetics and/or critical care, trauma and orthopaedics and general surgery. Increasingly, radiology and haematology doctors are contributing.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: How does the BACH classification system guide multidisciplinary planning for chronic osteomyelitis?
back: It stages patients based on Bone involvement, Antimicrobial options, soft-tissue Coverage needs, and Host status. All infected non-unions are considered complex.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 605 (Book Page): The BACH classifcation divides patients into ‘uncomplicated’, ‘complex’ and ‘limited options available’ based on... (B), the antimicrobial profle (A), the need for soft-tissue cover (C) and the health of the host (H).

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Compare single-stage versus two-stage revision plans for managing prosthetic joint infections.
back: Single-stage involves removal and reimplantation in one session. Two-stage uses a temporary antibiotic spacer for six weeks before reimplantation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 602 (Book Page): Single-stage joint revision... removal and reimplantation are undertaken in the same operating session... Two-stage joint revision... A new prosthesis is implanted after the course of antibiotics has been completed.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What is the plan for managing persistent arterial pelvic bleeding in a multidisciplinary setting?
back: If compression and extraperitoneal packing fail, interventional angioembolisation is the choice. Complex cases require coordination between orthopaedic surgery and interventional radiology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): If the bleeding is of arterial origin, interventional angioembolisation is the next choice for bleeding control... Severe pelvic injuries require a multidisciplinary team approach.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Outline the multidisciplinary antibiotic protocol required for the surgical phase of open fractures.
back: Administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms. Therapy must continue until 48 hours after definitive wound closure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): Continue intravenous antibiotics until 48 hours after defnitive wound closure.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What definitive surgical management is mandatory for native joint septic arthritis?
back: Prompt removal of pus via formal open washout or repeated aspiration/irrigation. The joint is opened to encourage free drainage through a capsulotomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus... the joint must be opened, irrigated and free drainage encouraged via the capsulotomy.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Which key factors determine the multidisciplinary prognosis for neurological recovery in spinal injuries?
back: Recovery depends on the initial level and completeness of the injury, the patient's age at presentation, and whether they are ventilator dependent.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 403 (Book Page): The prognosis for neurological recovery is strongly infuenced by factors such as the level and completeness of the injury, ventilator dependence and the age at presentation.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Describe the role of Single-Event Multilevel Surgery (SEMLS) in managing cerebral palsy gait.
back: Multidisciplinary teams use computerised gait analysis to plan simultaneous bone and soft-tissue procedures. This corrects multiple lower limb abnormalities in one operative event.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 632 (Book Page): Single-event multilevel surgery (SEMLS) is popular, and gait analysis... contributes to the selection of an appropriate management plan... Appropriate bone and soft-tissue procedures can then be planned.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What are the three primary goals of the multidisciplinary Damage Control Surgery (DCS) plan?
back: Immediate goals are limited to stopping active surgical bleeding, controlling contamination, and restoring normal physiology. Definitive reconstructive surgery is deferred.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): Damage control surgery is restricted to only three goals: ● stopping any active surgical bleeding; ● controlling any contamination; ● restoring normal physiology.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Outline the multidisciplinary phases of the Ponseti method for club foot management.
back: Phases include serial manipulation/casting (CAVE sequence), percutaneous Achilles tenotomy, and maintenance with a foot abduction orthosis (FAO) for up to four years.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 626 (Book Page): The Ponseti method... sequence of manipulations is: C... A... V... E... maintenance by a foot abduction orthosis (FAO).

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Which specific specialists comprise a standard multidisciplinary severe trauma team?
back:
- Senior clinicians from emergency medicine
- Anaesthesia/critical care
- Trauma and orthopaedics
- General surgery
- Contributing support from radiology and haematology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a dedicated trauma team... it will invariably involve doctors from the emergency department, anaesthetics and/ or critical care, trauma and orthopaedics and general surgery. Increasingly, radiology and haematology doctors are contributing to the trauma team]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Why is open arthrotomy preferred for the definitive management of hip septic arthritis?
back:
- Ensures prompt, thorough removal of destructive pus
- Facilitates joint irrigation
- Encourages free drainage via capsulotomy
- Prevents chondrolysis and avascular necrosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint... the joint must be opened, irrigated and free drainage encouraged via the capsulotomy.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Contrast definitive management strategies: Single-stage vs. Two-stage joint revision for infection.
back:
- Single-stage: Removal and reimplantation in one session; requires healthy soft tissues.
- Two-stage: Removal, antibiotic spacer placement, then reimplantation after 6 weeks of antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [Two-stage joint revision surgery... A new prosthesis is implanted after the course of antibiotics... Single-stage joint revision surgery... removal and reimplantation are undertaken in the same operating session.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Outline the multidisciplinary plan for managing complex Chronic Osteomyelitis using BACH criteria.
back:
- Bone: Radical segmental resection/stabilization
- Antimicrobials: Targeted long-term therapy
- Coverage: Plastic surgical soft-tissue reconstruction
- Host: Optimization of comorbidities (e.g., smoking, diabetes).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 605 (Book Page): [The BACH classifcation divides patients into ‘uncomplicated’, ‘complex’... based on... anatomical location (B), antimicrobial profle (A), the need for soft-tissue cover (C) and the health of the host (H).]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What are the criteria for the DAIR definitive management plan in PJI?
back:
- Prosthesis must be well-fixed
- Modular components must be exchanged
- Full excision of infected soft tissue/necrotic bone
- Good soft-tissue cover available.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 602 (Book Page): [This can only be undertaken if the prosthesis is well fxed... all infected soft tissue and necrotic bone must be fully excised and modular components exchanged... Good soft-tissue cover is essential.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: State the standard non-surgical management sequence for Idiopathic Club Foot (Ponseti).
back:
- Serial manipulation and casting (weekly)
- Percutaneous Achilles tenotomy (for residual equinus)
- Maintenance with Foot Abduction Orthosis (FAO) until age 4.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 626 (Book Page): [The Ponseti method... A specifc set of manoeuvres, followed by a series of well-moulded above-knee plaster casts... most feet lack 15° of dorsifexion and require a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy... foot position is maintained by a foot abduction orthosis]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What is the definitive management plan for DDH in a child aged 6–24 months?
back:
- Medial or anterior approach open reduction
- Simultaneous capsulorrhaphy
- Possible femoral/pelvic osteotomy for stability
- Postoperative maintenance in a spica cast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 618 (Book Page): [A medial approach open reduction can be performed between 6 and 24 months of age... anterior approach... allows for a simultaneous capsulorrhaphy... femoral shortening or derotation osteotomies will improve stability.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Outline the 'top-down' surgical sequencing plan for Panfacial fractures.
back:
1. Frontal bone and zygomatic arch
2. Orbital rim and nasoethmoidal complex
3. Mandible
4. Le Fort I and orbital floor (last).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 415 (Book Page): [One of the most common sequencing techniques is a ‘top down’... frst repairing the frontal bone and zygomatic arch fractures followed by orbital rim, nasoethmoidal and mandible fractures. The Le Fort I level maxillary and orbital foor fractures are repaired last.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What is the primary definitive management goal for geriatric lower limb osteoporotic fractures?
back:
- Rigid internal fixation using locking plate/nail technology
- Primary objective is immediate full weight-bearing and mobilization
- Prevents complications of prolonged recumbency.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [fxation should be strong enough to allow immediate weight-bearing and to hold the position until union. Locking plate technology improves fxation in osteoporotic bone]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Describe the urgent management plan for an acute unstable SCFE.
back:
- Considered a surgical emergency
- Gentle repositioning under anaesthesia (no force)
- Capsulotomy (to reduce tamponade)
- Definitive internal screw fixation within 24 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 622 (Book Page): [acute unstable SCFE is an emergency... gentle repositioning... A capsulotomy reduces the tamponade efect... such treatment should take place within 24 hours of injury.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Within what specific timeframe should Early Total Care (ETC) achieve definitive fixation for stable long bone and spinal fractures?
back: Within 36 hours of injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): For musculoskeletal injuries, ETC allows defnitive fxation of all unstable long bone, spinal and pelvic fractures within 36 hours of injury.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: How does biofilm formation on orthopaedic implants increase bacterial resistance to definitive medical management?
back: Bacteria within the polysaccharide matrix alter their metabolic state, becoming resistant to host immune responses and standard systemic antibiotic therapy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): Bacteria can adhere to... implant surfaces, forming a complex community... known as a bioflm. These bacteria alter their metabolic state, making them more resistant both to the host immune system and to antibiotics.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
coreConcept: Surgical Staging of Prosthetic Joint Infection
front: Q: Contrast the procedural approaches of single-stage versus two-stage revision for prosthetic joint infection (PJI).
back:
● Single-stage: Removal and reimplantation in one surgical session.
● Two-stage: Removal and spacer placement, followed by delayed reimplantation after 6 weeks of antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 602 (Book Page): Single-stage joint revision surgery... removal and reimplantation are undertaken in the same operating session... Two-stage joint revision surgery... A new prosthesis is implanted after the course of antibiotics has been completed.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What definitive surgical options are indicated for a child with chronic, severe (>66%) slipped capital femoral epiphysis?
back: Realignment osteotomy (e.g., intertrochanteric) or head-neck osteoplasty to restore head-neck offset and correct femoroacetabular impingement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 622 (Book Page): In the chronic severe slip... a realignment osteotomy may be considered... the slipped epiphysis is associated with a ‘cam’ type of femoroacetabular impingement and this may require treatment with a head–neck osteoplasty.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What is the standard antibiotic prophylaxis protocol for definitive surgical management of penetrating abdominal trauma?
back: Prophylactic antibiotics must be administered prior to surgery; a single dose is usually sufficient unless major contamination is present.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 408 (Book Page): However, prophylactic antibiotics prior to surgery should be used in all cases of penetrating abdominal trauma. Unless there is major contamination, a single dose is sufcient.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Which specific specialties are responsible for the multidisciplinary decision between Early Total Care and Damage Control Surgery?
back: Senior surgeons and anesthetists/critical care doctors.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): The identifcation of patients suitable for ETC versus DCS should be made by senior surgeons and anaesthetists/critical care doctors.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Why is early transfer considered for severe pelvic fractures in institutions lacking a specialized multidisciplinary team?
back: MDT care is required to coordinate complex management including angioembolisation, extraperitoneal packing, and orthopedic stabilization, which are essential for survival.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): Severe pelvic injuries require a multidisciplinary team approach. If adequate orthopaedic experience is unavailable, consideration should be given towards early transfer.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: In severe multi-system trauma, when is limb amputation prioritized over definitive revascularization for an arterial injury?
back: When revascularization would increase the total operating time and metabolic load, threatening life through the development of the 'triad of death'.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): Revascularisation of a limb following arterial injury may... increase the threat to life and therefore amputation may be the better option.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Describe the secondary injury physiological loop that multidisciplinary care aims to interrupt in traumatic brain injury (TBI).
back: Raised ICP reduces cerebral perfusion, causing hypoxia and secondary brain injury; this leads to further brain swelling, which increases ICP further.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): Brain swelling and mass lesions contribute to raised intracranial pressure, which compromises perfusion, leading to secondary brain injury and further swelling.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Which anatomical law explains referred knee pain in pediatric hip pathology, necessitating multidisciplinary joint assessment?
back: Hilton’s Law: a joint is supplied by the same nerves as the muscles that move the joint (e.g., obturator and femoral nerves).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): Hilton’s law, which states that a joint is supplied by the same nerves as the muscles that move the joint, explains why many children present with knee pain although the pathology is in the hip.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: List the specialists typically required for a dedicated multidisciplinary trauma team.
back: Emergency Medicine, Anaesthetics/Critical Care, Trauma and Orthopaedics, General Surgery, Radiology, and Haematology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): [it will invariably involve doctors from the emergency department, anaesthetics and/ or critical care, trauma and orthopaedics and general surgery. Increasingly, radiology and haematology doctors are contributing...]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: How is the decision to proceed with sequential definitive fixations managed by the multidisciplinary team?
back: At the conclusion of each procedure, the surgeon and anaesthetist collaboratively determine if the patient's physiological status (lactate, temperature, etc.) remains stable enough for the next step.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [at the conclusion of each procedure the surgeon and anaesthetist should determine whether the patient’s physiological status has been maintained sufciently to allow the next procedure, or whether the patient should return to critical care...]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Contrast the definitive management of a stable versus an unstable unhealed fracture-related infection (FRI).
back: Stable fractures use debridement, sampling, and suppression (DAIR). Unstable fractures require implant removal, radical segmental excision, and restabilization with an external fixator.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 603 (Book Page): [Unhealed fracture with stable fxation... managed with deep sampling, debridement... (DAIR) approach... Unhealed fracture with unstable fxation... implant... should be removed and replaced by an external fxator.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What is the definitive management plan for a complex segmental bone infection (BACH complex)?
back: Segmental curative resection, bone stabilization (e.g., Ilizarov method), soft-tissue reconstruction (often free tissue transfer), and long-term (6–12 weeks) antibiotics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 606 (Book Page): [Curative resection must be segmental and bone stabilisation will always be required. The Ilizarov method... is a powerful and successful technique in these cases. It can be combined with free tissue transfer.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: State the definitive multidisciplinary nutritional protocol for severe Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI).
back: Initiate enteral nutrition within 72 hours of injury; use prokinetics (metoclopramide or erythromycin) to enhance absorption and mitigate gastric stasis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): [Enteral nutrition is preferred to intravenous parenteral nutri- tion... should be commenced within 72 hours of injury. Prokinetics (e.g. metoclopramide, erythromycin) can be administered to promote absorption.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Which clinical bundle of indices confirms a trauma patient is sufficiently resuscitated for Early Total Care (ETC)?
back: Pulse <100/min, normal blood pressure, urine output >30 mL/h, normal coagulation screen, and lactate <2 mmol/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [physiological indices are used to evaluate the response to resuscitation, including a pulse rate less than 100 per minute, normal blood pressure and respiratory rate, as well as urine output >30 mL/h... normal coagulation screen. Lactate levels... <2 mmol/L...]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Outline the definitive management plan for persistent CSF rhinorrhoea following skull base trauma.
back: Maintain high suspicion for meningitis and perform surgical repair if spontaneous resolution fails; blind nasogastric tube insertion is strictly contraindicated.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [CSF leak will generally resolve spontaneously but persistent leak can result in meningitis so repair may be required. Blind nasogastric tube placement is contraindicated in these patients.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Compare the definitive surgical approaches for lower esophageal versus anterior cardiac injuries.
back: Lower esophageal injuries utilize a left anterolateral thoracotomy. Anterior cardiac injuries utilize a median sternotomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): [Table 29.5: Left anterolateral thoracotomy: Lower oesophagus; Left side of heart. Median sternotomy: Anterior aspect of heart; Anterior mediastinum.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What is the primary objective of a multidisciplinary 'Tertiary Survey' in polytrauma care?
back: To identify missed minor injuries (e.g., scaphoid fractures) once the patient is extubated and communicative, preventing long-term disability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Such patients should have a ‘tertiary survey’ when extubated and alert to identify any missed ‘minor’ injuries... these injuries have the potential to cause signifcant long-term disability.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: List the four clinical predictors used to differentiate paediatric septic arthritis from transient synovitis.
back: 1. History of fever >38.5°C. 2. Non-weight-bearing status. 3. ESR >40 mm/h. 4. White cell count >12 × 10^9/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 656 (Book Page): [Table 44.17: History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What is the typical specialist composition of a dedicated multidisciplinary trauma team?
back:
● Emergency department physicians
● Anaesthetics and/or Critical Care
● Trauma and Orthopaedics
● General surgery
● Radiology and Haematology doctors
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): [The composition of the team will depend on local policies but it will invariably involve doctors from the emergency department, anaesthetics and/ or critical care, trauma and orthopaedics and general surgery. Increasingly, radiology and haematology doctors are contributing to the trauma team]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What four parameters define the BACH classification for planning chronic osteomyelitis management?
back:
● Bone involvement (B)
● Antimicrobial options (A)
● Coverage of soft tissue (C)
● Host status (H)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 627 (Book Page): [The BACH classifcation divides patients into ‘uncomplicated’, ‘complex’ and ‘limited options available’ based on the four important features of the infection... anatomical location in the bone (B), the antimicrobial profle (A), the need for soft-tissue cover (C) and the health of the host (H).]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Contrast single-stage versus two-stage revision in the management of prosthetic joint infection (PJI).
back:
● Single-stage: Removal and reimplantation are performed in the same operation.
● Two-stage: Removal, 6-week antibiotic/spacer therapy, followed by new prosthesis reimplantation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [Two-stage joint revision surgery... A new prosthesis is implanted after the course of antibiotics has been completed... Single-stage joint revision surgery. The procedure is the same as above, but removal and reimplantation are undertaken in the same operating session.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What are the primary objectives during the definitive surgical phase of open fracture management?
back:
● Thorough debridement of contaminated/non-vital tissue
● Stable bone stabilization (internal or external fixation)
● Soft-tissue reconstruction (primary or delayed closure/flaps)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 465 (Book Page): [Surgical phase... stable fxation of the bony injury is very important... Thorough debridement of any contaminated or non-vital soft tissue is important... Soft-tissue reconstruction may involve primary or delayed primary closure of the wound]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What is the management sequence for idiopathic club foot using the Ponseti method?
back:
1. Serial above-knee casting (Corrects cavus, abduction, varus)
2. Percutaneous Achilles tenotomy (Corrects equinus)
3. Foot Abduction Orthosis (FAO) full-time then nights/naps for 4 years
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 648 (Book Page): [C – correction of the apparent forefoot cavus... A – gradual forefoot abduction to 60°... V – correction of the hindfoot varus... E – correction of hindfoot equinus usually follows a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy... foot abduction orthosis (FAO)... for up to 4 years.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Outline the treatment hierarchy for controlling arterial versus venous pelvic haemorrhage.
back:
● Venous (85%): Pelvic binding, external fixation, or extraperitoneal packing.
● Arterial: Interventional angioembolisation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [Eighty-fve per cent of bleeding originating from the pelvis is of venous origin and can be controlled by non-operative means, including compression either by binding or external fxator or by extraperitoneal pelvic packing... If the bleeding is of arterial origin, interventional angioembolisation is the next choice]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: At what age does the management plan for DDH typically transition to surgical reconstruction?
back:
● Splinting/Pavlik harness: Under 6 months.
● Closed reduction/Spica: 6–24 months.
● Open reduction/Osteotomies: Over 2 years.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 639 (Book Page)-640: [Successful harness treatment is unusual after the age of 4–6 months... closed reduction... A medial approach open reduction can be performed between 6 and 24 months of age. In the older child, a pelvic osteotomy may be required]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Why is an acute unstable slip of the capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) managed as a surgical emergency?
back:
● Equivalent to a displaced femoral neck fracture
● High risk of Avascular Necrosis (AVN)
● Requires gentle repositioning and internal fixation within 24 hours
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 644 (Book Page): [This situation is equivalent to a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. This means that an acute unstable SCFE is an emergency. The AVN risk is considerable... To be efective such treatment should take place within 24 hours of injury.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: State the target physiological parameters for managing a head-injured patient in neurointensive care.
back:
● ICP <20 mmHg
● CPP >60 mmHg
● MAP 80–90 mmHg
● PaCO2 4.5–5.0 kPa
● PaO2 >11 kPa
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): [Table 28.5 Key parameters to maintain in head-injured patients... PaCO 2 = 4.5–5.0 kPa; PaO 2 >11 kPa; MAP = 80–90 mmHg; ICP <20 mmHg; CPP >60 mmHg]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
coreConcept: Diagnostic Planning for Frontal Sinus Trauma
front: Q: Which biochemical assay is used to plan management for suspected CSF rhinorrhoea in facial trauma?
back: ● β2 transferrin assay
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 436 (Book Page): [If combined with a dural tear, there may be cerebrospinal fuid (CSF) rhinorrhoea, which can be confrmed by sending the fuid sample for β 2 transferrin assay.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: What is the clinical definition of thoracic trauma within the framework of torso injury?
back: Injury to the chest focal point of the torso, including the rib cage, heart, lungs, and mediastinal structures. It accounts for 25% of severe trauma deaths, primarily due to haemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [Thoracic injury accounts for 25% of all severe injuries. In a further 25%, it may be a signifcant contributor to the subsequent death of the patient. In most of these patients, the cause of death is haemorrhage.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: How is thoracic trauma primarily classified based on the mechanism of injury?
back: 1. Blunt Trauma: Caused by compression or deceleration (e.g., RTA, falls). 2. Penetrating Trauma: Caused by direct entry of objects (e.g., stabbings, gunshot wounds, blasts).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [In penetrating injury, most patients... can be managed with appropriate resuscitation and insertion of an intercostal drain. In blunt injury, most bleeding occurs from the intercostal or internal mammary vessels.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: What radiological approach distinguishes the initial assessment of penetrating from blunt thoracic trauma?
back: Penetrating: Erect radiographs are preferred to reveal small pneumothorax or air under the diaphragm. Blunt: CT scan with contrast is the gold standard for defining skeletal and visceral injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [In penetrating injury, it may be more helpful for the radiograph to be performed with the patient positioned erect... In blunt chest trauma, the CT scan... has become the principal and most reliable examination for major injury.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: A patient arrives with a gunshot wound below the nipples. How is this injury classified?
back: Classified as a junctional zone penetrating injury. Because the diaphragm moves between the 4th and 8th intercostal spaces, it must be investigated as both thoracic and abdominal penetration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [Any penetrating injury below the nipples on the chest may therefore have penetrated the diaphragm and entered the abdomen. Injuries in this junctional zone, therefore, should be investigated as if both cavities had been penetrated.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: What specific intravenous drug is indicated to reduce mortality in both blunt and penetrating haemorrhagic trauma?
back: Tranexamic acid (TXA). Administer 1g IV over 10 minutes, then 1g over 8 hours. It must be given ideally within the first hour and no later than 3 hours post-injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Tranexamic acid is an antifbrinolytic drug that reduces the risk of mortality from bleeding in both blunt and penetrating trauma. One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: List the 'Deadly Six' immediately life-threatening thoracic injuries managed during the primary survey.
back: 1. Airway obstruction. 2. Tension pneumothorax. 3. Pericardial tamponade. 4. Open pneumothorax. 5. Massive haemothorax. 6. Flail chest.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Six are immediately life-threatening and should be sought and managed during the primary survey... Airway obstruction, Tension pneumothorax, Pericardial tamponade, Open pneumothorax, Massive haemothorax, Flail chest.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Why is an erect chest radiograph specifically indicated for suspected penetrating abdominal viscus perforation?
back: To identify free gas under the diaphragm. Blunt injury often presents with large diaphragmatic ruptures and visceral migration, whereas penetrating wounds require erect views for subtle gas leaks.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [In penetrating injury... erect [radiograph]... will best reveal... free gas under the diaphragm, indicating the presence of a hollow abdominal viscus perforation.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Distinguish the mechanism of lung contusion between blunt compressive injury and penetrating gunshot wounds.
back: In blunt trauma, contusion is caused by direct chest compression or flail segments. In penetrating trauma (gunshots), contusion results from the kinetic shock wave of the bullet.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 398 (Book Page): [In blunt chest compressive injury, particularly in the presence of a flail chest, there can be an associated lung contusion... Following gunshot wounds, there is an area of contusion from the shock wave of the bullet.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: How do blunt and penetrating mechanisms typically cause traumatic diaphragmatic injury differently?
back: Blunt mechanisms involve large compressive forces causing large ruptures and herniation. Penetrating mechanisms involve sharp defects and are often 'silent,' requiring surgical repair via the abdomen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 398 (Book Page): [Blunt injury to the diaphragm is usually caused by a compressive force applied to the torso. The diaphragmatic rupture is usually large... Most diaphragmatic injuries are silent and the presenting features are those of injury to the surrounding organs.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: What force mechanism causes traumatic aortic disruption in blunt thoracic trauma?
back: Sudden impact creates shear forces that disrupt the vessel's intima and media. This typically occurs distal to the ligamentum arteriosum, near the origin of the left subclavian artery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Traumatic aortic rupture is a common cause of sudden death after a vehicle collision or fall... The shear forces from a sudden impact disrupt the intima and media.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Define thoracic trauma in terms of its incidence and clinical impact in severe injuries.
back: Thoracic trauma accounts for 25% of all severe injuries and contributes significantly to trauma-related deaths, with hemorrhage being the primary cause of mortality.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [Thoracic injury accounts for 25% of all severe injuries. In a further 25%, it may be a signifcant contributor to the subsequent death of the patient. In most of these patients, the cause of death is haemorrhage.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Classify thoracic trauma into its two primary categories based on the mechanism of injury.
back:
1. Blunt Trauma: Results from compression or deceleration forces (e.g., RTAs, falls).
2. Penetrating Trauma: Results from direct entry of objects (e.g., stabs, gunshots).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [In penetrating injury, most patients... can be managed with appropriate resuscitation... In blunt injury, most bleeding occurs from the intercostal or internal mammary vessels.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: How is the 'Deadly Dozen' of thoracic trauma clinically classified for assessment?
back:
1. Immediately life-threatening: Detected and managed during the Primary Survey.
2. Potentially life-threatening: Detected during the Secondary Survey.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [Life-threatening injuries can be remembered as the ‘deadly dozen’. Six are immediately life-threatening and should be sought and managed during the primary survey and six are potentially life-threatening and should be detected during the secondary survey.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Classify the specific anatomical 'junctional zones' relevant to thoracic trauma.
back:
• Neck and Thorax
• Thorax and Upper Limbs
• Thorax and Abdomen (Diaphragm)
• Abdominopelvic structures and Groin
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 392 (Book Page): [The key junctional zones are: ● between the neck and the thorax; ● between the thorax and the upper limbs; ● between the thorax and the abdomen; ● between the abdominopelvic structures and the groin.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Distinguish between the force mechanisms involved in blunt thoracic trauma pathology.
back:
• Direct Compression: Bursts organ substance (e.g., liver or heart).
• Deceleration/Shear Forces: Disrupts fixed anatomical structures (e.g., the aorta at the ligamentum arteriosum).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Blunt injury to the diaphragm is usually caused by a compressive force applied to the torso. ... Page 397 (Book Page): Traumatic aortic rupture... The shear forces from a sudden impact disrupt the intima and media.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Why is penetrating trauma below the nipple line classified as a 'thoraco-abdominal' injury?
back: The diaphragm moves between the 4th and 8th intercostal spaces during respiration; any injury below the nipples may have penetrated both thoracic and abdominal cavities.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [The thorax and abdomen are separated by the diaphragm... allowing movement during breathing between the fourth and eighth intercostal space. Any penetrating injury below the nipples on the chest may therefore have penetrated the diaphragm and entered the abdomen.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Define a 'Massive Haemothorax' based on the quantitative surgical classification.
back:
Accumulation of blood in the pleural space meeting one of two criteria:
1. Initial drainage of >1500 mL.
2. Ongoing bleeding of >200 mL/h for 3–4 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Define the clinical and radiological criteria for classifying a 'Flail Chest'.
back: Clinical/Radiological definition: Three or more adjacent ribs fractured in two or more places, resulting in paradoxical chest wall movement (segment moves inwards on inspiration).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Flail chest... is defned as three or more ribs fractured in two or more places. ... paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment. On inspiration, the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Classify an 'Open Pneumothorax' by its size threshold and physiological effect.
back: Defined by a chest wall defect >3 cm (or 2/3 the diameter of the trachea); leads to preferential air entry through the wound rather than the trachea, causing profound hypoventilation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Open pneumothorax (‘sucking chest wound’) ... due to a large open defect in the chest (>3 cm)... If the opening in the chest wall exceeds about two-thirds of the diameter of the trachea, then with each inspiratory cycle air will be preferentially drawn through the defect.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: How are thoracic trauma patients categorized for management based on physiological status?
back:
1. Physiologically Normal: Full investigation before treatment.
2. Physiologically Non-compromised: Limited investigation to determine operative vs. non-operative need.
3. Physiologically Compromised: Immediate surgery (e.g., Thoracotomy) required without delay for imaging.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): [Abdominal trauma can generally be classifed into... physiologically ‘normal’... physiologically ‘non-compromised’... physiologically ‘compromised’ – investigations need to be suspended as immediate surgical correction of the bleeding is required.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Outline the definitive management options for a patient with confirmed traumatic thoracic aortic disruption.
back:
- Control systolic blood pressure (<120 mmHg).
- Endovascular intra-aortic stent placement (TEVAR).
- Operative repair via direct suturing or Dacron grafting.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [In the presence of thoracic aortic injury, initial management consists of control of the systolic arterial blood pressure (to less than 120 mmHg). Thereafter, an endovascular intra-aortic stent ... can be placed, or the tear can be operatively repaired by direct repair or by excision and grafting using a Dacron graft.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What are the criteria for selecting Debridement, Antibiotics, and Implant Retention (DAIR) in prosthetic joint infection?
back:
- Firmly fixed prosthesis.
- Healthy soft-tissue envelope.
- Acute onset (<3 weeks) or early postoperative infection.
- Requires modular component exchange and radical debridement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 623 (Book Page): [This can only be undertaken if the prosthesis is well fxed. ...DAIR is not a form of washout as all infected soft tissue and necrotic bone must be fully excised and modular components exchanged.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Contrast single-stage versus two-stage revision for the definitive management of chronic prosthetic joint infection (PJI).
back:
- Single-stage: Removal and reimplantation in one session; requires healthy soft tissues.
- Two-stage: Removal, antibiotic spacer placement (6 weeks), followed by delayed reimplantation after infection clearance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 623 (Book Page): [Two-stage joint revision surgery ... A new prosthesis is implanted after the course of antibiotics has been completed. ... Single-stage joint revision surgery ... removal and reimplantation are undertaken in the same operating session.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Outline the definitive multidisciplinary management plan for acute limb compartment syndrome.
back:
- Immediate removal of all restrictive dressings/casts.
- Emergent surgical fasciotomy of all involved compartments.
- Senior input for monitoring and delayed primary closure or skin grafting.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 465 (Book Page): [Emergency treatment involves splitting casts and/or dressings to the skin and elevating the extremity. Senior input should be sought and arrangements put in place to perform defnitive treatment with fasciotomies.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: How does the OVIVA trial influence the definitive pharmacological management of musculoskeletal infections?
back:
- Validates targeted oral antibiotic therapy as non-inferior to intravenous therapy.
- Prerequisites: Organism susceptibility and patient tolerance of the oral regimen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 620 (Book Page): [The recent OVIVA trial has shown that oral therapy is equally efective, providing that the organism(s) is susceptible and the patient can tolerate the chosen antibiotic.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: State the sequential phases of the Ponseti method for definitive clubfoot (CTEV) management.
back:
- CAVE sequence: Cavus, Abduction, and Varus serial casting.
- Percutaneous Achilles tenotomy for Equinus correction.
- Foot Abduction Orthosis (FAO) splinting until age 4.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 647 (Book Page): [The standard sequence of manipulations is: C – correction of the apparent forefoot cavus ... A – gradual forefoot abduction to 60° ... V – correction of the hindfoot varus ... E – correction of hindfoot equinus usually follows a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Outline the multidisciplinary plan for definitive management of a Gustilo Type III open fracture.
back:
- Early broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
- Urgent radical debridement and skeletal stabilization.
- Multidisciplinary involvement for early soft-tissue cover (Plastic Surgery flaps).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 464 (Book Page): [The aim of open fracture management is to achieve bony union, optimise function and avoid infection. ...early administration of intravenous antibiotics ... Radical excision of the infected fracture is needed ... soft-tissue reconstruction.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Why is an acute unstable Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) treated as a surgical emergency?
back:
- Biomechanically equivalent to a displaced intracapsular neck fracture.
- Requires fixation within 24 hours to prevent epiphyseal avascular necrosis (AVN).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 643 (Book Page): [This situation is equivalent to a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. This means that an acute unstable SCFE is an emergency. ...treatment should take place within 24 hours of injury.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: Describe the multidisciplinary components addressed by the BACH classification for chronic osteomyelitis.
back:
- B: Bone resection and stabilization (e.g., Ilizarov).
- A: Targeted Antimicrobial therapy.
- C: Soft tissue Coverage (Plastic Surgery).
- H: Host optimization (e.g., managing diabetes/smoking).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 626 (Book Page): [The BACH classifcation ... B (bone), A (antimicrobial), C (soft tissue coverage), H (host status). ...multidisciplinary approach ...Ilizarov method ... distractions osteogenesis.]

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
front: Q: What surgical intervention is mandatory for the definitive management of confirmed native joint septic arthritis?
back:
- Prompt formal surgical washout (irrigation and drainage).
- Objective: Prevent protease-mediated chondrolysis and epiphyseal avascular necrosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 655 (Book Page): [The treatment of a presumed septic arthritis therefore requires the prompt removal of pus from the joint ... The joint is aspirated and, if pus is confrmed, a formal washout is mandatory.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
coreConcept: Immediate life-threatening chest injuries (The Deadly Dozen)
front: Q: List the six chest injuries identified as immediately life-threatening during the trauma primary survey.
back:
1. Airway obstruction
2. Tension pneumothorax
3. Pericardial tamponade
4. Open pneumothorax
5. Massive haemothorax
6. Flail chest.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Table 29.3] Immediately life-threatening: Airway obstruction, Tension pneumothorax, Pericardial tamponade, Open pneumothorax, Massive haemothorax, Flail chest.

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism of a tension pneumothorax?
back: A 'one-way valve' air leak allows air into the thorax but not out, collapsing the ipsilateral lung and displacing the mediastinum, which decreases venous return and compresses the opposite lung.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): A tension pneumothorax develops when a ‘one-way valve’ air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall. Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape... The mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side, decreasing venous return.

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Which physical examination findings distinguish tension pneumothorax from cardiac tamponade in a shocked patient?
back: Breath sounds and percussion: Tension pneumothorax presents with hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds on the affected side. Cardiac tamponade typically has normal breath sounds and muffled heart sounds.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): Pericardial tamponade needs to be differentiated from a tension pneumothorax in the shocked patient with distended neck veins... There will also be hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds over the affected hemithorax.

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: A restless trauma patient has tachypnoea, distended neck veins, and hyper-resonance on the right. Diagnosis?
back: Right-sided tension pneumothorax. It is a clinical diagnosis; treatment must never be delayed for radiological confirmation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): The patient is increasingly restless with tachypnoea, dyspnoea and distended neck veins... Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation.

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What is the immediate treatment for a tension pneumothorax according to current guidelines?
back: Immediate decompression in the 'safe triangle' (latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, and nipple line) or a finger thoracostomy at the same location.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): Treatment consists of immediate decompression... current teaching advocates undertaking decompression in the safe triangle – defned posteriorly by latissimus dorsi, anteriorly by the lateral border of pectoralis major and inferiorly by a line perpendicular to the nipple.

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What are the primary diagnostic criteria for a massive hemothorax requiring urgent thoracotomy?
back: Initial chest tube drainage of >1500 mL of blood, or ongoing hemorrhage exceeding 200 mL/h for 3–4 consecutive hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: How is an open pneumothorax ('sucking chest wound') initially managed to prevent tension conversion?
back: Promptly close the defect with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides (acting as a one-way valve) and insert a separate remote chest tube.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): Initial management consists of promptly closing the defect with a sterile occlusive plastic dressing... taped on three sides to act as a futter-type valve. A chest tube is inserted as soon as possible in a site remote from the injury site.

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Why is pericardiocentesis avoided in the management of traumatic cardiac tamponade from penetrating injury?
back: Traumatic tamponade usually involves substantial clotted blood, making aspiration difficult. Definitive treatment requires surgical evacuation (thoracotomy/sternotomy) and myocardial repair.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): In penetrating injury to the heart there is usually a substantial clot in the pericardium, which may prevent aspiration. Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury.

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Define flail chest and its characteristic clinical movement during respiration.
back: Defined as three or more ribs fractured in two or more places. It presents with paradoxical respiration: the loose segment moves inward on inspiration and outward on expiration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): flail chest... defned as three or more ribs fractured in two or more places... On inspiration, the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards... On expiration, the segment moves outwards (paradoxical respiration).

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What is the gold standard radiological investigation for identifying flail chest and underlying pulmonary contusion?
back: Computed Tomography (CT) scan is the gold standard for diagnosing flail segment and associated pulmonary contusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): The CT scan remains the gold standard for diagnosis of this condition [Flail Chest].

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What is the classic clinical triad used to identify traumatic cardiac tamponade?
back:
- Hypotension
- Distended neck veins
- Muffled heart sounds
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [Classically, the presentation consists of central venous pressure elevation, a decline in arterial pressure with tachycardia and mufed heart sounds.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What is the pathophysiological mechanism behind the development of a tension pneumothorax?
back:
- A 'one-way valve' air leak from the lung or chest wall
- Air enters the pleural space during inspiration but cannot escape
- Causes complete lung collapse and mediastinal displacement
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [A tension pneumothorax develops when a ‘one-way valve’ air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall. Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing and then compressing the afected lung.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Contrast the physical exam findings of tension pneumothorax and massive hemothorax regarding percussion and neck veins.
back:
- Tension Pneumothorax: Hyper-resonance and distended neck veins.
- Massive Hemothorax: Dullness to percussion and flat neck veins (hypovolemic).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Presentation is with haemorrhagic shock, fat neck veins, unilateral absence of breath sounds and dullness to percussion. ... The patient is increasingly restless with tachypnoea, dyspnoea and distended neck veins (similar to pericardial tamponade).]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: A shocked trauma patient has distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. What is the gold standard diagnostic tool?
back: Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (eFAST) showing fluid in the pericardial sac.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [These include an eFAST showing fuid in the pericardial sac, which is the most expeditious and reliable diagnostic tool, or chest radiography, looking for an enlarged heart shadow.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What is the initial emergency dressing requirement for an open pneumothorax (sucking chest wound)?
back: A sterile occlusive plastic dressing taped on only three sides to act as a flutter-type valve.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Initial management consists of promptly closing the defect with a sterile occlusive plastic dressing (e.g. OPSITE ◊ or similar product), taped on three sides to act as a futter-type valve.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What are the two specific blood loss thresholds for massive hemothorax requiring urgent thoracotomy?
back:
- Initial drainage >1500 mL
- Ongoing hemorrhage >200 mL/hour over 3–4 hours
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What is the specific anatomical definition of a flail chest?
back: Three or more ribs fractured in two or more places each.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [This condition usually results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures, and is defned as three or more ribs fractured in two or more places.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Differentiate the primary causes of hypoxia in flail chest versus open pneumothorax.
back:
- Flail Chest: Underlying pulmonary contusion and pain-restricted movement.
- Open Pneumothorax: Profound hypoventilation due to air preferentially entering the chest defect over the trachea.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [If the opening in the chest wall exceeds about two-thirds of the diameter of the trachea, then with each inspiratory cycle air will be preferentially drawn through the defect ... the associated lung contusion all contribute to the hypoxia.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Describe the respiratory mechanism of 'paradoxical respiration' in flail chest.
back:
- Inspiration: The loose segment moves inward.
- Expiration: The loose segment moves outward.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [On inspiration, the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards and therefore less air moves into the lungs. On expiration, the segment moves outwards (paradoxical respiration).]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Why is pericardiocentesis generally contraindicated in penetrating cardiac tamponade?
back:
- Pericardial blood is usually clotted (prevents aspiration)
- Definitive treatment requires surgical evacuation (thoracotomy or sternotomy) and repair.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [In penetrating injury to the heart there is usually a substantial clot in the pericardium, which may prevent aspiration. Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
coreConcept: Definition and Impact of Thoracic Trauma
front: Q: Define thoracic trauma and its significance in terms of incidence and mortality.
back: Thoracic trauma involves injury to the chest region. It accounts for 25% of all severe injuries and is a contributing factor in an additional 25% of trauma deaths, primarily due to major hemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [Thoracic injury accounts for 25% of all severe injuries. In a further 25%, it may be a signifcant contributor to the subsequent death of the patient. In most of these patients, the cause of death is haemorrhage.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: What is the specific pathophysiological mechanism of traumatic aortic rupture in blunt thoracic trauma?
back: Sudden impact (falls or collisions) creates extreme shear forces at the site distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. This force disrupts the intima and media of the vessel wall.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Traumatic aortic rupture is a common cause of sudden death after a vehicle collision or fall from a great height... The vessel is relatively fxed distal to the ligamentum arteriosum... The shear forces from a sudden impact disrupt the intima and media.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Contrast the nature of diaphragmatic injuries in blunt versus penetrating thoracic trauma.
back:
● Blunt: Typically large ruptures caused by compressive forces, leading to visceral herniation into the chest.
● Penetrating: Often small, 'silent' defects below the 5th intercostal space that risk later strangulation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Any penetrating injury below the ffth intercostal space should raise suspicion of diaphragmatic penetration... Blunt injury to the diaphragm is usually caused by a compressive force applied to the torso. The diaphragmatic rupture is usually large, with herniation of the abdominal contents into the chest.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: A patient with multiple rib fractures shows inward chest wall movement during inspiration. Identify the blunt trauma injury.
back: Flail Chest. It is defined as three or more ribs fractured in two or more places, resulting in paradoxical respiration where the loose segment moves opposite to the rest of the chest wall.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Flail chest... usually results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures, and is defned as three or more ribs fractured in two or more places... On inspiration, the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards... On expiration, the segment moves outwards (paradoxical respiration).]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: State the dosing and timing of Tranexamic Acid (TXA) for significant bleeding in thoracic trauma.
back: 1g IV administered over 10 minutes, followed by 1g over 8 hours. It should be given as early as possible, ideally within the first hour and no later than 3 hours post-injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Tranexamic acid is an antifbrinolytic drug that reduces the risk of mortality from bleeding in both blunt and penetrating trauma. One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... ideally within the frst hour... not administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
coreConcept: Clinical Diagnosis of Life-Threatening Thoracic Trauma
