front: Q: What are the specific clinical diagnostic criteria for a tension pneumothorax?
back: Restlessness, tachypnoea, dyspnoea, distended neck veins, hyper-resonance, and absent breath sounds on the affected side. Tracheal deviation is a late sign; diagnosis is strictly clinical.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [The patient is increasingly restless with tachypnoea, dyspnoea and distended neck veins... There will also be hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds over the afected hemithorax. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: How is the 'one-way valve' effect conceptually applied in managing a penetrating sucking chest wound?
back: An occlusive plastic dressing is taped on only three sides. This creates a flutter-valve that allows air to escape during expiration but prevents air entry during inspiration, preventing conversion to a tension pneumothorax.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Initial management consists of promptly closing the defect with a sterile occlusive plastic dressing... taped on three sides to act as a futter-type valve... no attempt should be made to close a sucking chest wound [completely]... in case a stable patient... is converted into an unstable patient with a tension pneumothorax.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Distinguish between Pericardial Tamponade and Tension Pneumothorax in a penetrating trauma patient with distended neck veins.
back:
● Tamponade: Characterized by muffled heart sounds and tachycardia; confirmed by eFAST showing fluid in the pericardial sac.
● Tension Pneumothorax: Characterized by hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds on the affected side.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Pericardial tamponade needs to be diferentiated from a tension pneumothorax in the shocked patient with distended neck veins. It is most commonly the result of penetrating trauma... presentation consists of central venous pressure elevation... and mufed heart sounds... eFAST showing fuid in the pericardial sac... is the most expeditious... tool.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop leading to shock in a tension pneumothorax.
back: Air leak acts as a one-way valve -> air accumulates in the pleura -> lung completely collapses -> mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side -> compression of the great vessels decreases venous return -> cardiac output drops.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing and then compressing the afected lung. The mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side, decreasing venous return and compressing the opposite lung.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Define the anatomical boundaries of the 'Safe Triangle' for thoracic decompression.
back:
● Posterior: Latissimus dorsi
● Anterior: Lateral border of pectoralis major
● Inferior: Line perpendicular to the nipple (5th intercostal space)
● Base: Apex of the axilla
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Current teaching advocates undertaking decompression in the safe triangle – defned posteriorly by latissimus dorsi, anteriorly by the lateral border of pectoralis major and inferiorly by a line perpendicular to the nipple... just anterior to the mid-axillary line.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What are the cardinal clinical findings that define a tension pneumothorax?
back:
- Respiratory distress and tachypnoea.
- Distended neck veins.
- Hyper-resonance on the affected side.
- Absent breath sounds and mediastinal/tracheal shift away from the injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [The clinical presentation is dramatic. The patient is increasingly restless with tachypnoea, dyspnoea and distended neck veins... There will also be hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds over the affected hemithorax.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Describe the "one-way valve" mechanism in the pathophysiology of tension pneumothorax.
back:
- Air enters the thoracic cavity during inspiration but cannot escape.
- Progressive air accumulation collapses the affected lung.
- Resultant mediastinal shift compresses the opposite lung and decreases venous return.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [A tension pneumothorax develops when a ‘one-way valve’ air leak occurs... Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing and then compressing the affected lung. The mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side, decreasing venous return.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Differentiate massive hemothorax from tension pneumothorax regarding percussion and neck veins.
back:
- Percussion: Dull in hemothorax versus hyper-resonant in tension pneumothorax.
- Neck Veins: Flat in hemothorax (due to hypovolaemic shock) versus distended in tension pneumothorax (due to obstructed venous return).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Presentation is with haemorrhagic shock, flat neck veins, unilateral absence of breath sounds and dullness to percussion.] Page 395 (Book Page): [The patient is increasingly restless with tachypnoea, dyspnoea and distended neck veins... There will also be hyper-resonance...]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: A penetrating trauma patient has shock and muffled heart sounds. What is the definitive management?
back:
- Immediate surgical intervention (sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy).
- Evacuation of the pericardial blood clot.
- Direct repair of the myocardial injury.
- Note: Pericardiocentesis is not indicated in traumatic tamponade.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury. The correct immediate treatment of tamponade is operative... with repair of the heart.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: In massive hemothorax, what specific drainage volumes necessitate urgent thoracotomy?
back:
- Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood.
- Ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h for 3–4 consecutive hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What is the clinical definition and hallmark of a flail chest segment?
back:
- Definition: Three or more adjacent ribs fractured in two or more places.
- Hallmark: Paradoxical respiration (segment moves inward during inspiration and outward during expiration).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [This condition usually results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures, and is defined as three or more ribs fractured in two or more places... the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards... On expiration, the segment moves outwards (paradoxical respiration).]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Explain why flail chest is associated with high mortality even if the airway is clear.
back:
- Associated underlying pulmonary contusion causes severe hypoxia.
- Mechanically impaired chest wall movement and voluntary splinting due to pain cause hypoventilation.
- High risk of concomitant pneumothorax or hemothorax.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [The blunt force typically also produces an underlying pulmonary contusion... mechanically impaired chest wall movement and the associated lung contusion all contribute to the hypoxia. There is a high risk of developing a pneumothorax or haemothorax.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Which three features constitute Beck’s Triad for cardiac tamponade diagnosis?
back:
- Elevated central venous pressure (distended neck veins).
- Decreased arterial pressure (hypotension).
- Muffled heart sounds.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Classically, the presentation consists of central venous pressure elevation, a decline in arterial pressure with tachycardia and muffled heart sounds.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Describe the physiological consequence of an open pneumothorax ("sucking chest wound").
back:
- If the chest wall defect is >2/3 tracheal diameter, air enters the pleura preferentially.
- This leads to immediate equilibration between intrathoracic and atmospheric pressure.
- Causes profound hypoventilation and hypoxia on the affected side.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [If the opening in the chest wall exceeds about two-thirds of the diameter of the trachea, then with each inspiratory cycle air will be preferentially drawn through the defect... leading to profound hypoventilation on the affected side and hypoxia.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: State the anatomical boundaries of the "safe triangle" used for finger thoracostomy.
back:
- Posterior: Latissimus dorsi.
- Anterior: Lateral border of pectoralis major.
- Inferior: A line perpendicular to the nipple (anterior axillary line at the 5th intercostal space).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [current teaching advocates undertaking decompression in the safe triangle – defined posteriorly by latissimus dorsi, anteriorly by the lateral border of pectoralis major and inferiorly by a line perpendicular to the nipple...]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What are the clinical hallmarks of a life-threatening tension pneumothorax during initial assessment?
back:
• Increasing restlessness and respiratory distress.
• Distended neck veins.
• Hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds on the affected side.
• Tracheal deviation (late finding).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [The clinical presentation is dramatic. The patient is increasingly restless with tachypnoea, dyspnoea and distended neck veins... There will also be hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds over the affected hemithorax. Clinical examination may reveal tracheal deviation; this is a late fnding]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Explain the physiological mechanism that converts a simple pneumothorax into a life-threatening tension pneumothorax.
back:
• A one-way valve air leak occurs from the lung or chest wall.
• Air enters the thoracic cavity but cannot escape.
• Rising pressure collapses the lung and shifts the mediastinum.
• Resulting displacement decreases venous return and compresses the opposite lung.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [A tension pneumothorax develops when a ‘one-way valve’ air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall. Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing and then compressing the afected lung. The mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side, decreasing venous return and compressing the opposite lung.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: How does percussion help differentiate massive haemothorax from tension pneumothorax in a shocked patient?
back:
• Tension Pneumothorax: Hyper-resonance (due to trapped air).
• Massive Haemothorax: Dullness to percussion (due to blood accumulation).
• Both present with unilateral absent breath sounds.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Presentation [of massive haemothorax] is with haemorrhagic shock, fat neck veins, unilateral absence of breath sounds and dullness to percussion.] Page 395 (Book Page): [There will also be hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds over the afected hemithorax [in tension pneumothorax].]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Which clinical triad suggests cardiac tamponade in a patient presenting with shock following penetrating trauma?
back:
• Beck’s Triad:
• Elevated central venous pressure (distended neck veins).
• Decline in arterial pressure (hypotension).
• Muffled heart sounds.
• Note: Neck veins may be flat if concurrent major bleeding exists.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Classically, the presentation consists of central venous pressure elevation, a decline in arterial pressure with tachycardia and mufed heart sounds. However, in cases in which major bleeding from other sites has taken place, the neck veins may be fat.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: What is the current recommended management strategy for a patient with a flail chest segment?
back:
• Oxygen administration and physiotherapy.
• Adequate analgesia (opiates or topical intrapleural local analgesia).
• Internal fixation of ribs in selected severe cases.
• Mechanical ventilation is reserved only for respiratory failure, not routine internal splinting.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Currently, treatment consists of oxygen administration, adequate analgesia (including opiates) and physiotherapy. If a chest tube is in place, topical intrapleural local analgesia introduced via the tube can also be used. Ventilation is reserved for patients developing respiratory failure]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: State the quantitative clinical criteria for a massive haemothorax necessitating an urgent thoracotomy.
back:
• Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood upon chest tube insertion.
• Ongoing haemorrhage exceeding 200 mL/hour for 3–4 consecutive hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Define the skeletal injury pattern and paradoxical motion seen in flail chest.
back:
• Skeletal pattern: Three or more ribs fractured in two or more places.
• Inspiration: The loose segment is displaced inwards (less air enters).
• Expiration: The segment moves outwards (paradoxical respiration).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [defned as three or more ribs fractured in two or more places... On inspiration, the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards and therefore less air moves into the lungs. On expiration, the segment moves outwards (paradoxical respiration).]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Why is pericardiocentesis avoided in the immediate management of traumatic cardiac tamponade?
back:
• Penetrating myocardial injuries usually result in substantial clot formation in the pericardium.
• Clots cannot be aspirated via a needle.
• Correct treatment is operative: subxiphoid window, sternotomy, or left anterolateral thoracotomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [In penetrating injury to the heart there is usually a substantial clot in the pericardium, which may prevent aspiration. Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Identify the three factors that contribute to hypoxia in a flail chest patient.
back:
• Underlying pulmonary contusion (primary cause).
• Mechanically impaired chest wall movement (paradoxical motion).
• Voluntary splinting of the chest wall due to pain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Voluntary splinting of the chest wall occurs as a result of pain, so mechanically impaired chest wall movement and the associated lung contusion all contribute to the hypoxia.]

category: Describe life-threatening chest injuries including tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, flail chest, cardiac tamponade
front: Q: Where is the current anatomical 'safe triangle' located for immediate tension pneumothorax decompression?
back:
• Posterior boundary: Latissimus dorsi.
• Anterior boundary: Lateral border of pectoralis major.
• Inferior boundary: Line perpendicular to the nipple (5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [current teaching advocates undertaking decompression in the safe triangle – defned posteriorly by latissimus dorsi, anteriorly by the lateral border of pectoralis major and inferiorly by a line perpendicular to the nipple going to the back, just anterior to the mid-axillary line]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
coreConcept: Definition and Mortality Impact of Thoracic Trauma
front: Q: Define thoracic trauma and its significance in severe injury mortality.
back:
A: Injury to the chest region. Significance:
• Accounts for 25% of all severe injuries.
• Acts as a significant contributor in another 25% of trauma deaths.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [Thoracic injury accounts for 25% of all severe injuries. In a further 25%, it may be a signifcant contributor to the subsequent death of the patient.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Explain the primary mechanisms involved in blunt thoracic trauma pathology.
back:
A: 1. Deceleration (e.g., vehicle collisions).
2. Falls from heights.
3. Direct compression forces that can burst solid organ substance or fracture the rib cage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 373 (Book Page)/394: [In blunt chest trauma, the CT scan will allow the defnition of fractures, as well as showing haematomas... Blunt liver trauma occurs as a result of direct injury... compressive forces can easily burst the liver substance.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
coreConcept: Diagnostic Imaging Modalities in Thoracic Trauma
front: Q: Contrast the diagnostic utility of upright versus supine chest radiographs in penetrating trauma.
back:
A: • Upright: Best reveals small pneumothorax, fluid meniscus, or free gas under the diaphragm.
• Supine: Often shows massive haemothorax only as a homogeneous increase in opacity (may mimic pneumothorax).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 373 (Book Page)/394: [In penetrating injury, it may be more helpful for the radiograph to be performed with the patient positioned erect, as this will best reveal a small pneumothorax... A supine chest radiograph can show a haemothorax as a homogeneous increase in opacity.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: A patient presents with a stab wound below the nipple line. Classify the likely cavity involvement.
back: A: Thoraco-abdominal injury. Penetrating injuries below the 4th to 5th intercostal space (nipple line) must be investigated for diaphragm breach and multi-cavity penetration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 372 (Book Page)/393: [Any penetrating injury below the nipples on the chest may therefore have penetrated the diaphragm and entered the abdomen. Injuries in this junctional zone, therefore, should be investigated as if both cavities had been penetrated.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
coreConcept: Biochemical resuscitaiton markers in Haemorrhagic Shock
front: Q: State the metabolic/physiological biochemical indicators used to classify ongoing internal bleeding.
back:
A: 1. Rising serum lactate (indicates tissue hypoperfusion).
2. Increasing respiratory/pulse rates.
3. Falling blood pressure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 372 (Book Page)/393: [Clinical indicators of potential ongoing bleeding in torso trauma. Physiological: Increasing respiratory rate, Increasing pulse rate, Falling blood pressure, Rising serum lactate]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: List the six immediately life-threatening thoracic injuries ('Deadly Dozen') classified during the Primary Survey.
back:
A: 1. Airway obstruction.
2. Tension pneumothorax.
3. Pericardial tamponade.
4. Open pneumothorax.
5. Massive haemothorax.
6. Flail chest.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 374 (Book Page)/395: [Six are immediately life-threatening and should be sought and managed during the primary survey... Airway obstruction, Tension pneumothorax, Pericardial tamponade, Open pneumothorax, Massive haemothorax, Flail chest]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Classify the five major sites of internal haemorrhage following torso trauma.
back:
A: Using the 'one on the floor and four more' rule:
1. Chest.
2. Abdomen/Retroperitoneum.
3. Pelvis.
4. Long bones (extremities).
5. External (floor).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 372 (Book Page)/393: [Bleeding occurs from fve major sites – ‘one on the foor and four more’: ● external – ‘foor’; ● chest; ● abdomen (including the retroperitoneum); ● pelvis; ● extremities.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Distinguish clinical hallmarks of Tension Pneumothorax from Pericardial Tamponade in a shocked patient.
back:
A: • Tension PTX: Tracheal deviation, hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds.
• Tamponade: Muffled heart sounds, central venous pressure elevation (distended veins), diagnostic eFAST pericardial fluid.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 374 (Book Page)/395: [Pericardial tamponade needs to be diferentiated from a tension pneumothorax in the shocked patient with distended neck veins... eFAST showing fuid in the pericardial sac... is the most expeditious and reliable diagnostic tool]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop that leads to profound hypoventilation in a 'sucking chest wound'.
back: A: Defect >2/3 tracheal diameter → Air enters the thoracic defect preferentially over the trachea during inspiration → Air accumulates in hemithorax instead of lung → Profound hypoventilation/hypoxia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page)/396: [If the opening in the chest wall exceeds about two-thirds of the diameter of the trachea, then with each inspiratory cycle air will be preferentially drawn through the defect... leading to profound hypoventilation on the afected side and hypoxia.]

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
coreConcept: Anatomical Junctional Zones of Torso Trauma
front: Q: Define the four critical 'Junctional Zones' where injury traverses torso anatomical boundaries.
back:
A: 1. Neck-Thorax.
2. Thorax-Upper limbs.
3. Thorax-Abdomen.
4. Abdominopelvic structures-Groin.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 371 (Book Page)/392: [Injury consistently traverses diferent anatomical zones... These zones are known as junctional zones. The key junctional zones are: ● between the neck and the thorax; ● between the thorax and the upper limbs; ● between the thorax and the abdomen; ● between the abdominopelvic structures and the groin.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What does the 'c' represent in the updated cABCDE primary survey sequence?
back: Exsanguinating external haemorrhage (catastrophic bleeding). It must be controlled by pressure or tourniquets even before airway management.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [The primary survey aims to identify and manage the most immediately life-threatening pathologies frst and follows cABCDE. c: Exsanguinating external haemorrhage]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Define the components of the 'triad of death' in severely traumatized patients.
back:
1. Acidosis
2. Coagulopathy
3. Hypothermia
These form a cycle resulting in multiorgan failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Distinguish between Early Total Care (ETC) and Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
back:
• ETC: Definitive management of all injuries within 36 hours.
• DCS: Early, rapid life-saving surgery (hemorrhage control) while deferring complex reconstruction until physiological stability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [ETC describes the defnitive management of a patient’s injuries within 36 hours... DCS describes simultaneous resuscitation with early rapid life- and limb-saving surgery.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: A hemodynamically unstable blunt trauma patient requires immediate laparotomy. What pelvic intervention is mandatory?
back: Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters and obtain a pelvic radiograph (without delaying transfer to theatre).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Any patient undergoing immediate trauma laparotomy after blunt trauma without a WBCT scan should have a pelvic binder applied and not removed until a pelvic fracture is excluded. Such patients should have an immediate pelvic radiograph]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the recommended dosing and time limit for Tranexamic acid in trauma?
back:
• Dose: 1g IV over 10 min, followed by 1g over 8 hours.
• Time: Must be given within 3 hours of injury (ideally within 1 hour).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the gold standard investigation for adult blunt trauma with deranged physiology?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) with IV contrast, scanning from the head to the pelvis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Define the systolic blood pressure targets for 'permissive hypotension'.
back:
• Standard: 70–90 mmHg.
• Suspected head injury: >90 mmHg.
Aim is to maintain vital organ perfusion while limiting further clot disruption.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: A trauma patient presents with a 'white' pulseless hand. What is the management priority?
back: Immediate surgical assessment for arterial repair or shunting to restore limb perfusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 441 (Book Page): [The white pulseless hand is a surgical emergency and requires immediate attention, assessment and urgent reduction.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Why is excessive crystalloid infusion avoided in severe hypovolaemia?
back: It causes haemodilution, exacerbates the 'triad of death' (coagulopathy), and increases the risk of ARDS.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulo - pathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
coreConcept: Lactate as a Surgical Triage Tool
front: Q: What venous lactate level is strongly indicative of a need for Damage Control Surgery?
back: Lactate >5 mmol/L signifies severe under-resuscitation requiring DCS approach.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [>5 mmol/L – DCS (see Chapters 26 and 29 )]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: In the trauma primary survey, what does the prefix 'c' represent in 'cABCDE'?
back:
A: Catastrophic exsanguinating external haemorrhage.
- Priorities: Control massive arterial bleeding before airway management.
- Methods: Direct pressure, packing, or proximal tourniquets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arte - rial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Why is excessive crystalloid resuscitation avoided in severely injured trauma patients?
back:
A: It causes haemodilution, exacerbates coagulopathy, and increases the risk of Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).
- Protocol: Use blood and blood products (1:1:1 ratio) instead.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulo - pathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: State the target Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP) during permissive hypotension.
back:
A: 
- Standard Trauma: 70–90 mmHg.
- Head Injury Suspected: >90 mmHg.
- Rationale: Maintains vital organ perfusion while minimizing clot disruption.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Where must a pelvic binder be positioned to ensure stability during the primary survey?
back:
A: At the level of the greater trochanters.
- Note: Correct positioning allows for trauma laparotomy without removal of the binder.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma lap - arotomy.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the dosing regimen and therapeutic window for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in trauma?
back:
A: 
- Loading: 1g IV over 10 minutes.
- Maintenance: 1g IV over 8 hours.
- Window: Best within 1 hour; do not administer after 3 hours from injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the clinical indicator that permissive hypotension has reached its adequate target?
back:
A: The presence of a palpable radial pulse.
- Note: Small fluid boluses (e.g., 250 mL) are titrated until this pulse is achieved.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [Small boluses of IV fuids... should be administered to achieve this target, which should result in a palpable radial pulse.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Define the role of the trauma team leader during a concurrent primary survey.
back:
A: Coordinates sequential activities and anticipates decisions by standing back from the patient.
- Goal: Facilitates simultaneous specialist actions (e.g., airway management and breathing assessment happening at once).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): [The importance of the trauma team leader cannot be overemphasised: they brief and prepare the team, coordinate these sequential activities, manage time, interpret fndings and plan the next move.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: How should a blunt trauma patient be moved during the primary survey if a pelvic fracture is suspected?
back:
A: Use a 20° roll with inline spinal stabilisation or a scoop stretcher.
- Rationale: Formal log-rolling must be deferred until radiographs exclude pelvic fracture to prevent disturbing blood clots.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [If patients need to be moved during their primary survey... a 20° roll with inline spinal stabilisation should be used... Log-rolling should not occur until a pelvic fracture has been radiographically excluded.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Contrast the timing objectives of Early Total Care (ETC) and Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
back:
A: 
- ETC: Definitive management of all injuries (including fractures) within 36 hours.
- DCS: Rapid life/limb-saving surgery only; definitive reconstruction is deferred for ICU resuscitation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.5: ETC describes the defnitive management... within 36 hours... DCS describes simultaneous resuscitation with early rapid life- and limb-saving surgery. Time-consuming defnitive surgery is deferred]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Which adjunct investigations are required for patients too unstable for Whole-Body CT (WBCT)?
back:
A: 
- Immediate chest radiograph.
- Immediate pelvic radiograph.
- FAST scan (Focused Abdominal Sonography for Trauma).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Some patients will be so haemodynamically unstable... immediate chest radio- graph will exclude catastrophic intrathoracic haemorrhage. An immediate pelvic radiograph is essential... FAST scan... may also be useful]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: In the ATLS Primary Survey, what specific priority must be managed even before the airway?
back: Control of exsanguinating external hemorrhage (massive arterial bleeding) using direct pressure, packs, or tourniquets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: List the components of the physiological 'triad of death' in severe trauma assessment.
back:
* Acidosis
* Coagulopathy
* Hypothermia
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: How is a Tension Pneumothorax diagnosed according to ATLS principles?
back: It is a clinical diagnosis. Treatment (decompression) must never be delayed for radiological confirmation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: At what anatomical level should a pelvic binder be positioned in an unstable blunt trauma patient?
back: At the level of the greater trochanters. This avoids obstructing emergency laparotomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What physiological criteria mandate the administration of Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in trauma patients?
back: Suspected significant hemorrhage with systolic blood pressure <110 mmHg or a pulse over 110 per minute.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have signifcant haemorrhage, including those with a systolic blood pressure of <110 mmHg or a pulse of over 110 per minute.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the initial volume of blood drainage that defines a Massive Hemothorax in the primary survey?
back: Initial drainage of >1500 mL or ongoing hemorrhage of >200 mL/h over 3–4 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the target systolic blood pressure during permissive hypotension in a patient with a suspected head injury?
back: >90 mmHg (compared to 70–90 mmHg in standard trauma without head injury).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the definitive initial management for cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury?
back: Urgent surgical repair via sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy. Pericardiocentesis is not indicated.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury . The correct immediate treatment of tamponade is operative]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Which venous lactate levels determine the choice between Early Total Care (ETC) and Damage Control Surgery (DCS)?
back:
* <2 mmol/L: Suitable for ETC
* >3 mmol/L: Under-resuscitated
* >5 mmol/L: Requires DCS
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [<2 mmol/L – ETC; >3 mmol/L – may be under-resuscitated... >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the standard ratio for blood products in a trauma Massive Transfusion Protocol?
back: 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the modified ATLS primary survey sequence used to prioritize catastrophic bleeding control?
back:
cABCDE.
• c: Control of exsanguinating external hemorrhage (packs, pressure, tourniquets).
• Managed even before the airway (A).
• Essential for ballistic and blast injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [The primary survey aims to identify and manage the most immediately life-threatening pathologies frst and follows cABCDE. c: Exsanguinating external haemorrhage... needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What physiological 'triad of death' must be prevented during damage control resuscitation?
back:
Acidosis, Coagulopathy, and Hypothermia.
• Occurs after lengthy surgical procedures in patients with impaired physiology.
• Leads to multiorgan failure and death.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Prolonged procedures result in additional trauma and further immune and physiological derangement; the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Distinguish the roles of Whole-body CT (WBCT) and FAST in blunt trauma assessment.
back:
WBCT: Gold standard for stable patients with suspected multisystem injury or deranged physiology.
• FAST: Rapid bedside tool for hemodynamically unstable patients to locate major hemorrhage before laparotomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury... A focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan (if immediately available) may also be useful in this scenario to locate the major source of haemorrhage.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: A blunt trauma patient presents in shock. What immediate step is taken regarding the pelvis during the 'C' survey?
back:
Apply a pelvic binder.
• Essential for all hemodynamically unstable blunt trauma patients.
• Do not remove until pelvic fracture is radiographically excluded.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [A pelvic binder should be applied to all haemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma and not removed until after a pelvic fracture has been excluded.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the specific dosing and time-limit for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) administration in major trauma?
back:
1g IV over 10 minutes, then 1g over 8 hours.
• Administer as early as possible, ideally within 1 hour.
• Contraindicated if more than 3 hours have passed since injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: According to the GCS scoring classification, what defines a 'severe' head injury?
back:
GCS 3–8.
• Moderate: GCS 9–13.
• Mild: GCS 14–15 (with loss of consciousness).
• Minor: GCS 15 (no loss of consciousness).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Head injury severity: clinical classifcation... Severe head injury GCS 3–8]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the target systolic blood pressure (SBP) during time-limited permissive hypotension?
back:
70–90 mmHg.
• Target >90 mmHg if head injury is suspected.
• Achieved with small IV fluid/blood boluses to maintain vital organ perfusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: Why is formal log-rolling deferred during the primary survey of blunt trauma patients?
back:
Risk of disrupting clots around pelvic fractures.
• May cause catastrophic hemorrhage in unstable patients.
• Use a 20° roll with inline stabilization if movement is essential.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): [Log-rolling patients with severe pelvic fractures may harm the patient by disturbing established blood clots. Log-rolling should not occur until a pelvic fracture has been radiographically excluded.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the specific component ratio required for a trauma Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP)?
back:
1:1:1 ratio.
• 1 unit Packed Red Cells.
• 1 unit Fresh-Frozen Plasma (FFP).
• 1 unit Platelets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization using the ATLS approach
front: Q: What is the standard requirement for intravenous access during the initial Primary Survey 'C' phase?
back:
At least two large-bore IV cannulae.
• Peripheral access preferred.
• Central or intraosseous access if peripheral sites are unobtainable.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [All patients require adequate intravenous (IV) access with at least two large-bore IV cannulae. Equipment and expertise for insertion of central or intraosseous venous access should be available where peripheral access is not easily obtainable.]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: What is the gold standard imaging modality for an adult blunt trauma patient with suspected multisystem injury?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) with IV contrast from the head to the pelvis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: In traumatic brain injury, how is Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) calculated?
back: CPP = Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) minus Intracranial Pressure (ICP).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [Flow depends on cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), which is the diference between the mean arterial pressure (MAP) and the intracranial pressure (ICP): CPP (75–105 mmHg) = MAP (90–110 mmHg) – ICP (5–15 mmHg)]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Contrast the age-based utility of ultrasound versus radiography in screening for neonatal DDH.
back:
● Ultrasound: Primary tool for anatomy/stability (4–6 weeks).
● Radiography: Useful only after 4–5 months (once the femoral ossific nucleus appears).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): [Ultrasonographic assessment... Screening scans should be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of age... Plain radiographs are used from 4–5 months of age, when the relationship of the femoral ossifc nucleus to the acetabulum can be assessed]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Which diagnostic tool differentiates pericardial tamponade from tension pneumothorax in a shocked trauma patient?
back: eFAST (extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma). It identifies fluid in the pericardial sac vs. air/fluid in hemithoraces.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [eFAST showing fuid in the pericardial sac, which is the most expeditious and reliable diagnostic tool... The presentation is similar to a tension pneumothorax – deteriorating cyanosis, tachycardia and agitation]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Which biochemical marker is used to determine if a trauma patient is resuscitated or requires damage control?
back:
Venous lactate.
● <2 mmol/L: Adequately resuscitated (suitable for Early Total Care).
● >5 mmol/L: Severely under-resuscitated (requires Damage Control Surgery).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [<2 mmol/L – ETC... >5 mmol/L – DCS... Venous lactate is an essential marker of resuscitation]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: List the four clinical predictors used to differentiate pediatric septic arthritis from transient synovitis.
back:
1. Fever >38.5°C.
2. Non-weight-bearing.
3. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) >40 mm/h.
4. White cell count (WCC) >12 × 10⁹/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: What is the mandatory diagnostic protocol for a suspected scaphoid fracture with normal initial X-rays?
back: Immobilize the wrist in a cast and repeat clinical examination and scaphoid-view radiographs in 10–14 days.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): [If a fracture is not evident on the initial radiographs... standard protocol of a suspected scaphoid fracture is to immobilise the wrist and examine again 10–14 days later. If tenderness remains, repeat the scaphoid views.]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: A pediatric patient presents with a rigid 'rocker-bottom' foot. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back: Congenital vertical talus (CVT). It typically involves dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 627 (Book Page): [Congenital vertical talus (CVT) is rare... Clinically, there is a stif ‘rocker-bottom’ foot with dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talus]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Describe the diagnostic significance of the 'too many toes' sign observed from behind a standing patient.
back: It indicates pes planus (flat foot) with increased forefoot abduction, often caused by tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 494 (Book Page): [The ‘too many toes’ sign demonstrates increased forefoot abduction (pes planus [fat foot]) and a splayed forefoot.]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Which imaging modality is most sensitive for early identification of acute osteomyelitis within the first 48 hours?
back: MRI. It shows bone edema and periosteal elevation within 2–3 days, whereas radiographs may stay normal for 7 days.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 603 (Book Page): [In the early phase (2–3 days) radiographs may be normal but MRI will show bone oedema and periosteal elevation.]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: What is the gold standard investigation for a severely injured adult blunt trauma patient?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from head to pelvis with IV contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: What diagnostic biomarker is used as an indicator of tissue perfusion and suitability for early total care (ETC)?
back: Venous lactate levels (<2 mmol/L indicates resuscitation).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Lactate levels are also a good indicator of tissue perfusion and should rapidly return to normal... A normal lactate (<2 mmol/L) is a sign that the patient is probably resuscitated and suitable for ETC.]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: What clinical indicators characterize the diagnosis of Tension Pneumothorax?
back: Dramatic tachypnoea, dyspnoea, distended neck veins, hyper-resonance, and absent breath sounds (Clinical diagnosis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation.]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: What are the specific components evaluated during an eFAST scan in trauma?
back: Cardiac tamponade, free blood/air in hemithoraces, and fluid in the abdominal paracolic gutters, subdiaphragmatic spaces, and pelvis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [The technique uses sonographic assessment in the chest, looking for a cardiac tamponade or free blood and air in the hemithoraces, and assessment for blood in the abdominal cavity, in the paracolic gutters, subdiaphragmatic spaces and pelvis.]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: What specific lab and volume parameters define a 'positive' Diagnostic Peritoneal Lavage (DPL)?
back: Aspiration of >10 mL frank blood, or >100,000 red cells/μL, or >500 white cells/μL.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): [The cannula is aspirated for blood (>10 mL is deemed as positive)... the presence of >100 000 red cells/μL or >500 white cells/μL is deemed positive]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: What are the Kocher clinical predictors for differentiating pediatric septic arthritis from transient synovitis?
back: Fever >38.5°C, non-weight-bearing status, ESR >40 mm/h, and WCC >12 x 10^9/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Table 44.17 The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: ● History of fever >38.5°C ● Non-weight-bearing ● Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h ● White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: How is the 'Real' Leg Length Discrepancy measured clinically?
back: Measured from the Anterior Superior Iliac Spine (ASIS) to the medial malleolus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 489 (Book Page): [The frst is called ‘real’ LLD, measured ASIS to medial malleolus.]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Which imaging modality is most sensitive for diagnosing Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI)?
back: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 389 (Book Page): [Magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive and is employed to evaluate for difuse axonal injury in patients who fail to improve neurologically.]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: What primary tool is used to evaluate the integrity of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL)?
back: Lachman test (Anterior translation of the tibia with a soft/no end point).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 492 (Book Page): [The most sensitive test for evaluation of the ACL is the Lachman test... Anterior translation of the tibia associated with a soft or no end point is a positive test.]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: What is the defining radiological finding for diagnosing a Chance fracture?
back: Flexion-distraction injury of the thoracolumbar junction (classically from lap belts).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 401 (Book Page): [Chance fractures are fexion–distraction injuries of the thoracolumbar junction and are classically associated with the use of lap belts]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: What is the 'cABCDE' sequence in the primary survey of a trauma patient?
back:
• c: Control exsanguinating external haemorrhage
• A: Airway with cervical spine control
• B: Breathing and ventilation
• C: Circulation and haemorrhage control (apply pelvic binder)
• D: Disability (neurological status)
• E: Exposure and environment
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [The cABCDE of trauma care ● c – Control of massive external haemorrhage ● A – Airway with cervical spine protection ● B – Breathing and ventilation ● C – Circulation and haemorrhage control: apply a pelvic binder... ● D – Disability (neurological status) ● E – Exposure (assess for other injuries)]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: Define the target blood pressure parameters for permissive hypotension in acute trauma.
back:
• Target Systolic BP: 70–90 mmHg for a limited time
• Head Injury Suspected: Target >90 mmHg
• Goal: Maintain vital organ supply (brain, heart, kidneys) without worsening coagulopathy or bleeding
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected. The initial aim of resuscitation is to maintain the blood supply to the vital organs: the brain, heart and kidneys.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: Contrast the principles of Early Total Care (ETC) and Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
back:
• ETC: Definitive management of all injuries within 36 hours post-resuscitation
• DCS: Immediate life/limb-saving surgery (bleeding/contamination control)
• Timing: DCS defers complex reconstruction until physiology is optimized in ICU
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [ETC describes the defnitive management of a patient’s injuries within 36 hours of injury after a period of initial resuscitation. DCS describes simultaneous resuscitation with early rapid life- and limb-saving surgery. Time-consuming defnitive surgery is deferred until the patient’s physiological status allows.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: What is the acute management protocol for a patient with traumatic cardiac tamponade?
back:
• Immediate operative repair (Sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy)
• Evacuation of pericardial haematoma
• Direct myocardial repair
• Note: Pericardiocentesis is contraindicated in penetrating myocardial injury
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury. The correct immediate treatment of tamponade is operative... sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy, with repair of the heart.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: What is the administration protocol for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in major trauma?
back:
• Loading Dose: 1g IV over 10 minutes
• Maintenance: 1g IV over 8 hours
• Timing: Must be given within 3 hours of injury (ideally within 1 hour)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: Define the standard blood product ratio for a Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP).
back:
• Ratio: 1 Packed Red Cells : 1 Fresh-Frozen Plasma : 1 Platelets
• Goal: Resuscitate with blood products instead of excessive crystalloids to avoid haemodilution and ARDS
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: What are the three primary surgical goals of Damage Control Surgery (DCS)?
back:
• 1. Control of active surgical haemorrhage
• 2. Control of contamination (e.g., bowel contents)
• 3. Restoration of normal physiology (interrupting Triad of Death)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Damage control surgery is restricted to only three goals: ● stopping any active surgical bleeding; ● controlling any contamination; ● restoring normal physiology.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: Outline the immediate management steps for a hemodynamically unstable pelvic fracture.
back:
• Apply pelvic binder at the greater trochanters immediately
• Resuscitate via MTP (1:1:1 ratio)
• Hemorrhage control: Extraperitoneal packing or interventional angioembolisation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Initial management requires the use of a compression binder or a sheet, applied around the true pelvis at the level of the greater trochanters... further bleeding control can be achieved either by angioembolisation or by extraperitoneal packing.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: Identify the components of the 'Triad of Death' in a severely traumatized patient.
back:
• 1. Acidosis
• 2. Coagulopathy
• 3. Hypothermia
• Consequence: Leads to multiorgan failure and death if not managed by DCS
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [The ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: How is the airway acutely managed in a patient with severe midface skeletal detachment?
back:
• Manually disimpact and pull maxilla forward
• Pull tongue forward with suture/towel clip
• High-volume suction to clear blood/debris
• Prepare for emergency surgical airway if intubation fails
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 426 (Book Page): [In the obtunded or unconscious patient, the maxilla can be disimpacted and pulled forwards using fngers. The tongue can be pulled and held forwards, with a large suture or a towel clip... the team must be prepared to undertake... an emergency surgical airway procedure.]

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Which metabolic marker is used to differentiate if a trauma patient is suitable for Early Total Care (ETC) vs Damage Control Surgery (DCS)?
back:
Venous lactate levels: 
- <2 mmol/L: Suitable for ETC. 
- >5 mmol/L: Indicates under-resuscitation, requiring DCS.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): Venous lactate is an essential marker of resuscitation ● <2 mmol/L – ETC ● 2–3 mmol/L – look at the trend ● >3 mmol/L – may be under-resuscitated ● >5 mmol/L – DCS

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Identify the four clinical predictors used to differentiate septic arthritis from transient synovitis in children.
back:
1. Fever >38.5°C
2. Inability to weight-bear
3. ESR >40 mm/h
4. White cell count >12 × 10^9/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: ● History of fever >38.5°C ● Non-weight-bearing ● Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h ● White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: What is the mandatory diagnostic protocol for a patient with anatomical snuffbox tenderness but normal initial radiographs?
back: Immobilize the wrist in a cast and repeat scaphoid-view radiographs in 10–14 days to identify an occult fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 433 (Book Page): If a fracture is not evident on the initial radiographs and the patient remains tender in the anatomical snuf box, then treat as a suspected scaphoid fracture until a fracture is actively excluded. The standard protocol... is to immobilise the wrist and examine again 10–14 days later.

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Why is tension pneumothorax classified strictly as a clinical diagnosis rather than a radiological one?
back: Radiological confirmation causes fatal delays; diagnosis relies on clinical signs (tracheal deviation, distended neck veins, hyper-resonance) to trigger immediate decompression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation. Always treat it with a high index of suspicion of being present.

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Which specific laboratory procedure is required to diagnose bacteria residing in a biofilm on removed orthopaedic implants?
back: Sonication: Subjecting removed hardware to ultrasonic vibration to disrupt the polysaccharide matrix before culture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 598 (Book Page): It is also possible to culture organisms from removed implants that have been subjected to ultrasonic vibration to disrupt bioflm (sonication).

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: According to the Ottawa Ankle Rules, what are the three indications for obtaining ankle radiographs?
back:
1. Bone tenderness at distal 6cm/tip of lateral malleolus.
2. Bone tenderness at distal 6cm/tip of medial malleolus.
3. Inability to bear weight immediately and at examination.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 505 (Book Page): Ottawa ankle rules... Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the lateral malleolus; Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the medial malleolus; Inability to bear weight at the time of the accident or at the time of examination.

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: How is a rigid flat foot distinguished from a flexible flat foot during clinical evaluation?
back: Rigid flat foot: Subtalar motion is restricted; the medial arch fails to return on tiptoe or with the Jack's test (lifting the great toe).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 497 (Book Page): Rigid [flat foot] ● On tiptoe the arch fails to return and the heel remains in valgus ● Subtalar joint movements are restricted and often painful... Jack’s test. With the patient standing, lift up the great toe. The arch should form in the fexible fat foot.

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Identify the four clinical findings that characterize a retrobulbar haemorrhage as an acute surgical emergency.
back:
1. Tense proptosis
2. Increasing pain
3. Reduced visual acuity
4. Loss of pupillary response to light.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness... It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response.

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Why is the synovial marker α-defensin utilized in the diagnostic criteria for prosthetic joint infection (PJI)?
back: It is a highly specific antimicrobial peptide marker that provides high diagnostic accuracy for infection compared to non-specific systemic markers like ESR/CRP.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): Raised infammatory markers... are neither sufciently sensitive nor sufciently specifc... new synovial fuid markers ( α-defensin and calprotectin) have shown high accuracy in diagnosis of PJI.

category: Identify key diagnostic tools for evaluation
front: Q: Name the two classification scoring systems used to assess the severity and treatment response of idiopathic club foot.
back: Pirani and Diméglio classification systems.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 625 (Book Page): Both the Pirani and Diméglio classifcation systems are based on the appearance of the foot in its position of max - imal correction. They predict treatment response and hence outcome.

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: What are the three primary goals of Damage Control Surgery (DCS) in acute trauma?
back:
1. Stopping any active surgical bleeding.
2. Controlling any contamination.
3. Restoring normal physiology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [Damage control surgery is restricted to only three goals: stopping any active surgical bleeding; controlling any contamination; restoring normal physiology.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: Identify the three physiological components of the "deadly triad" that mandate damage control.
back:
1. Hypothermia.
2. Acidosis.
3. Coagulopathy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [Patients with the ‘deadly triad’ (hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy) are those at highest risk.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: Contrast the management of acute trauma based on venous lactate levels of <2 vs. >5 mmol/L.
back:
<2 mmol/L: Suitable for Early Total Care (ETC).
>5 mmol/L: Requires Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.6 Venous lactate is an essential marker of resuscitation: <2 mmol/L – ETC; >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: What are the immediate emergency management steps for suspected compartment syndrome?
back:
1. Split all casts and dressings down to the skin.
2. Elevate the extremity.
3. Arrange for immediate emergency surgical fasciotomies.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Emergency treatment involves splitting casts and/or dressings to the skin and elevating the extremity... perform defnitive treatment with fasciotomies.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: List the essential presurgical management steps for an open fracture in the emergency department.
back:
1. Administer immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
2. Provide tetanus prophylaxis.
3. Apply sterile saline dressings.
4. Splint the limb.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [3. Once overall alignment is achieved, splint the afected limb... 4. Apply a moist saline dressing... 5. Administer intravenous antibiotics according to local protocols... 6. Obtain a tetanus immunisation history.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: Why is an acute unstable Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) treated as a surgical emergency?
back: It is equivalent to a displaced intracapsular neck fracture with high risk of Avascular Necrosis (AVN); requires reduction and capsulotomy within 24 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 622 (Book Page): [This situation is equivalent to a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. This means that an acute unstable SCFE is an emergency. The AVN risk is considerable.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: How must a retrobulbar haemorrhage be managed acutely to prevent permanent blindness?
back: Perform an immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under local anesthesia to reduce intraocular pressure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 413 (Book Page): [If this is suspected, preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under LA to allow the globe to bulge forwards and relieve the pressure.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: Identify the four Kocher clinical predictors used to diagnose septic arthritis in a limping child.
back:
1. History of fever >38.5°C.
2. Non-weight-bearing.
3. ESR >40 mm/h.
4. White cell count >12 × 10^9/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Table 44.17 (a) The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10^9/L]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: What is the immediate clinical management of a diagnosed tension pneumothorax?
back: Immediate decompression via finger thoracostomy or large-bore cannula in the safe triangle. Never delay for radiological confirmation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation... Treatment consists of immediate decompression... safe triangle.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: Contrast the role of pericardiocentesis versus thoracotomy in traumatic cardiac tamponade.
back: Pericardiocentesis has no role. Management requires operative sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy for clot evacuation and myocardial repair.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury. The correct immediate treatment of tamponade is operative... sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: What is the recommended ratio of blood products in a massive transfusion protocol?
back: 1:1:1 ratio. Consists of 1 part packed red cells, 1 part fresh-frozen plasma, and 1 part platelets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: What is the physiological goal and target pressure range for permissive hypotension?
back: Goal: Maintain perfusion to brain, heart, and kidneys while limiting coagulopathy. Target: Systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg (time-limited).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [The initial aim of resuscitation is to maintain the blood supply to the vital organs: the brain, heart and kidneys. For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg]

category: Outline principles of acute management
front: Q: Distinguish between the management indications for Damage Control Surgery versus Early Total Care.
back: Damage Control: Rapid life/limb-saving procedures for physiologically unstable patients. Early Total Care: Definitive fixation within 36 hours for resuscitated, stable patients.
