citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 382 (Book Page): [Digital rectal examination will reveal the presence of blood, which is evidence of intestinal or rectal injury. These injuries are often associated with bladder and proximal urethral injury.]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: Why is pancreatic injury frequently 'hidden' and missed during initial assessment?
back: The pancreas is a retroperitoneal organ, meaning injuries are masked. Furthermore, amylase and lipase levels are insensitive for acute diagnosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): [The major problem is that of diagnosis because the pancreas is a retroperitoneal organ. Amylase or lipase estimation is insensitive.]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: What radiographic finding involving a nasogastric tube identifies a diaphragmatic rupture?
back: A chest radiograph showing the nasogastric tube coiled or apparently within the chest cavity, suggesting stomach herniation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 373 (Book Page): [a chest radiograph will show the nasogastric tube apparently within the chest cavity; Page 377 (Book Page): chest radiography after placement of a nasogastric tube may be helpful (as this may show the stomach herniated into the chest).]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: Identify the systemic red flags for the development of Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS).
back:
- Increased ventilation/airway pressures
- Reduced urine output (<30 mL/h)
- Decreased cardiac output (reduced preload)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Respiratory: Increased ventilation pressures; Cardiovascular: Decrease in venous return resulting in decreased cardiac output; Renal: reduction in glomerular fltration rate.]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: In a haemodynamically unstable trauma patient, which two anatomical sites are the most likely sources of bleeding?
back: Abdominal or pelvic bleeding. These require immediate surgical control or FAST locating before CT can be safely performed.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [The most likely sources are abdominal or pelvic bleeding. A focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan (if immediately available) may also be useful in this scenario to locate the major source of haemorrhage.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What is the mandatory 'Rule of 2s' for initial radiographic assessment of extremity trauma?
back:
• 2 views: Orthogonal planes.
• 2 joints: Joint above and below injury.
• 2 occasions: Repeat after 10–14 days if occult injury suspected.
• 2 sides: Compare with contralateral limb (especially in children).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [The rule of 2s should be remembered: 2 views – ensure acquisition of two views in orthogonal planes... 2 joints – radiographs are required of the joint above and the joint below the fracture. 2 occasions – sometimes the fracture may not be initially visible... 2 sides – in paediatric injuries it can be useful to consider a radiograph from the opposite and uninjured side.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Compare the diagnostic sensitivity of MRI versus plain radiographs in early acute osteomyelitis.
back:
• MRI: Investigation of choice; shows bone edema/periosteal elevation within 2–3 days.
• Radiographs: Often normal for the frst 5–7 days; subsequent subtle osteopenia or periosteal new bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 603 (Book Page): [In the early phase (2–3 days) radiographs may be normal but MRI will show bone oedema and periosteal elevation. After 5–7 days, plain radiographs may show subtle abnormality.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: List the four Kocher clinical predictors used to diagnose pediatric septic arthritis over transient synovitis.
back:
1. History of fever >38.5°C.
2. Non-weight-bearing status.
3. ESR >40 mm/h.
4. WCC >12 × 10⁹/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Four clinical predictors can diferentiate between septic arthritis and transient synovitis (Table 44.17)... History of fever >38.5°C; Non-weight-bearing; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h; White cell count >12 × 10⁹/L.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What is the gold standard investigation for diagnosing bone detail and intra-articular fractures?
back:
• Computed Tomography (CT).
• Provides multiplanar reconstruction and three-dimensional characterization.
• Essential for periarticular injuries to define exact bony anatomy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [Computed axial tomography (CT) is very good for characterising the bony anatomy of injuries, allowing for multiplanar reconstruction... It is very useful for periarticular injuries, where the exact characterisation of the bony injury is essential.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Identify two high-yield synovial fluid biomarkers recently used to diagnose prosthetic joint infection (PJI).
back:
• α-defensin.
• Calprotectin.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 596 (Book Page): [Recently, new synovial fuid markers (α-defensin and calprotectin) have shown high accuracy in diagnosis of PJI.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing and screening DDH in infants aged 4–6 weeks?
back:
• Ultrasonography (USG).
• Defines anatomy and assesses dynamic stability.
• Replaces plain radiographs, as the femoral head is not yet ossified.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): [Ultrasonographic assessment. Ultrasonography defnes the anatomy and the stability of the hip joint. It is used as a screening tool... Screening scans should be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of age.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Differentiate between the bedside measurement of 'real' and 'apparent' leg length discrepancy (LLD).
back:
• Real: Measured from Anterior Superior Iliac Spine (ASIS) to medial malleolus.
• Apparent: Measured from a midline point (e.g., xiphisternum or umbilicus) to medial malleolus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 489 (Book Page): [The frst is called ‘real’ LLD, measured ASIS to medial malleolus. The second is called ‘apparent’ LLD, measured midline, e.g. xiphisternum to medial malleolus.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Which specific radiographic view is critical to avoid missing a posterior shoulder dislocation?
back:
• Axillary view (or modified axillary/Velpeau view).
• Routine AP and Scapular Y views frequently appear normal or deceptive in posterior dislocations.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 420 (Book Page): [Figure 32.3... (a) Anteroposterior (AP) view of the shoulder, initially reported as normal. (b) Lateral scapula radiograph, initially reported as normal... (c) Axillary view – true value of the axillary view shown with obvious posterior dislocation.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Define the radiological criteria for 'non-union' of a fracture.
back:
• Failure to demonstrate clinical or radiological improvement over 3 months.
• Usually formally diagnosed only after 6 months post-injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 424 (Book Page): [A non-union can also be defned as a fracture that fails to demonstrate clinical or radiological improvement over 3 months. In general, you do not describe a fracture as ‘non-union’ until 6 months after the injury.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What radiological sign on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury?
back:
• Segond fracture.
• Represents an avulsion of the anterolateral ligament complex during knee subluxation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 504 (Book Page): [A Segond fracture located on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury.]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: What anatomical clinical indicators suggest potential ongoing internal bleeding in torso trauma?
back:
• Visible bleeding
• Injury in close proximity to major vessels
• Penetrating injury with a retained missile
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [Anatomical: Visible bleeding; Injury in close proximity to major vessels; Penetrating injury with a retained missile]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: Why is blood pressure monitoring often an unreliable early indicator of severe intra-abdominal injury?
back:
• In young, fit patients, BP drop is a very late sign
• Compensatory mechanisms maintain BP despite significant loss
• Hypotensive patients should be treated as hypovolaemic until proven otherwise
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): [Distension is subjective, and a drop in the blood pressure may be a very late sign in a young ft patient. ... Blood is not an irritant and does not initially cause any abdominal pain.]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: Contrast the diagnostic utility of abdominal distension versus tenderness in identifying intra-abdominal hemorrhage.
back:
• Distension: Subjective and often difficult to assess initially
• Tenderness: May be absent as blood is not a chemical irritant to the peritoneum
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 399 (Book Page): [Blood loss into the abdomen can be subtle and there may be no clear clinical signs. Blood is not an irritant and does not initially cause any abdominal pain. Distension is subjective]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: A patient presents with bruising over the mastoid and seatbelt marks on the abdomen. What is the significance of the latter?
back:
• Suggests a high-energy accident
• Strong clinical indicator for underlying abdominal visceral injury
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Seatbelt marks on the abdomen and chest must be noted, as these suggest a high-energy accident.]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
coreConcept: Massive Transfusion Protocol in Abdominal Bleeding
front: Q: What immediate resuscitation protocol is indicated for a hemodynamically unstable patient with suspected abdominal bleeding?
back:
• 1:1:1 ratio of packed red cells : fresh-frozen plasma : platelets
• Immediate surgical control (laparotomy) if too unstable for CT
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: List the physiological red flags for ongoing internal bleeding in torso trauma.
back:
• Increasing respiratory rate
• Increasing pulse rate
• Falling blood pressure
• Rising serum lactate
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): [Physiological: Increasing respiratory rate; Increasing pulse rate; Falling blood pressure; Rising serum lactate]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: Describe the clinical presentation of a 'shocked' trauma patient indicating severe hemorrhage.
back:
• Skin: Cool and sweaty
• Pulse: Rate >100 per minute
• BP: Low (hypotensive)
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [An assessment of the haemodynamic status should be made to identify shocked patients: the skin may be cool and sweaty, the pulse rate raised to over 100 per minute and the blood pressure low.]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
coreConcept: Pelvic Fracture and Abdominal Bleeding Link
front: Q: Which specific injury increases the risk of associated intra-abdominal bleeding to 30%?
back: • Severe pelvic fracture in a hemodynamically unstable patient
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): [The haemodynamically unstable patient with severe pelvic fracture has a 90% risk of associated injuries and a 30% risk of intra-abdominal bleeding.]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: What is the clinical significance of a venous lactate level >3 mmol/L in torso trauma?
back:
• Indicates the patient is under-resuscitated
• Suggests need for further resuscitation or Damage Control Surgery (DCS) if urgent
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [An elevated lactate (>3 mmol/L) suggests the patient is under-resuscitated and should either have a period of further resuscitation or DCS if surgery is urgent.]

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
front: Q: Which anatomical region is the most frequent site of missed or difficult-to-diagnose internal bleeding?
back:
• The retroperitoneum
• Diagnostic tests like ultrasound and DPL may be negative here
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 403 (Book Page): [Injury to the retroperitoneum is often diffcult to diagnose, especially in the presence of other injury, when the signs may be masked. Diagnostic tests (such as ultrasound and DPL) may be negative.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What is the gold standard imaging investigation for a severely injured adult blunt trauma patient?
back:
- Whole-body CT (WBCT) from head to pelvis with IV contrast.
- Should be performed as early as possible during resuscitation.
- Avoid selective scanning of individual body systems.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Which specific clinical findings at the bedside identify a life-threatening tension pneumothorax?
back:
- Restlessness with tachypnoea/dyspnoea.
- Distended neck veins.
- Hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds on the affected side.
- NOTE: Diagnosis is clinical; never delay for imaging.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [The patient is increasingly restless with tachypnoea, dyspnoea and distended neck veins... There will also be hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds... Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Contrast the CT imaging appearance of extradural versus acute subdural haematomas.
back:
- Extradural: Lentiform (biconvex/lens-shaped) hyperdense lesion constrained by dural adherence.
- Subdural: Diffuse concave (crescent-shaped) appearance free to expand across the brain surface.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... Page 388 (Book Page): Since the dura is not as adherent to the brain as it is to the skull, subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: In suspected thoracic aortic disruption, what initial imaging findings are typically sought?
back:
- Bedside: Erect chest radiograph showing a widened mediastinum.
- Definitive: CT scan of the mediastinum or endovascular intra-aortic stent run.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum ( Figure 29.4 ). The diagnosis is confrmed by a CT scan of the mediastinum]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What four clinical predictors distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip?
back:
- History of fever >38.5°C.
- Inability to weight-bear.
- ESR >40 mm/h.
- Serum WCC >12 × 10^9/L.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Four clinical predictors can diferentiate between septic arthritis and transient synovitis ( Table 44.17 )... History of fever >38.5°C, Non-weight-bearing, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h, White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What is the 'too many toes' sign used to diagnose at the bedside?
back:
- Pes planus (flat foot).
- Indicates increased forefoot abduction as seen from behind the standing patient.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 515 (Book Page): [The ‘too many toes’ sign demonstrates increased forefoot abduction (pes planus [fat foot]) and a splayed forefoot.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Describe the diagnostic role of ultrasound in Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH).
back:
- Gold standard for neonates (4-6 weeks).
- Defines anatomy (alpha angle) and dynamic stability (Barlow/Ortolani).
- Used as a selective screening tool for 'at-risk' infants.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): [Ultrasonographic assessment... defnes the anatomy and the stability of the hip joint. It is used as a screening tool (universally or selectively for ‘at-risk’ patients)... Screening scans should be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of age]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Which imaging investigation is most sensitive for diagnosing early acute osteomyelitis and why?
back:
- MRI scanning.
- Shows bone marrow oedema and periosteal elevation within 2-3 days.
- (Plain radiographs may stay normal for 5-7 days).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 624 (Book Page): [In the early phase (2–3 days) radiographs may be normal but MRI will show bone oedema and periosteal elevation... Page 598 (Book Page): MRI is the investigation of choice... It is highly sensitive and specifc]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: How is venous lactate used at the bedside to guide trauma management?
back:
- Marker of tissue perfusion/resuscitation status.
- <2 mmol/L: Suitable for Early Total Care (ETC).
- >3-5 mmol/L: Indicates under-resuscitation; requires Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Venous lactate is a useful marker of resuscitation and physiological state. A normal lactate (<2 mmol/L) is a sign that the patient is probably resuscitated and suitable for ETC. An elevated lactate (>3 mmol/L) suggests the patient is under-resuscitated]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What radiographic finding is pathognomonic for an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture?
back:
- Segond fracture.
- An avulsion fracture located on the anterolateral aspect of the tibia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 525 (Book Page): [A Segond fracture located on the anterolateral tibia is pathognomonic for an ACL injury.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the recommended ratio of blood products for a massive transfusion protocol in severe trauma?
back:
- 1:1:1 ratio of products
- Includes 1 unit packed red cells : 1 unit fresh-frozen plasma : 1 unit platelets
- Prevents haemodilution and coagulopathy
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Which three physiological derangements constitute the 'triad of death' leading to multiorgan failure in trauma?
back:
- Acidosis
- Coagulopathy
- Hypothermia
- This cycle occurs when severely traumatized patients undergo lengthy reconstructive procedures instead of damage control.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: How do the treatment goals of Early Total Care (ETC) differ from Damage Control Surgery (DCS)?
back:
- ETC: Definitive fixation/repair of all injuries within 36 hours for stable patients.
- DCS: Rapid life/limb-saving procedures; defers definitive reconstruction until physiology is optimized.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [ETC describes the defnitive management of a patient’s injuries within 36 hours of injury after a period of initial resuscitation... DCS describes simultaneous resuscitation with early rapid life- and limb-saving surgery. Time-consuming defnitive surgery is deferred.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: How is life-threatening pelvic hemorrhage stabilized in the emergency department for a 'type C' pelvic fracture?
back:
- Immediate application of a compression binder or sheet
- Positioned at the level of the greater trochanters
- Reduces pelvic volume to tamponade venous bleeding
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [Initial management requires the use of a compression binder or a sheet, applied around the true pelvis at the level of the greater trochanters (‘reduce the pelvic volume’), a potentially life-saving procedure.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the specific dosing and timing protocol for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in severe trauma?
back:
- 1g IV over 10 minutes
- Followed by 1g IV over 8 hours
- Administer ideally within 1 hour; must be within 3 hours of injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: List three critical physiological markers indicating the need to transition to Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
back:
- Temperature <34°C
- pH <7.2
- Serum lactate >5 mmol/L
- Other markers include PT >16s and PTT >60s.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 386 (Book Page): [Indications for damage control surgery... Temperature <34°C; pH <7.2; Serum lactate >5 mmol/L (normal: <2.5 mmol/L).]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What defines the philosophy of Damage Control Resuscitation (DCR) in the early management plan?
back:
- Minimizes ED time; resuscitation occurs in the operating theatre
- Employs point-of-care testing (pH, lactate, Hb)
- Focuses on early delivery of whole blood and clotting products over crystalloids.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [The time in the emergency department is minimised and the majority of resuscitation of the patient is carried out in the operating theatre... directed towards the early delivery of biologically active colloids, clotting products and whole blood in order to buy time.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the emergency treatment for a patient with a clinical diagnosis of tension pneumothorax?
back:
- Immediate decompression in the 'safe triangle'
- Safe triangle: Latissimus dorsi, lateral pectoralis major, and superior to the nipple line
- Use finger thoracostomy in extremis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 374 (Book Page): [Treatment consists of immediate decompression... current teaching advocates undertaking decompression in the safe triangle – defned posteriorly by latissimus dorsi, anteriorly by the lateral border of pectoralis major and inferiorly by a line perpendicular to the nipple.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: In Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), which physiological parameters are targeted to prevent secondary brain injury?
back:
- Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) >60 mmHg
- Intracranial Pressure (ICP) <20 mmHg
- Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) 80–90 mmHg
- PaO2 >11 kPa and Sodium >140 mmol/L
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 390 (Book Page): [Key parameters to maintain... PaO2 >11 kPa; MAP = 80–90 mmHg; ICP <20 mmHg; CPP >60 mmHg; [Na+] >140 mmol/L.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the Pringle manoeuvre and when is it utilized during trauma laparotomy?
back:
- Manual or soft-clamp compression of the portal triad
- Reduces arterial and portal venous inflow to the liver
- Utilized for rapid control of massive liver hemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [The inflow from the portal triad is controlled by a Pringle’s manoeuvre, with direct compression of the portal triad, either digitally or using a soft clamp... This has the efect of reducing arterial and portal venous infow into the liver.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What is the gold standard imaging investigation for severely injured adult blunt trauma patients?
back:
- Whole-body CT (WBCT) with IV contrast.
- Covers head to pelvis.
- Performed as early as possible during resuscitation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology...]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Explain the mechanism by which venous lactate levels guide trauma management decisions.
back:
- Marker of tissue perfusion and physiological state.
- <2 mmol/L: Adequate resuscitation (Early Total Care).
- >5 mmol/L: Severe under-resuscitation (Damage Control Surgery).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Venous lactate is a useful marker of resuscitation and physiological state. A normal lactate (<2 mmol/L) is a sign that the patient is probably resuscitated and suitable for ETC... >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Contrast the utility of CT and MRI in diagnosing Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI).
back:
- CT: May identify small haemorrhagic foci in the corpus callosum but often appears normal.
- MRI: Significantly more sensitive for identifying primary white matter injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 388 (Book Page): [It is strictly a pathological diagnosis made at postmortem, but haemorrhagic foci in the corpus callosum and dorsolateral rostral brainstem on CT may be suggestive. Magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive and is employed to evaluate for difuse axonal injury in patients who fail to improve neurologically.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What bedside diagnostic priority is mandatory before decompressing a suspected tension pneumothorax?
back:
- Clinical diagnosis only: respiratory distress, absent breath sounds, and hyper-resonance.
- Do NOT delay for radiographic confirmation in unstable patients.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation. Always treat it with a high index of suspicion of being present]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Which specific clinical assessment parameters trigger the early administration of Tranexamic Acid (TXA)?
back:
- Significant suspected haemorrhage.
- Systolic BP <110 mmHg.
- Pulse >110 beats per minute.
- Administer ideally within 1 hour.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have signifcant haemorrhage, including those with a systolic blood pressure of <110 mmHg or a pulse of over 110 per minute. It needs to be administered as early as possible and ideally within the frst hour from injury]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What diagnostic finding on a bedside eFAST scan is definitive for traumatic pericardial tamponade?
back:
- Visualization of free fluid within the pericardial sac.
- This bedside sonographic assessment is the most expeditious and reliable tool in shocked patients.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 374 (Book Page): [These include an eFAST showing fuid in the pericardial sac, which is the most expeditious and reliable diagnostic tool, or chest radiography, looking for an enlarged heart shadow.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Why is an immediate pelvic radiograph essential even if a WBCT is planned for an unstable patient?
back:
- To exclude catastrophic pelvic bleeding as a source of shock.
- Allows early application/check of a pelvic binder prior to transfer to theatre.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [An immediate pelvic radiograph is essential but should not delay transfer to the operating theatre. A focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan (if immediately available) may also be useful in this scenario to locate the major source of haemorrhage.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: A pediatric patient presents with hip pain; which two radiographic views are necessary for diagnosis?
back:
- Anteroposterior (AP) pelvis view.
- "Frog" lateral view.
- The lateral view is more sensitive for detecting subtle Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 621 (Book Page): [The diagnosis is suggested by the history and examination and confrmed on plain radiographs. Displacement is often more obvious on a lateral view and the diagnosis can be missed if only the anteroposterior radiograph is checked.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: Describe the diagnostic loop involving the 'probe-to-bone' test in suspected diabetic osteomyelitis.
back:
- Bedside probe touching bone in a foot ulcer.
- Positive result combined with elevated CRP and abnormal radiographs confirms deep-seated infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 628 (Book Page): [A combination of the ‘probe-to-bone’ test with elevated infammatory markers and abnormal plain radiographs confrms the diagnosis.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
front: Q: What bedside/imaging modality is the gold standard for screening Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH)?
back:
- Ultrasonography.
- Best performed between 4 and 6 weeks of age.
- Assesses both anatomy and stability (Morin index).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 618 (Book Page): [Ultrasonography defnes the anatomy and the stability of the hip joint. It is used as a screening tool (universally or selectively for ‘at-risk’ patients). Screening scans should be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of age]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the recommended ratio of blood products in a trauma massive transfusion protocol?
back: A 1:1:1 ratio: 1 unit Packed Red Cells to 1 unit Fresh-Frozen Plasma to 1 unit Platelets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the systolic blood pressure target in permissive hypotension for trauma stabilization?
back: 70–90 mmHg (Target >90 mmHg if head injury is suspected). This is used for a limited time.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Contrast the primary surgical goals of Damage Control Surgery (DCS) versus Early Total Care (ETC).
back:
• DCS: Rapid life/limb-saving only (bleeding control, decompression).
• ETC: Definitive management of all injuries within 36 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [DCS describes simultaneous resuscitation with early rapid life- and limb-saving surgery. Time-consuming defnitive surgery is deferred... ETC describes the defnitive management of a patient’s injuries within 36 hours of injury after a period of initial resuscitation.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: When is it clinically indicated to switch from an Early Total Care (ETC) plan to Damage Control (DCS)?
back: If the patient's physiology (e.g., pH, temperature, or lactate) deteriorates during definitive surgical fixation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [An ETC approach can be changed to a damage control approach if the patient’s physiology deteriorates during defnitive surgery.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Outline the standard intravenous dosing regimen for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in trauma resuscitation.
back: 1 gram given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a second 1 gram dose infused over 8 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Which venous lactate threshold indicates that a patient must receive Damage Control Surgery (DCS)?
back: Lactate >5 mmol/L. (Levels <2 mmol/L are generally suitable for Early Total Care).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.6... >5 mmol/L – DCS; <2 mmol/L – ETC.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Where must a pelvic binder be positioned to ensure it does not obstruct a trauma laparotomy?
back: At the level of the greater trochanters.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Why is a 'tertiary survey' performed after the initial primary and secondary surveys?
back: Conducted when the patient is alert/extubated to find missed minor injuries (e.g., scaphoid fractures) causing long-term disability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [Such patients should have a ‘tertiary survey’ when extubated and alert to identify any missed ‘minor’ injuries, such as a scaphoid fracture in the wrist or a rotator cuf tear... potential to cause signifcant long-term disability.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Define the 'triad of death' that Damage Control Surgery aims to arrest.
back: A physiological cycle of Acidosis, Coagulopathy, and Hypothermia leading to multiorgan failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the clinical priority signified by 'c' in the primary survey (cABCDE)?
back: Control of exsanguinating external haemorrhage, which must be addressed prior to airway management.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed... c: Exsanguinating external haemorrhage.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What are the primary initial methods to control exsanguinating external limb hemorrhage in trauma?
back:
• Direct pressure to wound and proximal artery.
• Haemostatic dressings.
• Tourniquet application proximal to wound if pressure fails (record time).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [Bleeding must be controlled immediately by the application of packs and pressure directly onto the bleeding wound and proximal artery... Failure to control bleeding in the limb by direct pressure with surgical dressings should be followed by the application of a tourniquet.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the recommended ratio of blood products in a massive transfusion protocol for trauma patients?
back:
• 1 Unit Packed Red Cells (PRC).
• 1 Unit Fresh-Frozen Plasma (FFP).
• 1 Unit Platelets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Distinguish between the primary goals of Damage Control Surgery (DCS) and Early Total Care (ETC).
back:
• DCS: Rapid life-saving surgery (bleeding/contamination control) while deferring definitive repair until resuscitation.
• ETC: Definitive management/fixation of injuries within 36 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [ETC describes the defnitive management of a patient’s injuries within 36 hours of injury... DCS describes simultaneous resuscitation with early rapid life- and limb-saving surgery. Time-consuming defnitive surgery is deferred.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: How is a 'pink pulseless hand' managed following a paediatric supracondylar humeral fracture?
back:
• Urgent fracture reduction and stabilisation.
• Expectant observation for 24–48 hours if perfusion is satisfactory and no neurological injury exists.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 463 (Book Page): [The pink pulseless hand is more controversial... If there is satisfactory perfusion... then reduction and stabilisation of the fracture is warranted and a more expectant approach to the vascular injury can be taken.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the specific dosing and administration window for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in major trauma?
back:
• 1g IV over 10 minutes, followed by 1g over 8 hours.
• Ideally within 1 hour; do not administer after 3 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What specific volume thresholds of blood drainage mandate an urgent thoracotomy in massive haemothorax?
back:
• Initial drainage: >1500 mL of blood.
• Ongoing hemorrhage: >200 mL/h over 3–4 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 397 (Book Page): [Initial drainage of more than 1500 mL of blood or ongoing haemorrhage of more than 200 mL/h over 3–4 hours is generally considered an indication for urgent thoracotomy.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Contrast the surgical management of Zone 1 versus Zone 3 retroperitoneal haematomas in blunt trauma.
back:
• Zone 1 (Central): Always explored after proximal/distal vascular control.
• Zone 3 (Pelvic): Generally managed with extraperitoneal packing or angioembolisation; avoid opening.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): [Zone 1 (central): central haematomas should always be explored... Zone 3 (pelvic): ...best controlled with compression or extraperitoneal packing, or, if the bleeding is arterial in origin, with angioembolisation.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: In a limb with an open fracture and arterial injury, what is the recommended surgical priority?
back:
• Achieve temporary skeletal stability (External Fixation) first.
• Then perform arterial shunting/repair to ensure length, rotation, and alignment are restored.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): [Performing the arterial shunt before temporary stability has been achieved can compromise the later arterial reconstruction as length, rotation and alignment would not have been restored.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Which three physiological disturbances constitute the 'triad of death' in severely traumatised patients?
back:
• 1. Acidosis.
• 2. Coagulopathy.
• 3. Hypothermia.
• Damage Control Surgery (DCS) aims to stop this cycle.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: List the 'Four Ps' utilized in the operative management of traumatic liver injuries.
back:
• 1. Pressure (bimanual compression).
• 2. Pringle (portal triad compression).
• 3. Plug (silicone tubing).
• 4. Pack (definitive packing).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 401 (Book Page): [The operative management of liver injuries can be summarised as ‘the four Ps’: Pressure; Pringle; Plug; Pack.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Which specific trauma mechanisms are classically associated with posterior shoulder dislocation?
back:
● Electrocution
● Seizure activity
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [Certain injury mechanisms result in classical injury patterns; for example, electrocution or seizure activity may lead to a posterior dislocation of the shoulder.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Distinguish between the mechanisms causing Greenstick and Torus (buckle) fractures in children.
back:
● Greenstick: Tension cortex fails.
● Torus/Buckle: Compression cortex buckles.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Incomplete fractures are called greenstick fractures, where one tension cortex fails. If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus or buckle fractures.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Contrast the direction of distal fragment displacement in Colles and Smith’s fractures.
back:
● Colles: Dorsal displacement ('dinner fork').
● Smith’s: Volar (ventral) displacement.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 434 (Book Page): [It is possible to reduce volar displaced fractures (Smith’s fracture) of the distal radius... most dorsally displaced fractures (Colles fracture) can be addressed with closed reduction.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
coreConcept: Occult Vascular Injury in Extremity Trauma
front: Q: Why is a normal distal pulse insufficient to exclude vascular injury in acute knee dislocations?
back: An intimal flap may develop, progress, and thrombose over time; incidence is 30%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): [The presence of palpable pulses does not exclude a signifcant vascular injury and an intimal fap may develop, progress and thrombose over time. In 30% of knee dislocations... a vascular injury will occur.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: When is the critical timing for intravenous antibiotic administration in open fracture management?
back: Immediately in the emergency department (presurgical phase). Delay reduces efficacy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Administer intravenous antibiotics according to local protocols. It has been shown that early administration of intravenous antibiotics is one of the most important steps.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: What does the mnemonic STAR represent when assessing fracture displacement?
back:
● Shortening
● Translation
● Angulation
● Rotation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Type and degree of displacement: shortening, translation, angulation, rotation (mnemonic STAR).]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Describe the mechanical requirements to achieve direct (primary) bone healing.
back: Cortical apposition and absolute stability with zero movement/strain at the fracture site.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page): [Direct (primary) bone healing... happens in an environment of cortical apposition and absolute stability with no movement or gap between the fracture fragments.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
coreConcept: Referred Pain in Pediatric Hip Pathology
front: Q: In a child presenting with knee pain, which anatomical law mandates hip examination?
back: Hilton’s Law: A joint is supplied by the same nerves as the muscles moving that joint.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 442 (Book Page): [Hilton’s law, which states that a joint is supplied by the same nerves as the muscles that move the joint, explains why many children present with knee pain although the pathology is in the hip.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Define the Hueter-Volkmann principle governing pediatric skeletal remodelling.
back:
● Compressive forces: Inhibit growth.
● Tensile forces: Stimulate growth.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 609 (Book Page): [Hueter–Volkmann principle: Compressive forces inhibit growth; Tensile forces stimulate growth.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Identify the three types of nerve injury in the Seddon classification.
back:
● Neurapraxia
● Axonotmesis
● Neurotmesis
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Seddon classifed nerve injuries into neurapraxia, axonotmesis and neurotmesis.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the mandatory immediate action for exsanguinating external hemorrhage before airway management?
back:
• Application of packs and direct pressure.
• Application of a proximal tourniquet if pressure fails.
• Urgent surgical control for reperfusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed... bleeding must be controlled immediately by the application of packs and pressure... followed by the application of a tourniquet proximal to the wound.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What are the physiological target ranges for systolic blood pressure in permissive hypotension?
back:
• 70–90 mmHg for general trauma.
• >90 mmHg if head injury is suspected.
• Time-limited until primary hemorrhage source is controlled.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What defines the 'Early Total Care' (ETC) surgical strategy for musculoskeletal injuries?
back:
• Definitive management/fixation of all unstable fractures (long bone, spine, pelvis).
• Performed within 36 hours of injury.
• Requires the patient to be physiologically optimized.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [For musculoskeletal injuries, ETC allows defnitive fxation of all unstable long bone, spinal and pelvic fractures within 36 hours of injury. This facilitates nursing care, allows early mobilisation.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: A blunt trauma patient presents hemodynamically unstable. What immediate mechanical step is required for pelvic stabilization?
back:
• Application of a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters.
• Must not be removed until pelvic fracture is radiographically excluded.
• Do not perform 'springing' of the pelvis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [A pelvic binder should be applied to all haemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma and not removed until after a pelvic fracture has been excluded.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the specific dosing and timing protocol for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in trauma?
back:
• 1g IV loading dose over 10 minutes.
• Followed by 1g IV maintenance dose over 8 hours.
• Ideally within 1 hour; contra-indicated after 3 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What are the three primary objectives of Damage Control Surgery (DCS)?
back:
• Control of hemorrhage (e.g., packing, shunting).
• Limitation of contamination (e.g., stapling bowel).
• Restoration of normal physiology (interrupting the 'triad of death').
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 385 (Book Page): [Damage control surgery is restricted to only three goals: stopping any active surgical bleeding; controlling any contamination; restoring normal physiology.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What metabolic marker and threshold determine the need for Damage Control Surgery over Early Total Care?
back:
• Venous Lactate >5 mmol/L indicates DCS.
• Lactate <2 mmol/L indicates suitability for ETC.
• Values 2–3 mmol/L require trend observation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [Venous lactate is an essential marker of resuscitation: <2 mmol/L – ETC... >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: A patient develops tension pneumothorax. What is the immediate supportive management procedure?
back:
• Immediate needle decompression in the 'safe triangle' or 2nd intercostal space.
• Followed by insertion of an intercostal chest drain.
• High-flow oxygen administration.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [Life-threatening chest pathology such as tension pneumothorax... should be diagnosed and managed immediately. Equipment and expertise for rapid insertion of intercostal chest drains should be available.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Why is excessive crystalloid administration contraindicated in the early management of hypovolemic trauma?
back:
• Causes haemodilution of clotting factors.
• Increases coagulopathy.
• Increases risk of Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What components constitute the 'Triad of Death' in a severely traumatized patient?
back:
• Acidosis.
• Coagulopathy.
• Hypothermia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 379 (Book Page): [the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the initial systolic blood pressure target during permissive hypotension in trauma patients without head injury?
back:
● Target: 70–90 mmHg.
● Goal: Maintain minimal perfusion to vital organs (brain, heart, kidneys) while avoiding increased hemorrhage until definitive control is achieved.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What are the three primary physiological risks associated with excessive IV crystalloid administration in early trauma resuscitation?
back:
● Causes hemodilution.
● Increases coagulopathy.
● Increases the risk of Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Contrast the surgical management implications of a venous lactate level <2 mmol/L versus >5 mmol/L in trauma.
back:
● <2 mmol/L: Adequate resuscitation; suitable for Early Total Care (ETC).
● >5 mmol/L: Severe under-resuscitation; mandates Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): [Summary box 27.6: Venous lactate is an essential marker of resuscitation: <2 mmol/L – ETC... >5 mmol/L – DCS]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the immediate management plan for exsanguinating limb hemorrhage when direct pressure fails?
back:
● Apply a proximal tourniquet immediately.
● Record the exact time of application.
● Arrange urgent surgical control to restore limb reperfusion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): [Failure to control bleeding in the limb by direct pressure with surgical dressings should be followed by the application of a tourniquet proximal to the wound... the length of time for which the tourniquet is applied must be recorded... the patient requires urgent surgical control of the bleeding in order to reperfuse the limb.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the standardized intravenous dosing and critical time limit for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) administration in major trauma?
back:
● Dose: 1g IV over 10 minutes, followed by 1g IV over 8 hours.
● Time Limit: Must be started within 3 hours of injury (ideally within 1 hour).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the definitive emergency management sequence for a clinically diagnosed tension pneumothorax?
back:
● Immediate needle or finger decompression in the "safe triangle" (5th intercostal space, anterior to mid-axillary line).
● Subsequent insertion of an intercostal chest drain.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 395 (Book Page): [Treatment consists of immediate decompression... current teaching advocates undertaking decompression in the safe triangle... or, in extremis, a fnger thoracostomy at the same location.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Describe the supportive management plan for a sucking chest wound (open pneumothorax) before drain insertion.
back:
● Apply a sterile occlusive plastic dressing.
● Tape on three sides only to form a one-way flutter valve.
● Insert an intercostal chest tube at a remote site.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Initial management consists of promptly closing the defect with a sterile occlusive plastic dressing (e.g. OPSITE or similar product), taped on three sides to act as a futter-type valve. A chest tube is inserted as soon as possible in a site remote from the injury site.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: What is the definitive surgical management plan for traumatic cardiac tamponade following penetrating injury?
back:
● Urgent sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy.
● Evacuate pericardial clotted blood and repair the myocardium.
● Note: Pericardiocentesis is usually ineffective due to clotted blood.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 396 (Book Page): [Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury. The correct immediate treatment of tamponade is operative, either via a subxiphoid window or by open surgery (sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy), with repair of the heart]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
front: Q: Outline the three core goals of the initial operative phase in Damage Control Surgery (DCS).
back:
● Immediate control of active surgical hemorrhage.
● Control of contamination (e.g., bowel/fecal spillage).
● Restoring normal physiology (correcting acidosis, coagulopathy, and hypothermia).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 406 (Book Page): [Damage control surgery is restricted to only three goals: ● stopping any active surgical bleeding; ● controlling any contamination; ● restoring normal physiology.]

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
coreConcept: Absolute Surgical Indication in Spinal Trauma
front: Q: What is the only absolute surgical indication in the early management of acute spinal trauma?
back:
● Deteriorating neurological function.
● Note: Timing is critical to prevent permanent paralysis and minimize secondary cord injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 416 (Book Page): [The only absolute indication for surgery in spinal trauma is deteriorating neurological function.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: List the four components of the 'STAR' mnemonic for describing fracture displacement.
back:
* Shortening
* Translation
* Angulation
* Rotation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [type and degree of displacement: shortening, translation, angulation, rotation (mnemonic STAR) ( Figure 32.5 )]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Explain the mechanical conditions required for direct (primary) versus indirect (secondary) bone healing.
back:
* Direct: Requires absolute stability, cortical apposition, and no movement at the fracture site.
* Indirect: Occurs under relative stability; requires some movement (strain) to stimulate callus formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page)-424: [Direct bone healing... environment of cortical apposition and absolute stability with no movement... Indirect bone healing involves a transition from one tissue to another with callus formation... requires some movement]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Contrast the bone failure mechanisms in paediatric greenstick versus torus (buckle) fractures.
back:
* Greenstick: The bone fails on the tension side while the compression side remains intact.
* Torus (Buckle): The bone fails on the compression side, resulting in a buckling of the cortex.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [greenstick ( Figure 32.8 ) fractures, where one tension cortex fails. If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus ( Figure 32.9 ) or buckle fractures.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: A patient with a humeral shaft fracture develops a new radial nerve palsy after cast application. What is the management?
back: The nerve must be surgically explored and the fracture stabilized with internal fixation, as the palsy likely occurred during the intervention.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 418 (Book Page): [If, however, radial nerve function is lost after application of a cast or brace, the nerve should be explored. When exploring the radial nerve, plate and screw fxation is then undertaken to stabilise the humerus.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: What is the recommended antimicrobial duration and protocol for initial management of an open fracture?
back:
* Administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering Gram-positives, Gram-negatives, and anaerobes (if severe contamination).
* Therapy should continue until 48 hours after definitive wound closure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [Administer intravenous antibiotics... broad-spectrum antibiotic should be chosen covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative and... anaerobic... Continue intravenous antibiotics until 48 hours after defnitive wound closure.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Identify the anatomical defining features of a Salter-Harris Type IV growth plate injury.
back: A single fracture line that extends through the epiphysis, across the physis, and through the metaphysis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 423 (Book Page): [Type IV – fracture line across the epiphysis, across the physis and across the metaphysis. This injury can cause focal fusion of the physis, leading to abnormal growth.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Why is anatomical reduction mandatory for intra-articular fractures compared to extra-articular diaphyseal fractures?
back:
* Intra-articular: Restores joint congruity to prevent early stiffness and long-term degenerative arthritis.
* Extra-articular: Requires only mechanical alignment (restoration of length, rotation, and alignment) for function.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): [intra-articular fracture = anatomical reduction... to avoid degenerative joint disease... extra-articular fracture = mechanical alignment . In children an extra-articular fracture has the ability to remodel]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: In paediatric supracondylar fractures, distinguish the clinical management of a 'white' versus a 'pink' pulseless hand.
back:
* White: A surgical emergency; requires immediate reduction and vessel exploration if the pulse does not return.
* Pink: Satisfactory perfusion without compartment syndrome; requires reduction but can be observed expectantly.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 441 (Book Page): [The white pulseless hand is a surgical emergency... urgent reduction... If the pulse does not return... vessels should be explored... The pink pulseless hand... satisfactory perfusion... more expectant approach to the vascular injury can be taken.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological loop that compromises tissue perfusion in compartment syndrome.
back: Increased fascial compartment pressure leads to reduced microperfusion, resulting in tissue ischaemia and irreversible muscle damage from cellular anoxia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 444 (Book Page): [increased tissue pressure, which leads to reduced microperfusion, resulting in tissue ischaemia and irreversible muscle damage from cellular anoxia.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Distinguish between axonotmesis and neurotmesis using the Seddon classification of peripheral nerve injuries.
back:
* Axonotmesis: Nerve sheath remains intact; axon is damaged; potential for 1mm/day regeneration.
* Neurotmesis: Complete division of the nerve, sheath, and fiber; requires surgery for recovery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 421 (Book Page): [Axonotmesis – nerve sheath remains intact... potential for recovery; nerve fbre regrowth is at 1 mm per day. Neurotmesis – complete division of the nerve, nerve sheath and nerve fbre. Functionally poor outcome without surgical intervention]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: What does the STAR mnemonic represent in the description of fracture displacement?
back:
- Shortening
- Translation
- Angulation
- Rotation
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Describing the bony injury depends on... type and degree of displacement: shortening, translation, angulation, rotation (mnemonic STAR)]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Contrast the pathological features of Axonotmesis versus Neurotmesis in nerve injuries.
back:
- Axonotmesis: Intact sheath, internal fiber damage, potential for recovery (1mm/day).
- Neurotmesis: Complete division of nerve and sheath; surgical repair required.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [Axonotmesis – nerve sheath remains intact, with internal nerve fbre damage and associated Wallerian degeneration... Neurotmesis – complete division of the nerve, nerve sheath and nerve fbre.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: How does Perren’s theory relate tissue strain percentages to fracture healing?
back:
- <2% strain: Hard callus/primary mineralisation.
- <10% strain: Soft callus (indirect healing).
- <100% strain: Fibrous tissue formation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 446 (Book Page): [The amount of strain determines the nature of tissue it diferentiates into: under 100% leads to fbrous tissue, under 10% soft callus, less than 2% hard callus and progressive mineralisation (Perren’s theory of bone healing).]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Define a 'Nightstick fracture' of the upper extremity.
back: An isolated diaphyseal fracture of the ulna, typically occurring from defensive direct trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 457 (Book Page): [Isolated fractures of the ulna, the so-called nightstick fracture, are a little more controversial, as non-operative management is possible]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: What specific microbial coverage is required for open fracture antibiotic prophylaxis?
back: Broad-spectrum coverage for Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms (if severely contaminated).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 465 (Book Page): [A broad-spectrum antibiotic should be chosen covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative and, if there is severe contamination, anaerobic organisms.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: What is the primary clinical discriminator between Gustilo-Anderson Type IIIA and IIIB open fractures?
back: Availability of soft-tissue cover: IIIA has adequate cover; IIIB requires a flap for reconstruction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [IIIA: Adequate soft-tissue cover of a fractured bone after stabilisation; IIIB: Inadequate soft-tissue cover of a fractured bone after stabilisation (i.e. fap coverage required)]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: When is 'Absolute Stability' the mandatory mechanical objective in fracture fixation?
back: Intra-articular fractures; it ensures anatomical reduction and prevents callus formation that could inhibit joint motion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 452 (Book Page): [Intra-articular fractures (types B and C) of the distal radius require anatomical reduction of the joint surface... absolute stability... is desirable in intra-articular fractures, where callus at the fracture site might inhibit movement.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Which specific complication results from a missed forearm compartment syndrome following a pediatric supracondylar fracture?
back: Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture, caused by cellular anoxia and irreversible muscle damage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 463 (Book Page): [A very rare but feared complication of paediatric supracondylar fractures is Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture. This is due to excessive swelling and missed compartment syndrome in the forearm.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: What is the 'Delta Pressure' threshold indicating the need for emergency fasciotomy in compartment syndrome?
back: A difference (Diastolic BP – Compartment Pressure) of ≤ 30 mmHg.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 466 (Book Page): [Generally accepted pressure thresholds include... pressure diference (diastolic pressure – compartment pressure) less than or equal to 30 mmHg. Emergency treatment involves... fasciotomies.]

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
front: Q: Distinguish the bony failure mechanisms of Greenstick versus Torus (Buckle) fractures.
back:
- Greenstick: Tension cortex fails (breaks).
- Torus: Compression cortex buckles.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 443 (Book Page): [greenstick fractures, where one tension cortex fails. If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus or buckle fractures.]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
coreConcept: WBCT as Gold Standard in Trauma
front: Q: What is the gold standard imaging investigation for a severely injured adult blunt trauma patient?
back: Whole-body CT (WBCT) with IV contrast from the head to the pelvis. It is a time-critical investigation and should be obtained as early as possible during the resuscitation phase.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): [Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
coreConcept: Role of eFAST in Torso Trauma
front: Q: What is the primary diagnostic role of bedside eFAST during the initial assessment of torso trauma?
back:
● Detects free fluid in the abdominal cavity or pericardium.
● Identifies air or blood in the hemithoraces (pneumothorax/hemothorax).
● Locates sources of major hemorrhage in hemodynamically unstable patients prior to surgery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 394 (Book Page): [Extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (eFAST) is becoming the most common investigation. The technique uses sonographic assessment in the chest, looking for a cardiac tamponade or free blood and air in the hemithoraces, and assessment for blood in the abdominal cavity]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
coreConcept: Diagnostic Imaging Modalities for Pelvis Injury
front: Q: Contrast the roles of plain radiographs versus CT in assessing the stability of pelvic ring fractures.
back:
● Plain Radiographs: Initial screening; often appear normal if a pelvic binder is in situ.
● CT/CT Angiography: Gold standard for non-compromised patients; provides precise fracture anatomy and identifies arterial versus venous bleeding sources.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): [CT is the diagnostic modality of choice in the physiologically non-compromised patient, and CT angiography is particularly helpful in providing details of both the anatomy of the fracture and the origin of the bleeding (venous or arterial).]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
coreConcept: Differentiating Septic Arthritis from Transient Synovitis
front: Q: Which clinical and laboratory predictors help differentiate between pediatric septic arthritis and transient synovitis of the hip?
back:
The Kocher criteria include:
● History of fever >38.5°C
● Non-weight-bearing status
● ESR >40 mm/h
● White cell count >12 × 10^9/L
All four positive predictors indicate a 93% probability of joint sepsis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 634 (Book Page): [Table 44.17 (a) The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: ● History of fever >38.5°C ● Non-weight-bearing ● Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h ● White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L]

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
coreConcept: Clinical Indications for TXA in Hemorrhage
front: Q: What are the clinical criteria used at the bedside to initiate emergency Tranexamic Acid therapy in trauma?
back:
TXA should be administered if significant hemorrhage is suspected, characterized by:
● Systolic blood pressure <110 mmHg
